Russia preparing new AK-12+ rifle for serial production
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
07:25:20 UTC
16:25:20 KST

- Kalashnikov unveiled a mock-up of its new 5.45mm AK-12+ assault rifle at the Eastern Economic Forum in Vladivostok, saying serial production is being prepared.
- The rifle, built for special forces, has a thicker barrel, modified sights and removed sling, bayonet and grenade launcher fittings compared to the standard AK-12.
Kalashnikov Concern unveiled a mock-up of its new AK-12+ assault rifle at the Eastern Economic Forum in Vladivostok, presenting a 5.45mm weapon built for improved shooting precision.
The rifle is on display in the Voin Center pavilion at the Far East Street exhibition, part of the 11th Eastern Economic Forum, running September 1-4 on the campus of Far Eastern Federal University.
Kalashnikov, part of the state defense conglomerate Rostec, said the weapon is now being prepared for serial production. The company described the AK-12+ as a high-precision small-arms system built on the existing AK-12 platform, intended primarily for special forces units.
The system was developed under the supervision of Russian Deputy Prime Minister and Presidential Plenipotentiary Envoy to the Far Eastern Federal District Yury Trutnev, the company said.
The AK-12+ carries a thicker barrel than the standard AK-12, with a threaded muzzle designed to accept a flash suppressor or a muzzle brake. Kalashnikov modified the rifle’s mechanical sights and widened the contour of the gas cylinder to match the new barrel profile. Fittings previously used to attach a sling swivel, an underbarrel grenade launcher and a bayonet have been removed. The mock-up shown in Vladivostok featured an extended stock.
The rifle will also carry electro-optical sights. Kalashnikov said the sights are meant to improve accuracy at medium range in both daytime and nighttime conditions.
At the forum, Kalashnikov and the Voin Center signed a cooperation agreement. Under the deal, the two organizations will jointly develop engineering skills among the center’s cadets and expand the material and technical resources at its regional branches.
The Voin Center, formally the Center for Military-Sports Training and Patriotic Education of Youth, was created on presidential order in 2023. It trains teenagers aged 14 to 18 and reservists aged 18 to 35, and now operates branches in more than 20 Russian regions.
Kalashnikov already produces several variants of the AK-12 platform. The baseline AK-12 is chambered in 5.45x39mm, weighs about 3.6 kg (7.9 pounds) unloaded, has a 415 mm (16.3 inch) barrel and fires at a cyclic rate of roughly 700 rounds per minute. The family also includes the AK-15, chambered in 7.62x39mm, and the export-oriented AK-19, chambered in 5.56x45mm NATO.

Former Taipei Vice Mayor Huang Shan-shan announces end of political career
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
07:22:56 UTC
16:22:56 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) – Former Taipei Vice Mayor Huang Shan-shan (黃珊珊) said Thursday she will no longer run for election after 30 years in politics.
Huang was first elected to Taipei City Council for the pro-China New Party in 1998. From 2002 to 2023, she was a member of James Soong’s (宋楚瑜) People First Party.
Huang gained her most prominent political position as vice mayor of Taipei under Mayor Ko Wen-je (柯文哲) from 2019 to 2022, when she ran for mayor as an independent. From 2024 to 2026, she represented Ko’s TPP in the Legislative Yuan, but was suspended from the party amid allegations of campaign funding irregularities.
As candidates registered for the Nov. 28 local elections this week, Huang said she had been thinking of the future, per UDN. She said that she had spent most of her life since the age of 28 either running in elections or campaigning for other candidates.
In a post on Facebook, she related how she had decided during a grave illness in 2015 to stop fighting elections. If she made it out of the hospital, she would devote the rest of her life to her family, Huang said Thursday. However, after her illness, she spent another 10 years in politics.
The former vice mayor said she held no regrets about her long political career.

Chalmers can't avoid questions on house prices, Marles learns from melon saga
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

analysis
Chalmers questioned about house prices, Marles learns from melon saga
Welcome back to your weekly federal politics update, where Courtney Gould gets you up to speed on the happenings from Parliament House.
Jim Chalmers sits alone in a darkened press conference room, selfie camera on, chatting to his social media followers about the latest economic data.
But of course he wasn't asked any questions in his pre-filmed video. It was more an avenue for him to declare the economy was "robust" despite challenges from the Middle East war, point out more people are switching to EVs and that housing construction is up before he had to face reporters half an hour later.
He fronted up to the press conference for a tense back and forth where almost every single question was house prices.
When the government made the U-turn on its promise not to wind back negative gearing and the capital gains tax discount, it did so armed with Treasury forecasts. Growth, the budget papers said, would slow by 2 per cent over a number of years.
Property data firm Cotality this week flagged drops in every capital city in August, and predictions from the Commonwealth Bank that prices could drop as much as 13 per cent have some mortgage holders understandably worried.
Chalmers has largely brushed off movements in price as not unusual and backed in his department's forecast. "Buying a house is a long-term proposition," he said.
The major factor at play here is recent interest rate rises, he argued, not the government's tax changes.
That argument wasn't made easier for him either, after fellow frontbencher Matt Thistlethwaite declared on News24 (formerly Sky News Australia) there was "no doubt" the tax changes contributed to house prices falling.
"I think that's one of a number of reasons," Chalmers told ABC's Sally Sara when asked again this morning.
Opting out of algorithms?
Thistlethwaite may have made the sell a little bit harder for Chalmers, but the treasurer named the "disturbing rubbish" pushed by social media algorithms as the thing making his job more difficult.
"Our society, our social cohesion, the way that we come at big problems including in my part of the shop in the economy is hampered, not helped, by the way algorithms are dominating people's day," Chalmers said.
It's a similar argument that's been put before by Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, who has said algorithms are fuelling polarisation. Albanese is supportive of the idea that Australians should have more control over what they are shown online.
But that doesn't go as far as what consent advocate Chanel Contos has put forward: an opt-in algorithm for social media accounts. If adopted, it would be a world where we'd return to chronological feeds where our friends' content is shown instead of strangers. It's an idea backed by some of the crossbench and the Greens amid concerns social media is exposing young people to misogynistic content.
There seems to be no disagreement among the leaders of the major political parties that some of the content fed to people is toxic. But for some it's a bit of a chicken and egg argument.
Nationals leader Matt Canavan, for example, this week argued it is the "feminisation" of the school curriculum and a lack of male teachers that pushes boys towards such content. Opposition Leader Angus Taylor also accused teachers of running agendas in the classroom.
Contos argued the algorithm is the missing piece here — young boys are being shown this content whether they seek it out or not.
Coalition focuses on tobacco
Meanwhile, the Coalition finally released its plan to slash the tobacco excise. The plan also included a proposal to legalise and tax vapes and nicotine pouches.
An estimated 80 per cent of the cigarettes and other nicotine products consumed in Australia last year were illegal, according to the Australian Bureau of Statistics.
Last month, One Nation revealed its own plan to slash the excise by 75 per cent. The opposition went one further, revealing a proposal to cut the excise by 80 per cent. It argues it would be enough to tip the scales and redirect customers towards legal tobacco.
The Parliamentary Budget Office costed the policy but the Coalition has not released the costings or the assumptions underpinning them.
It says its plan, paired with a further $200 million spend on law enforcement to support more raids, arrests and closure of illegal tobacco shops, would increase tax revenue by about $8 billion over the first four years — double the current forecasts.
That hinges on the idea that cutting the price would encourage Australians to ditch the black market and that illegal distributers wouldn't also drop prices to compete — something Taylor disagrees with.
Back in the Pacific
While this was all going down at home, Albanese returned to palm tree-lined beaches and crystal clear blue water of Palau for the Pacific Islands Forum (PIF).
It's not the first time the prime minister has visited — he made the trip to the small Pacific nation last year for a pre-wedding holiday with now wife Jodie Haydon.
The early stages of the meeting were overshadowed by tensions between China and Taiwan about Taipei's increased presence at the gathering (Palau has diplomatic ties with Taiwan) and the number of leaders who decided to skip the annual forum.
Albanese said he wasn't distracted by all that as he pressed on with discussions about climate change and tackling the issue of drug trafficking in the Pacific, where Australia and New Zealand's appetite for illegal drugs has caused real issues.
Leaders were also due to discuss the matter of China's test-fire of a nuclear-capable missile carrying a dummy warhead in the Pacific — with host nation Palau indicating it would like to issue a united statement about the test.
Despite escaping PIF without another T-shirt faux pas, it wasn't all smooth sailing for Albanese, who had a tense press conference of his own at the forum about United Nations climate event being held in Fiji and Tuvalu next month.
The pre-COP events are organised by Australia and are part of the compromise Australia struck with Türkiye last year after we bowed out of hosting the climate conference in Adelaide.
But so far just five leaders from outside of the Pacific have confirmed they're making the trip, which was designed to highlight the impact of climate change on Pacific nations. It's not typical that leaders usually attend a pre-COP event.
Asked about this, Albanese said the focus on the non-Pacific leaders was "disrespectful".

Treaty yourself
And finally, have you been looking for the perfect gift for the Kiwi in your family? Or perhaps you have a long-distance American pen pal you need a stocking stuffer for?
Don't worry, Defence Minister Richard Marles has you covered for inspiration. He presented a framed copy of the full text of the ANZUS Treaty on vellum, and signed by Albanese, to a member of the Trump administration.
Vellum is a thin, translucent material made of calfskin and commonly used by artists.
Why are we presenting Albanese autographed military treaties to our allies? To mark the 75th anniversary. You can't get that at the shops.

Iranian-backed militia Badr admits it killed, wounded thousands of protesters in Iraq in 2019
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
07:19:29 UTC
16:19:29 KST

The head of the powerful Badr militia, Hadi al-Amiri, appears to have admitted that his group was behind the killing of thousands of protesters in Iraq in October 2019. For years, it was known that Iranian-backed militias were likely unleashed by the government to suppress the protests. However, there was a lack of confirmation and evidence for the role of the militias. Now, the head of the powerful Badr militia. In Iraq, social media is focused on this story.
In 2019, Iraq was in a transition period. Adil Abdul-Mahdi was prime minister. He was relatively weak and ineffectual. Powerful Iranian-backed militias that had been empowered by the war on ISIS were increasing their control across Iraq. Instead of Iraq receiving a kind of “peace dividend” when the war on ISIS largely ended in 2018, Iraq transitioned to new rounds of violence and economic stagnation. Militias also began targeting US-led Coalition forces.
Tishreen movement
This led to protests in October 2019. The protests have often been called the Tishreen movement. Amnesty International noted in 2025 that “Iraqi authorities continue to persecute activists and protestors while failing to deliver meaningful justice and accountability for the killings of hundreds and the maiming of thousands of protesters by security forces and militias or to reveal the fate and whereabouts of those disappeared, Amnesty International said today.”
Amiri uses the word “fitna,” which has a number of meanings but essentially accuses the protesters of sedition and heresy. It accuses the protesters of undermining the state and trying to create civil strife. Amiri was basically admitting that the Iranian-backed militias, such as Badr, massacred hundreds or thousands of people. He was accusing the protesters of being traitors who were then put down.
Amiri’s speech comes as Iraq is seeking to disarm and rein in the militias. Several of the most powerful militias have said they will not disarm or have presented new conditions to placing their arms under state control. These include Harakat Hezbollah al Nujaba, Kataib Hezbollah and Kataib Sayyid al-Shuhada. Badr is not usually seen as one of the most extreme militias. However, Amiri has long played a role as a power behind the throne in Iraq, with Badr as an enforcer of Iran’s agenda.
Lawyer submits report to Prosecutor General
Amiri’s comments have now led to controversy in Iraq. Some social media have been circulating images from the October 2019 protests showing the protesters being oppressed. A report on September 2 said that a lawyer has now submitted a report to the Prosecutor General of Wasit Province, demanding an investigation and lawsuit into Badr and the comments by Amiri. Al-Sharqiya TV in Iraq described the lawyer as seeking to sue Amiri after his statements.
There is debate in Arabic media in the region now about what Amiri said.
Has he revealed the “true face” of the “resistance” by appearing to admit the mass killings? “Was it a slip of the tongue by Hadi al-Amiri, head of the Badr Organization and one of the most prominent leaders of the Coordinating Framework that runs the sectarian power structure in Iraq?” another report asks. One question is whether his statement is actually a threat today that the militias could use force again against protesters or against a government that seeks to disarm them.
Asharq al Awsat in Arabic notes that “the wave of anger and popular criticism against the head of the Badr Organization, Hadi al-Amiri, continues, following statements in which he admitted the involvement of what he called the ‘resistance’ in the events that accompanied the ‘October Movement’ of 2019, which lasted for about two years and during which more than 600 demonstrators were killed and more than 20,000 others were injured.” Families of victims now say they will file lawsuits. There are calls to prosecute Amiri.
This is important because unlike some of the other militia leaders, Amiri has always been able to avoid sanctions and controversy. Badr has been the one major Iranian-backed militia in Iraq that is not sanctioned by the US. Most of the others are seen as Foreign Terrorist Organizations or Specially Designated Terrorist Groups. As such, Badr has a unique role. It continues to play a major role in the Interior Ministry and other parts of Iraq.
The role of the militias in the massacres is very similar to the IRGC’s role in Iran in massacring protesters. In January 2026, Iran was accused of massacring tens of thousands of people. It has done this before, and it has exported this model to Iraq and other countries. The militias have also kidnapped journalists and assassinated people. They have also attacked Americans and targeted the Kurdistan Region.

US, China arm for space warfare, raising stakes in race for military control of orbit
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
07:18:42 UTC
16:18:42 KST

In June, a secretive unmanned Chinese spaceplane closely monitored by US military analysts released a small satellite hundreds of miles above Earth in an orbital region crowded with commercial and military satellites. The object then looped around another Chinese satellite before returning towards the spaceplane, according to US space-tracking firm LeoLabs.
Little is known about the satellite or the mission. But the US military operates a similarly secretive spaceplane resembling a small shuttle, also with no crew. Both programs reflect the rapidly evolving field of military space operations as Beijing and Washington prepare for the possibility of conflict extending into space, according to a Reuters review of documents, space-tracking data and interviews with current and former military officials.
Chinese researchers linked to the military are developing technologies ranging from satellites designed to pursue and even capture other spacecraft to systems that could extend fuel supplies while doing so, according to a Reuters review of patent-related documents, procurement notices and academic papers. And the United States and Britain conducted their first joint military operation in space in the path of a suspected Chinese spy satellite, according to commercial space-tracking data.
"The Chinese are rapidly developing capabilities," including ground- and space-based weapons designed to interfere with or destroy targets, US Space Force’s Chief of Space Operations General Chance Saltzman said in July. The threat from China is "substantial," added Saltzman, who is retiring.
Satellites have become indispensable to modern warfare, as conflicts in Ukraine and the Middle East have demonstrated. For decades they have provided communications, navigation and intelligence services to armed forces on Earth, and once placed in orbit typically remained on fixed paths. Increasingly, however, militaries view them as active weapons platforms capable of launching attacks by disrupting a satellite’s operations through jamming or laser dazzling, or even capturing enemy spacecraft.
Disruption of US space capabilities would "cripple our massive military in the terrestrial sphere," affecting everything from surveillance to missile defense, said Everett Dolman, a former professor at the US Air Force's Air War College. Spaceplanes, because they are agile and capable of deploying satellites or carrying cargo, could appear to opponents as potential "space fighters," he said.
Allies join the US effort
The growing competition comes as Earth's orbit becomes increasingly crowded. SpaceX, which recently debuted on public markets, operates about 11,000 Starlink satellites and plans a constellation of larger AI-enabled data centers in space. China is building rival networks, while US President Donald Trump's Golden Dome missile defense program envisions space-based interceptors.
The United States is also refining capabilities that could prove important in a future conflict.
In the joint US-British operation in September last year, US space forces working from a base in Colorado directed a US military satellite to swoop in close to a U.K. one as China's Shiyan 12-01 satellite passed about 83 kilometers beneath them, according to space intelligence company Slingshot Aerospace. At that altitude, specialists consider the distance relatively close.
Three space experts with military backgrounds told Reuters it appeared intended as a signal to Beijing, including at space-tracking firm COMSPOC. Andrew Turner, a retired senior British air force officer who is now a space consultant, said it was “almost certainly a strategic signal to China” to demonstrate allied unity, capability and a warning to not interfere with the UK satellite.
The US and Britain publicly announced the operation, the first known one between two members of the "Five Eyes" intelligence alliance, but did not disclose its proximity to a Chinese spacecraft. Much of what occurs in space remains classified because of its intelligence implications.
US Space Command told Reuters the mission demonstrated the ability to work with allies in space. Britain's defense ministry said space is increasingly important to military operations and the UK and its partners were conducting advanced orbital operations to protect their national and military interests. Neither commented on the operation’s proximity to the Chinese satellite.
The US Space Force’s next chief of space operations, Lieutenant General Douglas Schiess, had been involved in the operation. In an interview shortly after, he said operating close to another spacecraft could help verify whether an allied satellite is functioning properly or determine whether an adversary is "doing something it shouldn't." He declined to say at the time whether another country's satellite had been nearby.
Britain recently disclosed that the mission was conducted alongside a maritime deployment to the Indo-Pacific region.
Using space not only to support military operations on Earth but also to influence their outcome is "really, really important," then U.K. Space Command chief Major General Paul Tedman said in April at a conference. He has since retired from the military.
China's foreign ministry said it was not familiar with the specific details of the US-British operation. More broadly, Beijing opposes the weaponization of space and supports its peaceful use, the ministry said, while accusing Washington of stoking an arms race through efforts including the missile defense system Golden Dome and potential space-based weapons.
Asked about Shiyan 12-01 and the Chinese spaceplane, the ministry said it had no information. State news agency Xinhua has described Shiyan 12-01 as conducting space environment surveys, and the spaceplane as an experimental craft supporting the peaceful use of space.
US Space Force says its own spaceplane is carrying out a range of tests and experiments.
Space Weapons
US Space Command head General Stephen Whiting has repeatedly emphasized the importance of space to modern warfare, warning that adversaries are developing capabilities to deny the United States access to key systems and reduce military effectiveness. He has said adversaries would likely seek to target US space assets early in a conflict.
To counter such threats, the US must adopt a more active warfighting posture in space, Whiting argues. That means not only protecting US systems but also being prepared to threaten or strike hostile assets if necessary. He has called for orbital interceptors and other weapons.
"We must be well-prepared for conflict in space. And if deterrence fails, we will fight and win," he told a conference in April.
Western officials warn of a range of threats, including ground-based lasers, electronic jammers, cyberattacks and anti-satellite missiles.
In orbit, the United States, China and Russia all operate maneuverable satellites capable of approaching and inspecting other spacecraft. Such systems could be adapted to carry weapons, including lasers or projectiles. Western officials say Beijing and Moscow have demonstrated technologies that could be used to threaten US and allied satellites.
The US has also accused Russia of developing an anti-satellite capability involving a satellite designed to carry a nuclear weapon. Moscow has denied that it is developing a space-based anti-satellite nuclear weapon.
The U.K.'s Tedman, in an interview last fall, said militaries now see satellites as “weapons systems” that need to maneuver and fight. The West is “working hard to retain our strategic advantage in space,” he said.
Some specialists note that disrupting satellites remains easier from Earth than through spacecraft-on-spacecraft attacks.
In a rare disclosure about its own capabilities, the US Space Force announced in June that it had introduced an earthbound electromagnetic weapon from L3Harris Technologies designed to disable or disrupt adversary satellites.
"Dogfighting" and hunter satellites
Although the United States remains the world's leading space power, China is rapidly expanding both the number of satellites it operates and the complexity of its missions.
Chinese satellites have demonstrated what US officials describe as orbital "dogfighting," which includes multiple satellites moving in a synchronized way in proximity. Chinese spacecraft have also shown the ability to capture a defunct satellite and move it into a different orbit.
Last year, China conducted what was likely an on-orbit refueling attempt, according to a US Space Force official. Refueling would be a major breakthrough because satellites are normally constrained by the fuel they launch with. The ability to replenish fuel could determine whether a spacecraft remains a hunter or becomes the hunted.
Chinese institutions continue to pursue new capabilities. Patent-related documents show the maker of some of China's most advanced military aircraft acquired technology that allows satellites to autonomously calculate fuel-efficient maneuvers while pursuing another spacecraft.
Meanwhile, a technology-transfer notice published by the National University of Defense Technology described a mature system capable of managing hundreds of satellites simultaneously for both defensive and operational purposes.
Researchers at another major Chinese university with close military ties have also been developing pursuit satellites, including concepts involving multiple spacecraft using nets to capture targets, according to patent-related documents.
The institutions and the People's Liberation Army did not respond to requests for comment. On-orbit capabilities such as refueling and capturing another satellite could have non-military uses.
China's official military newspaper, PLA Daily, said in a 2022 editorial that controlling space was essential for safeguarding national security, seizing the strategic initiative and achieving victory in war.

Norway seizes Russian ship to enforce $4.2 billion claim by Ukrainian energy firm
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
07:18:37 UTC
16:18:37 KST

Norway has seized a Russian ship in the Arctic to enforce a $4.22 billion compensation claim won by Ukrainian energy firm Naftogaz over Moscow's seizure of its assets when Russia annexed Crimea in 2014, officials said late on Wednesday.
The vessel, the Professor Molchanov, was seized off the Norwegian Arctic archipelago of Svalbard after a 24-hour standoff with the Norwegian Coast Guard, according to Covington, the US law firm representing Naftogaz.
Russian state news agency TASS quoted a Foreign Ministry spokesperson as saying the Norwegian action was "piracy."
Naftogaz has been pursuing legal action against Russia since 2016 to seek compensation for the expropriation of its property in Crimea.
A tribunal in The Hague in April 2023 ordered Russia to pay Naftogaz $4.22 billion plus interest and legal costs, but Moscow has not done so.
"Russia cannot evade responsibility simply by refusing to comply with an international arbitral award," said Naftogaz Acting CEO Sergii Fedorenko.
Covington tracks the Professor Molchanov for months
Covington, the law firm, said it had been tracking the Professor Molchanov, a Russian-owned vessel that is used for commercial cruises, for months.
Anticipating the ship's arrival in Svalbard en route to Barentsburg, a Russian mining settlement, Naftogaz's lawyers applied to a Norwegian court for the vessel to be arrested there and subject to a compulsory sale.
The application was approved by the Nord-Troms and Senja District Court on Monday. In its ruling, it required the governor of Svalbard to enforce the order, supervise the vessel, and ensure that it is not moved.
The governor's office issued a statement confirming that the ship had been seized and would be held in Svalbard.
Naftogaz has said it is coordinating enforcement measures across multiple jurisdictions, including the United States, France, the United Kingdom and Finland, where Russian assets have been frozen. Russia is appealing the process, saying no notice was given.
"We will continue to pursue Russian assets around the world until the compensation awarded to Naftogaz and other Naftogaz Group companies is paid," the Ukrainian company said.
Russia calls Norway's seizure of its ship 'piracy', TASS reports
The Russian Foreign Ministry on Thursday called Norway's seizure of a Russian vessel at the request of Ukrainian state firm Naftogaz "piracy."
The Ukrainian company has been pursuing legal action against Russia since 2016 to seek compensation for Moscow's expropriation of Naftogaz property when Russia annexed Crimea in 2014.
Norway seized the ship on Wednesday, after Moscow failed to pay Naftogaz $4.22 billion plus interest and legal costs to compensate for assets it seized in Crimea following a 2023 ruling by a tribunal in The Hague.
Alexei Chekunkov, Russia's Minister for the Development of the Russian Far East and Arctic, said Moscow would challenge the ruling, saying the seizure of the vessel, "Professor Molchanov," was "another example of Western countries' legal nihilism and lawlessness," according to the Interfax news agency.

From his home in Hornbæk, northern Copenhagen-born, retired Danish pilot, airline captain, and businessman Percy Beck Rørvigre calls living in Manhattan at an early age, joining the Danish Air Force at 18, starting a 30-year long career at Scandinavian Airlines at 24, and piloting the CPH-JFK route for years.
From his home in Hornbæk, northern Copenhagen-born, retired Danish pilot, airline captain, and businessman Percy Beck Rørvigre calls living in Manhattan at an early age, joining the Danish Air Force at 18, starting a 30-year long career at Scandinavian Airlines at 24, and piloting the CPH-JFK route for years.

house-like concrete play structures frame community arc park in chihuahua
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
07:15:48 UTC
16:15:48 KST

Urbánika builds ARC Park, a gathering and play area in Chihuahua
ARC Park by Urbánika is a community park located at the center of a mixed-use development in Chihuahua, northern Mexico. Named for Activity, Recreation and Community, the park serves as the social heart of the complex, bringing together spaces for play, sport, events, and everyday gathering within a landscape adapted to the Chihuahuan Desert climate.
The program includes a children’s play area, café, service areas, pickleball, basketball, table tennis, and volleyball courts, outdoor play spaces, and a multipurpose area for events and concerts. Shaded areas and spaces for social interaction complement the sports facilities, with the overall layout intended to encourage community gathering, physical activity, and health.
House-like concrete volumes form ARC Park’s main play area
The children’s play area forms the main public space within ARC Park. It is organized around a series of small, house-like concrete volumes, each offering a different type of spatial and physical experience. The first structure is designed for climbing and scaling, the second encourages descent, while the third provides a space for meeting and interaction.
A central platform connects and articulates the different volumes, creating a continuous play environment. With this configuration, Urbánika’s design team aims to stimulate imagination and free play, while supporting social, motor, cognitive, and sensory development. The structures provide a framework for play that can be completed through the children’s own interpretation and use.
The park’s recreational program extends beyond the play area. Pickleball courts are distinguished by different colors to facilitate identification and encourage a sense of ownership and appropriation among users. A fire pit provides a gathering point during the cold winter months, while a pet shower and public restrooms complete the supporting facilities.
pickleball courts use different colors to distinguish the recreational spaces
More than 120 trees establish a landscape in transformation
Landscape design forms an integral part of the park’s response to the desert climate. More than 120 trees were planted throughout the site, including eldarica pines, oak trees, cypress trees, and lilacs. The species were selected for their adaptability to the Chihuahuan Desert and their low maintenance requirements.
The vegetation is intended to develop alongside the park’s built elements. As the trees mature, their growing canopy will gradually integrate the children’s concrete structures into the landscape and extend the areas of shade across the site.
ARC Park is therefore conceived as a landscape that changes over time. Its environmental performance and spatial qualities are expected to evolve as the vegetation matures, providing increasing shade and supporting the daily use of the park by surrounding residents, visitors, children, and their caregivers.

Little help for girls in NL caught up in crime: study
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
07:14:44 UTC
16:14:44 KST

Little help for girls in NL caught up in crime: study
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
There is very little help for girls and young women who get caught up in the Dutch criminal justice system, a new government-backed study has found. The findings show the majority of treatment options are aimed at boys, who have different needs and problems.
The study is by the justice ministry’s research centre WODC and Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam. They looked at 22 international treatment methods for young female criminal offenders.
Only one such method is studied, used and seen as promising for girls in the Netherlands: a treatment that helps them manage aggression. For most other kinds of help, it is simply not known whether they do any good.
Different problems
 Most programmes are built around boys, who make up the majority of young offenders. But girls and young women usually end up in the system for different reasons.
Their behaviour more often traces back to issues such as anxiety, trouble with their parents, or sexual abuse. Boys are more likely to struggle with aggression, poor self-control, or falling in with the wrong crowd.
Because of that, help designed for boys does not always help girls – especially the lighter support given at home or through youth care.
Divided opinions
 Not all experts and researchers agree this is a problem. Some say programmes are always tailored to the individual anyway, so they work for boys and girls alike. Others want clearer guidance for working with girls.
Girls and young women are behind only a small share of recorded crime, usually less serious, such as theft.
Among the youngest, under 16, there has been a slight rise in violent offences. Why is not clear. It follows a wider rise in teen crime recorded last year.

"Smart javelin" brings sensors and real-time data analysis to athletics
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

TDK will debut its new sensor-powered Smart Javelin at the World Athletics Ultimate Championship in Budapest.
Javelins are about to get smart. TDK Corporation will fit throws with sensor technology at the World Athletics Ultimate Championship in Budapest, recording and analysing the physics behind every throw in real time.
As an official global supporter of the event, running in the Hungarian capital from 11 to 13 September, TDK will fit javelins with its sensors for a special demonstration featuring leading athletes.
The technology captures data invisible in a conventional result, where distance remains the only metric that counts. TDK's sensors track the javelin's release angle, rotation, speed, height and flight path.
TDK's software analyses that data in real time and turns it into visualisations displayed at the venue. The goal is twofold: giving athletes a sharper picture of their technique and performance, and helping spectators grasp the mechanics behind a top-level throw.
The initiative builds on TDK's partnership with World Athletics ahead of the World Athletics Championships Tokyo 25, when the two organisations first explored how sensor technology could capture previously "invisible" javelin data and present it accessibly.
TDK says upgrades to both the sensor unit and the software have since enabled instant analysis and visualisation of the javelin's movement, opening the door to new uses of the data in training, performance analysis and the spectator experience.
The Budapest demonstration
The special Smart Javelin presentation is scheduled for Friday, 11 September 2026, from 09:00 to 13:00 local time, at the training and warm-up area of the Gyula Zsivotzky National Athletics Centre.
International-level athletes are expected to take part in the demonstration, including:
- Rumesh Tharanga Pathirage (Sri Lanka), world No.1 in the men's javelin rankings for 2026.
- Keshorn Walcott (Trinidad and Tobago), 2025 world champion, 2012 Olympic gold medallist and 2016 bronze medallist.
- Haruka Kitaguchi (Japan), 2024 Olympic gold medallist, 2023 world champion and holder of the Japanese record. Kitaguchi will take part in the discussion on sensor technology but will not throw.
- Máté Horváth (Hungary), Hungarian champion in 2025 and European U18 silver medallist in 2022.
- Fanni Kövér (Hungary), Hungarian champion in 2024 and European U20 bronze medallist in 2023.
- Máté Járvás (Hungary), Hungarian bronze medallist in 2026.
From sensors to sports analytics
The project forms part of TDK's long-term "TDK Transformation" vision and "In Everything, Better." philosophy. Through its "TDK Sensing Within" initiative, the company aims to integrate sensor technology into products and solutions across multiple sectors, working with external partners.
TDK has been an official partner of World Athletics since 1983, and in recent years the collaboration has expanded into technology projects using sensors and data to give new insight into athletes' performances.
The World Athletics Ultimate Championship is a new global competition that will bring together world and Olympic champions, Wanda Diamond League winners and the leading athletes in the world rankings every two years.
The inaugural edition takes place in Budapest from 11 to 13 September, with a prize fund of $10 million (about €8.6 million).

Foreign support, drones fuel Sudan war and possible war crimes, UN probe says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
07:11:12 UTC
16:11:12 KST

Foreign support, drones fuel Sudan war and possible war crimes, UN probe says
GENEVA, Sept 3 - Foreign weapons, military technology, fighters and logistical networks are helping sustain Sudan's conflict and expanding the warring parties' ability to strike deep into civilian areas, a United Nations fact-finding mission said in a report published on Thursday, warning that some attacks may amount to war crimes.
Sudan's war erupted in April 2023 following a power struggle between Sudan's military and the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) ahead of a planned transition to civilian rule. The conflict has devastated the country, displaced more than 14 million people and created what the United Nations has described as one of the world's worst humanitarian crises.
The U.N. mission said investigators found reasonable grounds to believe that a transnational network involving individuals and entities in the United Arab Emirates, Chad, Libya and Somalia supplied the RSF with weapons, military equipment, logistics, training and foreign personnel.
The UAE, Chad, Libya and Somalia, the RSF and Sudan's military did not immediately respond to requests for comment from Reuters.
The UAE rejected allegations that it had provided military, logistical, financial or political support to the RSF, and Chad said it remained neutral in the war and denied knowledge of weapons transfers through its territory, according to the report.
The U.N. mission also said it obtained evidence that Colombian contractors played a significant role in operating and maintaining drone systems and other advanced weapons used by the RSF. It estimated the total number of Colombian contractors involved could approach 2,000 and said some were present during operations around al-Fashir in Darfur.
Colombia told investigators it opposed mercenarism and was taking steps to address the participation of Colombian nationals in foreign conflicts.
Mass killings of non‑Arab communities when the RSF captured al‑Fashir bore hallmarks that point to genocide, the U.N. mission said in a previous report in February.
In the past, the RSF has denied such abuses, saying the accounts have been manufactured by its enemies and making counter-accusations against them.
The mission said its investigation into external support for Sudan's military was at an early stage but had found evidence that foreign-supplied combat drones and loitering munitions — which can hover over an area before striking a target — had expanded the army's long-range strike capabilities.
It said some of those weapons were used in attacks on civilian locations, including Yabus Market in Blue Nile State.
DRONE WARFARE
The report found both sides committed serious violations of international human rights law and international humanitarian law in their drone operations, with some conduct amounting to war crimes. Both sides have previously denied allegations of human rights abuses.
Expanded range, persistence and increasingly sophisticated capabilities enabled Sudan's military and the RSF to strike far beyond immediate front lines, and evidence points to both sides carrying out drone attacks that killed civilians and hit hospitals, schools, markets and displacement sites.
More than 1,000 civilians were killed in drone strikes between January and May 2026, according to figures cited by the report.
Between May and July 2026, repeated RSF drone attacks damaged electricity and fuel facilities in the North Kordofan capital of El Obeid, which was under SAF control as RSF pressure intensified in June this year. Strikes disrupted water supplies, healthcare, transport and other basic services in a city already under severe strain and partial siege, the mission said.
Among the cases highlighted in the report were SAF strikes on Ad-Da'ein Teaching Hospital in East Darfur that investigators said killed at least 70 people and left the facility non-functional.
The mission reiterated calls for enforcement of the Darfur arms embargo and urged the U.N. Security Council to extend it across all of Sudan. REUTERS

Cassandra Wilson, the celebrated Grammy Award-winning jazz singer, dies aged 70
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
07:09:21 UTC
16:09:21 KST

Cassandra Wilson, known for her deep, moody and genre-bending contralto, was one of the most influential American jazz vocalists of the last 40 years. She redefined the boundaries of contemporary blues, jazz and folk.
American jazz singer and songwriter Cassandra Wilson has died in her hometown of Jackson, Mississippi, aged 70.
The two-time Grammy winning vocalist was named TIME magazine’s “America’s Best Singer” in 2001 and was best known for her distinctive and genre-bending contralto. She redefined the boundaries of traditional blues-jazz and folk sounds, and worked across various genres including pop, country, and R&B.
"It is with profound sadness that we announce the passing of Cassandra Wilson, the Grammy Award-winning and legendary jazz artist," her manager Robert Torre wrote in a statement (via jazz radio station WBGO). "Cassandra Wilson transitioned peacefully at home, surrounded by family, close friends, and her manager. Her family and close friends respectfully ask for privacy during this difficult time as they grieve her loss."
No cause of death was disclosed.
Jackson Mayor John Horhn also released statement: "Jackson has lost an extraordinary native daughter, and the world has lost a singular musical voice. Cassandra Wilson carried the sound, spirit and history of Mississippi with her wherever her music reached. She built a remarkable career rooted in jazz, blues, gospel, folk and the many traditions that shape our state’s musical identity.”
He added: "Her work had rare depth of character and a profound understanding of how music moves people, tells stories and connects generations."
As Jon Batiste put it in a eulogy yesterday, Wilson sounded like the South.
“She had an unmistakable vocal tone, phrasing and her approach of weaving folkloric, R&B and diasporic music together with experimental and popular genres had a major impact on me,” Batiste added.
Wilson gained critical acclaim in 1988 for her third album 'Blue Skies' and later signed to Blue Note Records in the early 90s, achieving breakthrough success with albums like 'Blue Light 'Til Dawn' (1993) and 1996's 'New Moon Daughter' - the latter of which won the Grammy for Best Jazz Vocal Performance. She received her second Grammy in 2009 for her album 'Loverly', crowned Best Jazz Vocal Album.
Throughout her solo career, she also contributed to albums by Steve Coleman, Greg Obsy and two of The Roots’ records, 'Do you Want More?!!!??!' and 'Illadelph Halflife', and recorded with the likes of Luther Vandross, Regina Carter, Angelique Kidjo, John Legend, Ravi Coltrane, and the Count Basie Orchestra. She was also a major voice in Wynton Marsalis' oratorio 'Blood on the Fields',which became the first jazz work to win a Pulitzer Prize for Music in 1997.
In 2015, Wilson gave a special concert at the famed Apollo Theater to commemorate the 100th birthday of blues singer Billie Holiday. That same year, she released her last studio album, 'Coming Forth By Day', an homage to Holiday.
She then formed a supergroup called Dopamine in 2020, alongside Elvis Costello, DJ Premier, T-Bone Burnett and Nathaniel Rateliff.
In 2022, Wilson received the National Endowment For The Arts Jazz Master Fellowship, one of the highest honours awarded to jazz musicians in the US.
RIP Cassandra Wilson 1955 - 2026

US, Australia to boost defense ties amid China's growing influence

US, Australia to boost defense ties amid China's influence
September 3, 2026
The United States and Australia have announced plans to boost defense ties and strengthen deterrence amid China's growing influence in the Pacific.
US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth met his Australian counterpart, Richard Marles, in Washington on Wednesday, saying Canberra understood "the gravity of maintaining a favorable balance of power in the region."
Marles told reporters that "American force posture in Australia is growing" and that the expanding cooperation was a response to "the biggest conventional military build-up by any country in the world since the Second World War in the form of China."
"We need to be ensuring that we build deterrence, that we build balance, so that we can provide for the peace and stability of the region in which we live," he added.
What did the two countries agree?
The Pentagon said the two countries agreed to "accelerate force posture initiatives at Australian bases, bolster cooperation in combined logistics, and build greater interoperability through joint exercises."
The force posture initiatives are agreements allowing the US military to train and store equipment in Australia, including the rotational deployment of aircraft and logistics support for US vessels.
While Australia does not permit foreign military bases on its soil, it does host several key joint exercises and rotations of US Marines in the northern city of Darwin. It was not clear if the agreement will see more US troops stationed in Australia.
According to the Pentagon, the two countries also discussed progress on cooperation "to enable shared capacity for guided weapons and next-generation capabilities."
Hegseth said in a statement that there was "strong alignment" between the national defense strategies of both countries.
He also stressed the importance of allies investing in their own sovereign security and the need for them to "both plan together but also ensure our capabilities match and are complementary."
Australia has sought to strengthen its defense force in recent years, focusing on boosting its missile strike capability and deepening strategic alliances.
Cooperation between the US and Australia also includes the AUKUS defense pact with Britain. As part of that pact, American defense personnel are working at the HMAS Stirling naval base in Western Australia, which is set to host a rotating force of US-commanded submarines from 2027.
China has called the AUKUS pact dangerous and warned it could spark a regional arms race.

MOD targets two-year contract deadline for major platforms
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
08:05:36 BST
16:05:36 KST

The Ministry of Defence has set a target of reducing the average time to first contract for major platforms such as tanks, frigates and aircraft from six years to two, alongside faster targets for upgrades and uncrewed systems, according to a written answer published this week.
Luke Pollard, Minister of State for Defence Readiness and Industry, was responding to Stuart Anderson, the Conservative MP for South Shropshire, who had asked about the planned reforms set out at paragraph 27 on page 64 of the Defence Investment Plan.
Mr Pollard said the National Armaments Director Group launched a segmented approach to procurement on 1 April 2026, tailoring acquisition routes to the type of capability, the supplier and the level of risk.
Three segments have been established, the Minister says. Major platforms, covering tanks, frigates and aircraft, carry the target of moving from six years to two. Pace-setting modular upgrades, covering communications, sensors and weapons improvements, are to come down from three years to one. Rapid commercial exploitation, which the answer illustrates with uncrewed systems, carries a target of three-month acquisition cycles.
On the commercial machinery behind that, Mr Pollard said: “These reforms are supported by the Accelerating Commercial Pathways (ACP) programme, which aims to improve the Ministry of Defence’s ability to harness flexibilities in the commercial process and ensure that commercial approaches are tailored to the needs of individual procurements, including through the use of flexibilities provided by the Procurement Act 2023. The programme has launched six Commercial Pathways and, since March 2025, over 300 procurements have self-selected one or more pathways.”
What the targets mean
Time to first contract measures the period between a requirement being identified and a supplier being placed under contract to deliver it, which is the stage before any metal is cut and where a great deal of British procurement time has historically been consumed.
The three-month target for uncrewed systems is the one that departs furthest from existing practice, and it reflects a problem the war in Ukraine has made unavoidable, where the useful life of a small drone design is measured in months before countermeasures catch up.
The segmented approach is the same framework that appeared in a market engagement notice published on 18 August, which set out a £1.9 billion requirement running from 2028 to 2037 and described the department as considering multi-supplier frameworks alongside individual contracts, with details of the competition promised no later than the first quarter of 2027.
The National Armaments Director Group was established on 1 April 2025 as one of the four groups now making up the Ministry of Defence, bringing together Defence Equipment and Support, the Defence Infrastructure Organisation, the Defence Science and Technology Laboratory, Defence Digital and the commercial, international collaboration and exports functions.
Rupert Pearce took over as National Armaments Director on a five-year fixed-term contract from October 2025.
The Procurement Act 2023 introduced the notice structure and the competitive flexible procedure now used across British public contracting, replacing the previous set of public contracts regulations, and the flexibilities Mr Pollard refers to include the ability to design a procedure around a particular requirement rather than following a fixed process.

====================================================================================================

China’s demise was gleefully predicted by the west – meanwhile, it built an AI revolution | Larry Elliott
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
07:00:47 UTC
16:00:47 KST

Almost from the moment it began, the end of the Chinese economic miracle has been much anticipated. Thick and fast, the books have come explaining how it will end badly. Overinvestment. A country wallowing in debt. The collapse of the property market. Political repression. The demand for democracy from a growing middle class. All have been put forward as reasons for the inevitable terminal crisis.
Even those impressed by the country’s rapid growth took comfort from the notion that the west would continue to dominate advanced manufacturing while China would be stuck assembling TVs. And while the wait for its much-predicted demise has gone on and on, China has become the workshop of the world.
This process has come in two distinct phases. Initially, it is true, there was a concentration on low-cost manufactured goods because cheap labour costs provided a competitive advantage. Firms left for east Asia in search of higher profits. Without China 1.0, Donald Trump would have remained a New York property developer and Brexit might never have happened.
Yet, the Chinese were not content to remain solely the producers of low-cost consumer goods and began to invest heavily in higher-end manufacturing. China 2.0 shattered the illusion that it would forever remain a developing economy destined to produce low-grade products and little else.
The market in solar panels was captured. It became the world leader in batteries and electric vehicles. It no longer has to import machine tools from Germany because it is now capable of making its own. The rise of the far-right Alternative für Deutschland is in no small measure due to the threat posed by China to German manufacturing jobs.
Of course, China’s critics have a point. The model relies too heavily on investment and has much excess capacity. The country produces far more goods than it can consume domestically, particularly given the low level of wages and a relatively ungenerous welfare system. As a result, China can only keep growing at a rate that prevents rising unemployment from leading to social unrest if it exports its surfeit of goods to the rest of the world. China found itself isolated at the recent meeting of finance ministers of the G20 group of leading developed and developing countries, facing criticism from all sides for failing to boost domestic demand for its products.
Perhaps this means the rest of the world has finally woken up to the threat. If it has, that would not be a moment too soon because China is now competing with the US for dominance in the race to develop artificial intelligence. Welcome to China 3.0.
In July, a Chinese startup called Moonshot unveiled its Kimi K3 model and it was an instant success. Just two days after its launch, the company suspended new subscriptions because demand was too great for its computing capacity. That was not surprising given that Kimi K3 was marketed as being able to match the models of its US rivals – such as the latest versions of OpenAI’s ChatGPT – at no cost. This was not a fluke or a random event.
As Edoardo Campanella of UniCredit notes, Beijing is pursuing a clear AI strategy: staying close to the technological frontier, diffusing its models throughout the global economy, and setting standards across international markets. “If this strategy succeeds, the third China shock might not just disrupt the global economy, but also the global balance of power,” says Campanella.
Beijing’s strategy might not succeed but even so there are three things that are striking about the AI development race. The first is that this would appear to be the worst possible time for Washington to antagonise its traditional allies by whacking them with punitive tariffs. The US needs all the friends it can muster.
The second is that the arrival on the scene of free Chinese AI models could spell big trouble for global markets. Until now, the US has been confident its technological prowess will give it the upper hand in the AI development race and that has justified massive investment in technology companies.
Despite rising oil prices, share prices on Wall Street have reflected confidence not just that AI will transform economies but that the US will be the main beneficiary. But if China can develop its AI models at a lower cost and offer them for nothing, investors will soon start to question whether the massive investment in the US justifies the sky-high share prices of tech companies. China’s success in AI could prick the stock market bubble.
Finally, there are lessons that countries such as Britain need to learn from China if it is to re-industrialise. When China began to build up its manufacturing strength almost 50 years ago, it saw itself as a developing country. It had no illusions about the scale of the challenge but had a plan and stuck to it.
There was no aversion to picking winners. Nor would the strategy be left exposed to the whims of speculators. Instead, there was a willingness to use all the policy tools available: subsidies, tariffs, exchange controls and state investment.
The result is what we see now: a China that has shifted through the gears from an industrial policy dominated by cheap goods to an industrial policy of everything. Sure, China’s model has its flaws but there is a stark contrast with Britain’s negligent approach since the late 1970s. One country is serious about manufacturing and the other isn’t.
- 
  Larry Elliott is a Guardian columnist

For first time, Ukraine shows its British Rapid Ranger air-defense system mounted on Spanish off-road chassis. Its crews call it “close-range storm”
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
07:00:31 UTC
16:00:31 KST

Ukraine’s Third Army Corps has released photos of the RapidRanger air defense system mounted on a URO VAMTAC armored vehicle. The troops themselves described the system as a “short-range storm.”
The system defends the sky in areas where radar cannot spot a target and other weapons cannot reach it, filling the gap between mobile fire groups and heavy, less-mobile air-defense systems. That niche — fast, cheap, and radar-independent — is exactly where Russia's Shaheds and small reconnaissance drones have been slipping through.
The images show a crew of the 1030th "Aquila" Anti-Aircraft Missile-Artillery Regiment arming the launcher with missiles before going on combat duty for the first time, RBC-Ukraine reports.
Light enough to ride a pickup
Rapid Ranger weighs only 500 kilograms and has a modular design that allows it to be mounted on pickups, armored cars, or even tracked platforms.
The systems in Ukrainian service ride Spanish URO VAMTAC tactical off-roaders, which reach 135 km/h, drive on public roads, and can change position quickly or cover long distances.
That mobility is the point: a launcher that can shoot and move is far harder for Russian forces to find and destroy than a fixed battery.
Laser guidance beats the decoys
The system's LMM Martlet missiles are 1.3 meters long, weigh 13 kilograms, and reach 1,800 km/h, striking targets up to seven kilometers away. Crucially, the missiles use laser guidance, not only infrared, so Rapid Ranger can hit targets with a low thermal signature or those carrying heat-emitting decoys. That makes it effective against Russian reconnaissance drones like the Orlan-10, whose small heat trail slips past heat-seeking weapons.
A 360-degree electro-optical surveillance suite gives the crew all-around coverage, and the system detects targets out to about 15 kilometers, which is more than twice its engagement range, giving the crew time to track a threat before firing.
Rapid Ranger reached Ukrainian units as part of a British military aid package, and Euromaidan Press reported in April that the system was already downing Shaheds from its Spanish mounts. The 3rd Corps' photos are the newest confirmation that Ukraine's newest Western air-defense hardware is now integrated and standing combat duty at the front.
