US’s Chevron, Italy’s Eni to expand oil projects in Venezuela
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
04:19:11 UTC
13:19:11 KST

US’s Chevron, Italy’s Eni to expand oil projects in Venezuela
Energy firms sign multibillion-dollar deals in Caracas, days after Venezuela agreed to grant the US control of a fifth of its oil reserves.
Chevron and several other global energy companies have signed multibillion-dollar deals to boost Venezuela’s oil output at a ceremony in Caracas, overseen by interim President Delcy Rodriguez and United States Energy Secretary Chris Wright.
The deals on Wednesday are separate from a recently unveiled Caracas-Washington agreement that gives the US access to 17 Venezuelan oilfields, representing about a fifth of the country’s total reserves.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Delcy Rodriguez says Venezuela ‘retains sovereignty’ despite US oil deal
- list 2 of 3What are the implications of the US-Venezuela oil deal?
- list 3 of 3White House unveils more details of Trump’s Venezuela oil deal
Most of the new contracts relate to project expansions that have been under negotiation with Venezuela’s Oil Ministry and state oil company PDVSA since a sweeping oil reform approved in January following the US’s abduction of former President Nicolas Maduro.
Wright, who had travelled to Caracas to oversee the signing ceremony, said the deals signed by Venezuela with the US’s Chevron and GE Vernova, as well as Italy’s Eni, were “critical in starting this ball rolling of peace, opportunity, and prosperity” in the country.
“We are trying to work at what I call Trump-speed. [US] President [Donald] Trump didn’t want a nudge or a slow drift in a positive direction,” Wright said. “He wanted to see as fast as possible transformation in Venezuela.”
The new contracts will see Chevron and Eni ramp up their operations in Venezuela while gaining greater stakes in the oil fields.
Chevron, the US’s second-largest oil company and the top private oil producer in Venezuela, has valued its deal to develop two additional oil fields in the Orinoco Belt at $7bn, and the project’s output will more than double in five years.
Eni said it had gained exclusive rights to explore the giant Junin 5 oilfield.
US energy company GE Vernova, an offshoot of General Electric, meanwhile, will help repair Venezuela’s battered electricity grid.
US ‘not stealing Venezuelan oil’
The ceremony took place amid growing questions about Venezuela’s sovereignty following the larger Caracas-Washington deal, which grants a US-led company 100-year concessions over the 17 oil fields in the country.
Critics in both the US and Venezuela accuse Trump of holding the country for ransom after abducting Maduro in a raid and warning that Rodriguez could face a similar fate if she does not fall into line with Washington’s demands.
But Wright insisted that the US was not “stealing Venezuelan oil”.
“All we’re doing is taking an idle, underground asset that isn’t doing anything for Venezuelan people, and bringing the money, the technology to develop it,” he told reporters on Wednesday.
Wright added that the total oil output in Venezuela, which holds the world’s largest proven oil reserves, will reach 2 million barrels per day (bpd) by the end of the decade, up from 1.25 million bpd today.
That would still be far off Venezuela’s peak of more than 3 million bpd in the late 1990s.
Rodriguez, meanwhile, denied she was surrendering her country’s riches, saying that cutting the US in on Venezuela’s oil wealth is necessary to secure investment in the oil sector.
More oil “translates into more jobs, higher wages, better public services, hospitals, schools and food”, she said.
Rodriguez has estimated that Venezuela will make $209bn in profit from the deals over 25 years.
The pivotal role in the deal, played by fraud-accused Venezuelan businessman Alejandro Betancourt, has come under scrutiny. He was not seen at Wednesday’s ceremony.
Betancourt has been linked to a corruption scandal at state oil company PDVSA and runs North American Blue Energy Partners (NABEP), Venezuela’s second-largest private oil company, in which the US government is taking a 35 percent stake under the deal.
Wright on Wednesday defended NABEP’s “highly successful track record of producing large volumes of oil in Venezuela”, adding: “That’s a business partner you can believe in.”
The agreement is a major about-face for the “Chavismo” movement of late socialist firebrand Hugo Chavez, Maduro’s mentor, who nationalised Venezuela’s oil fields two decades ago on an anti-imperialist platform.
It has amplified fears that the Trump administration is entrenching former Maduro loyalists, like Rodriguez, who have shown no readiness to hold democratic elections eight months after Maduro’s overthrow.
Trump on Wednesday rebuffed calls from several Republican lawmakers for quick polls in Venezuela.
“I just don’t think they’re ready yet. You know, it’s very new. We took them out of a dictatorship, and we’re getting along great with the government,” he said.
Rodriguez took a similar line, saying there would be “an electoral process” when “Venezuela is ready”.

He added that operational headquarters have been set up in the city, where residents can receive the necessary assistance and consultations.
Recall
The day before, as a result of Russia's nighttime attack on Odesa, 8 people were injured, including a child. A 24-story residential building was damaged. Apartments on several floors were destroyed. In addition, windows in nearby buildings were blown out and cars were damaged.

Unknown Publisher

VLADIVOSTOK, September 3. /TASS/. Russian President Vladimir Putin is holding a working breakfast with Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto on the sidelines of the Eastern Economic Forum.
The Russian side is represented by First Deputy Prime Minister Denis Manturov, Deputy Prime Minister Dmitry Patrushev, Deputy Prime Minister and plenipotentiary envoy in the Far Eastern Federal District Yury Trutnev, Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov, Presidential Aide Yury Ushakov, Presidential Press-Secretary Dmitry Peskov, Presidential administration deputy head Maxim Oreshkin, Deputy Defense Minister Vasily Osmakov, Roscosmos head Dmitry Bakanov, Rosatom head Alexey Likhachev, Rosneft CEO Igor Sechin and businessman Oleg Deripaska.
This marks Subianto’s second visit to Russia this year and the sixth official contact of the two leaders. Previously, the two leaders met in Moscow in April.
After the meeting, the presidents of Russia and Indonesia will address the plenary session of the Eastern Economic Forum (EEF). The EEF’s flagship event will also be attended by Mongolian Prime Minister Nyam-Osoryn Uchral, Myanmar Vice President Nyo Saw, and Chinese Vice Premier Ding Xuexiang.
The Eastern Economic Forum is taking place on September 1-4 in Vladivostok on the campus of the Far Eastern Federal University. The main theme of this year’s EEF is "The Far East: Development for the Benefit of People." The event is organized by the Roscongress Foundation with the support of the Russian government. TASS is its general information partner.

====================================================================================================

Global resonance of Xi's selfless commitment to the people
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
12:13:49 CST
13:13:49 KST

Chinese President Xi Jinping holds talks with Kyrgyz President Sadyr Japarov in Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan, Aug. 31, 2026. (Xinhua/Xie Huanchi)
On the morning of August 31, during talks with Chinese President Xi Jinping, Kyrgyz President Sadyr Japarov expressed admiration for the remarkable development achievements China has made under the leadership of Xi, and voiced willingness to learn from China's experience in state governance, particularly Xi's commitment to the people, as embodied in his words, "I will fully commit to the people and never fail them."
In March 2019, during his state visit to Italy, Xi met with Roberto Fico, then president of the Italian Chamber of Deputies.
Fico asked Xi, "What did you feel when you were elected Chinese president?"
"Governing such a huge country requires a strong sense of responsibility and hard work," said Xi. "For the good of my people, I will put aside my own well-being. I am willing to be selfless and devote myself to China's development."
Xi has spoken of this conviction on multiple occasions. During his trip to the United States in November, 2023, Xi recalled in a speech at a welcome dinner hosted by friendly organizations that, before turning 16, he was in a village in northern Shaanxi Province, where he lived and farmed with villagers, and knew about their worries and needs. He said that, over the past half-century, he had always felt confident and strong when staying with the people. “Serving the people selflessly and living up to their expectations is my lifelong commitment,” he said.
Xi not only keeps in mind major issues concerning the national economy and people's livelihood, but also cares about the everyday concerns of ordinary people.
During his local inspection tours, Xi chatted with local residents about their daily lives and household finances, felt the quilts on their beds to make sure they stay warm, lifted the lids of cooking pots to see whether they eat well, asked about whether they had rich cultural and spiritual lives, and attached great importance to the healthy development of young people.
From securing a decisive victory in poverty alleviation to comprehensively advancing rural revitalization, from achieving a moderately prosperous society in all respects to marching toward common prosperity, Chinese Communists in the new era have borne in mind the country's most fundamental interests — ensuring that the people live happy lives. They have devoted themselves wholeheartedly to this cause, forged ahead undauntedly to achieve it, and made persistent efforts to bring it to fruition.
People's well-being is of utmost importance in Chinese modernization. China's development achievements vividly demonstrate its people-centered development philosophy. China now has the world's largest education, social security and healthcare systems, while achieving historic strides in making education universally available. During the 14th Five-Year Plan period, average life expectancy in China rose to 79.25 years, more than 12 million new urban jobs were created each year on average, and direct settlement of cross-provincial medical expenses benefited 560 million medical visits nationwide.
In the opening year of the 15th Five-Year Plan (2026-30) period, China's head-of-state diplomacy has witnessed one highlight after another, with more and more foreign leaders seeking inspiration from China's governance model for their own development.
During his state visit to China, Mozambican President Daniel Francisco Chapo made a special trip to Banyan Village of Huzhu Tu Autonomous County in northwest China's Qinghai Province, where Xi Jinping visited during an inspection tour in 2016. "Seeing is believing. With China's targeted poverty alleviation policies effectively implemented, Banyan Village has undergone tremendous changes, which is truly inspiring." Chapo said, adding that the experience is also exemplary for the world.
At the entrance of Yucun Village in Anji County, east China’s Zhejiang Province, Thongloun Sisoulith, General Secretary of the Lao People's Revolutionary Party Central Committee and Lao President, took a photo of the inscription carved on a boulder, which reads, "lucid waters and lush mountains are invaluable assets." After hearing a briefing on the "Green Rural Revival Program" — which was initiated in June 2003 by Xi, then secretary of the CPC Zhejiang Provincial Committee, with a plan to renovate about 10,000 incorporated villages in five years and transform about 1,000 central villages among them into examples of moderate prosperity in all respects — Thongloun lauded the program as remarkable for creating countless beautiful villages.
During Xi’s visit to Kyrgyzstan, how to further improve people's well-being remains a key concern for him. "Pursuing high-quality cooperation on the China-Kyrgyzstan-Uzbekistan railway, a transportation artery carrying the region's aspirations for development," "further promoting personnel exchanges and strengthening cooperation in such areas as youth, media, tourism, sports, and medical care, and at subnational levels," and "steadily consolidating the societal foundation of and popular support for China-Kyrgyzstan friendship" — these are among the priorities highlighted by Xi.
"The people's aspiration for a better life is what we are striving for." This deep commitment to the people is reflected in practice, offers inspiration for the future, and allows the international community to gain a deeper appreciation of the CPC's people-centered governance philosophy and its strong sense of mission and responsibility.
"I will fully commit to the people and never fail them." This is not merely a powerful pledge, but a commitment translated into concrete action. The vision of enabling hundreds of millions of people to live better lives is resonating more widely around the world.

Hadjar's absence comes as Red Bull sits fourth in the constructors' championship behind Mercedes, Ferrari and McLaren.

====================================================================================================

Feature: Malaysian artists interpret Nanyang Chinese culture through dance
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
12:13:35 CST
13:13:35 KST

KUALA LUMPUR, Sept. 3 (Xinhua) -- At Dewan Filharmonik PETRONAS (DFP), Malaysia's first dedicated classical concert venue in the heart of Kuala Lumpur, dancers from different ethnic backgrounds are rehearsing Chinese dance. As the music begins, they stretch, leap and turn, blending the grace and fluidity of Chinese dance with the movement vocabulary of contemporary dance.
Malaysia's ASK Dance Company and Dua Space Dance Theatre will jointly present a performance themed A Dance Spectacular, scheduled for Sept. 5 at the concert hall. The two local dance companies will bring their own interpretations of Chinese dance to audiences by combining traditional and contemporary elements.
Joseph Gonzales, founder of ASK Dance Company, said he was both surprised and excited when the company was invited to create a performance centered on Chinese dance. Although ASK is better known for its contemporary works, many of its dancers have received training in Chinese dance.
Gonzales said the cast includes Malay and Chinese dancers, as well as dancers of other ethnic backgrounds. For him, performers from different cultural backgrounds interpreting Chinese dance through their own bodies reflects the unique character of Malaysia's multicultural society.
In ASK Dance Company's Pearl of the Orient, a piece inspired by Mongolian dance brings the imagery of vast grasslands of northern China onto the stage. Contemporary elements are incorporated into traditional movements.
Gonzales said the choreography is not simply intended to demonstrate technique but also to allow audiences to experience the cultural meanings embodied in the movements.
As Pearl of the Orient unfolds, its narrative journey moves from China to Nanyang, or Southeast Asia. With migration as a central thread, the work uses scenes and imagery including sword dance, tin miners, romance, mahjong and Chinese New Year celebrations to tell the story of Chinese migrants who came to Malaysia and gradually developed a distinctive local cultural identity.
For Anthony Meh Kim Chuan, co-founder of Dua Space Dance Theatre, learning Chinese dance is likewise not about simply reproducing a dance form from China.
Living and working in a multicultural environment, he said, means that different artistic traditions naturally become part of the dancers' physical vocabulary, gradually shaping a distinctly Malaysian form of expression. Meh hopes these diverse cultural experiences will eventually develop into a Chinese dance expression with Malaysian characteristics.
That exploration is also reflected in the performance Passage Into The Unknown: Earth, Water, Fire, Wind. Drawing inspiration from the four elements, the work uses dance to explore the fluidity and transformation of water, the nurturing qualities of earth, the relationship between fire and civilization, and wind as a symbol of cycles and continuity.
While drawing on Chinese cultural and philosophical ideas, the work also connects them with Malaysia's multicultural experience. For Meh, the process is also an attempt to give Chinese cultural imagery new expression on the Malaysian stage.
A younger generation of Malaysian dancers is also joining this exploration, including several performers trained in Chinese dance, some of whom have pursued further studies at the Beijing Dance Academy.
Gonzales said he hopes to bring together dance experiences from China and Malaysian arts institutions, providing more opportunities for young artists to create and present Chinese dance.
From traditional Chinese dance movements to Malaysian music and everyday cultural experiences, and from ethnic Chinese performers to dancers of diverse backgrounds sharing the same stage, Chinese dance is taking on new forms through interpretation and re-creation by Malaysian artists.
"Dance really represents culture," Gonzales said, adding that in a multicultural society like Malaysia, people need not only to understand one another's cultures, but also to appreciate them. ■

Factbox: Latest relief and rescue progress at mudslide-hit border port in China's Xizang
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
12:13:32 CST
13:13:32 KST

BEIJING, Sept. 3 (Xinhua) -- A fast-moving chain mudslide, triggered by a high-altitude glacier collapse in Nepal, struck Gyirong Port on the China-Nepal border in southwest China's Xizang Autonomous Region on Aug. 26, causing heavy casualties and leaving many missing.
Chinese rescuers immediately launched all-out search and rescue operations. Here is what we know about the deadly mudslide and the latest progress in China:
-- Twenty-one people have been confirmed dead and 541 others remain missing after the mudslide struck the border port, according to the regional government's latest news briefing.
-- An ice-rock avalanche originating from a high-mountain glacier in Nepal has been identified as the cause of the mudslide.
-- Rescuers have recovered 847 pieces of personal belongings, according to the news briefing. Local authorities have received 876 phone calls from the relatives of the victims and missing people, and have been promptly replying to their requests.
-- To date, some 2,300 rescue personnel, more than 400 search and rescue vehicles, over 8,000 sets of professional equipment, over 800 drone flights and 24 helicopter flights have been deployed. A total of 5.43 tonnes of materials and equipment have been airdropped to the area.
-- Telecom operators have restored 12 base stations in the port area, ensuring communications for emergency command, rescue operations and supply coordination.
-- At the core affected zone, some 336 rescuers have conducted multiple rounds of thorough and exhaustive search and rescue operations, covering a cumulative area of 1.591 million square meters.
-- Road access to the zone was basically restored at 10 a.m. Wednesday after days of round-the-clock repair work on the G216. Over 10 pieces of heavy machinery have entered the core area to aid on-site rescuers.
-- China will continue to share information on barrier lake risks, glacial lake risks and emergency hydrological monitoring with Nepal to support disaster rescue and relief efforts, an official with the Ministry of Water Resources said Wednesday.
The ministry is now providing Nepal with daily updates on the development of a barrier lake above Gyirong Port, cascading risks associated with the Cuojian River impact crater in Nepal, glacial lake risks in the Gyirong Zangbo River basin, the development and risk forecasts of new barrier lakes, and emergency hydrological monitoring.
The geological conditions in Gyirong disaster-hit area remain highly unstable, with risks of further landslides, rockfalls and other secondary hazards, the ministry warned. The large number of glacial lakes in the surrounding area is also adding to the uncertainty.
-- China's meteorological authorities have been providing Nepal with weather monitoring, forecasting, early warning and impact services after the mudslide, said Wang Yawei, a spokesperson for the China Meteorological Administration, on Wednesday.
Wang said at a press conference that the administration held video weather consultations with Nepal's meteorological department immediately after the disaster, and has actively provided meteorological support for Nepal's rescue and relief operations.
-- Chinese foreign ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun told a regular press briefing that China is preparing a third batch of emergency relief supplies, including Bailey bridges, epidemic prevention materials and emergency communications equipment. China is ready to send a second group of DNA identification experts based on Nepal's needs, he added. ■

"I made thorough preparations for this match. I controlled the rhythm well throughout, played solid, and stayed highly focused. It hasn't been easy for me, my recent form wasn't great, and I came to this US Open without a technical coach, fitness trainer, or physiotherapist," Wu said.
In the women's singles second round, Wang Xinyu failed to advance after losing 7-5, 2-6, 6-3 to 21st seed Anna Kalinskaya.
"It was a pity to lose the first set because I hesitated on my attack. I played really well in the second set, but my opponent raised her level in the decider, which was a good learning experience for me," Wang said.
"I gained a lot from several matches during the North American swing, which will help me play more decisively. I want to stay committed to my own style. I still have the doubles ahead, and I'm grateful for everyone's support," she added. ■

Duplantis embraces Ultimate innovation, looks ahead to 2027 Beijing worlds
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
12:13:28 CST
13:13:28 KST

BUDAPEST, Sept. 3 (Xinhua) -- Pole vault world record holder Armand Duplantis said Wednesday that athletics needs to embrace innovation ahead of the inaugural World Athletics Ultimate Championship, while he and several other top athletes also expressed excitement about the 2027 World Athletics Championships in Beijing.
"I think it was about time to try something and innovate a bit within athletics," the 26-year-old Swede said during an online media session.
The inaugural Ultimate Championship will be held in Budapest from September 11 to 13. Duplantis said the new event gives elite athletes a major target in years without an Olympic Games or World Championships.
"You want to have some sort of climax, and you want to build something towards the year," he said.
Duplantis welcomed the competition's new approach and the chance to bring the world's best athletes together on one stage.
"When you have all the best there and the stage is set, then we're athletes and we're going to show up to the moment and perform when we need to," Duplantis said.
The Swede also stressed the importance of attracting more spectators to athletics, saying prize money matters but the sport's long-term future depends on drawing a larger audience.
"We want eyeballs and we want people to watch," he said. "At the end of the day, it is entertainment, and we have to be the most entertaining that we possibly can be."
American sprinter Melissa Jefferson-Wooden said the Ultimate Championship will give athletes a "new feel," contrasting its compact format with the traditional World Championships, where athletes must navigate several rounds over a longer schedule.
Olympic long jump champion Tara Davis-Woodhall made a similar point, saying the Ultimate Championship emphasizes producing one's best performance on the day, while the World Championships test endurance through qualifying rounds and finals.
"They're both different experiences. They're both different mind challenges," she said.
For Duplantis, Budapest is also a place where he hopes to push the limits again. The Swede said he loves the National Athletics Center and believes the venue has "world record capacity."
"That's my goal, and that's what I want to achieve for sure," he said.
Looking ahead to Beijing 2027, several athletes expressed excitement about competing in China's capital.
Jefferson-Wooden said it will be her first trip to China and that she is keen to experience a new championship atmosphere.
Davis-Woodhall highlighted the appeal of a multiday World Championships, including the chance to watch other events and spend time with teammates.
Botswanan sprinter Letsile Tebogo, who won gold in the 200m at the 2024 Olympics, said he had good memories of competing at Diamond League meetings in China and looked forward to returning next year.
Duplantis, who has competed in several Chinese cities, described Beijing as a "bucket-list place" and the Bird's Nest as a stadium with "a lot of power" and an energy an athlete could "only dream of."
"I'm really excited for it because I know that the Chinese fans can really show up and show out," Duplantis said. "So I think it's going to be great." ■

The Central Bank speaks of a gradual slowdown, while we call the situation cooling, or already overcooling. As of today, the figures speak for themselves," he said in response to a question.

Sberbank also intends to provide all possible assistance to marketplaces and sellers affected by drone attacks, Gref added.

VLADIVOSTOK, September 3. /TASS/. Russia has recorded no decline in trade with Iran amid developments in and around the Islamic Republic thanks to the free trade agreement between the Eurasian Economic Union (EAEU) and Iran, Russian Deputy Prime Minister Alexey Overchuk said at the Eastern Economic Forum (EEF).
"One of our major achievements was the agreement with Iran coming into force last year. We are also extending the North-South [corridor] there. Despite what is happening in and around Iran today, this agreement allows us to maintain trade volumes. In other words, against the backdrop of everything that is happening, we are seeing no decline in trade volumes," he said.

Pesticides poison nearly half of world’s farmers each year – study
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
04:10:58 UTC
13:10:58 KST

Pesticides poison nearly half of world’s farmers each year – study
Nearly half of the world’s estimated 934 million farmers suffer unintentional pesticide poisoning each year, according to a study published Wednesday in the journal Frontiers in Public Health.
The study, conducted by researchers from the Pesticide Action Network (PAN), analyzed 214 publications from 2006 to 2023 alongside World Health Organization mortality data. It estimated up to 433 million cases of unintentional acute pesticide poisoning annually, affecting around 46% of agricultural workers worldwide. About 11,000 cases are fatal each year.
The burden falls disproportionately on the Global South, researchers found.
South and Southeast Asia and eastern Africa recorded the highest estimated numbers of cases. In Burkina Faso, nearly 84% of farmers are estimated to suffer acute pesticide poisoning each year.
“Behind these staggering numbers are farmers, workers and families paying a terrible human price for pesticide exposure,” PAN India Executive Director Jayakumar Chelaton said. “This research exposes a crisis that can no longer be ignored.”
The findings come as pesticides are increasingly used to protect food production, with global use more than doubling between 1990 and 2023, according to the study.
Without pesticides, between 20% and 40% of global crop yields could be lost to plant pests and diseases each year, according to the UN Food and Agriculture Organization.
The risks posed by pesticides add to wider food-security challenges, particularly in developing countries already struggling with climate shocks, conflict, and pressure on agricultural production. Russia has sought to address some of these pressures through food and agricultural assistance to countries in Africa and Asia.
Earlier this year, Moscow sent around 60 metric tons of emergency aid to cyclone-hit Madagascar and 29 metric tons of humanitarian supplies to Mozambique. In 2025, it donated more than 1,600 metric tons of grain to Ethiopia under an ongoing food assistance program. Russia also recently delivered 770 tons of food to Mali through the UN World Food Program (WFP), enough to support more than 57,000 vulnerable people for three months.
Russian companies have also provided fertilizer to countries facing food insecurity. Fertilizer producer Uralchem recently donated 30,000 metric tons of potash to Bangladesh in a shipment facilitated by the WFP. The company says it has donated more than 220,000 tons of mineral fertilizers free of charge since 2022, with shipments reaching Malawi, Kenya, Nigeria, Zimbabwe, Sri Lanka and Bangladesh.

He said severe damage in Nuwakot, a rugged district in northern Nepal, has cut off physical connectivity. Because roads and bridges have been completely swept away, helicopters are the primary means of reaching isolated communities, said Khanal.

Khanal emphasized that rescue teams are working purely from a "humanitarian perspective," with no discrimination between local and foreign citizens.

2026-09-03

US officials denied accusations that the deal was holding Venezuela for ransom, stressing that it is mutually beneficial deal for all, developing an unutilised underground asset.
US energy firms signed a series of multi-billion-dollar deals with Venezuela on Wednesday, days after the South American country agreed to grant Washington control of a huge chunk, roughly one-fifth, of its vast oil reserves.
US Energy Secretary Chris Wright travelled to Venezuela’s capital Caracas to oversee the signing of deals worth "tens of billions of dollars of investment," seen as a quid pro quo for Washington winning majority control of 65 billion barrels of Venezuelan oil reserves.
Wright said the deals signed by Venezuela with US oil major Chevron, GE Vernova – a General Electric offshoot – and Italy's ENI were "critical in starting this ball rolling of peace, opportunity, and prosperity" in the country.
US President Donald Trump has talked up the agreement on Venezuela's oil reserves as the "biggest oil deal in world history."
It comes as US Republicans brace for possible losses in November midterm elections due to spiralling fuel costs brought on by his war against Iran, and a broader national affordability crisis in housing, food, utilities and other basic needs.
But the deals have raised major questions about Venezuela's sovereignty. Critics in both the US and Venezuela accuse Trump of holding the country for ransom after ousting former president Nicolas Maduro in a raid and warning that Rodriguez could face a similar fate if she doesn't fall into line with Washington's demands.
The US was not "stealing Venezuelan oil," Wright insisted. "All we're doing is taking an idle, underground asset that isn't doing anything for Venezuelan people and bringing the money, the technology to develop it.”
Interim President Delcy Rodriguez earlier denied she was surrendering her country's riches, saying that cutting the US in on Venezuela's oil wealth is necessary to secure investment in the oil sector.
More oil "translates into more jobs, higher wages, better public services, hospitals, schools and food," she said. Rodriguez has estimated that Venezuela will make $209 billion (€180 billion) in profit from the deals over 25 years.
US Oil giant Chevron confirmed that it will expand operations in Venezuela after President Donald Trump announced an ambitious deal to develop the nation’s oil reserves and give the Pentagon a stake in the profits.
Chevron, the only US oil company with a major presence in Venezuela, said on Wednesday that it has been assigned additional acreage in the Orinoco Belt, where it has active operations.
The company plans to invest more than $7 billion (€6 billion) over the next five years, with the goal of more than doubling its current production to about 600,000 barrels a day.
“Chevron’s history in Venezuela spans more than a century, and our expanded position reflects our confidence in the country’s deep resource potential,” said CEO Mike Wirth in a prepared statement.
Venezuela holds the world's largest proven reserves, totalling more than 303 billion barrels of crude oil, according to OPEC's 2025 Annual Statistical Bulletin. Saudi Arabia is a distant second with 267 billion barrels.
The agreement has been met with scepticism from energy experts who say it will take years to revive Venezuela’s oil industry, which is in disarray after years of neglect.
There are also questions about whether Venezuela’s acting president, Delcy Rodríguez, has the authority to give North American Blue Energy Partners (NABEP) 100-year rights over 17 oil fields with reserves of 65 billion barrels — and whether future Venezuelan or American administrations would overturn the deal.
Venezuela's constitution states that arrangements like the one that the United States has entered must be approved by the National Assembly, which has not happened, wrote Ian Vásquez, vice president for international studies at the Cato Institute.
“The deal lacks legitimacy since it was agreed to with a dictatorship that has clung to power for decades through violence and by committing what was probably the largest electoral fraud in Latin American history in 2024,” Vásquez wrote.
“The agreement was also reached under overwhelming pressure, military and otherwise, from the United States. As such, any future Venezuelan democracy will question the deal, thus undermining confidence in the current arrangement,” he added.

Government offers small businesses a trust tax workaround
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
04:02:48 UTC
13:02:48 KST

Government offers small businesses a trust tax workaround
In short:
The federal government has proposed a workaround for small businesses who were worried about paying state stamp duties when they restructure out of discretionary trusts to avoid the proposed minimum tax.
They will instead be able to restructure their affairs without actually changing their trust structures, remaining exempt from the tax as long as they do not vary their distributions.
What's next?
The draft legislation is open for consultation for two weeks.
Small businesses could avoid being stung by stamp duty when they restructure to escape Labor's minimum tax on discretionary trusts, under a workaround proposed by Treasurer Jim Chalmers.
Draft laws to enact the 30 per cent trust tax were released for feedback on Thursday. The tax is the last of the major tax changes from the May federal budget to be legislated.
Fears about stamp duty had been raised with the government during consultation, with small business lobby COSBOA warning those who used discretionary trusts could be left with "an impossible choice between a higher tax burden or a costly restructure".
The workaround would allow trustees to avoid an official restructure, exempting them from the tax if they agreed to shift their existing beneficiaries to a fixed-income structure.
Why stamp duty loomed as an issue
Stamp duties are collected by states and territories when property is transferred or transacted.
Financial assets count as property, so small business restructures usually trigger stamp duty.
Many businesses were expected to restructure to avoid the new trust tax.
Labor's tax applies only to discretionary trusts, a type of financial vehicle which gives their owners flexibility to shift income between an array of companies and beneficiaries and across time.
The government has argued the trusts are used to minimise tax.
By restructuring into a company structure or a "fixed" trust, which doles out income in steady proportions, trustees would forfeit the flexibility benefits but avoid the new tax.
But doing so would be expensive. The budget papers promised "rollover relief" for "small businesses and others".
But similar federal rollover programs do not cover state stamp duties, applying to federal income taxes only.
How Labor is proposing to swerve the stamp duty issue
The government had indicated it wanted to fix the issue and sought ideas through the consultation process.
But state treasurers had responded with reluctance or even outright hostility to suggestions they may be asked to waive stamp duty.
This workaround is designed to avoid triggering a stamp duty event, effectively by allowing small business to keep their discretionary trusts, but opt out of actually using their discretion.
Rather than converting to a fixed trust and triggering stamp duty, the legislation would allow trustees to choose to make fixed distributions to their existing beneficiaries, making them exempt from the trust tax as long as they keep the fix in place.
Another change would exempt from the tax any donations made from discretionary trusts to registered charities, deductible gift recipients, or "income-tax exempt entities" such as religious groups or sporting clubs.
Some trustees had raised concerns that charitable giving would be discouraged without such an exemption.
The trust tax will begin in mid-2028, a year later than capital gains and negative gearing changes.
There are many exemptions, including for super funds, disability trusts, deceased estates, testamentary trusts, charitable trusts, and farm income.
Business groups have also called for help with the cost of legal and financial advice to restructure.
Andrew McKellar of business group ACCI said in July that these costs were "extensive … not to mention the serious costs in time and stress".
Consultation on the draft is open for two weeks, closing on September 18.

====================================================================================================

‘Internal exclusion’ of England secondary school students almost triples in three years
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
04:00:44 UTC
13:00:44 KST

The proportion of secondary school students in England removed from class and placed in “internal exclusion” as a disciplinary measure has almost trebled in three years, according to new data.
The data shows the proportion of secondary pupils removed from normal lessons went up from 5% in the 2022/2023 academic year to 13% in 2025/26 – a 160% increase.
Poorer children are disproportionately affected, with more than one in five (22%) disadvantaged youngsters taken out of lessons at least once in 2025/26, up from 8% three years ago – a 175% increase, according to analysis of the data. The figure was one in ten (10%) for non-disadvantaged pupils.
Children with special educational needs and disabilities (Send) are also overrepresented, with 18% of students with an education, health and care plan removed from class at least once in 2025/26.
Critics say that putting pupils into internal exclusion – which varies between schools but is sometimes described as an “isolation room” – can damage mental wellbeing and result in lost learning. Others say it is an effective tool in behaviour management.
The data was collected and analysed by Arbor, a management information system used by 13,000 schools across England, and shared exclusively with the Guardian.
Fewer than 1% of primary pupils were internally excluded at least once in a year. In 2025/6 the number of under-11s affected was almost 5,000, though the real figure is likely to be significantly higher, as Arbor does not have data for every school.
Unlike permanent exclusions and fixed term suspensions, when pupils are sent home, internal exclusions require children to remain on site and they are returned to their class at the end of the exclusion. While the government collects data on exclusions and suspensions, it does not for internal exclusions.
Arbor’s CEO and co-founder, James Weatherill, said: “Schools clearly need effective ways to respond when behaviour disrupts learning, and we know from schools that internal exclusion can be an important alternative to sending a pupil home. But the scale of this increase, particularly among disadvantaged pupils, should prompt us to look more closely at what is driving it.”
The rise in internal exclusions, as recorded by Arbor’s live national data, comes at a time when official figures published by the Department for Education (DfE) showed formal suspensions and exclusions fell last year.
“We cannot tell from these figures whether one is replacing the other, but the divergence underlines why government needs a more complete picture of how many pupils are being removed from their normal lessons, for how long, and with what consequences,” said Weatherill.
Pepe Di’Iasio, general secretary of the Association of School and College Leaders, said: “Internal exclusions are never used lightly but only after other avenues have been exhausted. They are a step short of an external exclusion and are designed to keep the student in school with appropriate learning support.”
Lily Wielar, researcher at the Education Policy Institute, said: “Classroom removal has become a deeply embedded feature of behaviour management in England’s secondary schools.
“We urgently need to know more about how classroom removal is being used, and to ensure that removed pupils have the same legal protections and transparency that apply elsewhere.”
Tom Bennett, a leading expert in behaviour management, said: “Internal exclusions are, of course, a form of inclusion. A way to show students who disrupt the learning or safety of others that their actions have consequences, but in a way that means they aren’t simply sitting at home doing nothing, or worse, exposed to unsupportive environments.
“It means that learning can be delivered on site, and in an environment where staff ratios are higher, work can be done on their social skills and behaviour, but away from the students whose learning and safety has been damaged – because they matter too.”
Dame Rachel de Souza, children’s commissioner for England, said: “Excluding a child from the classroom can be necessary to protect other children, but every child should be supported to learn alongside their peers. Where that isn’t possible, children should still be receiving a high-quality education as part of internal exclusion – and I’m concerned that might not always be the case.”
The DfE has been contacted for comment.

====================================================================================================

The people of France are in an extraordinary funk about their future – here’s why | Paul Taylor
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
04:00:44 UTC
13:00:44 KST

France, as the French travel writer Sylvain Tesson once noted, “is a paradise inhabited by people who think they live in hell”. As the campaign for next year’s presidential election hits its stride with ever more wannabes declaring their candidacies, the country is in a particularly sullen mood.
If the vote were held now, the anti-immigration populist Marine Le Pen would have a strong chance of romping into the Élysée palace, riding a wave of voter disillusionment with the entire political class and a sense that “we’ve tried everything else”. But a lot can happen between now and 18 April 2027, the date of the first round. France is also a country of sudden shocks.
In spring 2011, Dominique Strauss-Kahn, the then head of the IMF and an admired former finance minister, was hot favourite to become the Socialist party candidate who would beat the incumbent conservative Nicolas Sarkozy in the 2012 race. But Strauss-Kahn was felled by a sexual harassment scandal and the unfancied socialist politician François Hollande ended up in the Élysée. In 2016, the former conservative prime minister François Fillon was well ahead in the race to succeed Hollande, then he was exposed as having arranged taxpayer-funded phoney parliamentary jobs for his wife. He finished third and a young centrist outsider without a party machine, Emmanuel Macron, went on to triumph.
To understand the backdrop to next year’s election – with huge stakes for Europe and the western alliance as well as for France – it’s worth examining the unique features that distinguish the French funk from the crisis facing other advanced democracies. After all, politics has become more raw and polarised in many countries. Other big European economies are stagnating. Mainstream parties are shrinking and fragmenting across Europe under growing challenges from insurgent rightwing national populists as well as a new radical, often ecologist, left. Political instability is accelerated everywhere by social-media frenzy and the 24/7 news cycle.
But several historical factors make the French malaise special, as I explored in a recent conversation with Michel Wieviorka, an eminent sociologist and author of numerous studies on French society, including Où va la France: Métamorphose ou Déchéance? (Where is France Headed: Metamorphosis or Decline?).
France was Europe’s first centralised state, with a culture of dirigiste economic development harking back to Cardinal Richelieu, Louis XIV and his minister Jean-Baptiste Colbert in the 17th century. That tradition was revived by Charles de Gaulle and postwar governments that used a powerful national economic planning commissariat to drive industrial modernisation, including the nuclear programme, the aerospace sector and massive public infrastructure investment.
This helps explain why French people have great expectations of the state and accept some of the highest levels of taxation, income redistribution and public spending as a proportion of economic output of any major economy. It also helps explain why France’s debt-to-GDP ratio of 118% is among the highest and fastest rising in Europe.
“The French are very attached to public services and anxious about their degradation, which is spectacular in public education but also in the justice system, the police, the tax system and health services, as revealed by the Covid-19 pandemic,” Wieviorka said. “They have the feeling that we used to be a great country at the forefront of modernity, but it is now falling apart.”
Another unique characteristic is a multi-century tradition of often violent protest. From the peasant jacqueries and Paris barricades of the 16th and 17th centuries to the landmark upheaval of the 1789 French revolution, revolt against authority has long been seen as legitimate by a large part of society. As Jean-Paul Sartre put it, “It is right to rebel.” The French labour movement, too, was rooted in anarcho-syndicalism before being dominated by the communist party, and lacks the British or German trade unions’ tradition of reformist compromise.
Like the English did in the 17th century, the French executed their king in the 18th century, but it took almost another century to finally abolish monarchy after two royal restorations and two emperors. The French left fought for the republican principle, prevailing over authoritarian forces backed by the Catholic church in the Dreyfus affair at the end of the 19th century. That led to a strict separation of church and state and the principle of secularism that enjoys consensus support today.
However, as Wieviorka noted, the decline of France’s Christian identity and religious observance has coincided with the rise of Islam, mostly among people of immigrant origin. This has stirred anxieties fanned by mainstream conservative and hard-right politicians and the new-right media empire of the billionaire Vincent Bolloré.
These fears explain the rise of the extreme-right Front National founded by Jean-Marie Le Pen in 1972, which Wieviorka called “the pioneering national-populist party in Europe”, putting the fight against immigration at the centre of its agenda. Rebranded in 2018 as the National Rally (RN) by his daughter, Marine, in a quest for respectability, the party has roots in the Vichy regime that collaborated with Nazi Germany but swapped antisemitism for anti-Islamism, advocating “national priority” for French citizens in welfare, housing and healthcare.
Another distinguishing feature is France’s political and administrative elite, rebuilt on meritocratic lines after the second world war with the creation of L’École nationale d’administration (ENA) to train top civil servants and captains of nationalised enterprises, many of whom made a career in politics. The system has become ossified and spawned a self-perpetuating elite – the so-called énarques – increasingly seen as remote from ordinary French people’s concerns.
These factors combined explain the state of public opinion on the eve of the campaign – deeply pessimistic about the state of the country, anxious about identity, declining public services and the cost of living, and disillusioned with a political establishment seen as having failed on all these fronts.
To Wieviorka’s matrix of factors underlying the political malaise, I would add a widespread lack of economic realism and a belief that what the French call “public money”, which in the UK or Germany is known as “taxpayers’ money”, is infinitely extendable.
Economic unrealism makes France particularly susceptible to magic money solutions such as RN’s fantasy that the debt and deficit would melt away if the government only stopped welfare payments to immigrants and slashed its EU contribution, or the radical leftist Jean-Luc Mélenchon’s claim that France just needs to write off “cost free” 18% of its debt held by the European Central Bank and confiscate all inheritances of more than €12m.
No wonder there’s little time for politicians who propose dreary real-world solutions such as raising the retirement age or curbing some welfare benefits. A famous slogan in the student uprisings of May 1968 proclaimed: “Be realistic, demand the impossible”. The big risk now is that the French vote with their gut rather than with their head. At a time of such geopolitical and fiscal peril for France and Europe, that is an alarming prospect.
- 
  Paul Taylor is a senior visiting fellow at the European Policy Centre

‘A crisis of authenticity’: the truth about food influencers
