Israel's election mudslinging hits a new low with toxic October 7 treason theories - editorial
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
03:06:15 UTC
12:06:15 KST

We’re still almost two months away from the fateful October 27 election, but the level of personal mudslinging has already reached a dismal nadir.
The worst are this week’s claims by Sara Netanyahu, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s wife, that Yair Golan, leader of The Democrats party, had prior knowledge of Hamas’s October 7, 2023, attack in which over 1,200 Israelis were slaughtered and that launched the war that continues to this day.
Golan is a former deputy IDF chief of staff, and as the events of October 7 unfolded, he donned his IDF uniform and drove to the Supernova music festival in the South to help.
Golan is no saint, however. By May 2025, he had soured on the war efforts and proclaimed that Israel was killing babies in Gaza “as a hobby.” As a result, Defense Minister Israel Katz was permanently barred from reserve duty and called his remarks a “blood libel.”
His political views are one thing, but thinly veiled claims of treason are another. Sara Netanyahu, in an interview with the right-wing Channel 14 on Monday, said he must have had advanced warning of the Hamas attack.
Claims Netanyahu intentionally not informed of October 7 attack
“A military man of such high rank, claiming that you fought on October 7, that already early in the morning you were there, already dressed and ready at a very, very early hour when others didn’t know, such as the prime minister...” she said.
In an Instagram post, the prime minister did not go as far as his wife, but he did say that IDF officers deliberately did not wake him for over an hour because they knew he would prevent the massacre.
According to Yaakov Katz, co-author of While Israel Slept and a former The Jerusalem Post chief editor - who wrote about Netanyahu’s comments and the failure to prevent October 7 - the prime minister would likely not have done anything differently after receiving flawed assessments from the military and intelligence echelon that Hamas was probably not preparing for a major attack.
But in election season, apparently, anything goes.
According to N12’s Dafna Liel, the media statements by both Netanyahus weren’t random but part of a deliberate Likud campaign ahead of the election to spread conspiracy theories and distance the premier from the massacre.
The October 7 conspiracy theory is nothing new and is bandied about by those on the Right whenever it comes in handy.
In a Knesset session only three weeks after the October 7 attack, Likud MK Tali Gotliev referred to a social media post by Golan in September 2023 that said, “October is approaching; the hour of decision is coming.”
Golan’s post was referring to the opening of the Knesset’s winter session and the judicial reform issue, but Gotliev’s comments unleashed a floodgate of unfounded claims that have gained steam over the ensuing three years.
Threat of lawsuit against Sara Netanyahu, conspiracy theories likely to expand
It’s time to put them to rest.
Whether Golan’s demand for an apology and threat of a hefty lawsuit against Sara Netanyahu will deter future outrageous statements about a conspiracy is questionable.
As Yashar party chief Gadi Eisenkot, Netanyahu’s main rival, wrote on Tuesday on X/Twitter: “The outrageous conspiracy theory of treason... is intended solely to fan hatred and perpetuate the Netanyahu government, whose only way of ruling is to divide.
“Netanyahu is running from responsibility for the worst failure in Israel’s history, to which he led us blindly - through negligence and by ignoring every warning sign. Some people claim that they ‘weren’t woken up,’ while others got up and rushed into action -without asking questions.”
The surest way to get to the bottom would be to hold an official state inquiry.
However, those opposed to the inquiry and those who have prevented it are the same ones perpetuating the conspiracy theories. Interesting.
The most infuriating aspect of the attention this issue has received is that it takes up the bandwidth that should be provided to the real, critical issues facing the country as it heads to Election Day.
Here’s some advice for all of the candidates: Instead of blaming others for what they did or didn’t do, focus the campaign on what you intend to do to help the country.

Tehran maintains deliberate opacity regarding the minefields, asserting that only Iranian forces know their exact locations.

Explosion near railway station in Augsburg, Germany injures two Ukrainians
Two Ukrainian citizens – a 17-year-old girl and an 18-year-old man – were injured when an unidentified object exploded in the German city of Augsburg.
Source: Bavarian police (Polizeipräsidium Schwaben Nord); Augsburger Allgemeine; DAZ
Details: The explosion occurred at around 03:15 on 2 September on Bahnhofstrasse, near the city's main railway station.
According to law enforcement, an unidentified object detonated in a passageway between buildings in a retail and office complex.
The explosion left two Ukrainian citizens with minor injuries and acoustic trauma. According to police, the Ukrainians were passers-by who happened to be at the scene when the incident occurred.
The blast wave also damaged the facades and shop windows of nearby buildings, including a jeweller's, a bank branch and a household chemicals shop.
Investigators are currently determining what type of explosive device was used and examining all possible explanations for the incident, including a possible criminal dispute.
In addition, another suspicious object was found at around 08:30 in a pedestrian underpass at the main railway station. Police evacuated the station and completely halted rail traffic.
"With the help of a sniffer dog trained to detect explosives and specialists from the Bavarian State Criminal Police Office, it was ultimately established that the object posed no danger," the police said.
Background:
- In February 2024, a group of teenagers attacked Ukrainian basketball players with knives in the German city of Oberhausen, killing 17-year-old Volodymyr Yermakov and 18-year-old Artem Kozachenko.
- In April 2024, a Russian man attacked two Ukrainian servicemen who were undergoing rehabilitation at a shopping centre in the city of Murnau. Both defenders died of stab wounds.
- On 7 March 2025, the Munich Regional Court sentenced a 58-year-old Russian man to life imprisonment for the murders of the two Ukrainian servicemen.

The inaugural flight to Ishigaki was on Wednesday, while the Komatsu flight is on Thursday, according to the airline.
Tigerair Taiwan Chair Huang Shih-hui (黃世惠) said the new Kaohsiung routes will significantly improve travel convenience for passengers in southern Taiwan and make travel planning easier for Japanese visitors. Foreign travelers can take advantage of Tigerair Taiwan’s extensive network to explore the south or use flexible multi-city itineraries to experience the nation’s diverse culture and cuisine, Huang said.
The chair added that Ishigaki is known for its stunning ocean scenery and island charm, while Komatsu serves as an ideal gateway to Japan’s Hokuriku region, the Kaga Onsen, and other natural attractions. Huang will board the inaugural flight to Komatsu on Thursday to meet with Yamano Yukiyoshi, the Ishikawa Prefecture governor.
With these two additions, Tigerair Taiwan's Kaohsiung network now has 14 routes. The airline is Taiwan’s only low-cost carrier. It currently operates routes to Japan, South Korea, Macau, Thailand, and Vietnam.

====================================================================================================

The world is expected to overshoot a critical climate target. But there's still hope
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
02:55:28 UTC
11:55:28 KST

In brief
- A UN report says the world will likely exceed the 1.5C warming target by 2030.
- Experts say rapid emissions cuts could still return temperatures below 1.5C.
For over a decade, the world has been trying to limit global warming to 1.5C.
That's no longer possible, according to a new United Nations report. We will likely pass 1.5C in 2030. That's not good news for anyone, least of all Australia's Pacific Island neighbours who face rapidly rising seas.
In response to the report, Palau's President Surangel Whipps Jr said: "It is hard to overstate the depth of emotion for those of us living on the front-line after having fought so hard to put the 1.5 degree limit at the heart of the Paris Agreement … calls for greater ambition are no longer enough — we need to see an urgent and unprecedented increase in political will and investment in a climate safe future."
The small silver lining is that it's still possible for this to be a temporary overshoot of the target.
If nations redouble their efforts to phase out fossil fuels and reduce other sources of emissions, they could limit peak warming to 1.8C and then use carbon removal methods to bring temperatures back to 1.5C or below this century.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
In 2026, the world is already about 1.4C warmer than pre-industrial levels, and the damage and death toll from climate-boosted disasters is ramping up.
The United Kingdom is warning of possible food shortages amid a historic drought.
Wildfires hit new areas in France and Spain, while glaciers are melting rapidly and the oceans are at their hottest level on record.
The enormous El Niño event emerging in the Pacific is likely to bring major disruption. Every fraction of a degree makes things worse.
There are no good outcomes if we remain above 1.5C. Urgent cuts to emissions and efforts to protect the most vulnerable are our best remaining options. Failure to do so risks irreversible harm.
Why does 1.5C matter so much?
The 2015 Paris Agreement established a shared goal for the world: keep the rise in global average temperatures above pre-industrial levels "well below" 2C and "pursue efforts" to hold warming to 1.5C.
This goal was set based on expert scientific assessments that warming of more than 2C would be dangerous and that limiting warming to 1.5C was necessary to minimise climate risks.
Pacific nations fought hard to include 1.5C in the agreement, arguing it was essential for their communities to "stay alive" in the face of rising sea levels and other climate-fuelled threats.
Last year, the world's top court — the International Court of Justice — ruled that 1.5C is the primary temperature limit nations have committed to work towards.
This ruling means that if governments fail to act as ambitiously as they can, they could be sued in international courts.
In May this year, a majority of nations voted in the UN General Assembly to endorse the court's ruling and urge action to keep to 1.5C.
It's not time to give up
Warming of 1.5C will be bad. But 1.6C will be worse, and 1.7C worse again. Every increase will bring more extreme weather, more loss of nature, more loss of land to the sea and more harm to humans.
If we stay over 1.5C, we risk triggering climate tipping points — sudden shifts which cannot be undone on human timescales. These include the Greenland and West Antarctic ice sheets melting, the collapse of crucial heat-distributing currents in the Atlantic Ocean or the Amazon rainforest becoming a source of emissions.
Overshooting 1.5C doesn't mean it's time to throw out the Paris Agreement. It's not working fast enough, but it is working.
Solar power and electric vehicles have boomed and electrification has accelerated. Nations have cut emissions enough to avoid the worst climate futures of a 3C rise or even higher.
According to the Climate Action Tracker, the Paris Agreement has averted the equivalent of 1C of warming. Rather than hitting 3.6C by 2100, the world is on track for 2.6C.
While this is progress, it is not enough. Global emissions are plateauing, but have still not begun to fall in earnest.
As damage from climate change mounts, leaders must do the work and begin rapidly cutting emissions to keep the goal of net-zero by 2050 alive.
To get temperatures back under 1.5C, we will also need to pull gigatonnes of carbon dioxide back out of the atmosphere using tree planting and nature restoration.
We may also need technological approaches such as rock weathering or ocean alkalinity enhancement, though these are not proven at scale and can come with other risks.
We are all in this together
It may seem as if climate action faces impossible headwinds, as populism surges and the current United States administration doubles down on fossil fuels.
It's worth looking beyond these headlines.
It took almost 70 years for the world to install a terawatt of solar power, but then just two years for the second and another two for the third terawatt.
In ten years, that figure will likely have tripled. Developing nations are moving rapidly to take up non-polluting electric transport.
Climate change can no longer be ignored.
As damage mounts, nations will have to cooperate to cut emissions as rapidly as possible and figure out how to safely and equitably pull carbon back out of the atmosphere. Action depends on strong political will, inclusive governance, and finance to help developing countries cut emissions and adapt.
In November, Australia will lead negotiations at the next international climate summit, COP31, in Turkey. Leaders and diplomats will work to keep 1.5C in reach — even after overshoot.
Australia can point to its own rapid clean energy transition and urge others to set clear pathways to go electric – and wean themselves off the production and use of fossil fuels.
Climate change has been described as a super wicked problem — big, complex and impossible to solve simply.
The solution is to see the urgency of the issue and act cooperatively to tackle it.
If we make it a problem for the next generation, there may be no way back to a safe climate.
Jacqueline Peel receives funding from the Australian Research Council for her Laureate Program on Global Corporate Climate Accountability. She is affiliated with the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, serving as a Coordinating Lead Author in Working Group III (mitigation) for the Seventh Assessment Report.
Wesley Morgan is a fellow with the Climate Council of Australia.

Pentagon limits classified access amid Iran war concerns - report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
02:49:13 UTC
11:49:13 KST

The Pentagon has restricted access to decades of classified military documents on an internal computer system, The Washington Post reported on Wednesday, days after the newspaper reported that senior US commanders had raised concerns about sustaining large-scale military operations against Iran.
Documents associated with the Secretary of Defense Orders Book (SDOB) were removed from an internal web portal on the Secret Internet Protocol Router Network (SIPRNet), according to three people familiar with the matter who spoke to The Washington Post on condition of anonymity.
It was not immediately clear whether the documents remained available to US personnel through other means or how the reduction in access could affect military planning, according to the report.
SIPRNet contains information classified as "secret," while top-secret information is held on more highly classified networks with fewer people granted access.
US military leaders raised concerns over Iran operations
The SDOB contains information on the location and availability of US warships, military units, weapons systems, and other resources. It also allows senior military leaders to formally register reservations about orders while continuing to carry them out through a process known as "non-concurring," The Washington Post reported.
The Jerusalem Post previously reported, citing the Washington Post, that several senior US military leaders raised concerns in the classified August 14 edition of the SDOB about continuing operations against Iran.
The officials warned that prolonging the war could weaken the US military's ability to respond to threats elsewhere. The SDOB reportedly called for some US troops deployed in the Middle East to remain in the region through September, while others would remain until 2027.
Gen. Alexus Grynkewich, head of US European Command; Gen. Francis Donovan, head of US Southern Command; Adm. Samuel Paparo, head of US Pacific Command; and Adm. Daryl Caudle, chief of naval operations, were among those who registered reservations with a "non-concur," according to people familiar with the discussion who spoke to the Washington Post.
Air Force Chief of Staff Gen. Kenneth Wilsbach and acting Army Chief of Staff Gen. Christopher LaNeve agreed with Hegseth's plan to extend some unit deployments but emphasized that doing so would carry significant risks, according to the report.
Pentagon declines to discuss access change
Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell declined to discuss the reported change with the Washington Post on Wednesday but did not dispute that it had occurred.
"As we have previously stated, the Department of War does not publicly discuss internal operational deliberative processes, including the management, handling, or access protocols for the Secretary of War Orders Book (SWOB)," Parnell said in a statement to the newspaper.
"The success of our service members is Secretary Hegseth's top priority, and for that reason, decisions regarding operational processes, force posture, and deliberative staffing are managed through appropriate security channels to ensure mission security and operational integrity," he added.
Following the Washington Post's Sunday report, Parnell said on social media that much of what the newspaper published was "inaccurate," though he did not specify which details he disputed.
"Non-concurs are standard," Parnell said. "The Secretary sees them constantly. That's how you run a real military. We are in great shape around the world."
Restricted access could complicate military planning
A former defense official who routinely reviewed the documents told the Washington Post that removing the SDOB from SIPRNet or moving it to systems with higher levels of classification would "dramatically reduce the number of people who have direct access to it."
Commanders and their staff rely on access to the SDOB for time-sensitive decisions and notifications, the former official told the newspaper.
Moving aircraft and weapons from one command to another, for example, requires urgent logistical work to redirect equipment and resources. Restricting access to the relevant information could make that process slower and more difficult, according to the former official.
The change does not make it impossible for personnel to access strategic and operational documents, but doing so is now "certainly more difficult," the former official said.

The warning came as Moscow airports faced widespread disruption and several foreign carriers canceled services.
Flight-tracking data cited by Reuters showed 21 cancellations and 235 delays at Sheremetyevo International Airport on Wednesday, while Vnukovo recorded 22 cancellations and 94 delays.
Independent Russian outlet Agentstvo, citing its analysis of Moscow airport schedules, said foreign airlines canceled 27 flights to and from the Russian capital on Wednesday – sharply more than the previous day.
The cancellations included services by Turkey’s Pegasus Airlines and Turkish Airlines, the UAE’s flydubai, Egypt’s Nesma Airlines, Armenia’s Shirak Avia, Kuwait Airways and Tajikistan’s Somon Air.

Kyiv warns of growing risk

“There will simply be drones in Russia’s skies on a scale that has to be taken into account,” he said.
Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said in a statement on X: “We want to prevent unintended incidents,” adding: “The war is returning home to Russia.”
Ukraine has formally notified the International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO) about the risks and urged the UN aviation agency to encourage member states to prohibit civilian flights in Russian airspace.
ICAO said civilian aircraft face heightened risks of being targeted or caught in crossfire in conflict zones.
Most European and US carriers have avoided Russian airspace since Moscow launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022, while airlines from countries including China, Turkey and Gulf states continue to operate there.
Moscow rejected Kyiv’s warning, with Russian aviation authorities insisting that airport and foreign airline operations were continuing.
Russia’s aviation sector already under strain
The latest disruption adds to mounting pressure on Russia’s aviation sector since the full-scale invasion, ranging from restricted access to Western parts to wartime air-defense risks and deadly military crashes.
In October 2022, an Su-34 fighter-bomber crashed into an apartment building in Yeysk, killing at least 15 people. Six days later, an Su-30 crashed into a house in Irkutsk during a test flight, killing both pilots.
In December 2024, an Azerbaijan Airlines passenger jet crashed after being hit during Russian air-defense operations against Ukrainian drones, killing 38 people. President Vladimir Putin later apologized for what the Kremlin called a “tragic incident” in Russian airspace, without explicitly acknowledging that Russia had shot down the plane.
In July 2025, an Antonov An-24 operated by Angara Airlines crashed near Tynda in Russia’s Far East, killing all 48 people on board.
A war returning to Russia
The disruption in Russian aviation comes as Ukraine continues to endure a far heavier toll from Moscow’s air campaign against civilians and infrastructure across the country.
Sept. 2 marked the seventh consecutive day of Russian missile and drone attacks on Kyiv, killing civilians, including children, damaging residential areas and repeatedly forcing residents into shelters.
Russian attacks have also continued elsewhere in Ukraine, damaging energy infrastructure and homes and causing civilian casualties.
The contrast is stark: while Russia is increasingly experiencing aviation disruption from a war reaching deeper into its territory, Ukrainians have lived with missile and drone attacks since Moscow launched its full-scale invasion on Feb. 24, 2022.
The growing disruption to Russian aviation is a reminder that Russia started this war and Russia can stop it.

Clarkson's game plan was eviscerated by North president Sonja Hood and football boss Todd Viney after he was axed with a season remaining on his deal.
What's next?
The Kangaroos are expected to begin the hunt for their next head coach next week.
A shocked Chris Fagan has labelled North Melbourne's public explanation of coach Alastair Clarkson's axing "unfair" and hopes his old friend was given a chance to act on any feedback before the rug was pulled.
Clarkson, who coached Hawthorn to four premierships in an era-defining stint from 2005 to 2021, arrived at North as head coach amid great fanfare after being appointed in August 2022.
Yesterday, with a year to run on his contract, he was unceremoniously axed by football boss Todd Viney, a close friend, and club president Sonja Hood.
Asked what type of coach the Kangaroos wanted, Hood, who declared Clarkson's appointment had not been an error, said: "This club needs a coach who can coach for the modern game.
"It'll be a coach who knows what they're doing, and it'll be a coach who's the best fit for this football club."
Viney said there were "still some gaping holes in our game plan" and Clarkson's efforts to fill them only led to "more meetings, more information and players … becoming a bit more confused".
The pair said a canvassing of the club, including players, revealed he no longer had the belief of enough people that he was the right coach to take the group forward.
"I hope he's okay," Brisbane Lions coach Fagan, who first worked with Clarkson at Melbourne in the late 90s before they joined forces at Hawthorn, said.
"I just hope that the feedback that was given at the press conference yesterday about him was given to him in person at some stage during this year, so that he had a chance to act on it.
"It was a pretty fierce press conference. The way that he was spoken about. I reckon probably an unfair description of the man that's done awful lot for footy."
The 58-year-old's departure comes despite the Kangaroos's improved season in 2026, when they finished 14th and claimed nine wins.
"It was a big shock to me. I actually thought, 'That can't be right,'" Fagan said of the call.
"Under his guidance, North really started to improve. It just reminded me of how tough coaching can be.
"That when a bloke that's been as successful as him as a coach can be jettisoned as quickly as that."
The pair were central figures in Hawthorn's racism saga that was settled after two years of legal turmoil in 2024.
Clarkson took a mental health break in 2023 while Fagan, who has the Brisbane Lions in sight of a third-straight flag, admitted he came close to doing the same before opting to coach on.
Fagan, who has yet to speak to Clarkson, hopes his old mate is not lost to the game, and chuckled at the thought of him in a media role, given his typically frosty relationship with that industry.
"We go back a long way and we'll still be friends and still talk a lot about footy, and I'll still seek his advice, no doubt," Fagan said.

Venezuela signs major energy deals with Chevron, Eni during US visit
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
02:37:00 UTC
11:37:00 KST

Laura Gamba Fadul, Mariam Ashalem De Andres
03 September 2026•Update: 03 September 2026
Venezuela signed major energy investment agreements Wednesday with US oil company Chevron and Italian energy major Eni during a visit to Caracas by US Energy Secretary Chris Wright.
The agreements were signed in the presence of Acting President Delcy Rodriguez and Wright, less than a week after Washington announced a historic energy agreement with Caracas aimed at expanding Venezuela's oil production and attracting foreign investment.
Chevron confirmed it will invest more than $7 billion over the next five years across its Venezuelan joint ventures with state oil company Petroleos de Venezuela (PDVSA), aiming to raise output to approximately 600,000 barrels per day.
Under the new terms, Chevron was granted additional acreage in the resource-rich Orinoco Belt adjacent to its existing operations.
"Chevron's history in Venezuela spans more than a century, and our expanded position reflects our confidence in the country's deep resource potential and its ability to compete for investments within our portfolio for decades," Chevron CEO Mike Wirth said in a statement.
"With improved conditions and additional land, we are strengthening a portfolio that we believe can deliver attractive, low-cost oil growth, support energy supply, and create differentiated value over the long term."
Chevron has maintained a continuous presence in Venezuela since 1923 and operates major heavy crude projects including the Petropiar and Petroindependencia joint ventures in the Orinoco Belt, as well as Petroboscán in western Zulia state.
Eni also finalized a 25-year strategic contract under which it will become the exclusive operator of the Junin 5 heavy oil field in the Orinoco Belt.
Moving away from a joint venture model with PDVSA, Eni will assume full technical, financial and commercial management of the field, which holds an estimated 35 billion barrels of certified oil in place.
Eni, which has operated in Venezuela since 1998, aims to increase Junín 5 production to 400,000 barrels per day by the end of the decade, with estimated annual investment of $1.5 billion.
Beyond heavy crude, Eni is also a major supplier to Venezuela's domestic energy system. Through its Cardon IV venture with Spain's Repsol, the company operates the offshore Perla field, the largest gas discovery in Latin America, which accounts for nearly 35% of Venezuela's natural gas consumption.
“This agreement represents a new pillar for the revival of the country's oil and gas sector, at a historic time when energy security ... is vital to global stability,” Eni Chief Executive Officer Claudio Descalzi stated following the signing.
PDVSA also signed a strategic alliance with US-based GE Vernova to rehabilitate electrical infrastructure serving Venezuela's petroleum industry.
GE Vernova separately signed an agreement with state-owned National Electric Corporation, known as Corpoelec, aimed at strengthening the national electricity system.
The agreements come as Venezuela seeks to restore an energy sector weakened by years of underinvestment, operational problems and US sanctions.
The announcements build on President Donald Trump's plan to unlock Venezuela's crude reserves, which OPEC data puts at more than 303 billion barrels, the world's largest proven reserves.
Wright, who previously visited Chevron's Orinoco Belt operations alongside Rodriguez during bilateral talks in February, highlighted the diplomatic and economic goals of the agreements.
“These investment agreements in Venezuela seek to bring peace, opportunity, and prosperity to the people of Venezuela and the people of the United States," Wright said upon his arrival.

Australia, US to boost defence ties as China’s Pacific influence grows

Australia, US to boost defence ties as China’s Pacific influence grows
- Australia and the US are increasing defence cooperation, including expanded US military presence and equipment storage in Australia to boost Indo-Pacific stability.
- The AUKUS pact involves US, UK, and Australia, with US submarines stationed at HMAS Stirling from 2027, despite China’s warnings of a regional arms race.
- Australia and the US pledged US$580 million to Pacific Island nations to counter China’s growing influence through aid and infrastructure projects.
AI generated
WASHINGTON – Australia and the United States said they would boost their defence ties in a move that could expand the US military presence in Australia, while strengthening deterrence across the Pacific, where China has been expanding its influence.
After meeting US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth in Washington DC, Defence Minister Richard Marles told reporters on Sept 2 that “American force posture in Australia is growing” and was on the rise across every domain.
The US-Australia Force Posture Initiatives are agreements that allow US military forces to train and store equipment in Australia, including the rotational deployment of aircraft and logistics support for US vessels.
“We think that’s really important in terms of providing deterrence in the Indo-Pacific, providing for stability and peace in the Indo-Pacific, and that’s very much in Australia’s national interest.”
Marles did not specify if the greater level of cooperation would mean more US troops being stationed in Australia, but said further details would be provided at the next meeting of Australian and US defence ministers later in 2026.
Australia-US defence cooperation also includes the AUKUS defence pact between the US, Britain and Australia.
Some US defence personnel are working at the HMAS Stirling naval base on Australia’s west coast, which will house four US-commanded Virginia-class submarines from 2027.
China calls the AUKUS pact dangerous and has warned it could spur a regional arms race.
Hegseth said in a statement that there was “strong alignment” between the national defence strategies of both countries, and stressed the importance of allies investing in their own sovereign security to contribute to collective defence.
“We share a common (understanding) of the complex threat picture in the world today and the need for allies to, both plan together but also ensure our capabilities match and are complementary,” he said.
The meeting comes as the Pacific Islands Forum (PIF) headed into its final day in Palau on Sept 3, with the summit overshadowed by the absence of several leaders and China’s protest over the presence of Taiwan’s foreign minister.
Australia and the United States have announced a combined US$580 million (S$736.77 million) in funding for Pacific Island nations as China continues to expand its influence in the region through grants, infrastructure projects and aid. REUTERS

Preview: New-look China faces stern test at Women's Basketball World Cup
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
10:34:34 CST
11:34:34 KST

by sportswriters Su Bin and Zhao Jiantong
BEIJING, Sept. 3 (Xinhua) -- Returning to the FIBA Women's Basketball World Cup after a record-tying runner-up finish, China faces a critical generational transition and needs to address its squad cohesion, offensive coordination and outside shooting to stay competitive.
The 2026 FIBA Women's World Cup will be held in Berlin from September 4 to 13, featuring 16 teams. China has been drawn in Group D with defending champion the United States, Czechia and Italy.
With the return of WNBA-based center Han Xu, China finalised its World Cup roster. The squad began training in mid-April and spent more than four months in preparation, yet full-team practices were rare. Yang Shuyu and Chen Mingling, who competed in Australia's second-tier National Basketball League 1 South league, rejoined the national team in late July. Guards Wang Siyu and Li Yuan headed to Australia to play for clubs there, while several players had to balance training with academic study.
Han's late return presents tactical challenges: how quickly she can merge the team's offensive and defensive systems remains uncertain, and the absence of fellow WNBA centre Li Yueru reduces China's interior strength.
China needs smart off-ball movement to open up court space, which calls for both positioning from centers and well-timed passing from their teammates.
Also, that strength will create open looks for outside shooters, and the team's ability to convert those opportunities will weigh heavily on match results. In some recent warmup games, China's three-point shooting success rate dipped below 20 percent.
Compared with the silver-medal winning squad four years ago, the current group is younger and lacks major competition experience. China has to keep its composure against defensive pressure, reduce mistakes and limit opponents' fast breaks.
Coach Gong Luming, who took charge last year, said the young roster is gradually taking shape. "Ever since we assembled this squad, we have worked on physical conditioning, technical skills, tactics and accumulating big-game experience. Now we can see tangible progress," he said.
China will open its campaign against the United States in a rematch of the 2022 World Cup final. Seeking its fifth straight title, the U.S. roster is stacked with elite talents, including six WNBA No. 1 draft picks and multiple players who averaged over 20 points per game in the league. Even with stars A'ja Wilson and Kelsey Plum sidelined by injury, the U.S. remains the title favorite.
With the U.S. seemingly difficult to beat, Czechia and Italy will be China's main targets in the group stage. China beat Czechia 84-74 in the World Cup qualifiers after a hard-fought battle in March. However, Czechia center Emma Cechova, who scored 23 points and grabbed 13 rebounds in that game, will be sidelined due to injury, dealing a blow to their overall strength.
Italy's main scoring threat comes from WNBA-based forward Cecilia Zandalasini, who averaged 13.8 points in the qualifiers. China lost both warmups against Italy in August and needs to figure out ways to break Italy's pressure defense.
16 teams are divided into four groups. Group winners directly qualify for the quarterfinals, while second- and third-placed sides will compete in a qualification to quarterfinals round to decide the remaining four berths.
Over the past month, China has played a series of warmup games to face varied styles. China played three matches against Nigeria at home to simulate the U.S. game, followed by six games in Europe against five opponents to adapt to European team play and physical contact.
Gong said the team will progress step by step to build major tournament experience. "Our ultimate goal is the 2028 Los Angeles Olympic Games. We will give our all in every game and strive for the best possible results," he said. ■

11th–13th-century Polovtsian stone sculpture disappears from beach in Kharkiv
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
02:28:00 UTC
11:28:00 KST

11th–13th-century Polovtsian stone sculpture disappears from beach in Kharkiv
Alina Kharlamova, an archaeologist and researcher from Kharkiv, drew attention to this and spoke to Ukrinform about it.
“There used to be a stone Polovtsian sculpture on the beach. I study these sculptures and can confirm that it is authentic and dates back to the 11th–13th centuries. When I recently visited the beach, I saw that the statue was gone,” says Kharlamova.
According to her, it is not known exactly when the sculpture first appeared at the resort, but even before the full-scale Russian invasion, the archaeologist had approached the beach’s leaseholders—representatives of “Aquazhur”—with a request to transfer the artifact to the appropriate institutions.
“They simply ignored me. When I told the representative of what was then a paid beach that this sculpture should be handed over to a museum, she made a face as if I were joking. Perhaps people really didn’t view the statue as something valuable, but considered it a prop,” Kharlamova speculates.
The sculpture may have been brought from the Azov region, the researcher believes.
Currently, the municipal enterprise “Kharkivzelenbud” is responsible for the beach in question. The enterprise’s press office told the agency’s correspondent that the sculpture was not present when the territory was taken over, adding that before the municipal workers began landscaping the area, the former tenants had the opportunity to remove their property.
“It is very unfortunate that while our defenders are evacuating such monuments from areas under fire, they are disappearing right here in our city. I urge anyone who may have taken the sculpture or knows where it is to contact me personally or the Museum of Archaeology at V. N. Karazin Kharkiv National University at 067-397-97-59,” Kharlamova said.
The beach in Zhuravlivka has been leased since January 17, 2008. The term of the agreement, signed between the Kharkiv City Council and “Kontakt Plus” LLC, was 49 years—until April 1, 2056. In 2018, the city council attempted to terminate this agreement through the courts, but its request was denied.
In May 2026, Mayor Ihor Terekhov said in an interview with Ukrinform that Zhuravlivka Island had been returned to the ownership of the local community.
“I fought very hard, and I can say that we won this battle—and it really was a battle, as you can imagine! After all, land like this is very attractive. Not only that, but they (the tenants—ed.) weren’t paying under this contract, yet they were charging people money (for admission and access—ed.). I can tell you what a struggle I went through and how many enemies I made,” the mayor said at the time.
According to the NGO “Kharkiv Anti-Corruption Center,” “Contact Plus” LLC is linked to the business structures of former People’s Deputy Dmytro Shentsev of the now-banned “Party of Regions” and former Kharkiv Regional Council deputy Davyd Chikhladze (who served twice for the “Party of Regions” and once for “Vidrodzhennia”).
As previously reported, in February, soldiers from the Sicheslav Brigade, together with museum staff, volunteers, and philanthropists, evacuated 11th–13th-century Polovtsian stone statues—unique stone monuments from the Steppe era—from Vasylkivka in the Synelnykivsky District of Dnipropetrovsk region.

Iran warns U.S. against Israeli attack on south Lebanon ridge held by Hezbollah, sources say
Iran has warned the United States that it would respond forcefully to an Israeli offensive on a mountainous ridge in southern Lebanon where Iranian military personnel are holed up alongside Hezbollah fighters, three officials briefed on the message told Reuters.
The message, delivered last month, highlights Iran's continued direct involvement in the ground fighting in southern Lebanon and its readiness to retaliate against Israeli attacks there as the regional war enters its seventh month.
Hezbollah is believed to have built an underground command center and weapons stores within the Ali al-Taher ridge, which has a commanding view of southeastern Lebanon, according to Lebanese security sources and has become one of the most contested pieces of ground in the Israel-Hezbollah war.
Hezbollah has said in public statements that it controls the hill and will confront any Israeli advances. Its officials have referred to a "facility" there, but have declined to provide details.
The Israeli military has occupied swathes of territory to Ali al-Taher's south and has identified the ridge as one of its "primary operational focuses" in public statements.
In its message to Washington, Tehran threatened that any full-fledged Israeli offensive on the ridge would be met with a large-scale Iranian attack, said the three officials in the region, who spoke to Reuters on condition of anonymity.
Hezbollah declined to comment on whether Iranian forces were present in Ali al-Taher.
In response to Reuters questions about the message, or whether the U.S. had put pressure on Israel not to attack Ali al-Taher, a White House official said, "this is not accurate."
There was no immediate comment from Iran's permanent mission in Geneva, the U.S. Defense Department, or Oman's foreign ministry. The Israeli military declined to comment.

US not ‘stealing Venezuelan oil’, energy secretary insists
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
02:22:00 UTC
11:22:00 KST

US not ‘stealing Venezuelan oil’, energy secretary insists
- US Energy Secretary Chris Wright denied claims that the US is stealing Venezuelan oil, emphasising the oil belongs to the Venezuelan people and benefits go to their government.
- The US will take majority control of nearly 20% of Venezuela's oil reserves, with expected earnings of US$209 billion over 25 years from the energy deals.
- Wright highlighted the need to fix Venezuela's electricity sector, linking it to oil production, and said elections will occur when the country is ready after necessary reforms.
AI generated
CARACAS – US Energy Secretary Chris Wright on Sept 2 dismissed claims that Washington was “stealing Venezuelan oil” after the South American nation granted its northern neighbour access to a huge chunk of its natural resources.
Wright, who travelled to Venezuela to oversee the signing of a series of energy deals worth billions of dollars, sought to dispel criticism in comments made to AFP and other outlets at Caracas airport.
The United States is due to take majority control of more than 65 billion barrels – almost 20 per cent – of oil in Venezuela, which holds the largest proven reserves in the world.
Caracas has projected earnings of US$209 billion (S$265.57 billion) over 25 years from the accord.
“I’ve seen those headlines. ‘We’re stealing Venezuelan oil’. Of course, that’s not true at all,” Wright said, adding that “the oil in Venezuela is indeed owned by the people of Venezuela”.
“Private companies are bringing the money to produce the oil, but the benefits, the royalties and the taxes all go to the government of Venezuela and the people of Venezuela,” he said.
“All we’re doing is taking an idle, underground asset that isn’t doing anything for Venezuelan people and bringing the money, the technology to develop it.”
Wright also stressed the importance of fixing Venezuela’s electricity sector, with much of the country enduring hours-long power cuts on a daily basis.
The oil sector also needed electricity to function, he added.
“You need them both,” he said, voicing optimism given the “existing (electricity) infrastructure” in Venezuela that he believes can be put to use again under a five-year plan.
US President Donald Trump has described the pact announced on Aug 28 as “the biggest oil deal in world history”.
Earlier on Sept 2, the US leader rebuffed calls for elections in Venezuela, amid high hopes that Washington-backed talks between the interim government and parts of the opposition might lead to a democratic ballot.
“I just don’t think they’re ready yet. You know, it’s very new. We took them out of a dictatorship, and we’re getting along great with the government,” he said.
US forces ousted Venezuelan president Nicolas Maduro in January, and Maduro’s former vice-president Delcy Rodriguez has been governing on an interim basis ever since.
Rodriguez, who effectively rules under Trump’s thumb, echoed that elections would take place when “Venezuela is ready”.
Wright sought to clarify that elections were a “process”, pointing out that reforms including an overhaul of Venezuela’s Supreme Court were necessary first.
“The plan for elections has not changed at all. It’s to continue to get the infrastructure ready and have elections at the appropriate time,” he said.
The secretary said the country and its economy had to be stabilised before a popular vote could occur.
“You don’t want to wait, sit on your hands for whatever time it takes to get through elections,” he said. AFP

Berlin approves $930 million in weapons sales to Israel

Berlin approves $930 million in weapons sales to Israel
The German government approved nearly €800 million ($930 million) in weapons exports to Israel between January and June, Der Spiegel reports, citing a government response to a parliamentary inquiry. The sum is already four times higher than the total value Berlin greenlighted last year.
Around one-fifth of the exports was linked to German-Israeli defense-industry cooperation benefiting the German Armed Forces, according to the government. Just over two-thirds of the approved value is tied to the INS Drakon, a nearly 70-meter-long Dolphin II-class submarine built for Israel by German shipbuilder TKMS. The vessel, which can remain submerged for weeks, left Kiel on Tuesday and is reportedly on its way to Israel.
Berlin said the remainder covered equipment not classified as ‘weapons of war’, including small arms, ammunition, explosives, and drones, according to Der Spiegel.
The Left Party accused Berlin of “boundless double standards” over the deals.
“As [Chancellor] Friedrich Merz was supposedly outraged by [Israeli Security Minister Itamar] Ben-Gvir’s inhumane statements, his federal government was pushing ahead with cooperation with a government and an army facing genocide charges before the International Criminal Court, supporting settler violence in the West Bank, and continuing to occupy southern Lebanon,” MP Lea Reisner said.
The controversial Israeli minister stated last month that he considers the enclave “to be ours” and urged the IDF to carry out dozens of “targeted assassinations” there every night, claiming that some in the Palestinian enclave “are not people.”
Germany’s War Weapons Control Act requires licenses to “always be denied” where weapons risk being used in “peace-disturbing acts” or where Germany’s obligations under international law could be impaired.
Berlin temporarily halted weapons exports to Israel in August 2025 over West Jerusalem’s plans to occupy Gaza City, but lifted the restrictions in November after a US-backed ceasefire with Hamas. Israeli forces have since continued operations in Gaza and against Hezbollah in Lebanon, where they still occupy parts of the south.
Germany is meanwhile expanding military cooperation with Israel. On Wednesday, the German Navy said it had successfully tested an Israeli ballistic missile in the North Atlantic with a range of up to 500 kilometers. Germany has no ballistic missiles of its own, with Taurus cruise missiles being its longest-range missile systems.
Germany’s unwavering support for Israel, which is facing genocide accusations before the International Court of Justice in a case filed by South Africa, has arguably cost Berlin international support, as it failed to secure a seat on the Security Council in June.

China rivalry ‘no excuse’: US Democrats allege corruption in Trump’s mining deals

4-MIN READ4-MIN

Nayan Sethin Washington
US Democratic lawmakers on Wednesday accused the Donald Trump administration of using the critical minerals contest with China as an excuse for corruption – alleging billions of dollars in deals were enriching the president’s family and friends.

The Trump administration has poured billions of dollars into domestic and overseas mining projects, acquired stakes in US mining companies and established bilateral and international partnerships in a bid to break China’s chokehold on critical mineral supply chains.
Beijing holds a near monopoly in the processing of major minerals such as graphite, gallium, tungsten, germanium and rare earth elements – metals that are critical to military systems, semiconductor manufacturing and robotics.
While US industry leaders and mining experts have welcomed the investments on national security grounds, many have raised concerns about a lack of transparency and favouritism in awarding mining contracts.

Iran war escalation raises concern over civilian death toll
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
02:06:11 UTC
11:06:11 KST

Iran war escalation raises concern over civilian death toll
CAIRO/WASHINGTON – The sudden recent escalation of the Iran war has cast renewed attention on its civilian toll after Iran reported 18 dead in the last US assault, including four killed and dozens wounded at a wedding.
Iran’s health minister said 18 people were killed and 108 wounded in the US strikes across Iran on the night of Sept 1.
The Iranian Red Crescent Society said four people were killed and 67 wounded at a wedding ceremony near the coast of the Strait of Hormuz.
The return of combat operations has alarmed countries throughout the region, as Iran launched missile and drone attacks against what it said were US assets in Bahrain, Jordan, Kuwait and Iraq.
Kuwait’s army reported further missile and drone attacks early on Sept 3, saying they were intercepted by air defence systems.
The guns had largely gone silent since the previous exchange in July, although peace talks failed to advance in the interim.
US President Donald Trump threatened to unleash yet more military force, even though the war is unpopular at home and has driven up the cost of petrol.
Top aides to Trump are pushing to keep the war from escalating before November’s midterm elections to staunch Republican electoral losses, and White House officials will consider ramping up military action after the vote on Nov 3, four people familiar with the discussions said.
Iran, for its part, has remained defiant, despite suffering heavy military and economic losses.
United Nations Secretary-General Antonio Guterres was “deeply alarmed by reports of civilian casualties, including a strike that reportedly hit a wedding ceremony in Iran”, and called for an immediate cessation of military action, his spokesman Stephane Dujarric said.
“The Secretary-General condemns all attacks against civilians. He recalls that all parties must respect their obligations under international humanitarian law, including the principles of distinction, proportionality, and precaution,” Dujarric said.
The deaths would be in addition to the 3,636 people documented as killed in Iran as at April 7, including 1,701 civilians, according to the Human Rights Activists News Agency (HRANA), an independent Iranian rights group.
The US has reported 18 military personnel killed and more than 750 wounded.
“We are aware of reports, which originated from Iranian state media. The US military never targets civilians, unlike the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps,” US Navy Captain Tim Hawkins, a spokesman for the US military’s Central Command, said in an e-mail.
The Iranian Red Crescent Society released a video showing debris strewn on the ground next to a building with a large hole in the roof, accompanied by still images showing people, some in Red Crescent vests, at a damaged building and a utility tower lying on the ground.
Reuters was able to verify the location using satellite imagery, which showed the fallen tower was 136m from the damaged building.
The wedding incident recalled the blast at a school in Minab that killed 160 people at a girls’ school on the first day of the war.
The Pentagon has yet to issue an official finding on the Minab strike, which would be the US military’s largest civilian casualty incident in decades.
It may have been the result of US use of outdated targeting data, two sources familiar with the matter told Reuters.
Democratic members of the US Congress have called on the administration to release findings of its investigation of the incident, but the report has not been sent to lawmakers.
US defenders of the Iran war also point to civilian deaths that resulted from Iranian attempts to put down street protests that embroiled the country in December and January, before the US and Israel attacked Iran on Feb 28.
HRANA has put that death toll at more than 7,000, while Iranian exile groups claim the number is much higher.
Trump has cited an incentive for Iranians to overthrow their government as one reason for the war, in addition to seeking to halt Iran’s nuclear programme and ending its support for militant groups abroad such as Hamas, Hezbollah and the Houthis.
Iran has also responded to the US attacks by threatening any oil tankers that transit the Strait of Hormuz without Iranian authorisation, severely curtailing traffic in a waterway that before the war carried 20 per cent of the world’s oil supply. REUTERS

The far-right leader pushing Germans to forget the Nazi past
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
02:01:00 UTC
11:01:00 KST

The man leading the charge to make Germany proud again won’t say he wants his fellow Germans to “forget” the Nazi past, but that is where his ideas invariably lead.
Hans-Thomas Tillschneider, a 48-year-old lawmaker for the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt, was until recently little known beyond his largely rural constituency. But he may soon be in a position to help realize one of the greatest ambitions of the party’s most extreme faction: remaking his country’s postwar identity and steering Germans toward leaving behind the Nazi past.
That history “remains present in a peculiar way — yes, like a zombie,” Tillschneider told POLITICO in July on the sidelines of an AfD conference in the eastern city of Magdeburg. “It’s an undead entity. And that is not normal. That is not good.”
Advertisement
Germany’s much-vaunted Erinnerungskultur, or culture of remembrance, is central to its self-conception — and long served as an existential imperative. Though halting, West Germany’s reckoning with Nazi crimes and the Holocaust in the decades after the end of World War II served to help restore the country’s standing among democratic nations, making possible its membership in Western alliances. The country’s constitution was shaped in repudiation of Nazism, with safeguards intended to prevent its resurgence.
But for the AfD’s most extreme leaders — many now concentrated in rural areas of the former East Germany — the culture of remembrance has merely perpetuated what some, including Tillschneider, call a “guilt cult” designed to instill self-loathing in the German Volk, a term for “people” which is imbued with near-mystical significance on the far right. Without openly denying Nazi crimes, they argue the cultural and political reckoning with them has damaged the Volk’s identity, leaving Germans weak, atomized, and vulnerable to “globalist” forces such as the EU and the U.S., long viewed by the far-right as a corrosive force due to the homogenizing influence of its individualist, consumerist culture — at least until U.S. President Donald Trump’s arrival.
Tillschneider’s ideas aren’t new. The backlash against Germany’s culture of remembrance is as old as the effort to reckon with the past itself. But as the intellectual architect of the party’s blueprint for governing in Saxony-Anhalt ahead of a Sept. 6 election in the state — where the AfD is so far ahead in the polls it’s within striking distance of an outright majority in parliament — he could soon wield more tangible power than any other far-right figure in Germany’s postwar history to turn those ideas into reality. Tillschneider, currently the AfD’s spokesperson for culture and education policy in the state parliament, is a leading candidate to become the head of a future ministry that would oversee school curricula and cultural funding in the state.
“We want to spread the joy of being German,” Tillschneider said at a pre-election AfD “family fest” on an overcast August afternoon in Querfurt, a small medieval fortress city in his Saxony-Anhalt constituency. “It’s a celebration. Celebrate the fact that you’re German.”
This did not mean, he added, that the AfD would eliminate school lessons on Nazi crimes. Rather, it would “shift the emphasis,” he said, so the Nazi past loses its contemporary urgency.
“Of course, I’d also like to see history classes on the Third Reich,” he said, “But good history classes. Good history classes convey a sense of the otherness of the past.”
‘More Bismarck, less Hitler’
In some ways, Tillschneider, a bearded, bespectacled former university lecturer, seems an unlikely figure to advance the revolution in German identity the far-right has long sought.
Born in Romania during the Cold War, Tillschneider grew up in a German-speaking minority community whose roots in the region stretched back to Habsburg rule. His family moved to West Germany when he was still a child. At university, he became interested in Islamic studies, drawn — as he now explains it — to the subject because it was foreign and unfamiliar. He later studied in Syria before earning a doctorate and publishing a book on “the origins of legal hermeneutics in early Islam.”
Advertisement
After moving to eastern Germany in subsequent years, Tillschneider came to depict Islam as fundamentally incompatible with German society and became a prominent figure in the so-called “New Right,” a network of radical intellectuals known for recasting old, extremist ideas in more culturally palatable terms. He also became associated with an extreme faction within the AfD called Der Flügel (“the Wing”) alongside Thuringian politician Björn Höcke, who drew widespread condemnation in 2017 for calling Berlin’s prominent Holocaust memorial, located near the Brandenburg Gate, a “monument of shame” and demanding a “180-degree turn” in Germany’s memory politics. Der Flügel was dissolved in 2020, but its members, including Tillschneider, have only grown more influential in the party since then.
Tillschneider was the main author of the AfD’s program for how it will wield power in Saxony-Anhalt. At the root are myriad measures aimed at “stabilizing” German identity by redirecting cultural funding and revising school curricula, over which states have primary authority. Tillschneider has announced plans for changing history lessons so that they are oriented toward “more Bismarck, less Hitler,” — controversial phrasing that has recently been removed from the governing manifesto. The party’s program also proposes cutting funding for “anti-German art” and developing a “patriotic tourism” strategy for the state.
Party leaders say they don’t intend to eradicate memorials to Nazi crimes but will fund and restore those that “honor the sacrifices of soldiers” in both world wars. “This support should benefit all monuments equally, without petty political judgments,” the program reads. “Fallen soldiers gave their lives to defend their country. Recognizing and honoring this great sacrifice is a first sign of a patriotic turnaround.”
It’s perhaps no coincidence that such a revolution in German identity would take root in the former East Germany, where the AfD is ascendant. While West Germany was attempting to undertake a confrontation with the past, imperfect as it was, the state narrative in the former East Germany was that its people had vanquished fascism, which in any case was a product of the West. Many of the AfD’s supporters in the East believe a West German narrative about the Nazi past was imposed on them after the fall of the Berlin Wall.
But for Tillschneider, there’s another reason the revolution will begin in the East — because eastern Germans already know what it means to see a political regime collapse.
“As a result of the peaceful revolution, people have witnessed a change in systems and, as a result, have gained some distance, are more reflective,” he said at the AfD family festival, speaking in a breathless torrent. By contrast, he added, western Germans “have been stewing in the same soup for 80 years.”
‘Love for the homeland is not a crime’
As attendees queued for beer and free bratwurst at the AfD family festival — held on an arid field on the outskirts of Querfurt, beside an agricultural-machinery plant — Tillschneider took the stage before an “Our Country First” placard and declared that they had ample reason to celebrate: the establishment parties, he said, were nearing their demise.
“We’re celebrating the fact that the policies that are directed against us — which take away our freedom, which strip us of our autonomy, which impoverish us — will come to an end,” he yelled, his booming voice saturating the speakers. “On Sept. 6, for the first time, we have a realistic chance — and this isn’t just campaign rhetoric — a realistic chance to end this nightmare, to put an end to this horror!”
Advertisement
Ulrich Siegmund, the AfD’s top candidate in Saxony-Anhalt and its potential future premier, then took to the stage to a rock-star reception. Charismatic and very popular online, his quick smile belies the radical politics of the state branch of his party, which domestic intelligence authorities have classified as an extremist organization seeking “to abolish parliamentary democracy in its current form.” AfD politicians in the state, including Siegmund and Tillschneider, deny being extremists, portraying the label as state repression that undermines the democratic will of their supporters.
If Siegmund is the face of the AfD in Saxony-Anhalt, Tillschneider supplies much of the brains. Siegmund alluded to this during his speech, thanking Tillschneider for spending “hundreds of hours” on the party’s governing manifesto.
“I’ll need him over the next five years because we’re making history together,” Siegmund said of Tillschneider. “The sun rises in the east, but it will shine over all of Germany!”
As people waited in line for hours to get Siegmund’s autograph, Tillschneider darted frantically from tent to tent, making sure things were running smoothly. “Don’t sell them for less than €10!” he shouted to a group of volunteers as he handed them a box of tote bags emblazoned with Siegmund’s face.
One of those volunteers, Gesine Sauer, a 48-year-old social worker from the area, said she agreed with Tillschneider’s ideas about making Germans proud of their history.
“People always focus on just a very small part of German history — and that has nothing to do with anyone trying to deny it, or trying to dismiss it — but German history is so much more than that,” she said. “And time and again, from all sides, we’re being forced to grapple with this question of guilt. That’s wrong, and it’s not a positive development. Instead, we should reflect on what we were once capable of achieving,” she added, going on to list German historical accomplishments in medicine and industry.
Others put it more simply. “I’d say that was all 90 years ago, and at some point we should just let the past be the past,” said one woman in her 60s wearing a bracelet in the colors of the German flag.
Advertisement
“With us, if you say you love your homeland, you’re stamped as a Nazi,” said one man, a 51-year-old railroad track worker, as he waited in the long line for beer wearing a shirt that read “Love for the homeland is not a crime.”
Most attendees, however, cited other reasons for voting for the AfD: economic and industrial decline; refugees receiving state support while Germans struggled to pay their bills; the government’s refusal to accept cheap Russian natural gas while sending billions in federal aid to Ukraine.
For Tillschneider and his fellow far-right ideologues, these more tangible issues are all connected to the crisis of German identity: the country’s reluctance to pursue its own interests, they argue, stems from an “anti-German” strain of thinking within the country.
“That’s why we have policies that are self-destructive in every area — because we have a cracked identity,” Tillschneider said from underneath a tent at the festival.
He rattled off ideas for repairing the German soul: a “pride month” celebrating German cultural heritage and a festival of German music — not “Baroque music or European music,” he clarified, but “German music.”
He denied the goal was to make Germans forget the Nazi past. Yet he went on to describe a process that seemed to amount to just that.
The goal, he said, was for this history to “no longer be so urgent, no longer so intrusive, no longer so present.”
He added: “Just because something is no longer present doesn’t mean it will be forgotten.”
Nette Nöstlinger contributed reporting.

Pedro Sánchez’s Ceuta crisis just got a lot worse

A new report alleging Moroccan involvement in the migrant surge threatens to upend the Spanish PM’s narrative and further erode his standing with voters.
A large group of migrants crowd outside the entrance of the Loma del Colmenar reception center, waiting for admission, in Ceuta on September 1, 2026. | Antonio Sempere / AFP via Getty Images
When Pedro Sánchez agreed to appear in the Spanish parliament’s hearings on the Ceuta migration crisis, he knew he would face a hostile audience.
But Thursday’s session promises to be a political reckoning for the Spanish leader, with an emboldened opposition and increasingly distrustful coalition partners seizing on a police report claiming that Morocco played a direct role in last month’s sudden arrival of 72,000 migrants in the autonomous city in North Africa.
The report has dramatically raised the stakes for Sánchez. With the prime minister’s credibility eroding, lawmakers are demanding to know how Spain’s security services failed to detect a hostile operation by a supposedly close ally — and whether the government knew more about Morocco’s role than it previously admitted.
Advertisement
“This wasn’t a spontaneous migration movement, but rather an operation that originated in Morocco and was spearheaded and coordinated by Morocco,” center-right People’s Party leader Alberto Núñez Feijóo said at a rally in Ceuta on Wednesday.
“The government knew and covered it up,” he added, calling for snap elections. “They lied to our faces.”
In the immediate aftermath of the surge, Sánchez described it as an “attack on the territorial integrity of Spain,” but insisted Rabat had nothing to do with it.
He doubled down on that position on Monday, assuring the public he had “no information from Spanish security forces or our intelligence services that would cast any doubt on Moroccan authorities,” and instead accusing Russia, Israel and “an international far-right group” of orchestrating the operation.
But according to the police report, first revealed by Spanish newspaper El Español, Moroccan agents helped orchestrate the mass entry of migrants into the exclave. El País later published a page from the document with images that appeared to show uniformed Moroccan security officers guiding groups of people toward the beach from which they could cross into Ceuta.
The document was commissioned by a judge investigating the surge and drawn up by the National Center for Immigration and Borders, a specialized intelligence unit within Spain’s National Police.
Advertisement
In a letter to National Police Director Francisco Pardo, Interior Minister Fernando Grande-Marlaska on Wednesday denied knowing of the report’s existence and expressed irritation that its contents had not been shared with the top officials convened to manage the crisis.
Justice and Presidency Minister Félix Bolaños said the government had only learned of the document through the press and declined to comment on it until it had been properly examined.
The report complicates the government’s efforts to avoid a direct clash with Rabat, whose assistance is needed both to deport unauthorized migrants and to prevent future surges. Sánchez on Monday insisted the crisis could “only be resolved with cooperation,” and that “showing a lack of confidence in Morocco will only aggravate this situation.”
Political reckoning
The report has turned Thursday’s hearing into a much more consequential political test for Sánchez.
Far-right Vox party MEP Jorge Buxadé on Wednesday urged Spain’s parliament to invoke Article 102 of the Constitution, which provides for criminal proceedings against members of the government in certain circumstances.
“This was an invasion of our territory, an act of hybrid war orchestrated by Morocco,” he said. “And this report shows the government knew about it beforehand and did nothing to stop it.”
Advertisement
Demands for accountability are also now coming from Sánchez’s own coalition government.
The junior partner in the executive, Sumar, has long questioned Rabat’s role in the crisis, and on Wednesday one of its member parties demanded Interior Minister Fernando Grande-Marlaska — who has always attributed the surge to human smuggling mafias — to step down if the information in the police report is proven to be true.
“Not a leaf stirs in Morocco without the government knowing about it, and between 70,000 and 80,000 people don’t move en masse to the Ceuta border in trucks or on foot without being detected,” said Antonio Maíllo, coordinator of the United Left party, which is part of Sumar. “The Moroccan government’s involvement in the crisis is obvious.”
The government’s parliamentary allies — among them the Republican Left of Catalonia and the Basque Nationalist Party — are expected to grill Sánchez on who knew what when, potentially exposing just how little room the prime minister has left in an increasingly uneasy coalition.
That political isolation was also on display on Spain’s streets on Wednesday evening, with tens of thousands of protestors in participating in nationwide demonstrations condemning the situation in Ceuta. Protests were held in more than 260 cities, with dozens of Socialist mayors defying orders from the party leadership and taking part in rallies in support of the exclave.
Their revolt underscores Sánchez’s difficulty enforcing party discipline among local politicians who increasingly see him as a political liability. With municipal and regional elections next May, the protests are a stark sign of the prime minister’s fragile standing heading into a crucial political year.

Nigel Farage’s Reform show gets a reboot
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
02:00:00 UTC
11:00:00 KST

The Reform UK leader will use his conference to strike a ‘very serious tone’ after spending the summer fighting a by-election challenge from Count Binface.
LONDON — Nigel Farage had a silly summer squaring off against Count Binface. Now he wants to get serious.
The Reform UK leader will use his annual party conference, kicking off in Birmingham Thursday, to attempt to move on from a by-election dominated by novelty candidates and questions over his finances. He will try to signal how he would govern if he wins power at the next U.K. general election.
The leader and his four top lieutenants will use their speeches in Britain’s second-largest city to unveil what one senior party official described as “key pledges” for the first 100 days of a Farage premiership.
Advertisement
“It will be a very serious tone this conference,” the official — granted anonymity to discuss internal planning — said.
That’s the hope anyway, because public infighting, questions over undeclared donations, and splits on the right of British politics have dogged Farage’s summer — and could still overshadow proceedings.
Bardella and Farage show
Reform says the conference will be the party’s biggest yet — up by 2,000 attendees on last year, according to internal figures.
They’re boasting big business attendance and a diplomatic presence, too. Jordan Bardella, the president of the far-right French party National Rally, will provide a set-piece attraction. Farage and Bardella have bonded over tackling small boat crossings in the Channel — the major public grievance that has fueled Reform’s success.
But Farage knows this event must offer more than a shift in tone. Not only has his party’s polling slumped as Labour rebounds after the ousting of Keir Starmer, but Farage is suffering a severe dent to his personal figures too.
A YouGov survey released this week suggests his net favorability rating has fallen from its peak of -27 last summer to -44. Just 19 percent of Brits now see him as a prime minister-in-waiting — down seven points since June, before he called his “people versus the establishment” by-election in Clacton.
Advertisement
The party knows looking credible is key. That’s why Farage will be leading the pledge-making to the public, culminating in a policy-laced but unscripted speech on Friday. Robert Jenrick, Zia Yusuf and Richard Tice — his spokespeople for the Treasury, home affairs and business briefs, respectively — will be making them too.
“It will be very serious about the problems the country faces and how we intend to fix them in the first 100 days,” the official cited above said.
Some in Reform had hoped the conference would mark the moment Farage announced an expanded front bench. Key posts like health and defense remain unfilled, despite Farage trying to demonstrate the party is no one-man band. But the party will hold off until after the Birmingham jamboree is over, instead announcing “a couple of new people” later this month and in October, according to the official.
Summer of scrutiny
Farage’s return to the limelight, which he has uncharacteristically dodged ever since his re-election in Clacton, began on Wednesday, with an interview with the BBC’s political editor.
The Reform leader has faced repeated questions over a £5 million donation from crypto-entrepreneur Christopher Harborne, as well as support from convicted fraudster George Cottrell.
Farage continued to insist Wednesday that he has “done nothing wrong” in not declaring the support in the run-up to the 2024 general election. He argued that the intense scrutiny of Reform’s funding is down to an “establishment” stitch-up, and railed against living in a “complainants’ society.” He compared his situation to the investigations faced by fellow “outsider” Donald Trump.
Advertisement
But Farage’s victory in Clacton last month served to restart the parliamentary standards commissioner’s investigation into the Harborne funding. Farage himself suggested that an interview with the investigator is on the horizon — and a sanction could well trigger another by-election for the Reform leader. He is keen to press the need to fund personal security for politicians in a dangerous world.
Reform’s conference opens Thursday with a day of trying to charm businesses, while the main event gets underway Friday.
Underlining the threat that Farage argues politicians now face, the conference will start with a tribute to Ann Widdecombe, the 78-year-old Reform spokesperson killed in her own home in July.
Restore a ‘shiny object’
Reform top brass seems keen to avoid talking about one elephant in the room: Restore Britain.
The right-wing splinter group, formed by sacked Reform MP Rupert Lowe, has been sucking small but significant support from Farage’s right flank in recent months.
Restore is talked of derisively as a “statistical anomaly” inside Reform, but tackling the threat is likely to be a topic of conversation in the conference center. “New shiny objects often attract support. That’s the way human beings are,” Farage dismissively told the BBC Wednesday, in an indication he believes support for Lowe’s outfit could tail off.
Advertisement
For Restore’s part, a disruptive intervention this week seems unlikely. “Let’s let them fight among themselves,” said one well-connected figure in Restore circles.
Indeed, the plea for unity that Farage wrapped last year’s conference with will be put to the test again in Birmingham. The party goes into this conference with open disagreement in its ranks.
Farage this summer publicly reprimanded his home affairs spokesperson, Zia Yusuf, for calling a Conservative former defense secretary a “traitor” in a series of angry online arguments. Reform then suspended political commentator Tim Montgomerie for criticizing senior party figures — including Yusuf.
Trade unions meanwhile look unlikely to leap at Farage’s call to ditch their historic ties with Labour and attend Reform’s conference. “I don’t think any unions are seriously going to take up his invitation to attend Reform conference,” predicted one union leader.
But for all the sniggering at Farage’s fight with Binface this summer, there are more optimistic takes inside the party about the resilience of its base.
Farage not only saw increased support in Clacton — but Reform’s polling is not collapsing in the face of its most intense scrutiny to date.
Advertisement
“Despite a summer that you might say hasn’t been brilliant,” said a second Reform official, “what we’ve learned is that our polling base is around 20-21, which is a step up in two years.”
It’s this core that will be drinking up the Farage show in Birmingham. But it’s the rest of Britain he’ll need to aim at this week.
