Trump's $1 coin enters circulation in century-old first
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
21:56:56 UTC
06:56:56 KST

Halis Sünnetci
03 September 2026•Update: 03 September 2026
The US Mint announced Wednesday that new $1 coins featuring President Donald Trump have entered circulation, making him the first living US president to appear on a circulating coin.
The Mint, a bureau of the Treasury Department responsible for producing US coinage, said the coins were available for purchase.
“Available for purchase today at 12PM ET: 2026 President Donald J. Trump $1 Coin. These coins are also in circulation, so check your pocket change. Collect them today!' the Mint wrote on US social media platform X.
The obverse of the coin features a portrait of Trump along with the inscriptions 'LIBERTY,' 'IN GOD WE TRUST' and '1776 ~ 2026.'
The reverse features the Presidential Seal, depicting an eagle holding an olive branch and a bundle of arrows, with a shield bearing the number '250' to mark the 250th anniversary of US independence.
A banner in the eagle's beak bears the Latin motto: 'E PLURIBUS UNUM,' meaning 'Out of many, one.' The coin also carries the inscriptions 'UNITED STATES OF AMERICA' and 'ONE DOLLAR.'
The Mint said 250,000 Trump $1 coins were struck July 4 at the Philadelphia Mint with a special July 4th privy mark and randomly included in bags and rolls offered through its online catalog.
The coins are available through the US Mint at $61 for a 25-coin roll and $154.50 for a 100-coin bag.
The release is part of the US Semiquincentennial coin program commemorating 250 years since the Declaration of Independence in 1776.
The only previous instance of a living US president appearing on US coinage came in 1926, when a commemorative silver half dollar marking the country's 150th anniversary featured President Calvin Coolidge alongside George Washington.
Critics have questioned the legality of featuring Trump on the coin, pointing to federal restrictions on depicting living people on US currency, and a longstanding tradition against placing sitting presidents on the nation's money.
The Citizens Coinage Advisory Committee, a bipartisan panel that advises the Treasury secretary on coin designs, declined to review an earlier Trump coin proposal. Some members warned that issuing the coin without the panel's review could violate federal law.

A Maltese court on Wednesday acquitted tycoon Yorgen Fenech of orchestrating the car-bomb killing of investigative reporter Daphne Caruana Galizia, sparking outrage from her family and media freedom advocates.
The wealthy businessman had stood accused of masterminding the 2017 assassination of 53-year-old Caruana Galizia, which sparked unprecedented protests and brought down a government.
Caruana Galizia's family said in a statement that Fenech's acquittal was "denying her the justice she deserves".
Her son Matthew Caruana Galizia said jurors had made a "terrible decision... that our country may never recover from".
The European Centre for Press and Media Freedom said the verdict sent "a disturbing message to those who attack and kill journalists".
Dubbed a "one-woman WikiLeaks", Caruana Galizia had exposed corruption at the highest level in the country, shining a spotlight on murky links between Malta's business and political elites.
Her slaying shocked the world and put Malta, the European Union's smallest member state, in the spotlight over its apparent rule-of-law failings.
The killing also led to a political crisis, and the resignation of then-premier Joseph Muscat in January 2020 after widespread anger and mass protests over his perceived efforts to protect friends and allies from the investigation.
A two-year public inquiry published in July 2021 concluded that the state should "shoulder responsibility" for the murder due to the "atmosphere of impunity" the government had created.
Fenech, a tycoon whose business interests spanned the energy and tourism sectors, was arrested on his yacht in 2019 as he tried to sail out of Malta after a middleman in the murder was offered a pardon to identify those involved.
Prosecutors had accused Fenech of ordering the journalist to be killed because she was on the brink of publishing a compromising article about his uncle.

'Beyond outraged'
Five people have been convicted so far in relation to the murder for supplying the explosives and carrying out the killing.
In June 2025, Robert Agius and Jamie Vella were convicted of supplying the bomb that killed Caruana Galizia and sentenced to life in prison.
The three men who carried out the murder – brothers George and Alfred Degiorgio together with Vince Muscat – are serving prison sentences after being found guilty of their role.
A 437-page report written by a panel of three judges in 2021 found that the state had shirked its duty to protect Caruana Galizia and subjected her to personal attacks and verbal abuse from politicians.
The atmosphere created a "favourable climate" for her assassination, and there was "convincing evidence" that her killers knew they would be protected by "persons in the highest state positions".
"Accountability is now overdue for all those who enabled, facilitated, or protected her murderers," the family said in their statement on Tuesday.
"Nine years after Daphne's brutal assassination, the institutional failures that enabled her murder remain unaddressed and unreformed."
Media watchdog Reporters Without Borders (RSF) said it was "beyond outraged".
"The verdict means that almost nine years since the assassination of Daphne Caruana Galizia, the Maltese authorities have failed to identify and convict the mastermind.
"Full justice must be served and Maltese authorities must implement the long overdue measures protecting journalists and media freedom," it added.
The Maltese government issued a statement saying it "took note" of the verdict and was "committed to ensuring that justice is served".

An Arkansas federal judge on Wednesday denied a request by an energy company to temporarily block the Arkansas Democrat-Gazette from publishing additional details from confidential documents that the newspaper obtained about the company's involvement in building a facility that will supply power to a $4 billion Google data center in that state, a court filing showed.
The company, Entergy Arkansas, also had asked Judge Lee Rudofsky to order that the Democrat-Gazette remove from its website information in an article published on Monday about the documents.
"I think you have a strong case here," Rudofsky told a lawyer for Entergy at a hearing Tuesday in U.S. District Court in Little Rock, according to a report in the El Dorado News Times. "But the First Amendment gives me pause here."
The judge said, "It would take a lot to get me to do a prior restraint," the News Times reported.
The Freedom of the Press Foundation has noted that "The Supreme Court has made clear time and again that prior restraints" — barring a media outlet from publishing certain stories — "can be justified in only the most extreme circumstances."
Rudofsky in his order Wednesday denied Entergy's request for a temporary restraining order against the Democrat-Gazette and other defendants. A court filing showed he plans to set a briefing schedule on Entergy's request for a preliminary injunction in the case at a later date.
The Arkansas Times, which was also a defendant in the case, reported that during a hearing Wednesday, Rudofsky said the case involved an issue of "significant public concern."
"Public utility companies' special arrangements with a large data center may very well have repercussions across the state, presumably, or at least potentially, in both very positive and potentially, or presumably, negative ways," the judge said, according to the Times.
He also said that Entergy was a utility that could be considered a monopoly "and the details of its business arrangement, especially with large users of power, for example … Google, are matters that an ordinary Arkansas citizen may very well want to be aware of."
Entergy, in a statement after the order was issued, said, "We will never waver when it comes to protecting our customers' privacy and confidential information. It is both the right thing to do and required by law."
"We protect all customer information — whether it involves a household, a local manufacturer, or a global company," the company said.
Lee Wolverton, executive editor of the Democrat-Gazette, in a statement Wednesday, said, "This case is first, foremost and in its entirety about the First Amendment. Our duty as a news organization and the duty of all news organizations is to inform the public as fully as possible about issues of high public interest."
"Any attempt to impede that effort by using the courts to apply prior restraint to any news organization's First Amendment rights represents an attack on the very freedoms that define our country," Wolverton said. "That must not stand."
Entergy said in a court filing Tuesday that the documents, which contained "trade secrets" and "highly sensitive protected information," were "disclosed in error" by the Arkansas Public Service Commission to a woman, Jessica Kivell, who had requested them under the state's Freedom of Information Act.
Kivell then gave the documents to a reporter for the Democrat-Gazette, which published a story on Monday under the headline "Google to pay Entergy Arkansas $526 million for solar facility to feed West Memphis data center."
The reporter, Sydney Sasser, wrote that the $526 million payment will cover "about one-third of the $1.6 billion price tag of the facility known as Cypress Solar," a 600-megawatt solar field and 350-megawatt battery facility that will "feed the grid from which Google's West Memphis data center will draw massive power."
Sasser noted that the state's Public Service Commission in December approved a special rate contract between Google and Entergy, the details of which "have been mostly kept secret."
"In June, Entergy residential customers began paying an added $5.77 monthly increase to cover three new power generation projects, one of them being Cypress Solar," Sasser wrote.
Entergy Arkansas, in a civil complaint filed Tuesday in U.S. District Court in Little Rock, asked Rudofsky to issue a temporary restraining order barring the Democrat-Gazette, Sasser, Kivell,, the Arkansas Times, and its managing editor Byron Tate from further disclosing what it said were the trade secrets disclosed by the Public Service Commission. Tate told CNBC that his news outlet never received the documents.
Entergy also wanted Rudofsky to order that the Democrat-Gazette and the other defendants remove from their websites any disclosure of information from the documents "that has already occurred."
Tate, in an interview Wednesday with CNBC after Rudofsky ruled against Entergy, said, "I'm grateful that press freedom and the public's right to know won."
Rudofsky, a former assistant general counsel for Walmart whom President Donald Trump appointed to the federal district court in 2019, was nominated by the president in August for a seat on the 8th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals.
Entergy, in its statement Wednesday, said that the Democrat-Gazette's article contained a math error that understated Google's financial contributions to the project.
"Using the figures published in the article — $443 million plus $83 million minimum annually over 20 years — the total would be approximately $2.103 billion, not the amount reported," Entergy said. "That distinction is significant. In fact, as demonstrated by the evidence submitted to the Arkansas Public Service Commission, Google is not only paying its cost to serve but is delivering $1.1 billion in other benefits to Arkansas customers."
"Google's financial contributions to expand and improve the Arkansas power grid are substantial," Entergy said. "As we have stated publicly regarding Google's contract — and as state officials who regulate utilities and protect the public interest have reviewed — the agreement includes important protections for existing customers."
Those protections included Google "paying for 100% of its power needs and more," and Google's contracting including "termination penalties and guarantees designed to protect other customers," the statement said.
A spokesperson for Google, which is not a party to Entergy's civil action, in a statement, said, "Google is fully committed to covering 100% of the power and infrastructure costs for our West Memphis data center."
"While upfront payments total $526 million, our ongoing monthly rates over the 20-year agreement will completely fund our operational footprint," the spokesperson said. "Entergy's regulatory filings demonstrate that this project will actually lower overall system costs, providing more than $1.1 billion in net benefits to Arkansas residents."

OpenAI gets Trump backing in blockbuster battle over AI and journalism
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
21:54:11 UTC
06:54:11 KST

The Trump administration has intervened in the closely watched legal dispute between OpenAI and The New York Times over the use of news content to train artificial intelligence models.
In court papers filed on Tuesday, the US Justice Department supported OpenAI’s argument that training its models on troves of writings found on the internet is protected by the “fair use” doctrine of copyright law.
The Justice Department wrote that “the creative possibilities and public benefits” of training large language models on such content “far outweigh any competitive harm.”
It told the court that siding with The New York Times and other publishers who argue OpenAI’s practice violates copyright law would thwart “creative and scientific progress while hindering American prosperity and economic mobility.”
“The entire reason that AI models are rapidly reshaping the economy and national security is that they help people, including those working in creative fields, make things and get things done,” Justice Department attorneys wrote.
The “creative benefits often overlap with national security interests,” the department added, because AI models can “help national security officials analyse and draw inferences from (unprotected) real-world facts such as those conveyed in New York Times articles.”
Times criticises government’s position
The lawsuit and the government’s involvement reflect a broader global debate over how legal and regulatory frameworks are adapting to the rapid growth of AI technologies.
In many cases, disputes about AI and its practices are winding their way through courts that still lack precedents — and in some cases language — to match the subject matter.
The New York Times said on Wednesday that the administration “is siding with a handful of trillion-dollar AI companies at the expense of the countless American creators whose work they stole.”
“Both AI and creators can thrive — AI companies simply need to pay fairly for the content that makes their products possible, as copyright law requires,” Graham James, a spokesperson for the paper, said in an emailed statement.
“The Administration’s proposal to let companies take that content without permission or compensation would undermine the sustainability of the human-created content that a healthy society depends on, and which AI needs to function.”
“OpenAI threatens financial livelihood”
The Times sued OpenAI in 2023, arguing that the company was threatening its journalists’ livelihoods by effectively stealing billions of dollars’ worth of their work, in some cases spitting out The Times’ material verbatim to people seeking answers from generative artificial intelligence like ChatGPT.
The threat to news publications became even more apparent when, in 2024, Google introduced AI-generated summaries at the top of online search results, cutting off the advertising dollars that come when people click a link to the information’s original source.
The Times has since been joined by other news organisations, including MediaNews Group-owned newspapers the New York Daily News and the Chicago Tribune, digital media publisher Ziff Davis and the nonprofit Centre for Investigative Reporting.
In its original lawsuit and an amended complaint filed earlier this year, it focused on the unfair competition of companies that “seek to free-ride on The Times’s massive investment in its journalism by using it to build substitutive products without permission or payment.”

Palestine accuses Israel of ‘stealing artifacts’ from West Bank Sebastia archaeological site
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
21:53:32 UTC
06:53:32 KST

Zein Khali, Mohammad Sio
03 September 2026•Update: 03 September 2026
The Palestinian Foreign Ministry on Wednesday accused Israel of “stealing artifacts” from the Sebastia archaeological site in the northern occupied West Bank in an effort to alter its features and identity.
The ministry said Israeli authorities were carrying out excavation and land-clearing work at archaeological sites in Sebastia, including bringing heavy machinery into the area around the Roman theater and excavating parts of the site.
The work also includes “stealing its artifacts,” the ministry said, adding that signs bearing the name “Samaria Park” had been placed at the archaeological site.
The ministry described the actions as a “flagrant violation of international law and an attempt to annex the occupied West Bank and impose colonial facts” at one of Palestine’s most prominent heritage sites.
It warned of threats facing Sebastia, particularly after the town was placed on UNESCO’s World Heritage in Danger list, saying the designation underscored the urgent need to protect the site.
The ministry said the excavation and land-clearing work violated Israel’s obligations as an occupying power under international humanitarian law, which requires the protection of cultural property and prohibits its exploitation or alteration for purposes related to occupation.
It also said the actions violated the 1954 Hague Convention for the Protection of Cultural Property in the Event of Armed Conflict and the 1972 World Heritage Convention.
“Plundering Palestinian artifacts or distorting them or changing their significance,” said the ministry, constitutes an attack on Palestinian presence and world heritage, and an attempt to control the site and erase its historical identity.
 
It urged UNESCO, the World Heritage Committee, international organizations and the international community to take urgent action to halt excavation, land-clearing and tampering at the site, as well as the “theft of artifacts.”
The ministry also demanded measures to protect the site and preserve its authenticity and integrity, while preventing any projects that could undermine its outstanding universal value.
It urged the adoption of “concrete” measures to stop what it described as the looting of Palestinian cultural heritage and to hold Israel accountable for violations.
The ministry said protecting Palestinian heritage required effective measures on the ground, an end to the occupation and allowing the State of Palestine to exercise sovereignty over its land, resources and heritage.
Sebastia, northwest of Nablus, contains a historic archaeological site considered one of the most prominent in the West Bank.

German investigators identify Russian and Belarusian suspects in Leipzig airport drone attack plot
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
21:47:00 UTC
06:47:00 KST

Investigators in Germany believe they have identified two likely perpetrators of a failed plot to blow up cargo aircraft at Leipzig/Halle Airport in early August, according to a report by Süddeutsche Zeitung, NDR, and WDR. One suspect was born in Russia and holds a Latvian passport; the other was born in Belarus, holds a Russian passport, and has previously faced legal proceedings in several countries. Investigators believe both are linked to the attempted bombing of a Ukrainian An-124 cargo transport plane on Aug. 4, which German authorities this week formally blamed on Russia.
At a news conference, German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt said the attempted terrorist attack had been planned and carried out professionally, adding that the attack involved “a high level of technical expertise and considerable organizational effort.”
Dobrindt added that the Aug. 4 incident bore the hallmarks of a “familiar pattern of Russian hybrid operations in Europe.” He said available information pointed to people acting “on behalf of Russian state authorities,” referring to them as “low-level agents.” Dobrindt did not name the suspects or explain why investigators linked the attack’s organizers to Russian intelligence services, saying that the probe was ongoing and required “the highest level of information protection.” Later that evening, Die Zeit reported that Germany’s federal prosecutor’s office was pursuing a case against two defendants.
German investigators believe the first suspect served as a logistics coordinator and instructor for the planned attack. According to Süddeutsche Zeitung, NDR, and WDR, he entered Germany in late July through Berlin’s Brandenburg Airport, then drove in a rental car toward Leipzig. Two days before the attempted attack, he departed Germany via the airport in Berlin.
The second suspect was identified through DNA found at the scene of the crime — on the inside of a tin can containing explosives, and on an antenna mounted on a tree near the airport. A check of the samples against European databases produced matches in Lithuania and Finland. Investigators determined that the suspect had entered Germany on an Italian tourist visa, which they believe was issued in late April by the Italian consulate in Minsk.
Investigators are reportedly skeptical about the chances of bringing the suspects to justice. In past instances, including after the 2015 hack of Bundestag servers, German authorities were unable to detain agents who did not return to Europe. Meanwhile, experts from the BKA, Germany’s federal criminal police office, say it is possible that drones in addition to the three found at the airport may have been used in the failed attack.
Meanwhile, the Russian Embassy in Berlin called the incident a “hastily concocted provocation,” claiming it was concerned about a “new wave of anti-Russian hysteria” in Germany.
On Sept. 1, German authorities for the first time formally blamed Russia for the events in Leipzig while announcing the closure of Russia’s consulate general in Bonn and the Russian House in Berlin in response to the incident.

No one is to be named as an accused without sufficient grounds, HC clarified."Suspicious circumstances'' surrounding the death necessitate the registration of an FIR, HC bench of Justices Sarang Kotwal and RR Bhonsale held. But HC said it has "not made any observations against any particular individual"."The police probe raises more questions than it answers. Therefore, an investigation by CBI is necessary.''A delayed spot panchanama nine hours later, on June 9, has “indications that the police were not treating the case as an accidental death case but they were suspecting foul play,’’ the high court observed.

Estonian parliament elects Ulle Madise as next president
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
21:44:58 UTC
06:44:58 KST

Şeyma Erkul Dayanç
03 September 2026•Update: 03 September 2026
Estonia’s parliament elected Chancellor of Justice Ulle Madise as the country’s next president Wednesday, according to Estonian public broadcaster ERR.
Madise received 71 votes in a secret ballot, surpassing the 68 votes required to win the presidency.
Seven ballots were left unmarked, while none were declared invalid.
A total of 78 members of the 101-seat parliament, known as the Riigikogu, took part in the vote.
“I will do my best to be worthy of this trust,” Madise told lawmakers after the result was announced.
“I hope that through mutual understanding, debating vigorously when necessary while still supporting one another, we can accomplish a great deal together for Estonia, so that life in Estonia is happy, good and safe,” she added.
Madise will become Estonia’s seventh president and the second woman to serve as head of state.
She will be sworn into office Oct. 12.
She will succeed Alar Karis, who announced in June that he would not seek a second term.
Karis congratulated Madise following the vote.
“Serving as head of state is a great honour and an even greater responsibility. I wish you strength, wisdom and resolve,” he wrote on US social media platform X.
Madise, born Ulle Anton on Dec. 11, 1974, in Tartu, is a lawyer and legal scholar who has served as chancellor of justice since 2015.
She studied law at the University of Tartu and completed a doctorate in administrative management at Tallinn University of Technology in 2007.
Madise previously worked at Estonia’s Ministry of Justice, advised the Riigikogu Constitutional Committee and served as chief auditor at the National Audit Office.
From 2009 to 2015, she was legal adviser to then-President Toomas Hendrik Ilves.
She also taught public and constitutional law at several Estonian universities.
As chancellor of justice, Madise has focused on individual liberties and legal oversight, and has maintained a non-partisan role.
She is married to Lauri Madise, a judge at the General Court of the EU.

US and Iran Trade Strikes as Fighting Resumes in Gulf
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
21:42:31 UTC
06:42:31 KST

U.S. Central Command launched a wave of strikes against Iran on Sept. 1, and President Donald Trump said forces are “prepared to do another one” as Iran launched retaliatory attacks Sept. 2.
Fighting resumed Aug. 30, as CENTCOM officials announced strikes on “minelaying forces posing an imminent threat in the Strait of Hormuz.” Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps has been using land-based launchers to lob floating mines into the Strait.
Speaking in the Oval Office on Sept. 2, Trump said he ended the roughly monthlong pause in hostilities because of sea mines.
“They were trying to rebuild their radar systems and a missile system and … to build a rocket that drops mines,” Trump said at a White House event. “They were building it, it was almost finished, so we took it out. We saw that they were building it, we see everything that they’re doing.”
Iranian forces countered with ballistic missile attacks on U.S. forces in Jordan and on civilian ships transiting the Strait. A number of U.S. Air Force personnel and assets are stationed at the base in Jordan that has previously come under attack.
On Sept. 1, CENTCOM announced additional strikes on IRGC targets in retaliation for “attempted attacks by the IRGC against commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz and against American service members deployed to the region.” The command indicated its targets included “air defense sites, radar systems, maritime assets and facilities, mine-laying capabilities, and communications sites.”
Trump called the U.S. strikes “a very heavy attack” that “took out all of the new equipment that they tried to build along the Strait of Hormuz: some defensive, some offensive.”
Iranian state media outlets alleged the strikes also hit a wedding party in a coastal town, but those claims remain unconfirmed.
Iranian forces launched their latest retaliatory strikes Sept. 2. Officials and media outlets in the Middle East reported attempted strikes in Kuwait, Bahrain, Jordan, and Iraq. Saudi Arabia’s Foreign Ministry also said Iran targeted a Saudi tanker in the Strait of Hormuz and killed members of its crew.
As of 4 p.m. Eastern time and 11 p.m. in much of the Middle East, CENTCOM had not announced additional strikes. Trump told reporters that the U.S. is “prepared to do another one anytime we want.”
CENTCOM continues to enforce a blockade of Iranian ships and ports and said in a Sept. 2 social media post that it has redirected 86 commercial vessels, disabled three, and boarded two as part of the blockade.

GREENBELT, Maryland – A federal judge on Sept 2 blocked the Trump administration from enforcing a new executive order limiting the number of people eligible for birthright citizenship that President Donald Trump issued after the US Supreme Court rejected his previous effort.
US District Judge Deborah Boardman in Greenbelt, Maryland, issued a preliminary injunction at the request of immigrant rights advocates who had, in 2025, secured a ruling from her blocking the Trump administration from enforcing his initial 2025 executive order curtailing birthright citizenship.
The US Supreme Court on June 30 rejected that initial effort to end birthright citizenship for children whose parents were not American citizens or legal permanent residents, known as green card holders, finding it violated the citizenship clause of the US Constitution’s 14th Amendment.
The clause, which was the focus of the Supreme Court’s 6-3 ruling in Barbara v. Trump, confers citizenship to those born in the United States who are “subject to the jurisdiction thereof”.
Following that decision, Trump signed a new order on Aug 6 that took particular aim at “birth tourism”, in which women travel to the US to give birth so their children can obtain automatic citizenship.
Citizenship would also be denied to children if one of their parents works for foreign governments in the US, engages in fraud or a commercial transaction to obtain citizenship, or is classified as an “alien enemy”.
After he signed that order, lawyers pursuing a class-action lawsuit on behalf of babies who would be deprived citizenship under Trump’s 2025 order asked Boardman to block enforcement of the Republican President’s newest order, and ensure their clients’ citizenship continued to be honoured.
The judge, an appointee of Democratic President Joe Biden, agreed to do so, saying the latest order “is almost certainly unconstitutional as applied to the certified class for the simple reason that the Supreme Court in Barbara already decided that the children in the class are citizens at birth”.
“The Supreme Court has spoken: Children in the certified class are ‘citizens at birth’,” she wrote.
Her order bars agencies – including the US Department of State, the US Department of Homeland Security and the Social Security Administration – from taking any action to interfere with, deny or fail to recognise citizenship of people covered by the class action.
The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
The plaintiffs included the immigrant rights groups CASA and Asylum Seeker Advocacy Project, which in 2025 convinced Boardman to become one of four lower-court judges to block Trump’s initial order prior to the Supreme Court ruling.
“Immigrant families should not have to come back to court to defend the rights of their US-born children and others whose citizenship is being questioned by a new executive order,” Conchita Cruz, co-executive director of the Asylum Seeker Advocacy Project, said in a statement.
Justice Department attorneys argued that an injunction was inappropriate in this case, as Trump’s order was more narrow than the sweeping one the plaintiffs first sued over.
They also called the lawsuit premature, saying federal agencies had yet to issue the necessary public guidance detailing how the President’s directive would be implemented, which they are expected to do by Sept 5.
Any legal challenge should wait until then, the administration argued.
But Boardman said an injunction was needed now, saying that while the Justice Department claimed the order would be applied only prospectively, by its plain terms, it “applies to all children who meet its criteria, regardless of when they were born”.
“This Court must, once again, preliminarily enjoin enforcement of the President’s most recent attempt to strip the right to citizenship from them,” she wrote.
While Boardman blocked enforcement of Trump’s order, she said agencies could still issue guidance on how Trump’s order would be implemented.
Reuters reported on Sept 1 that the US State Department had drafted proposed guidance requiring parents applying for passports for their children to provide proof of their own citizenship or immigration status in order to implement that executive order. REUTERS

"Imposing a minimum 30 per cent tax on these small and family businesses will mean they have less money to reinvest and grow, fewer opportunities to take on new staff, and reduced capacity to pay down debt," Mr McKellar said.

Chinese hyperscalers accelerating AI investment but US peers retain sizable capacity lead: Moody’s
Heavy AI spending will weigh on hyperscaler free cash flow and increase leverage over the next 12–24 months, although ample cash buffers will cushion the strain, according to financial services firm Moody’s Ratings.
"Lower infrastructure costs, policy support and improving domestic AI capabilities allow Chinese hyperscalers to narrow the compute gap with US peers while investing far less," the company said.
"Still, substantially higher US capital spending and continued access to leading-edge chips will preserve a sizable advantage in overall compute capacity through the end of the decade."
Moody’s said cloud remained the primary AI monetisation channel, but scale and pricing diverge.
"US hyperscalers' larger, more mature cloud businesses, broad enterprise and consumer bases and substantial contracted revenue provide a clearer path to monetising AI, supporting their capacity to fund elevated capital spending," it noted.
"China's (A1 stable) lower-cost open-source models and growing domestic AI ecosystem are driving rapid growth in AI-related cloud demand and adoption, but monetisation remains at an earlier stage and on a materially smaller scale."
Despite rising AI investment pressuring cash flow and leverage, cash buffers remained substantial, Moody's added.
"AI investment is likely to weaken credit metrics for both Chinese and US hyperscalers," it said.
"Free cash flow will come under pressure, while debt and lease obligations will likely increase.
"Substantial cash balances, strong earnings and continued market access provide capacity to absorb elevated spending over the next 12-24 months."
Housing not like bananas
The current witness at the parliamentary committee looking at housing affordability and home ownership is economist Ben Spies-Butcher, a former academic who is now CEO of the Centre for Future Work.
He says the housing market behaves like an asset market, not a commodities market, meaning increasing supply is only a partial solution to improving housing affordability.
"Housing looks less like producing bananas and more like a derivative," he comments, pointing out that house prices are falling at the moment not because we have suddenly started building a lot more homes.

Corporate Travel facing 'existential threat'
Shares in travel services company Corporate Travel Management (CTM) have plunged 81%.
The company sells itself as an "award winning provider of innovative and cost-effective travel management solutions".
It ceased trading on the Australian Securities Exchange (ASX) in September last year because it did not lodge its preliminary final report for the year ended June 30, 2025.
It filed audited reports on Wednesday morning and was relisted (reinstatement to quotation) later in the day.
The market today has given a savage assessment of its earnings forecast.
"An 80%+ fall in Corporate Travel’s stock price is indicative of the existential threat the company faces," MooMoo's Michael McCarthy said.
"Even if CTM can negotiate its way out of the overpayment crisis, the question remains — is there a real business here?"
The business is in hot water after pocketing tens of millions of dollars in margins on air tickets and rebates from suppliers.
Corporate Travel is now refunding the amounts to customers because contracts obliged the company to hand on some of this money to clients.
For other customers, the problem is that contracts did not spell out what to do with the margins and so the cash is being handed back.
The method of overcharging was revealed in an announcement from Brisbane-based Corporate Travel to the share market and brings the total of remediation to almost $246 million.

The farm sector has held up better than expected given the rise in diesel, fertiliser and freight costs following the Middle East conflict.

Key Event
'Going for gold': J.P.Morgan on Australian trade
The Bureau of Statistics has published its International Trade in Goods report for July.
- The seasonally adjusted balance on goods decreased $418m in July
- Goods credits (exports) decreased $1,576m (3.3%) driven by non-monetary gold and coal, coke and briquettes
- Goods debits (imports) decreased $1,157m (2.5%) driven by fuel and lubricants and non-monetary gold
Here's a follow-up note from investment bank J.P.Morgan:
Australia’s monthly trade surplus for July landed at $A1.9 billion, a modest decline following upward revisions to the prior print ($A2.3 billion).
Exports value slipped 3.3%m/m, though the weakness was entirely concentrated in non-monetary gold, which sank 26%m/m following an unusually large increase the month prior.
The remainder of the export basket performed as expected, with rural goods bouncing (6%m/m) and non-rural holding steady.
Non-monetary gold was also influential on the import side, declining 31%m/m and dragging aggregate nominal imports 2.5%m/m lower.
Capital goods demand remained strong (7%m/m), led by data centre-related imports (captured in the broader capital goods – ADP equipment sub group), which jumped 50%m/m.
Fuel declined 12%m/m, which we think is more related to global energy prices rather than volumes, while the recent rally in WTI/Brent crude prices suggests import values will recover from August.
While early in the quarter, today’s print is consistent with our view that the quarterly trade surplus will rebound in 3Q given unexpectedly soft export growth around the middle of the year.
Alongside our forecast for relatively stable income flows, this outcome leaves the current account on track to post a modest improvement in 2H26.

UN agency urges civilian aircraft safety after Zelensky warns Russian airspace ‘not safe’
MONTREAL - The UN’s International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO) called on its members on Sept 2 to ensure the safety of civilian aircraft, shortly after Ukraine formally told the body that Russian airspace was “not safe” amid the war.
“Long-range weapons systems, unmanned aircraft systems (UAS), global navigation satellite system radio frequency interference, and advanced air defense systems are among the military technologies jeopardising civilian aviation,” the ICAO said in a statement that did not mention any specific country.
The Montreal-based UN agency also reiterated calls “for stronger commitments from all member states to protect civilian aircraft from all risks arising from conflict zones” because the risk of being “targeted or caught in crossfire is increasing.”
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky warned on Sept 1 that skies over Russia were becoming “extremely dangerous” because of Kyiv’s drones.
“Ukraine does not want innocent lives to be lost. That is why we are warning our partners: the safe days in the Russian sky are over,” Zelensky said, noting that while civilian flights aren’t being targeted, there is “no place” for them “in a sky swarming with drones.”
The Ukrainian leader called that a fair response to “Russia’s desire to prolong the war” by committing “terror against civilians.” AFP

Is Wintour still en Vogue? The Met navigates rough seas as Galliano's 'Horizons' sparks controversy
Unknown

Is Wintour still en vogue? Met navigates rough seas as Galliano retrospective sinks into 'Horizons'
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
Issued on: Modified:
François Picard is pleased to welcome Dana Thomas, author of Gods and Kings: The Rise and Fall of Alexander McQueen and John Galliano and the New York Times bestseller Deluxe: How Luxury Lost Its Luster. The fiery controversy surrounding the Met’s now-cancelled John Galliano retrospective revives the timeless debate over whether we can separate the art from the artist. But our guest argues that the central issue is one of institutional power, with the art itself almost relegated to an afterthought. From her perspective, Galliano’s stature as an artist and fashion designer was never in dispute. His character, however, is once again being called into question in a very public arena.
A retrospective at the Met does more than examine an artist’s legacy: it confers prestige and historical legitimacy. In this case, it would also have given its living subject a key role in shaping the homage to his own life and legacy. Against a backdrop of renewed scrutiny of Galliano’s past racist, antisemitic and misogynistic tirades, Thomas argues that such an exhibition cannot be treated as culturally neutral.
She also turns her attention to Anna Wintour and the concentration of influence surrounding the Met Gala. Wintour’s decades-long friendship with Galliano, coupled with her formidable presence in fashion spanning nearly half a century, casts a harsh light on the tensions that arise when the rarefied worlds of art, fashion and high society collide with the responsibilities of a world-renowned cultural institution.
What might be explained away within the tightly controlled, cut-throat world of fashion, prestige, power and celebrity becomes considerably more contentious at a New York museum cherished around the world, with a civic role, a formidable reputation and a diverse public to serve.
Ultimately, for Dana Thomas, this not about erasing Galliano’s legacy from the world of fashion, but rather which institutions confer legitimacy, and how history should be written.

Republican senator calls on Trump to fire Secretary of Defence Hegseth
Senator Thom Tillis accuses Pentagon chief of ‘inept mismanagement’ as US military is strained by war on Iran.
United States Senator Thom Tillis has called on President Donald Trump to fire Secretary of Defence Pete Hegseth for creating a “leadership void” within the military amid the ongoing war with Iran.
In a social media post on Wednesday, Tillis contrasted Hegseth unfavourably with former Army Secretary Dan Driscoll, who submitted his resignation on Monday amid reported disagreements with the Pentagon chief.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3US Army Secretary Daniel Driscoll submits resignation, media reports say
- list 2 of 3Why are US Republicans losing faith in War Secretary Pete Hegseth?
- list 3 of 3Iran targets American bases in Jordan in retaliation to US strikes
“I have never witnessed more inept management of the brave men and women who serve our country. He is intimidated by competence and retreats to ginning up culture wars instead of soberly attending to the vital work of our national defense and the health and well-being of our fighting force,” the North Carolina senator wrote.
“I urge the President to find a new leader at the Pentagon who will retain and empower our military talent rather than diminish it.”
Tillis is a member of Trump’s Republican Party. But in recent years, he has become an increasingly vocal critic from within the party over policies he fears harm democracy.
In June 2025, amid criticism from Trump, Tillis announced he would not be seeking re-election in November’s congressional midterm polls. His term ends in January.
Early in Trump’s second term as president, Tillis was among the senators who voted to confirm Hegseth, a military veteran and former TV host, despite criticisms of his conduct towards women and his past work.
Tillis only confirmed his vote in favour of Hegseth at the last minute, appearing to share some of the concerns being debated in the Senate.
Since taking office as defence secretary, Hegseth has pursued controversial changes to the Pentagon, including attempts to limit journalistic access to the Defence Department.
He has also undertaken a wide-ranging effort to root out what he calls “wokeness” from the military.
That effort has reportedly included firing top military leaders, blocking promotions, removing transgender service members and reviewing admissions standards for top military academies.
In Wednesday’s post, Tillis pointed to some of those efforts, questioning why Hegseth appeared fixated on culture war issues rather than modernising the military.
He pointed to evolving forms of warfare in Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, and in the US-Israeli war against Iran.
“Our understanding and assumptions of warfare are being challenged in places like Ukraine and Iran, and Dan [Driscoll] understands the old way of doing business no longer applies,” said Tillis.
The senator then proceeded to imply that Driscoll’s departure was a direct result of Hegseth’s mismanagement.
“If we had a Secretary of Defense who maintained the same priorities and forward-thinking, he would be fighting to retain talented leaders like Dan and the many flag officers he has forced into retirement. Instead, he is creating a leadership void at the top of our military ranks,” Tillis added.
Hegseth has faced growing scrutiny in recent months as the US struggles to achieve its goals in the war on Iran, launched on February 28. The war hit its six-month mark last week with no end in sight.
Media reports indicate that the war has left the Pentagon struggling with shrinking munitions stockpiles that could hinder the US military in future actions.
The war has also taken a toll on the popularity of the Trump administration, which has seen approval numbers sink ahead of the November congressional election.
Since the war began, fuel prices have skyrocketed, and the conflict has spread across the Middle East.
More than two-thirds of Americans disapprove of the administration’s handling of the war, according to a University of Massachusetts poll released on August 31.

Nearly 3,500 applicants choose military education this year
As reported by Ukrinform, the Ministry of Defense said this on Telegram.
“The largest numbers of applicants were admitted by: Kharkiv National Air Force University – more than 700; the Military Institute of Taras Shevchenko National University of Kyiv – more than 550; and the National Army Academy – more than 500,” the statement said.
It is noted that 100% of the planned number of applicants were admitted to the Military Institute of Taras Shevchenko National University of Kyiv, the Naval Institute of Odesa Maritime Academy National University, and the Military Law Institute of the Yaroslav Mudryi National Law University.
According to the Ministry of Defense, Ukraine’s military education system covers 121 specializations. They encompass a broad range of professional fields, from unit command, weapons and intelligence to law, medicine, psychology, logistics and international relations.
Military education is constantly adapting to the experience of modern warfare and the needs of the Defense Forces. Nearly half of the specializations offered at higher military educational institutions, military training units at higher education institutions and military colleges belong to the Security and Defense field of study, including military command, troop support, weapons and military equipment.
According to Deputy Defense Minister Liubov Halan, this broad range of training makes it possible to develop personnel not only for directly commanding units but also for the technical, medical, logistical, legal and other support of the Defense Forces.
One of the key changes in military education, the Defense Ministry emphasized, is the development of training for unmanned systems specialists.
“Military educational institutions offer specializations related to tactical and aviation unmanned systems, as well as the operation and repair of maritime unmanned systems. This responds to the challenges of modern warfare, where technological superiority, intelligence, strike precision and the ability to rapidly process information directly affect unit effectiveness,” the Defense Ministry said.
Ukraine is developing military education based on combat experience and the needs of the Defense Forces so that future officers are prepared to work with new technologies, effectively command units and make decisions in the conditions of modern warfare.
“This is an investment in the professionalism and technological capabilities of the military and its ability to ensure Ukraine’s reliable defense,” the Defense Ministry concluded.
As reported by Ukrinform, more than 300,000 applicants have been admitted to bachelor’s and master’s programs at universities. Overall, more than 1 million university students are beginning the new academic year.

Protests in Spain over government's handling of Ceuta migrant crisis

Protests in Spain against government's handling of Ceuta migrant crisis
- Published
Thousands of people have protested in cities across Spain against the government's handling of the influx of migrants to the Spanish exclave of Ceuta on the north African coast.
Spanish opposition parties accuse Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez of abandoning the residents of Ceuta, while the government says right-wing parties are exploiting the crisis.
On Wednesday a police report said Moroccan security forces showed "total permissiveness" during the unprecedented influx, days after Sánchez insisted Morocco was not responsible. Senior police officers have also stressed the report does not directly attribute what happened to the Moroccan government.
He has blamed trafficking gangs and online misinformation for encouraging people to cross the border. Morocco has denied orchestrating or being involved in the mass crossing.
At least 72,000 migrants crossed from Morocco into Ceuta on 30 and 31 July and although most have returned, as many as 5,000 remain in makeshift camps or scattered across the city's streets or on the beach - leading to unrest in the autonomous city in North Africa and a crisis for Sánchez.
There have been near-daily protests by locals, with demonstrators calling for the migrants to be sent back to their countries of origin or redistributed across Spain.
Wednesday's rallies were called by city councils across Spain where opposition parties - the conservative Partido Popular (PP) and the far-right Vox party - govern or have significant popularity.
Demonstrators called on Sánchez to resign.
PP leader Alberto Núñez Feijóo was at the rally in Madrid, where more than 50,000 people gathered, according to government figures.
"A Spanish city has been invaded, occupied and, unfortunately, this happened with the knowledge of the Government of Spain," he said.
Vox leader Santiago Abascal meanwhile said Sánchez was "at the service, like a lackey, of the Moroccan regime".
There was also a major rally in Ceuta itself, with participants chanting: "Ceuta is not for sale, Ceuta must be defended."
"The response has been inadequate, late and, to top it all, has involved a complete dereliction of duty on the part of the government," 45-year-old teacher David Hernandez told Reuters.
"We cannot be second-class citizens, and our border must not be sidelined."
Pressure on Sánchez's government has intensified after Spanish media said the report submitted by the National Police's National Immigration and Borders Centre (CENIF) to the National Court pointed to the involvement of Moroccan gendarmes in the migrant crossings.
The police report claimed that the Moroccan police deployment around the border "was clearly smaller than usual" and cited migrants who spoke of a "passive attitude" as the crossings happened.
However the report did not categorically accuse Morocco of being behind the influx.

Morocco has a long-standing claim over Ceuta and its fellow autonomous city of Melilla, which have long been a flashpoint in diplomatic relations between the two countries.
A large number of social media posts appeared in August portraying the border fence between Morocco and Ceuta as safe and easy, even though at least 100 people died while trying to swim around the border fence, according to figures from the mayor.
Spanish fact-checking website Maldita said before 30 July, when the influx began, messages circulated on Moroccan social media encouraging people to attempt the crossing, after a June ruling by Spain's Supreme Court.

Nepal’s Foreign Minister Shisir Khanal has urged international support following deadly floods to be treated as climate compensation rather than charity, saying it is a “question of justice and fairness."
The death toll from the flash floods and mudslides that struck the Nepal-China border Aug. 26 has climbed to 1,225, while nearly 4,757 victims, including 541 in China, are missing.
Nepalese authorities have said 1,204 people were found dead, while China confirmed 21 fatalities by Wednesday.
Khanal said Nepal was suffering disproportionately from climate change despite accounting for a tiny fraction of global greenhouse gas emissions.
"If you look at data, even our overall carbon footprint, greenhouse emission is less than a 10th of a percentage," Khanal told CNN’s Anderson Cooper 360°.
"The glaciers are melting. The permafrost are thawing, and there is a risk of glacier flood," he said, adding that the latest disaster involved a glacier collapse.
"What we are telling to the world is, look, our contribution in this changing climate is almost negligent," said Khanal.
He stressed that protecting the Himalayas should not be Nepal’s responsibility alone.
"Saving Himalayas has to be part of a global effort because today it’s impacting Nepal but it also impacted China," he said.
Khanal noted that Himalayan rivers eventually flow into India and, in some cases, Bangladesh, providing fresh water for agriculture and drinking to more than 2 billion people.
"Global communities have to come together and this cannot be seen merely as a charitable giving, but has to be part of a compensation process as well," he said.
"You don’t want foreign governments to look at this as giving aid to Nepal. You want this to be compensation," asked Cooper.
"Exactly, this should be seen from the perspective of justice and fairness," Khanal replied. "How fair is it for Nepali people and people of Himalayas to bear the burden of the climate change, where we have had very little contribution to it?"
Asked whether he regarded the disaster as a direct result of climate change, Khanal replied, "Absolutely, you know, there is no question that there is evidence."

Estonia's defence minister resigns amid scandal over ammunition purchases for Ukraine
Estonian Defence Minister Hanno Pevkur has announced his intention to resign amid criticism from the National Audit Office and a scandal over defence procurement, including ammunition intended for Ukraine.
Source: Pevkur in an interview on the ETV programme Aktuaalne kaamera, as reported by Estonia's public broadcaster ERR
Quote from Pevkur: "As defence minister, I of course have to recognise that I am responsible for the entire area under my ministry and if you are now waiting for that big answer, then, of course, a leader must have both the courage and the stature to take responsibility as a matter of political responsibility, even when there is no personal responsibility. I will take that responsibility and the prime minister will have to find a new defence minister."
Details: Pevkur said the findings of the state audit into the activities of the Estonian Defence Forces and the Estonian Centre for Defence Investments (RKIK) were serious enough to raise the issue of political responsibility.
He said he will hand over the post to his successor at a time convenient for the prime minister, expressing his conviction that his actions had been the right ones to strengthen Estonia's security.
"I do so with the firm knowledge that we have made the right decisions to strengthen national defence. Estonia is better defended than ever before," he said.
Pevkur has headed the defence ministry since 2022.
The resignation announcement came after information emerged that Estonia had attempted to purchase artillery shells for Ukraine and had paid a total of €70 million in advance to Indian companies that had not previously sold a single piece of ammunition.
Magnus-Valdemar Saar, the former head of RKIK, said that no important decisions had been made without the approval of the Defence Ministry's leadership. In addition to the minister, former permanent secretary Kusti Salm and current permanent secretary Kaimo Kuusk had been informed about the details of the contracts.
Pevkur said he had indeed not read the contracts, but confirmed that RKIK had provided him with the documents.
Quote from Pevkur: "Although the minister does not count socks and ammunition or conduct contract negotiations, the National Audit Office's criticisms, primarily concerning the activities of the Defence Forces and the Centre for Defence Investments, raise the question of political responsibility. I therefore believe it is right to take political responsibility today for the entire defence sector and hand over the defence minister's baton at a time suitable for the prime minister."
Background:
- Earlier, a special committee of the Estonian parliament (Riigikogu) held hearings following a summary report by the National Audit Office, which pointed to systemic problems and confusion in the defence sector's accounting.
- After the report was posted, Toomas Uibo, head of the Estonia 200 parliamentary faction, Lauri Läänemets, leader of the Social Democratic Party, and Urmas Reinsalu, leader of the Isamaa party, publicly called on Pevkur to resign.
- Prime Minister Kristen Michal convened a Cabinet meeting for the morning of 3 September to receive the Auditor General's report, noting that the absence of personal fault on the part of the minister did not rule out the need to assume political responsibility.

Nuclear bomb test veterans were victims of one of ‘greatest scandals in Britain’, says ex-defence minister
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
21:30:35 UTC
06:30:35 KST

A former defence minister has admitted misleading parliament over the existence of crucial medical records relating to nuclear bomb test veterans.
Tobias Ellwood has said he unwittingly gave MPs incorrect information in 2018 when he told them he had been unable to locate information on veterans’ blood tests after being given incorrect information by officials at the Ministry of Defence (MoD).
Veterans have been fighting for years to see the records as many look to prove that years of serious illnesses such as cancer were linked to their experiences testing nuclear weapons. Ellwood’s admission will increase pressure on the MoD to explain whether its officials have helped prevent those veterans get justice.
In a piece for the Guardian, Ellwood says: “In December 2018, as defence minister, I inadvertently misled parliament.
“Asked whether blood samples had been taken from service personnel for radiological monitoring during the nuclear bomb tests, I relayed the line provided to me by the Ministry of Defence: it was ‘unable to locate any information’ suggesting blood samples had been taken for radiological monitoring at the tests.
“I now know the reality was very different – these samples were taken across the armed services branches. But those veterans seeking compensation for serious illnesses developed after radiation exposure have been unable to access them.”
He added: “This is among the greatest scandals in Britain, and it must be addressed.”
An MoD spokesperson said: “This government commissioned and completed an extensive records discovery exercise, examining tens of thousands of documents to address long-standing questions from veterans about blood and urine testing policies during the nuclear testing programme.
“The findings have now been published in full, following regular engagement between ministers, nuclear test veterans and community groups throughout the process.”
Between 1952 and 1967, about 22,000 British military personnel took part in 45 large-scale nuclear weapons tests in Australia and the South Pacific. Some pilots flew through mushroom clouds, some troops crawled through fallout and many witnessed the first test wearing little more than short-sleeved shirts and shorts.
Large numbers later suffered blood disorders and cancers, which they believed were caused by exposure to radioactive fallout. Most were denied pensions because of their ill health.
Unlike other nuclear-armed countries such as France, the US and the Soviet Union, the UK has never compensated those involved in testing atomic bombs.
The case has been compared with the infected blood scandal, which saw more than 30,000 people contract HIV and Hepatitis C in the the 1970s and early 1990s after being given contaminated blood and blood products.
The prime minister, Andy Burnham, has previously said he was misled by officials when he claimed as health secretary in 2009 that there was no evidence that people were knowingly given contaminated blood. His claims echo those being made today by Ellwood.
Burnham has also been a vocal supporter of the nuclear test veterans in recent years.
As Greater Manchester mayor in 2022, Burnham said: “If the state was conducting medical tests upon servicemen and not informing them when they found serious irregularity, that is at least misconduct in public office, and more serious, perhaps gross negligence manslaughter, in respect of people who died as a result.
“Crimes have been committed.”
The prime minister is now coming under pressure to begin an inquiry and allocate government money for compensation to the victims.
One of the major problems with securing compensation so far has been the lack of medical evidence linking veterans’ health problems to their experiences helping with nuclear tests.
The government long maintained that it did not hold any such medical records – a claim that was proved incorrect in 2022 when the journalist Susie Boniface revealed the existence of a database of 28,000 documents known as Merlin.
That database had been put together in response to a 2007 lawsuit by 1,000 British test veterans and their families, but the information was classified.
Ellwood says he did not find out about the existence of this database until 2022, when details began to emerge in the press.
He writes in his piece: “If this information existed within the MoD, why had ministers not been given the full picture?”

====================================================================================================

I inadvertently misled parliament over a British nuclear scandal. Now I’m calling for justice | Tobias Ellwood
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
21:30:35 UTC
06:30:35 KST

In December 2018, as defence minister, I inadvertently misled parliament. Asked whether blood samples had been taken from service personnel for radiological monitoring during the nuclear bomb tests, I relayed the line provided to me by the Ministry of Defence: it was “unable to locate any information” suggesting blood samples had been taken for radiological monitoring at the tests.
I now know the reality was very different – these samples were taken across the armed services branches. But those veterans seeking compensation for serious illnesses developed after radiation exposure have been unable to access them. This is among the greatest scandals in Britain, and it must be addressed.
More than 20,000 armed forces personnel took part in dozens of nuclear tests and nearly 600 radiation experiments, the majority between 1952 and 1967. This was for the entirety of the cold war. The science was deemed necessary. How effective were our own bombs and, just as importantly, how well could our military function if the Soviet Union used theirs against us? Test after test was conducted in the Australian desert, at Christmas Island in the Pacific, and we also sent service personnel into the atomic clouds of allies and enemies. Yet their medical records for the period are missing.
Other nuclear nations, such as the US, France and the Soviet Union, did the same. Yet they acknowledged that it happened and created dedicated compensation schemes for nuclear test veterans who subsequently developed serious illnesses. Britain stands apart here. In Britain, the burden was placed on veterans to prove their case. But how do you claim what happened decades earlier when potentially vital records are missing or inaccessible?
In 2007, about 1,000 nuclear test veterans and families took the MoD to court seeking compensation. Pilots had been instructed to fly through mushroom clouds. Service personnel sailed and crawled through fallout. Others witnessed nuclear explosions, in some cases just two miles from ground zero. Surely our service personnel deserved better?
This is where the scandal turns ugly. To deal with the veterans’ litigation, the MoD instructed the Atomic Weapons Establishment (AWE) to collate relevant documentation into a searchable database called Merlin. More than 28,000 documents were eventually assembled, covering radiation, precautions, health monitoring and what was known about the possible biological effects of the tests. Yet the veterans’ lawyers had no practical access to this vast archive. Thanks to the extraordinary investigative journalism of Susie Boniface, historical documents began emerging referring to blood and urine testing.
When I saw the evidence, I raised it in November 2022 as chair of the defence committee. The MoD finally acknowledged that the AWE held copies of blood-test results and urine-radioactivity measurements for “a small number of individuals”. That took me straight back to my parliamentary answer four years earlier.
I challenged the then defence secretary, Ben Wallace. If this information existed within the MoD, why had ministers not been given the full picture? He agreed that withholding relevant medical information would be “deeply wrong” and undertook to investigate.
The dam was beginning to burst. Searches of Merlin for “blood” and “urine” subsequently identified 151 documents. Then another extraordinary twist. A software change meant the AWE could no longer provide a historical audit trail showing who had accessed Merlin.
In 2024 (after the general election), the government finally ordered a discovery exercise into what blood and urine testing had taken place. Its findings, published this July, are damning. Evidence indicates that medical examinations or blood testing were required for “the majority, if not all” of Britain’s nuclear-testing period, across all three armed services. Bizarrely, the review says it found no evidence of intentional concealment.
But after seven decades of incomplete answers and ministers kept in the dark, this cannot be where the story ends. Had veterans and their doctors known the full picture decades ago, cancers and other illnesses could have been diagnosed earlier. Lives could have been saved.
Merlin is now being transferred to the National Archives. But declassifying 28,000 documents into the public domain will take time and is not the same as giving veterans answers. Many are now in their 80s and 90s.
Given the numbers of veterans involved and the decades this has been allowed to drag on, this is arguably one of Britain’s biggest scandals – alongside infected blood, Windrush and the Post Office. It demands an apology to the nation from the prime minister, an independent tribunal to establish the truth, and a compensation scheme for veterans and widows similar to that provided in the US.
These men served their country. Their country failed them. Seventy years on, veterans should not still be fighting their own government for the truth.
- 
  Tobias Ellwood is a former defence minister and the author of Ten Steps to Prevent World War Three

Agriculture—and Farmers—Should Be at the Heart of Transforming Africa's Economy, Leading Voices Agree
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
21:30:33 UTC
06:30:33 KST

Africa’s agricultural productivity has grown in recent decades, but more progress needs to be made to improve the livelihoods of smallholder farmers and create lasting economic growth, experts agreed at the TIME Impact Dinner on Wednesday Sep. 2 in Kigali, Rwanda.
Moderated by TIME senior correspondent Justin Worland, leaders in agriculture, climate, and development discussed the progress that has been made in growing Africa’s agricultural productivity and the work that still remains.
A report released this week from AGRA, an African-led institution focused on scaling agricultural innovations for smallholder farmers and the event sponsor, shows that Africa’s farm output has roughly doubled in the last 20 years. Yet despite meaningful investments, not enough has been done to ensure that gains are not siloed, says Ismahane Elouafi, executive managing director of CGIAR, the world's largest, publicly-funded agrifood research network. “We have made increases in productivity, but not enough,” she says, noting that while a farmer might have healthy soil, they could still lack water or strong irrigation systems. “So basically, we have done it in piecemeal, but not as a food system as a whole.”
Many African countries do not treat food systems as an important part of economic and development agendas, says Kingsley Moghalu, founder of the Institute for Governance and Economic Transformation (IGET) Academy and CEO of Sogato Strategies LLC, a global risk advisory firm. “Our countries look at agriculture as some niche area, and that bypasses 80% of its potential,” he says.
Agriculture is central to Africa’s economy, contributing 20% to GDP and employing over 60% of the workforce, according to the World Economic Forum. That, coupled with a rising population that is expected to represent 25% of the global workforce by 2050, could present a new avenue for growth in Africa, Kingsley notes. "It's a huge opportunity if you make [the workforce] agri-food system skilled."
Yet strengthening the food system can only happen if the needs of smallholder farmers are taken into account, says Temiyeoluwa Alabi, head of corporate communications at ThriveAgric, which connects smallholder farmers across Africa to financing, support, and markets.
“We try to emphasize the need to look at the smallholder farmer as an important … entity within the value chain,” Alabi says. “Otherwise, we can't unlock the real value, because if the farmer just won't get value for what he does, then there cannot be prosperity for him.”
Technological advances present a promising opportunity for change, says Elouafi. “In Africa there is definitely a lack of infrastructure that makes the value chain very long,” she says. “But I think now with AI, with advisory services, with the way we can really look at big data, we could make a very quick and very fast impact and improvement.”
Those opportunities shouldn’t come at the cost of farmers. “If we are to have a change, we must invest in the entire value chain,” says Elizabeth Wathuti, climate activist and founder of Green Generation Initiative. “Technology and innovation is not supposed to make the farmers realign their lives to accommodate it. It's supposed to actually look at how it's addressing the realities on the ground and what exactly the farmer is doing on the ground.”
Success must be measured in different ways—beyond a farmer’s yield, Wathuti notes.
“For farmers that are in areas that are completely degraded, it is almost impossible for them to be able to continue adapting to a changing climate. How are we strengthening the farmers and ensuring that the farmers actually have more security?” she says. “We have to also look at the profitability and the value that the farmer gets from being able to put in the work to be able to produce our food.”
TIME Impact Dinner: Reimagining Farmer Prosperity: Building Africa’s Next Food Systems Frontier was presented by AGRA.

US-Iran strikes raise fears of renewed war across the Middle East
DUBAI/WASHINGTON – Fears of renewed escalation gripped the Middle East on Sept 2 after the US and Iran exchanged their biggest barrage since July, with Washington striking Iran’s southern coast and Tehran firing at US bases across the region.
With the US threatening further strikes, Iran accused Washington of hitting a wedding party, killing four people and wounding dozens. Its health minister later said 18 people had been killed and 108 injured in the latest wave of US strikes.
The US military said it struck air defences, radar systems, maritime assets, mine-laying capabilities and communications sites on Sept 1. Iran reported hits on multiple targets near the Strait of Hormuz.
The flare-up threatens to deepen a conflict that has dragged on since the US launched strikes on Iran in February, disrupting global energy supplies and drawing opposition from a majority of Americans ahead of November’s congressional elections.
“Last night was like the end of the world,” Mahmoud, 38, a municipal worker in Sirik County along the strait, told Reuters by telephone, describing attacks on the area that includes the city where the wedding was reported to have been hit.
US President Donald Trump said the US hit Iran “very hard” and that Iran responded with a “love tap”.
“It was a very heavy attack last night, and we’re prepared to do another one any time we want,” Trump told reporters at the White House.
Iran struck what it said were US assets in Bahrain, Jordan, Kuwait and Iraq, and said its aim was to drive US forces from the vast network of military bases they have maintained for decades across the Middle East.
“American evil in the region will be met with heavier, more widespread, and devastating responses, and any country that cooperates with the aggressive American army must accept its dangerous consequences,” Iran’s military command said.
Iran said it killed US forces in Jordan and at a base in northern Iraq, but US officials told Reuters there had not been any casualties, according to initial assessments.
In Kuwait, Iran said it had carried out a missile and drone attack on the US Ali Al Salem airbase and on a residential complex used by a US commander. Kuwait’s fire service said it put out a blaze at a residential complex hit by a drone.
Qatar, home of the largest US airbase in the Gulf, said it held Iran responsible for attacks and their repercussions. Bahrain, which houses the regional headquarters of the US Navy, said Iranian drones were intercepted and destroyed.
Iran also said two tankers had been struck by mines while being steered through the Strait of Hormuz by US personnel.
Washington says that despite Iranian attacks, it is guiding ships through the strait. Energy Secretary Chris Wright said more than 17 million barrels of oil exited on Aug 31.
Iran blacklisted 11 more ships, bringing the total number of such vessels to 56, a government website showed, meaning it would consider them subject to fines, confiscation or detention if they try to sail through the Strait of Hormuz without Tehran’s permission.
Trump repeated his assertion that the strait, which handled 20 per cent of global oil and liquefied natural gas shipments before the war, was open to shipping.
Iran says wedding struck
Iranians were fearful that the new strikes signalled war could restart at full scale.
“It’s very difficult to live like this. We don’t know when America will strike,” Mahpari, 28, a woman in the southern port city of Bandar Abbas, told Reuters by phone.
Iran said four people, including a four-year-old, were killed while celebrating a wedding at a home in Sirik. Iranian media said as many as 68 people were wounded there, and released images of injured children in hospital.
Reuters was unable to independently verify the incident.
US Navy Captain Tim Hawkins, a spokesman for Central Command, said: “We are aware of reports, which originated from Iranian state media. The US military never targets civilians, unlike the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps.”
Video shot by Iran’s West Asia News Agency at the purported site showed rubble strewn across rooms and a courtyard. A pair of strappy women’s dress sandals lay abandoned on a blood-soaked carpet.
Ali Molahi, identified as the father of the bride, said: “I am just glad the casualties weren’t even worse.”
Conflict draining both sides
The exchange of fire was the worst since July, when Trump abruptly halted two weeks of intense bombing of Iran after warnings from his military brass that they were using up munitions and running out of meaningful targets.
Trump has yet to achieve the aims he set when launching Operation Epic Fury in February – to end Iran’s nuclear programme, deprive it of the ability to strike its neighbours and create conditions for Iranians to topple their rulers.
But the US has seriously degraded Iran’s conventional military forces and taken a toll on Iran’s already weakening economy, US officials say.
Sources have told Reuters that Trump aides are trying to keep the war quiet for now to avert a defeat in the midterm elections in November. Polls show Americans oppose the war by more than a two-to-one margin. REUTERS
