Estonia's Defense Minister resigns after wasting 70 million euros on faulty ammunition for Ukraine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
21:29:53 UTC
06:29:53 KST

Estonia's Defense Minister resigns after wasting 70 million euros on faulty ammunition for Ukraine
Estonian Defense Minister Hanno Pevkur announced his resignation on Sept. 2 following revelations that the country had given a company 70 million euros (about $81.1 million) for artillery for Ukraine, despite the company having never previously sold a single shell.
Pevkur said he was not personally aware of the problems surrounding the ammunition deal but was prepared to take responsibility for the outcome.
"A leader must have strength and courage to take responsibility ... even though the minister does not count socks and cartridges and does not hold contract negotiations, the comments of the National Audit Office ... raise the question of political responsibility," Pevkur said in a Facebook post announcing his resignation.
"That is why I must take political responsibility for the entire defense field today and pass on the Minister of Defense's baton to the Prime Minister."
Estonia's National Audit Office on Aug. 28 released a report on the nation's defense spending, criticizing the defense ministry's military procurement in recent years. The report led to calls for Pevkur's resignation as the 70-million-euro mistake came to light, according to ERR News.
In 2024, Estonia entered into a deal to purchase artillery shells from the Italian-registered company Datasel S.R.L., owned by the Indian company Neco Defense Munitions, according to Eesti Ekspress. The deal would supply Ukraine with ammunition against Russian forces using money from the EU's European Peace Facility.
The deal came as Ukrainian troops faced a severe shortage of artillery shells, exacerbated by delays in U.S. aid packages and the EU's failure to reach its target of delivering one million shells by March 2024.
read also
Estonia's Center for Defense Investments (RKIK) sent millions of euros to Datasel in advance for the ammunition, but the company repeatedly reported delays, and shipments didn't arrive for months. When a shipment eventually arrived in 2025, Eesti Ekspress reported that the shells were faulty and "useless."
Current RKIK Director General Elmar Vaher, who did not oversee the original contract, told Eesti Ekspress that the deal should never have been signed. 
"In my opinion, we should not have signed a contract with them," Vaher said. "If I start building a house and hire a company that has never built houses before, there is a doubt that the house will not be finished," he said.
Estonia's defense spending has risen sharply since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. The nation's defense spending increased from 2% of its GDP in 2022 to 3.4% in 2025, according to the Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD).
In 2026, Estonia announced that its defense expenditure would increase to 5.4% of its GDP and that its defense budget would grow by 42%. Tallinn also pledged over $117 million in military aid to Ukraine for 2026.
Estonia's National Audit Office has repeatedly raised alarms over the risk of misuse of state funds during this time. The August report is the latest in a string of unfavorable audits of the defense ministry's spending.
"There is a risk that costs of around 70 million euros will have to be paid for from the Estonian state budget at the expense of other planned expenditures," the National Audit Office said.
Estonian Prime Minister Kristen Michal called for a cabinet meeting on Sept. 3 to discuss Pevkur’s resignation and the findings of the audit reports. The nation's Prosecutor's Office has also opened a criminal investigation into issues covered in the reports from 2025 and 2026.
Pevkur said he was submitting his resignation "with the firm knowledge that we have made the right decisions to strengthen national defense."
"Estonia is better protected than ever before," he wrote. "I wish the defense sector strength and success, because the Estonian people must be assured of the assets and resources of the Defense Forces and continue to unwaveringly support Ukraine, because they help ensure our security as well."
The Baltic nations continue to scale up defense capabilities in light of new Russian threats. Estonia reported drone incursions into its airspace on Sept. 1 as Russia launched a large-scale aerial attack on Ukraine and Ukrainian drones targeted western Russia.

U.N. admits exceeding the 1.5-degree-Celsius global warming target is ‘unavoidable’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
21:28:22 UTC
06:28:22 KST

The world is on track to exceed the Paris Agreement’s target of no more than 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit) of warming above preindustrial temperatures within the next few years, the United Nations admits in a new report.
The report from the U.N. Environment Program (UNEP) states that exceeding the 1.5-degree-C threshold is “unavoidable” and likely to occur “within the next few years.” Even under an “optimistic scenario,” the report says, global temperatures are expected to peak at 1.8 degrees C (3.24 degrees F) above preindustrial levels.
The forecast has been released less than a year after the U.N.’s climate change lead Simon Stiell told attendees at the organization’s annual climate conference in Brazil that the 1.5-degree-C goal may remain “within reach.”
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
“I’m not saying we’re winning the climate fight. But we are undeniably still in it, and we are fighting back,” he said.
Now the report urges the world to prepare for life past 1.5 degrees C of warming. As the planet heats up, the world is likely to see severe harms such as worsening heat waves, greater sea-level rise, extensive flooding and the possible collapse of coral reefs, as well as “profound changes” to glaciers, permafrost and other parts of the planet that are reliant on cold temperatures, the authors write.
The report comes hot on the heels of a summer marked by climate-related disasters and extreme weather, including record-breaking heat, extensive wildfires and a devastating flood in Nepal and Tibet. A strong El Niño that is forecast to peak in December could exacerbate heating, and 2027 could break the record for hottest year, scientists say.
If the report has any good news, it’s that the U.N. maintains that the warming trend is reversible with urgent action—even as many countries, and particularly the U.S., roll back climate protections and scale down clean-energy projects. Indeed, the U.S., the globe’s biggest historical greenhouse gas emitter, officially pulled out of the Paris Agreement in January.
“Every fraction of a degree avoided and every year by which overshoot is shortened will save lives, protect ecosystems and reduce economic losses,” the authors write.

Bihar Police’s case against six accused in 2001 firing case rejected by Supreme Court
NEW DELHI: Bihar police had proved its case before the trial court and Patna high court against six persons accused of firing indiscriminately to kill a man in broad daylight in 2001, but its evidence was trashed by the Supreme Court, which took more than a decade to acquit the accused by concluding that it was a case of "no investigation" having taken place.The snail-paced legal system saw one of the accused serving a life term awarded by the trial court and upheld by HC in 2015. The other five convicts had appealed against the HC decision. Acquitting them, a bench of Justices J B Pardiwala and K Vinod Chandran said, "There is complete lack of evidence in the present case, and testimonies (of eyewitnesses) do not inspire confidence." SC's remark that "the case is not of a faulty investigation but of no investigation having been carried out" indicates possible lack of judiciousness on the part of trial court or HC to separate grain from the chaff while appreciating evidence in the case. Otherwise, it is incomprehensible as to how the complete lack of evidence in the case, as pointed out by SC, had escaped the scrutiny of two judicial tiers.Justices Pardiwala and Chandran said it was aware that faulty investigation cannot be taken advantage of by the accused but added, "When there is no reliable evidence, merely because the IO was recalcitrant or a complaint of collusion was raised against him, the court cannot presume the guilt of the accused."
SC said, "We are unable to find the prosecution having established the culpability of the accused beyond reasonable doubt. As we noticed, the eye-witness testimony does not inspire confidence, and there are no recoveries made or seizures effected as would have been done in a proper investigation."SC said the murder motive projected by the prosecution was sticky, an expert medical opinion went against the witness testimony on how the incident occurred, and there was no recovery of weapons or cartridges from the scene of crime in the case that saw witnesses claiming indiscriminate firing by the accused. Disbelieving the eye-witness account that the assailants came from behind and fired indiscriminately at the victim, who was walking, the bench said, "Expert evidence that there was an indication from the nature of the wound that the victim was sitting and that the firing was made from close quarters persuades us to disbelieve the eyewitness testimony."

Malta: Businessman acquitted of journalist's murder
September 2, 2026
A Maltese businessman was acquitted after being accused of being behind the murder of investigative journalist Daphne Caruana Galizia.
Yorgen Fenech, 44, was accused of commissioning the car bomb killing of Caruana Galizia in 2017 in a case that sent waves across Europe.
Caruana Galizia, who was 53 years old at the time of her murder, was driving near her home when the bomb detonated.
Caruana Galizia's journalistic investigations included extensive information about suspected corruption in politics and business in Malta. She faced about 40 libel suits at the time of her murder.
Life in prison avoided
Fenech, who would have faced up to life in prison had he been found guilty, was cleared of both complicity for murder and criminal association to commit murder with a jury margin of 8-1. He denied the allegations that he had wanted the journalist dead due to an investigation about him being about to be published.
Fenech did not comment after leaving the courtroom, with a crowd of people waiting outside the court shouting insults in his direction.
Family's demand for justice continues
Caruana Galizia's family responded to the acquittal by saying that the institutional failures that led to the murder "remain unaddressed and unreformed."
"Lasting justice means no person should ever face the same risks again. Our country failed to protect Daphne's life. It owes it to her to prevent other lives being lost."
Daphne Caruana Galizia's sons were in the courtroom when the verdict was read out.
Five people were convicted in connection to the murder, with three of them being found guilty of carrying it out.
All five are currently in jail.

Israel still wants to remove Palestinians from Gaza, defence minister says
Israel Katz says ‘there is no real solution for Gaza’ without de-populating the territory.
Israel is still working to remove Palestinians from the Gaza Strip, Israeli Defence Minister Israel Katz has admitted, saying that US President Donald Trump has only frozen a plan that rights advocates say amounts to ethnic cleansing.
Speaking at a conference organised by Israeli publication Ynet on Wednesday, Katz said de-populating Gaza – which some Israeli officials euphemistically describe as voluntary “immigration” or “migration” of Palestinians – remains the “only solution”.

“In the end, there is no real solution for Gaza without this migration,” Katz said, according to the Times of Israel.

Japanese WWII crimes revisited: Soviet files detail mass beheadings in Manchuria
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
21:17:29 UTC
06:17:29 KST

Japanese WWII crimes revisited: Soviet files detail mass beheadings in Manchuria
On August 9, 1945, a notorious Japanese army unit executed dozens of civilian prisoners in the city of Hailar, on the day the Soviet Union launched an offensive against the Imperial Japanese puppet state of Manchukuo.
To mark Victory over Japan Day (V-J Day), the Russian authorities published historical documents for the first time detailing the killings. The files were compiled by the Soviet military counterintelligence service (SMERSH), which investigated the crimes and brought some of those responsible to justice.
Hailar, then a city of around 40,000 people, now part of China’s Inner Mongolia region, saw some of the fiercest fighting of the Soviet-Japanese conflict, which began on August 9, 1945. A major Japanese fortified complex in the area, built with forced Chinese labor during the occupation, has since become part of a memorial park.
The crimes described in the documents released by Russia’s Federal Security Service (FSB) took place elsewhere, at a secret police prison where the Japanese authorities held local residents suspected of harboring pro-Soviet sympathies.
Manchuria had a complicated history of Russian settlement. Its population included working-class railway builders, monarchists who had fled the Bolshevik Revolution, and even committed Russian fascists eager to ally themselves with the Axis powers.
How did the USSR go to war with Japan?
Despite fighting on opposing sides in World War II, the USSR and Japan avoided direct military confrontation through most of the deadliest conflict in human history. Soviet forces stopped a Japanese attempt to expand into Mongolia in 1939, but afterward, both powers concentrated on their principal enemies: Nazi Germany for Moscow and the United States for Tokyo.
The defeat of the Axis powers in Europe in May 1945 changed the strategic balance, while Moscow was also under pressure to honor a commitment to its Allied partners to enter the war in the Asia-Pacific.
Within weeks, battle-hardened Red Army forces overran Japan’s Kwantung Army in Manchuria and created a credible threat of an invasion of the Japanese home islands.
Japan ultimately chose to surrender to the Americans.
What was the Hailar massacre?
As the prospect of war with the USSR grew in 1944, the Japanese occupation authorities in Manchukuo compiled lists of Soviet citizens and other “subversives” and began arresting those deemed a threat. On August 9, another wave of arrests was followed by summary executions.
The organization tasked with the effort was the Tokumu Kikan, or Special Service Organizations, a network of elite military-civilian units specializing in human intelligence and fifth-column activities. The decentralized organization traced its origins to a force created in 1904 by Japanese intelligence officer Akashi Motojiro to conduct covert operations against the Russian Empire. It was reestablished in 1919 as Tokyo pursued plans for expansion on the Asian mainland.
Lt. Col. Amano Isamu, who headed the Tokumu Kikan branch in Hailar, ordered the killing of 43 people on August 9, 1945, with Japanese-commanded local police assisting in the operation.
Three weeks later, after the occupation regime collapsed, local residents exhumed the bodies so they could bury their relatives. SMERSH investigators established that many of those killed were Soviet citizens living in Hailar.
What evidence was found in Hailar?
The complete report assembled by Maj. Gen. Pyotr Popov, the SMERSH commander in Hailar, contained more than 100 pages of documents as well as a collection of photographs.
The FSB has declassified and published around 20% of the material, including excerpts from a medical examiner’s report, transcripts of interviews with witnesses and suspects, a description of the secret prison, and updates Popov sent to Moscow as the investigation proceeded.
Who were the victims?
According to the documents, Soviet forces learned about two mass graves exhumed by locals, while 19 bodies were still awaiting burial, allowing investigators to conduct proper post-mortem examinations. All of those killed were identified as ethnic Russians and Jews except for one Mongol man.
Messages left on the walls of prison cells provide a glimpse into the people held by the Tokumu Kikan. Many of the inscriptions simply contain victims’ names, including one reading ‘Gosha K’. Others include biographical details, dates of imprisonment, and complaints about torture, malnutrition, and deaths inside the prison.
A young man named Vinokhodov left a farewell message saying, “dying for the cause, I feel some relief,” suggesting that he sympathized with the Soviet Union.
How did the Japanese kill the prisoners?
The prisoners were killed by clean beheading carried out by a professional’s strong hand, the forensic report said. The evidence suggests that at least one of the executioners was an accomplished swordsman.
The documents state that several victims were not completely decapitated, with their heads left attached to their bodies by skin at the throat. Although Soviet investigators did not comment on this, it has significance in Japanese cultural tradition.
Traditional seppuku, a ceremonial form of self-disembowelment that also served as a form of capital punishment among the samurai class, was normally carried out with the assistance of a second person. The assistant would cut off the dying person’s head to end the suffering. A technically difficult cut that left the head partly attached was regarded as evidence of exceptional swordsmanship and was intended to preserve the dignity of the person being executed.
Seppuku was long outlawed by 1945, however, and it is highly unlikely that an Imperial Japanese officer intended to grant his prisoners an honorable death. A more plausible explanation is that the executioner was showing off.
One notorious episode during the Nanking massacre in 1937 involved two Japanese officers who were reported to have competed to see who could kill 100 people with a sword first. Contemporary Japanese newspapers portrayed the victims as battlefield combatants, although researchers have concluded that they were almost certainly prisoners of war.
What happened to the perpetrators?
In November 1945, a Soviet military tribunal sentenced Japanese military and police personnel involved in the mass arrests and executions in Hailar to death. Tokumu Kikan chief Amano and Maj. Gen. Haseki Kageyama, the head of the provincial gendarmerie, were among those executed by firing squad.
Their fate contrasted with that of many other Japanese officers, including Tokumu Kikan alumni, who were later incorporated into the US-backed postwar order. Former enemies, including individuals implicated in war crimes, offered their knowledge and experience to Washington as the Cold War began.
One example was Imperial Japanese spymaster Arisue Seizo. Gen. Charles Willoughby, who headed US military intelligence under Gen. Douglas MacArthur, recruited Arisue and similar figures to kickstart anti-Communist operations in Asia.
Why did Soviet citizens live in a hostile nation?
Russia became heavily involved in the development of Manchuria in the late 19th century as it sought greater access to Chinese markets. The Russian defeat in the Russo-Japanese War and the collapse of the Russian Empire during World War I, however, sharply reduced the country’s influence in the Far East.
Harbin, one of the main centers of Russian settlement in Manchuria, became a magnet both for people who wanted nothing to do with the new Soviet state and for those seeking to actively undermine it. Some younger Russian emigres in Manchuria came to believe that fascism could provide a path to restoring Russia, creating an organization that at its peak in the 1930s was estimated to have around 20,000 members.
The Russian community in Manchuria nevertheless remained sharply divided over the Soviet Union. According to historian Sergey Smirnov, around 120,000 people in the region in the 1920s were either Soviet citizens or sympathized with the new state, while more than 100,000 held opposing views.
The divide is also reflected in the newly released documents, which identify a “white emigree” surnamed Kaevich as a member of the Japanese police who took part in the Hailar massacre.
Where are the Hailar massacre archives?
The archives are held by three separate institutions.
The Central Archives of the Federal Security Service (CA FSB) holds interrogation transcripts, personal files and and background declarations of Japanese officers and medical personnel.
The Russian State Military Archive (RGVA) stores operational military records of the Soviet Red Army’s trans-Baikal offensive into Manchuria in August 1945.
The State Archive of the Russian Federation (GARF) stores the official state records, evidence compilations, and international legal paperwork regarding the 12 primary Japanese war criminals prosecuted by the Soviet Union for crimes against humanity in Northeast China.

Coalition promises to slash tobacco tax, legalise and regulate vapes

Coalition unveils plan to slash tobacco tax, legalise and regulate vapes
In short:
The Coalition has vowed to cut the tobacco excise by 80 per cent if elected, in a bid to shut down the black market.
It has also promised to legalise, regulate, and tax vapes and nicotine pouches for adults.
One Nation plans to slash the excise by 75 per cent, while Labor has argued there is no evidence a dramatic cut would end the illicit trade.
A future Coalition government would slash the tobacco excise by 80 per cent, legalise and tax vapes and nicotine pouches, and bolster law enforcement to shut down the illicit trade.
Opposition Leader Angus Taylor today pledged to reduce the excise on a standard packet of 20 cigarettes from about $30 to $6 if elected, declaring the dramatic price reduction would smash the thriving black market.
A 20-pack of cigarettes typically costs between $40 and $50. With the Coalition's proposed cut, the price would drop to about $16-$26, assuming the tobacco retailers passed on the full tax reduction.
More than half of the tobacco consumed in Australia last year was bought illegally, with the illicit market share jumping to 80 per cent when vapes and nicotine pouches are included.
Public health authorities have long used a tobacco excise to reduce smoking by making cigarettes more expensive, and they have consistently warned dropping the tax risked reversing this.
The Coalition has also vowed to legalise, regulate and tax vapes and nicotine pouches for adults.
Australians aged over 18 can purchase legal vapes through pharmacies, while pouches are banned.
Under the Coalition's plan, vapes would have a "low rate" of excise of 50 cents per millilitre of e-liquid, while pouches would be taxed at 2.5 cents per milligram of nicotine.
A $60 million three-year national public awareness and education campaign would "expose the organised crime" behind illegal tobacco and vapes and warn people of the dangers of smoking.
A further $200 million would be spent on a nationwide law enforcement "surge" to support more raids, arrests, border seizures and the closure of illegal tobacco shops.
The surge in illegal sales has cost the federal budget tens of billions of dollars in lost excise revenue, with the Coalition's policy assuming this trend would reverse if legal cigarette prices were lowered to attract customers away from illicit alternatives.
Modelling of the Coalition's policy package by the Parliamentary Budget Office (PBO) found it would increase tax revenue by about $8 billion over the first four years, about double current forecasts.
Last month, One Nation unveiled a plan to slash the excise by 75 per cent, while Labor has argued there is no evidence a dramatic cut would end the illicit trade.
Social Services Minister Tanya Plibersek said the Coalition's plan to slash the excise "will kill people".
"If we drop the excise, in the way that is being suggested by the Coalition, that's a guarantee we will see smoking and vaping rates in this country increase. That will lead to deaths," she told News24.
Monash MP Mary Aldred, who co-chaired an internal Coalition taskforce on illegal tobacco, said Ms Plibersek had the situation "backwards".
"What's killing people right now is the black market the excise created. More than 200 firebombings since 2023, and at least one innocent Australian, Katie Tangey, dead," she said.
Ms Aldred said illicit tobacco and nicotine products had no quality control, age checks or regulation.
"Every packet the black market sells is one the government has no oversight of. Bringing consumers back into a controlled and regulated market is a critical objective of our policy," she said.
Shadow Health Minister Anne Ruston has also defended the policy, which includes legalising vapes and nicotine pouches, arguing people were already accessing those products illegally.
"I think what we're seeking to do here today is a short-term trial for two years of a practical measure to see if we can smash this [illicit] market," she said.
"Because no matter how much you yell and scream about the issue, the reality is that 80 per cent of nicotine products are currently being purchased by Australians in the black market."
Taylor says excise cut will shut down black market
Mr Taylor argued the Coalition's policy would attack the source of the black market by taking away the profits enjoyed by organised criminals selling illicit tobacco and vapes.
"Organised crime is waging a campaign of economic terrorism on Australians," he said.
"Labor has allowed a criminal industry to thrive on our streets. We will shut it down."
Mr Taylor said Australians were getting the "worst of all worlds" with higher tobacco consumption, crime and the loss of billions of dollars in revenue.
"Tobacco consumption has gone up around 30 per cent since the end of 2021, while taxes have kept rising, clearly showing that the government's current approach has failed," he said.
University of Sydney public health professor Becky Freeman described the policy as a "terrible idea".
Dr Freeman, who made a submission to the Liberal-led Senate inquiry into illicit tobacco and has appeared as an expert witness, said the idea was in line with the "tired drumbeat of the tobacco industry".
"It is absolutely not going to reduce smoking rates in this country, which is what we need to focus on," she said.
Dr Freeman agreed that illicit tobacco had exploded in use and was a national crisis, but disagreed with the proposed solutions.
"If we were to lower the price of regulated products, the criminals can just lower their prices as well and it'll just be a race to the bottom for the cheapest cigarettes available," she said.
Mr Taylor disagreed with the suggestion illegal cigarettes would still be cheaper than legal ones under his plan.
"We don't agree with that. We're going to drive up the cost by putting $200 million into joint federal and state law enforcement," he told ABC News.
"We're going to bring down the tax, and we're going to smash the business model."
Asked if the policy would encourage more Australians to smoke, Mr Taylor argued they were already able to buy illegal cigarettes for $10 or $15 a packet.
"The horse has bolted on this," he said.
Cancer council warns against 'new generation' of smoker
Cancer Council Australia and Quit have both warned that making cigarettes and vapes more accessible and affordable risked creating a "new generation" of nicotine addiction.
Medical lead at Quit Liam Egan said the organisation did not want to make harmful, addictive nicotine products easier to access at the "very moment we should be doing everything possible to prevent another generation becoming hooked".
"These proposals go against hard-fought public health wins,"
Cancer Council's tobacco issues committee chair Alecia Brooks said people who vaped were five times more likely to go on to smoke tobacco products.
"At a time when smoking rates are at historic lows, creating a legal retail market for vapes risks reversing years of progress. Public policy should be focused on reducing addiction, not shifting consumers between addictive products," she said.
"Australians are not calling for easier access to nicotine products.
"What they want is effective policing of organised crime, stronger enforcement against illicit operators and retailers, and proper implementation of existing laws."
Smoking data differs from Coalition claims
In June, the Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS) estimated nicotine consumption had risen by about 30 per cent in the past four years, but this increase included the growing use of vapes and other nicotine products.
The ABS cautioned the estimates were experimental, and while its analysis suggested higher legal cigarette prices enabled the illicit market, it did not establish the excise caused overall tobacco consumption to increase.
The latest National Drug Strategy Health Survey found daily smoking among Australians aged 14 and over fell from 8.3 per cent in 2022-23 to a record low 5.6 per cent in 2025.
The survey, conducted by the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare (AIHW), found daily vaping was broadly unchanged at 3.6 per cent.
The AIHW specifically asked people about their smoking behaviour, while the ABS consumption estimates tried to capture the quantity of all nicotine consumed.
Question remains over black market prices
A legal packet of 20 cigarettes costs between $40 and $50, of which the excise makes up as much as $30.
Illicit cigarettes retail for between $15 and $20.
The Coalition said the PBO had estimated an 80 per cent excise cut was "sufficient" to bring the prices of legal and illegal cigarettes into "alignment", making it harder for the black market to compete.
It is not clear whether that calculation assumed black market prices would remain the same or drop to continue to undercut legal sales.
Nationals leader Matt Canavan said the current excise rate had created a "massive profit margin for organised crime".
"Cutting the excise will take billions of dollars out of the hands of criminal gangs, bring the market back under Australian law and give our police a fighting chance to shut down those who remain," he said.
The Coalition's excise cut would be reviewed after two years.

Inside Kallas’ fightback against plans to tear up the EU’s diplomatic service
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
21:13:30 UTC
06:13:30 KST

Inside Kallas’ fightback against plans to tear up the EU’s diplomatic service
Senior officials working for the foreign policy chief are sounding out capitals for ideas on how to reform the EEAS without drastic changes to its makeup.
European Commission High Representative and Vice President Kaja Kallas makes a point during a press conference with Ireland's Defence and Foreign Minister Helen McEntee in Wicklow, Ireland, on Sept. 1, 2026. | Paul Faith/AFP via Getty Images
Kaja Kallas, the EU’s chief diplomat, is leading a fierce behind-the-scenes push against Franco-German plans to overhaul her diplomatic service — courting capitals and using a new secretary-general to develop alternative reform plans.
Kallas’ campaign involves convincing EU governments that the bloc’s foreign-policy problems stem from unanimous decision-making rules and poor implementation of its treaties — not from the current institutional setup, according to three EU officials informed of her plans. They were granted anonymity to discuss sensitive internal strategy.
The fight comes as the 15-year-old European External Action Service faces criticism that it is no longer fit for purpose at a moment when Russia’s war against Ukraine, Donald Trump’s demands on Europe, conflict in the Middle East and a more confrontational China are all testing the bloc’s ability to act abroad. The Commission is also expanding its role in foreign policy, while Berlin is pressing to cut EU operating costs amid negotiations over the bloc’s next long-term budget.
Advertisement
Kallas’ allies fear that an overhaul intended to make EU foreign policy more effective could instead give President Ursula von der Leyen’s Commission greater control over the work overseen by the high representative.
“If I have somebody above me who is actually deciding, then it doesn’t work,” Kallas told journalists Wednesday after a debate with EU foreign ministers in Wicklow, Ireland.
One diplomat, referring to the Franco-German plans, said: “She [Kallas] wants to delay the whole process because she doesn’t want to be subject to von der Leyen.” Another said “she wants this whole thing to go away.”
The pushback is taking shape through Kajsa Ollongren, the EEAS’ new secretary-general, who has been touring EU capitals to discuss reform proposals with national governments.
Ollongren will brief staff on the findings from that tour at a town hall meeting with the EEAS this week, where Kallas will formally introduce her, according to the officials and an EU diplomat.
Ollongren is also expected to propose the creation of a “council of elders” task force to reflect on possible internal reforms, one of the officials said.
Advertisement
The group would include the EEAS’ former secretary-general, Belén Martínez Carbonell, who has delayed taking up a new role as head of the EU delegation in Mexico to advise Ollongren. Senior EEAS official Charles Fries is also set to contribute, according to the officials and the diplomat.
The push seeks to give the EEAS more control over a reform debate that could determine whether the service remains a distinct part of the EU’s foreign policy machinery or becomes more closely integrated into the Commission.
The Franco-German plans, set out in a paper seen by POLITICO, include moving much of the EEAS staff into the EU executive. Although they call for reinforcing Kallas’ formal role, her allies see them potentially allowing von der Leyen’s Commission to take greater control of foreign policy.
Kajsa Ollongren, who has been touring EU capitals to discuss reform proposals with national governments, making a statement during a meeting of NATO defense ministers in Brussels in June 2024. | Simon Wohlfahrt/AFP via Getty Images
The EEAS currently straddles the Council and the Commission: Kallas works with national governments in the Council, where foreign policy decisions are made, while the service coordinates with the Commission on its external-facing work.
Kallas signaled her concern about the plans on Wednesday, saying a “majority” of EU foreign ministers had opposed the institutional change.
The letter opens the door to the selective use of qualified majority voting for foreign and security policy decisions. Currently, any decision on topics under those headings requires unanimous backing — leading to major bottlenecks under former Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orbán, who opposed the bloc’s support for Ukraine.
While agreeing with the aim of making EU foreign policy faster-moving and better able to protect the bloc’s interests, Kallas argued Wednesday that the solution is to enforce EU treaties and legal texts that, in theory, give her oversight of the Commission’s external-facing policy units without requiring big reforms.
“The problem is not the treaties, the institutional setup,” she said. “The problem is the implementation.”
CORRECTION: A previous version of this article misstated the names of Kajsa Ollongren and Belén Martínez Carbonell.

Relatives of 2 loan scam accused may get Rs 3 crore after 35-year case
NEW DELHI: Relatives of two loan scam accused who died during the 35-year pendency of the criminal case may receive an unexpected windfall of Rs 3 crore, which may swell beyond this sum with compound interest for 15 years.Supreme Court, while acquitting the lone surviving accused in the 1991 loan scam case, discovered that the bank had auctioned the assets of two others for Rs 3.6 crore to satisfy a Rs 50 lakh loan liability but did not return the rest to their legal heirs.The lone survivor was a branch manager, accused of sanctioning loans of Rs 13.5 lakh and Rs 10 lakh but pocketing the amounts.After the registration of an FIR, the bank launched recovery proceedings in 2010. Auctioning the properties of one of the two accused fetched Rs 1.2 crore, from which Rs 16.4 lakh was adjusted towards satisfying the loan amount along with interest. In the recovery proceeding against a second person, the bank realised Rs 2.8 crore from the sale of his assets and adjusted Rs 40 lakh towards the loan liability.A bench of Justices J B Pardiwala and K Vinod Chandran said, "The loan was availed in the year 1991-1992 and the property was auctioned in the year 2010.
Admittedly, the auction of properties was completed and the entire amounts due to the bank were received. More intriguing is the fact - as coming out from the testimony of the official witnesses - that the amounts received in auction in excess of the appropriation to the loan accounts are still remaining with the bank.
"While granting a clean chit to the lone surviving accused bank official and terming the case a fabricated one, the bench said, "We are surprised that no attempt was made to find the legal heirs and pass on the money."Supreme Court asked the manager of Indian Bank's Anna Nagar Branch to produce records relating to the utilisation of the money received from the auction, and the title deeds of the properties mortgaged against loans. The court said though the criminal case was disposed of, it was posting the matter for further hearing on Oct 5 to ensure that the excess money received from auction reached the legal heirs.

Magbegor in her prime-time era, leading Opals' World Cup charge
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
21:11:06 UTC
06:11:06 KST

Ezi Magbegor in her prime-time era, will carry Opals' hopes at Women's Basketball World Cup
In short:
The Opals begin their Women's Basketball World Cup campaign in Berlin this weekend, hoping for their first title since 2006.
Australia is ranked third in the world behind the USA and France.
What's next?
The Opals' first game is against Puerto Rico on Friday night AEST.
The Opals have produced a consistent pipeline of global superstars throughout their silverware-packed history, an impressive feat in one of the world's most competitive sports.
In the 2026 incarnation of the Opals, Ezi Magbegor, 27, carries that tag.
After bursting onto the international stage as a highly promising 18-year-old, she is now a defensive linchpin, a leader, and the type of player whose influence will likely dictate how far the Opals go at the Women's Basketball World Cup.
And she is in her prime-time era.
Throwing a fit
Magbegor entered this WNBA season as a hot commodity — becoming the equal highest paid Australian player in the league, and one of the richest female Australian athletes overall.
But an Achilles injury, then broken nose, wiped her out for most of the season, delivering a harsh reality check for the Seattle Storm forward-centre.
"I've been so blessed to not have many injuries at all in my first seven years of my W season," she told ABC Sport.
"You just realise injuries are a part of sport and it's about how you reset your mind and bounce back and prepare for the next thing.
"And so, yes, I was injured, but I just used it as a great opportunity to work on my body and put myself in the best position to be ready."
It also gave her a chance to spend some time on her 'tunnel fits', aka the casual outfits that players wear when arriving at arenas, which have become a core part of the WNBA.
"This year I really wanted to lean into my Nigerian culture and heritage, and my mum's been begging me to wear traditional clothing," she said.
"My favourite was definitely my traditional attire. My parents had bought the material from Nigeria and then one of our friends had sewn it together in Melbourne.
"I worry about being too dressed up sometimes, but my mum's like, yeah, it's not enough, nothing's too dressed up. So, it was really fun to be able to share that with her."
She traded high fashion for a protective face mask when she returned to the court for the Storm in late July, adding to her already intimidating aura as one of the league's best shot blockers.
And while her domestic season has been stunted, she is coming back to full fitness and form just in time for the World Cup, tipping-off in Berlin this weekend.
Opals going big
Magbegor was part of the team that won World Cup silver in 2018, bronze at home in Sydney in 2022, and bronze at the Paris 2024 Olympics.
There has been substantial turnover since Paris with the emotional core of the team including Tess Madgen, Lauren Jackson, Cayla George, and Marianna Tolo, all missing.
And with captain and point guard Sami Whitcomb belatedly ruled out of this World Cup, the side's star power now largely shines around Magbegor and Alanna Smith.
"It's expected for me to pass on the cultural values and expectations onto the next group coming up," Magbegor said.
"But for me it's just about leading by example, touching base with my teammates, making sure that I'm being the best professional, best teammate, best person I can be come tournament play, and in the lead up as well.
"I've been in the Opals team and squad for a while now and I want to have an impact for the team in any way I can, whether that's on the floor, off the floor.
"But definitely looking to play my best basketball for the group and hopefully come away with the medal."
Smith, who was last year named WNBA defensive player of the year, had her own injury interrupted start to the season.
Coach Sandy Brondello is confident Magbegor and Smith are recovered and ready to lead Australia's charge in Berlin.
"They can hold themselves with any of the best post players in the world here. And that's what we're going to need from them without putting pressure," Brondello told ABC Sport.
"I've coached [Ezi] since she was 18. And this is her time, back healthy.
"The best is to come to her, but I'm just excited for her to get out, her athleticism, her rim protection. But now she's a three-level scorer, so that's a great asset.
"And Alanna was our best player in Paris, most consistent player over the whole tournament.
"And it's good to see her getting some rhythm now and getting that confidence back because we need them. We have to lean into them. They're our two best bigs."
Chasing the elusive gold
The Opals enter the World Cup ranked third. The Olympic bronze was followed by a breakthrough Asia Cup win last year, without any WNBA players, and they had a limited preparation for this tournament.
"The results that we've had, it shows that the continuity that we've developed over many years, not just one year, is showing because our chemistry is strong, our culture is strong," Brondello said.
"Everyone's accepting their roles and coming in and playing at a high level. And that's the beauty of Australian teams that we have."
Culture is always the constant with the Opals and what they attribute their sustained performance over decades to.
"It really just comes down our sisterhood and how gritty and tough we are and how we play together and we'll play whatever role to help us to have great success," Brondello said.
"These players, they've become family.
"Playing at the highest level just means everyone has to buy into the values for the success of the program. And there's no one player bigger than the program."
While the Opals are perennial podium finishers at major tournaments, gold has eluded them since their one and only world title in 2006.
"It's just something that comes with being an Opal, that legacy piece and recognising and acknowledging who put us in this position and who started that legacy," Magbegor said.
"Medals is quite synonymous with Opals, and we've won in the past and want to continue to win."
As had been the case for decades, the world number one USA is a seemingly immovable object from the top step of the podium, although was pushed all the way by France in the gold medal match at the Paris Olympics.
"[The USA are] the best of the best and they're great, but they've got the best talent," Brondello said.
"But we've got a talented group, we've built some more chemistry over the years, and that's what we have to lean into."
Growing the game
Half the Opals squad plays in the WNBA, the rest are in the local WNBL, and both leagues have experienced significant changes in the past year.
After drawn out, often bitter negotiations, the WNBA and players' association finally signed a new collective bargaining agreement which saw player salaries skyrocket.
Magbegor went from earning $US186,000 ($260,000) a year to $US1.25 million, a figure matched by Smith at the Dallas Wings, and significantly larger than the base salaries of other leading Australian female athletes in team sports, including the top Matildas and cricketers.
"I think that's just a testament to people that came before us and really pushing for the growth of women's basketball in particular, but just women's sports in general," Magbegor said.
"And I think now is a greater time than ever to push forward, invest in women's sports and just advocate for ourselves, but each other as well."
The WNBL has been making its own moves on a much smaller scale, including a new ownership group taking over last year.
And after starting her career there, Magbegor hopes it too can thrive.
"That's what is probably lacking right now, exposure, and knowing that it's going to pay off in the long run," she said.
"People need to see the product and see the game and realise that women's basketball, basketball is incredible.
"We have great athletes, especially coming up, and I think it's just a matter of investing, a matter of showing up and a matter of supporting."

Zelenskyy Urges ‘Accountability’ Following Kyiv Shootout Between Ukraine’s Security Agencies

21:10:52 UTC
06:10:52 KST

KYIV -- Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy called for “accountability” and “personnel decisions” after a shoot-out in Kyiv involving the country’s major security services.
In his daily evening video address, Zelenskyy said the incident took place between Ukraine’s Security Service, known as the SBU, and the country's military intelligence agency, the HUR, calling it “absolutely disgraceful.”
“The only people anyone should be shooting at are the Russian occupiers, in defense of Ukraine,” he added. “No other exchange of gunfire will ever be treated by our state as something anyone is permitted to engage in.”
Gunfire woke residents in Kyiv’s Bereznyaky district early on September 2, with witnesses saying they saw wounded people and traces of blood at the scene of the incident.
Shortly after the stand-off had ended, conflicting versions of what had happened emerged.
The SBU issued two contradictory statements: first, saying that it was working alongside the HUR to avert a Russian “terrorist attack,” and then, saying that it had resisted a “group of individuals” who had tried to block a search effort.
In a later comment to RFE/RL’s Ukrainian Service, a commander of HUR's “Tymur” special forces unit said that the SBU agents were “detaining HUR personnel and opening fire without warning” at them.
The Russian Volunteer Corps
The shoot-out appears to be connected to earlier reports concerning the arrest of Stepan Kaplunov, deputy commander of the Russian Volunteer Corps, a Ukrainian-backed paramilitary group affiliated with the HUR.
Taras Borovskiy, Kaplunov's lawyer, told RFE/RL’s Ukrainian Service that his client was “abducted” on August 23, and that his whereabouts remained unknown until September 1. He added that the SBU had not responded to his requests for comment.
From here the details of the story get even murkier.
According to Borovskiy, overnight on September 2, the SBU brought Kaplunov to his apartment to conduct a search. But HUR representatives and his friends were already present there.
The HUR commander said he reached an agreement with the SBU unit commander but “other SBU personnel” then opened fire.
Separately, Denis Nikitin, the commander of the Russian Volunteer Corps, told RFE/RL that the SBU had not found anything compromising in Kaplunov's apartment.
Later, Zelenskyy said prosecutors would investigate the incident.

====================================================================================================

Rubio Confirms Ukraine Patriot Talks As Experts Warn Production Is Years Away
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
21:08:16 UTC
06:08:16 KST

WASHINGTON -- US Secretary of State Marco Rubio has confirmed that Washington and Kyiv are negotiating a license that could allow Ukraine to produce missiles for the US-made Patriot air-defense system, reviving an idea that President Donald Trump appeared to downplay only weeks ago.
Rubio’s comments offer Ukraine a potential long-term path toward greater self-reliance in air defense. But he was clear that even if a license is granted, it would not address Kyiv’s immediate shortage of interceptors.
“That’s being negotiated as we speak,” Rubio said on September 2 when asked on The Brian Kilmeade Show whether he was opposed to giving Ukraine licenses to make its own Patriot missiles.
“But that is not an immediate solution,” he added, saying that “ramping up production” and building factories for such sophisticated weapons would take multiple years.
The remarks came as Ukraine seeks more air-defense interceptors ahead of another winter of Russian missile and drone attacks. Rubio said demand for interceptors has become “the number-one defense need on the planet,” with countries in the Middle East also seeking them.
He stressed, however, that the US has its own defense requirements and must maintain adequate stockpiles before supplying other countries.
For Kyiv, that leaves a difficult gap: the interceptors are needed now, while the industrial capability being discussed could take years to establish.
No Patriot Fix For This Winter
Rubio’s confirmation does not guarantee that an agreement will be reached, and it does not offer a quick answer to Ukraine’s immediate air-defense needs.
Retired Rear Admiral Mark Montgomery, a senior director at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies, told RFE/RL that Ukrainian Patriot production would be worthwhile but would not materially affect the war in the near term.
“The idea that the US is going to work with Ukraine for Ukraine to eventually license and build Patriots is admirable, but that's years away,” Montgomery said.
He estimated that licensing and establishing production could take at least 18 months and potentially two or three years.
“That will not produce Patriots for Ukraine anytime in 2026 or 2027, and maybe not even 2028,” he said. “So while that's interesting, that's not going to change the status quo of the conflict with Russia.”
Montgomery said he does not believe the US is currently offering Ukraine sufficient numbers of Patriots, which he said could make the coming winter difficult.
Instead, he pointed to ways Washington could help Ukraine strike Russian missile launchers before they fire.
He suggested providing targeting data that could help Ukrainian medium-range drones hit Russian Iskander ballistic-missile launchers, as well as software upgrades for Ukrainian F-16s to allow them to dynamically target those launchers.
A Signal To Kyiv -- And Moscow
The licensing talks nevertheless carry political and strategic significance.
Yevhenii Malik, a Ukrainian Marine veteran and Mariupol defender who heads national-security and defense programs at the Kyiv School of Economics, agreed that building a Ukrainian Patriot capability would be a long-term undertaking.
But he said the significance also lies in the signal that Washington is continuing to work with Kyiv on advanced defense capabilities.
“It’s more about the sign,” Malik told RFE/RL.
For ordinary Ukrainians and Americans, he said, the technical details of ballistic-missile interceptors may be difficult to understand. What is easier to see is the cooperation between the United States and Ukraine and the broader message of allied support.
Russia is also watching that relationship, Malik said.
The Patriot discussions come alongside US-Ukrainian talks on drone technology. Asked whether Washington had been reluctant to accept Ukraine’s offer of drone technology, Rubio said the United States was pursuing potential deals that made sense for it.
“If it’s a deal that makes sense for the US, I think we’re pursuing those,” Rubio said, describing the discussions as “a work in progress.”
He again stressed that such projects would be long-term efforts rather than capabilities that could come online immediately.
The discussions therefore point to a broader form of defense cooperation in which Ukraine could eventually become not only a recipient of Western weapons but also a source of battlefield-tested military technology.
Daunting Production Math
Even if Ukraine receives a license, the scale of the ballistic-missile threat presents a formidable challenge.
Malik said Russia could produce roughly 1,000 or more ballistic missiles a year, while US production of PAC-3 Patriot interceptors is slightly above 600 annually.
The imbalance becomes more pronounced because intercepting a ballistic missile does not necessarily require a single interceptor.
Malik cited Ukrainian estimates suggesting that two PAC-3 missiles could be needed to intercept one ballistic missile under optimistic assumptions, with other estimates putting the figure at three or even 3.5.
That underscores why a Ukrainian production capability would have to reach substantial scale to significantly affect the balance.
Malik also pointed to Russia’s military cooperation with North Korea and Iran, including the use of North Korean ballistic missiles against Ukraine. His broader argument is that Kyiv’s future air-defense needs must be measured against a wider and potentially growing ballistic-missile threat.
Kyiv Faces An Even Longer Road
Kateryna Bondar, a senior fellow at the Center for Strategic and International Studies and a former adviser to the Ukrainian government, is similarly skeptical about any near-term impact.
Bondar recently returned from Ukraine, where she spoke with Ukrainian missile specialists about the prospects for domestic Patriot production.
She told RFE/RL that the experts she consulted believed it could take several years simply to begin manufacturing.
Bondar said the Ukrainian specialists she spoke with estimated that it could take “up to five, six years just to start producing” because of the system’s complexity.
Even established manufacturers face significant scaling constraints.
Bondar said Lockheed Martin experts had told her that, despite existing technology, supply chains, production partners, and other infrastructure, increasing output from roughly 600 PAC-3 interceptors to at least 2,000 could take about three years.
For Ukraine, which would have to establish much of the industrial base, the challenge would be greater. “So it won't change calculus in any short-term perspective for sure, and even mid-term,” Bondar said.
Yet she sees a potentially important long-term purpose.
Some Ukrainians increasingly view access to advanced interceptors as part of a future security guarantee, she said. A credible ability to defend against Russian ballistic missiles could help deter Moscow from restarting a large-scale war after a cease-fire or peace agreement.
“Having interceptors, having [the] ability to intercept Russian ballistic missiles is something that can stop Russia from advancing,” Bondar said.
Moscow May Not Wait
Bondar said some Ukrainian experts fear Moscow could accelerate ballistic-missile production and develop countermeasures before Ukraine acquires the technology and infrastructure needed to manufacture PAC-3 interceptors.
“Russians are definitely getting the message,” Bondar said. “They’re not only getting the message. They already start thinking of countermeasures.”
That could turn the licensing effort into part of a longer technological competition. While Kyiv and Washington seek to establish a durable air-defense capability, Moscow could seek to increase missile production or develop ways to overwhelm it.

4 in 5 Americans Believe World Language Learning is Important
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
21:08:10 UTC
06:08:10 KST

In a recent Pew Research Center survey, 78% of the 3,507 Americans interviewed said it was extremely, very, or somewhat important for children growing up in the US to learn a language other than English.
Here are the survey’s findings about language learning in the U.S.:
Four-in-ten Americans say it is extremely or very important for children growing up in the U.S. to learn a language other than English. Another 38% say this is somewhat important, and 21% say it’s not too or not at all important.
Women are slightly more likely than men to say language learning is extremely or very important (42% vs. 38%). Adults with bachelor’s degrees are also more likely than adults with less education to say this (45% vs. 37%).
Additionally, U.S. adults who say they live in urban areas are particularly likely to say language learning is important (52%). Suburbanites (40%) are less likely to say this, and Americans who live in rural areas (28%) are the least likely.
More than half of Americans (53%) think it is highly important for U.S. schools to offer Spanish classes.
Spanish is the second-most common language spoken at home in the U.S., after English. Among those ages 5 and older, 14% of the U.S. population speaks Spanish at home, according to the Census Bureau’s 2024 American Community Survey (ACS). Another 77% speak only English at home.
Chinese comes up next in the survey. One-in-five Americans say it is important that U.S. schools offer it. But ACS estimates only around 1% of Americans speak Chinese languages, including Mandarin and Cantonese, at home.
There are some differences between the languages Americans think schools should teach and those that U.S. public schools offer. For example, 20% of U.S. adults surveyed say it’s important for schools to offer Mandarin Chinese as a language class, but only 3% of K-12 public schools offer Mandarin or Cantonese as an independent class, according to the 2024 NCES survey.
Meanwhile, Spanish is the world language that Americans think is most important for schools to offer, and it’s the most commonly taught. Four-in-ten K-12 public schools teach it as an independent class, including 79% of public high schools.
French is the second-most common language that U.S. public schools teach. But Americans say it’s less important to offer than Mandarin Chinese and about as important to offer as Latin.
Immigrants and Americans born in Puerto Rico are nearly twice as likely as those born elsewhere in the U.S. to say children learning a language other than English is extremely or very important (60% vs. 36%). There is a similar pattern when it comes to learning some specific languages, such as Spanish and Mandarin Chinese.
Among U.S.-born adults, second-generation Americans are more likely than third- or higher-generation Americans to say learning a language other than English is important (49% vs. 33%).
Immigrants are more likely than adults born in the U.S. to say it is important for U.S. children to learn a second language
People’s opinions of the importance of learning a language other than English vary by how they see the United States’ global power and influence. In general, those who see the U.S. as less powerful tend to say learning another language is more important.
U.S. adults were asked an open-ended question: “What country or countries are global superpowers, where ‘superpower’ means a country that is both militarily and economically dominant?”
- 27% of Americans who see the U.S. as the sole global superpower say learning a language other than English is extremely or very important.
- 43% of people who see the U.S. as one of several global superpowers say learning another language is important.
- 51% of people who do not name the U.S. as a superpower say learning another language is important.
Along the same lines, Americans who think their country’s influence in the world is waning (51%) are more likely than those who think U.S. influence is getting stronger (31%) or staying the same (34%) to say U.S. children should learn a language other than English.
Similarly, 23% of people who say China’s influence is growing say it’s important for U.S. schools to offer Mandarin Chinese, compared with 18% of those who say China is getting weaker and 12% who say China’s influence is staying the same.
Only 43% of K-12 public schools (43%) offer world language classes (NCES 2024 poll) —just 20% of elementary schools and 82% of high schools.

Trump floats renaming Strait of Hormuz the 'Trump Strait'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
21:07:10 UTC
06:07:10 KST

President Donald Trump on Wednesday floated renaming the Strait of Hormuz — the central point of contention in the ongoing war against Iran that the U.S. and Israel started — after himself.
The proposal via a Truth Social post came less than a week after Trump, who is locked in an intensifying feud with Canada, signed an executive order to change the name of Lake Ontario to "Lake America."
"Now that we have it under U.S.A. control, should we change the name Hormuz Strait to TRUMP STRAIT???" Trump wrote in the post Wednesday morning.
"Like America itself, it would be 'hotter' than ever before! Thank you for your attention to this matter. President DONALD J. TRUMP," he wrote.
It was not immediately clear how the president would attempt to implement a name change for the strait, which is not near the U.S.
The order renaming Lake Ontario directed Interior Secretary Doug Burgum and his department to update the Geographic Names Information System with the new name. Canada rejected the change, though Google and Apple have recently updated their maps.
Early in his second presidential term, Trump also declared he was renaming the Gulf of Mexico as the Gulf of America, a change also rejected by Mexico and other international counterparts. The U.S. borders Lake Ontario and the Gulf of Mexico, both of which have had their names for centuries.
It was also not immediately clear if Trump was serious about the latest plan to try to change the name of an international geographical feature.
Asked at the White House on Wednesday afternoon if he really intended to rename the strait, Trump suggested he did not.
"No, no ... it was just thrown out there," Trump said.
Trump and his administration have repeatedly insisted that Iran has lost control over the strait, which carried one-fifth of the world's oil trade before the war began in late February.
But transits through the waterway remain far below prewar levels, and ship trackers say they have dropped further in recent days, as military strikes in the region have resumed following a weekslong hiatus.
The Trump administration asserts that total oil exports from the region are now higher than they were before the war began, if the tally includes Saudi Arabia's and the United Arab Emirate's pipelines that bypass Hormuz.
U.S. Energy Secretary Chris Wright told CNBC on Wednesday that more than 17 million barrels of oil transited the strait on Monday, a wartime record. Around 20 million barrels per day of crude and products passed through the strait before the conflict started on Feb. 28.

Leaked Documents Reveal Covert Russian Missile Technology Transfer to Iran
Russia has been secretly helping Iran develop advanced supersonic cruise missiles through a multiyear covert technology transfer program, according to an investigation by the Financial Times, posted on September 1.
Codenamed “C430L,” the program began in 2023 and has continued into 2026.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
This advanced technology transfer is part of a broader military exchange between the two nations. It was previously reported that Russia is simultaneously using the landlocked Caspian Sea to ship explosives, ammunition, and drone components directly to Tehran, bypassing Western navies to help replenish Iranian military stocks following strikes by the US and Israel.
According to leaked Russian correspondence, travel records, and military patents obtained by the Financial Times, the initiative focuses on helping Tehran develop a ramjet propulsion system—a specialized engine that enables cruise missiles to sustain flight at several times the speed of sound.
Missile experts told the publication the technology is designed for anti-ship and land-attack cruise missiles capable of threatening naval vessels and missile defense systems in the Middle East.
The program was arranged by Russia’s state arms exporter, Rosoboronexport, in coordination with defense contractor NPO Mashinostroyenia. Financial Times noted that senior Russian missile designers and propulsion specialists made repeated trips to Iran to assist with the project.
According to the Financial Times, NPO Mashinostroyenia engineers received technical data from an Iranian flight test and provided detailed technical analysis to help troubleshoot combustion, fuel system, and airflow issues in the Iranian prototype.
While Iran has previously flight-tested ramjet components, mastering supersonic air-breathing propulsion has remained a key technological hurdle for its defense industry.
The Financial Times reported that correspondence between Russian and Iranian officials regarding the next development phase of C430L continued through mid-2026.
Russia’s export revenues have also temporarily surged by 27% year-over-year in the second quarter to $125.7 billion, driven by global energy price spikes and Middle East supply disruptions. Driven by climbing Urals crude prices and expanded agricultural quotas, the brief foreign currency influx strengthened the ruble through late May.

Ukraine’s Commander-in-Chief Unveils New Military Principles Focused on People and Frontline Efficiency
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
21:06:05 UTC
06:06:05 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Ukraine’s Commander-in-Chief Unveils New Military Principles Focused on People and Frontline Efficiency
Ukraine’s Commander-in-Chief Major General Mykhailo Drapatyi has published on September 2 a foundational document titled "Leadership Principles of the Commander-in-Chief of the Armed Forces of Ukraine and Military Development in Conditions of War."
The framework outlines his intent, eight key development priorities, fourteen requirements for commanders at all levels, and eight expectations for headquarters operations.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The policy obligates commanders to prepare service members for combat, mitigate unnecessary risk, provide care for the wounded, honor deceased soldiers, and support military families.
Further guidelines demand that officers distinguish between military decisiveness and recklessness during operations, emphasizing that every unjustified loss weakens the defense effort. Extended support for veterans will be coordinated alongside government ministries, local authorities, and volunteer groups.
Defending civilians, cities, villages, and critical infrastructure against enemy attacks stands as the top military priority. To achieve this, the strategy focuses on stabilizing the frontline, maintaining and building combat capabilities, taking the initiative where possible, and preventing the adversary from fulfilling its operational objectives.
The doctrine explicitly addresses long-standing concerns regarding military service timelines, rotations, and discharge procedures. The stated goal is to reform the systems of recruitment, training, deployment, and discharge to ensure military service becomes predictable, fair, and professional. Personnel decisions will rely on institutional requirements, professional performance, and practical results.
The document mandates objective assessments across all levels of command and prohibits personal ambition, fear, or false optimism from distorting operational reporting. A strict standard of conduct applies equally to generals, officers, non-commissioned officers, and civilian managers, prohibiting corruption, abuse of power, harassment, discrimination, and misuse of state resources.
Headquarters at all levels are instructed to evaluate processes through a single metric: whether an activity directly enhances combat effectiveness. Under these directives, excess reporting is reduced, duplicate tasks are eliminated, and staff structures are required to become smaller, faster, and more supportive of frontline units.
The framework stresses the necessity of rapid adaptation and the integration of new technologies to minimize risks for personnel holding the frontline. Commanders are required to foster environments where effective solutions can be proposed by any service member regardless of rank, while reinforcing that joint operations across all military branches are essential for success during Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
The implementation details, specific tasks, and performance indicators corresponding to these principles will be detailed in separate official documents.
Previously, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy stated that the new Commander-in-Chief of the Armed Forces of Ukraine, Mykhailo Drapatyi, and the acting Defense Minister, Yevhen Khmara, were tasked with strengthening the country’s air defense and reforming its mobilization system.
Speaking at a press conference in Kyiv alongside Irish Prime Minister Micheál Martin on July 23, 2026, Zelenskyy emphasized that the two defense leaders were required to work in close coordination to address critical challenges arising from Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, specifically focusing on securing the airspace, protecting border areas, and normalizing mobilization practices through Territorial Recruitment and Social Support Centers.

US-Iran war: Old videos falsely claim to show new attacks on American bases
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02

US-Iran war: Old videos falsely claim to show new attacks on American bases
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
Issued on:
As US-Iran hostilities flare up and strikes has resumed, so has a wave of misinformation online. Old and unrelated videos are flooding social media, falsely presented as footage of new attacks. As tensions escalate, lips filmed in Dubai, Russia and the US have been misrepresented as Iranian strikes on US bases in the Gulf. Another 68-year-old video of a US nuclear test has been falsely claimed to show Iran detonating mines in the Strait of Hormuz. Vedika Bahl fact-checks in Truth or Fake.
After a monthlong lull in hostilities, the United States launched fresh airstrikes on Iran on Sunday, prompting retaliation from Tehran and renewed fighting across the Middle East. But as the strikes have resumed, so has a wave of misinformation.
As Iran responded to the US strikes by targeting American allies and military sites across the region, social media users began sharing old and unrelated footage, falsely claiming it showed the latest attacks in Jordan, Kuwait and around the Strait of Hormuz.
One widely viewed video, gaining hundreds of thousands of views,claimed to show a US military base in Jordan engulfed in flames. However, it has been circulating online for around six months and was originally presented as footage of a drone attack on the US consulate in Dubai, which we confirmed via geolocation analysis.
Another account shared a blurry clip claiming to show the Iranian military "pounding American bases in Jordan with heavy missiles." In reality, the footage was filmed last year in Ryazan, southeast of Moscow, following a Ukrainian drone attack on a Russian oil refinery.
Similar false claims have also emerged around US facilities elsewhere in the Gulf. One video was shared as purported footage of Iran shelling the US consulate in Kuwait, except the original video is from a SWAT operation explosion on a house in Arlington, Virginia.
And the misleading information is not confined to attacks on US facilities.
As tensions remain high around the strategically important Strait of Hormuz, users have also circulated old footage claiming to show Iran detonating naval mines in the waterway. The video has appeared across platforms including X, Facebook and Instagram, with some posts claiming the alleged mine explosions were intended to intimidate the United States.
The footage however, is 68 years old, and not linked to the Strait of Hormuz. A reverse image search traces the video to Operation Hardtack I, a series of US nuclear tests conducted in 1958. The specific footage shows the underwater nuclear test known as “Wahoo”, which was carried out at Enewetak in the Pacific Ocean.
So while the video may look like a dramatic record of fighting in the Strait of Hormuz, it actually shows a 1958 American nuclear test in the Pacific.

Turning prison laundries into cells won’t fix overcrowding – former UK MP
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
20:56:31 UTC
05:56:31 KST

Turning prison laundries into cells won’t fix overcrowding – former UK MP
The British government’s plan to turn prison laundries and other unused spaces into cells will not solve the country’s jail overcrowding crisis, former MP Andrew Bridgen has told RT.
The Ministry of Justice has fast-tracked £110 million ($149 million) from existing budgets for the conversions, saying this week it could create between 200 and 900 additional places.
The adult male prison estate is operating at more than 98% capacity, with around 1,500 places reportedly available at the start of September, the lowest level this year.
Speaking to RT on Wednesday, Bridgen said that creating more space would not address the system’s deeper problems. “Quite honestly, we need a root and branch reform of these institutions,” he said.
Bridgen blamed years of chronic underfunding for worsening conditions, saying that “overcrowding is causing huge problems.” Around 30 people a day are arrested over social-media posts and that some 1,200 are imprisoned each year, he said.
He also accused the authorities of “two-tier policing,” saying: “If you call someone a pedophile, you’ll probably go to prison. But if you actually are a pedophile, it would appear the judicial system doesn’t put you in prison.”
With jails close to full, ministers have retained an early-release program due to begin in October. However, around 4,500 inmates are expected to be set free in ten stages through June 2027, down from approximately 6,000 under the original proposal.
The reduction followed a public outcry over the plan, prompting British Prime Minister Andy Burnham to tighten the eligibility rules and bar prisoners convicted of manslaughter, rape, grooming, serious child sex offenses, indecent assault, and death by dangerous driving.
The policy follows an emergency measure introduced in September 2024 that allowed eligible inmates to leave after serving 40% of their sentences, rather than half.
Under the new system, qualifying prisoners serving standard determinate sentences may be freed after completing one-third of their custodial term. Those convicted of more serious eligible offenses must serve at least half, while misconduct can keep an inmate behind bars for longer. The remainder of each sentence is served under supervision.
The Ministry projects that the prison population in England and Wales could rise from 87,332 in November 2025 to between 98,000 and 103,600 by March 2030.

Government bodies differ, Centre to test green crackers afresh

20:54:14 UTC

Centre Wednesday told Supreme Court that it intended to conduct fresh tests to assess the harmful impact of the use of barium
NEW DELHI: As two govt organisations took contradictory stands on commercial production of next-generation green firecrackers - with Council of Scientific and Industrial Research-NEERI approving new formulations and Central Pollution Control Board objecting - Centre Wednesday told Supreme Court that it intended to conduct fresh tests to assess the harmful impact of the use of barium.Additional solicitor general Aishwarya Bhati told a bench of Justices M M Sundresh and Augustine George Masih that govt, after consulting stakeholders, had decided to conduct the tests in New Delhi, Bhopal, Kolkata and Chennai.Centre had asked CSIR-NEERI to develop green/low-emission fireworks - with particulate matter (PM) emission reduction of more than 50% - in association with manufacturers. Tamil Nadu Fireworks and Amorces Manufacturers' Association (Tanfama) devised new-generation formulation crackers with a reduced quantity of barium salts/nitrates in combination with other oxidisers.In a report, CSIR-NEERI said with the new formulations, emission reductions achieved for PM10 and PM2.5 were between 45% and 60%, and recommended that the formulations for light-emission fireworks (such as flowerpots, sparklers, chakkars, pencils, twinkling stars and their hybrids) be considered for commercial production.It also approved the manufacture of 'joined crackers', known as 'ladis', which have been banned by a court order.
The report said there was a reduction in PM emissions by approximately 30% and a reduction in solid waste generation by up to 32% for joined crackers.CPCB asked how barium nitrate could be used in crackers when it was banned by SC. "This court, vide order dated Oct 23, 2018, has expressly banned the use of barium salts in firecrackers and, therefore, any formulation involving barium compounds, even in reduced quantities, is in contravention of the said order," it said in its communication to govt.
"The reported reduction in PM10 and PM2.5 levels has not been comparatively assessed with (i) improved low-emission crackers and (ii) green crackers formulated entirely without barium, rendering the claim incomplete and inconclusive," it added.The petitioners, on whose plea polluting firecrackers were banned, submitted that the court had over the years passed eight orders to ban the use of barium and its use in cracker manufacturing could not be allowed.SC asked Centre to get suggestions from experts, saying the court had no expertise in these matters.
