Kennedy Center removes ‘Blue’ sculpture as Trump presses on with Washington makeover
WASHINGTON – A crane removed the 7m sculpture “Blue” from the Kennedy Center grounds on Sept 2 in the latest move to redesign Washington’s public spaces under President Donald Trump.
The sculpture, made of rectangular blue aluminium blocks, had sat near where a tarp obscures the centre’s facade, as Trump allies continue court battles to try to keep his name on the front of the complex, created by an act of Congress to memorialise slain President John F. Kennedy.
Created by artist Joel Shapiro, “Blue” resembles a soaring stick figure with arms outstretched and one leg kicked up in the air. Since 2019, it was located on a grassy area between the main Kennedy Center building and a separate venue called “The Reach” used for arts education.
The Kennedy Center confirmed in a statement that the statue would be removed and said artwork deinstallations were common practice.
“We are deeply grateful to Joel Shapiro for the years Blue has spent animating our campus and connecting visitors to his vision,” a Kennedy Center spokesperson said.
Trump is pursuing an ambitious remaking of Washington, with plans for projects ranging from a new White House ballroom, which he calls a national security priority, to a 76m arch.
Administration lawyers argued in a court filing last week that the Kennedy Center could eventually face demolition without major repairs.
Since taking office in 2025, Trump has removed the centre’s leadership, changed its programming and appointed a board that has closed the centre for renovations. A US district court judge ordered in May that Trump’s name be removed from the facade.
The Kennedy Center board, controlled by Trump appointees, subsequently voted on Aug 13 to put Trump’s name back on the building, calling it “The John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts Restored and Renovated by President Donald J. Trump”. This move has set up a potential clash with the judge. REUTERS

What do you do when you can’t hear the bombs? Being deaf during the Gaza genocide.
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
16:04:00 UTC
01:04:00 KST

Zuhdi Murtaja, a deaf man working in a community kitchen serving children with hearing disabilities in Gaza City, posed a question in sign language.
“How can we protect ourselves if we can’t hear the bombings or the warnings? And where is the safe place?”
Fadl Kuraz, a sign-language interpreter and trainer who has spent more than three decades working with Gaza’s deaf community, paused before answering.
“There isn’t always a safe place,” he told him.
Instead, Kuraz gave him practical advice: watch the people around you. If they suddenly start running, run with them. Carry a card that says, “I am deaf. I need help.”
For Gaza’s deaf community, the war has added a layer of danger that is largely overlooked amidst the inhumane conditions with which the whole population grapples on a daily basis. Unable to hear incoming strikes, evacuation orders, or emergency sirens, they are fully dependent on others to interpret a rapidly changing reality — and in a war that has killed more than 73,000 people and displaced nearly the entire population of the Strip, that dependence has become a matter of survival.
A 2023 UNDRR survey of more than 6,000 people with disabilities across 132 countries found that 56 percent either were unaware of disaster-risk information available in accessible formats or could not access it. In Gaza, where the infrastructure for reaching people with disabilities has largely collapsed, this gap is acutely felt.
Kuraz has become one of the few people still trying to close it.
“The hardest thing deaf people face during the war is not only the bombing,” Kuraz says. “It is being unable to access information when they need it most.”
Kuraz — who holds a master’s degree in educational psychology and studied special education in Jordan with a focus on hearing impairment — dedicated the years before the genocide to helping the hearing impaired. This included sign-language education, supporting deaf students, helping teachers communicate with them, and running training sessions at the Atfaluna Society for Deaf Children, one of Gaza’s primary organizations serving people with hearing disabilities.
The war has entirely changed the demands of that work.
He now moves between educational points established by Atfaluna across displacement areas and neighborhoods, including al-Shati, al-Nasr, Sheikh Radwan, al-Jalaa, and Tal al-Hawa in Gaza City — all of them tent structures within shelter centers, lacking the basics. His work often starts with questions about the students rather than their lessons: How are they coping? Have new families arrived? Does anyone need batteries for a hearing aid? Has anyone developed hearing problems after another night of bombardment?
A different kind of access
At an educational point run by Atfaluna in the Jalaa area of Gaza City, a distant blast interrupts the activity. The vibrations cause some children to freeze. Others turn toward Kuraz.
He reassures them through sign language, and the teachers move them to simple games and activities. Within minutes, the children are laughing and competing for his attention.
Kuraz keeps his expression calm. This, he says, is among the most demanding parts of the work.
“I have to control my emotions and my facial expressions within seconds,” he says. “If I lose that control, the children will lose their sense of safety.”
The pressure does not end when he leaves. “The fear I suppress during the day catches up with me at night,” he says.
Many of the teachers working with deaf students are hearing educators whose sign-language skills continue to develop through practice. Kuraz works with them to strengthen their communication with students and better understand their needs.
“There are always new expressions, new situations, and signs that teachers don’t know,” he says. “I help strengthen their language because language is what connects these children to education.”
But education is only one part of the problem.
For deaf Palestinians, information that hearing people may receive automatically — through conversations, public announcements, television, or warning sirens — often has to be made accessible in another form.
During active Israeli attacks, that gap can have immediate consequences. When Kuraz meets students, they often want to know what has happened outside the classroom: Where was the bombing? Which neighborhoods were affected? Is there an evacuation? What is happening outside the shelter?
“They need someone to explain what is happening around them,” Kuraz says. “Political developments, humanitarian conditions, and changes in their communities — things that many hearing people receive naturally, but deaf people often cannot access.”
Murtaja himself has become part of that information network. A graduate of al-Rafa’i School for the Deaf in Gaza City, he completed university through a program specifically designed for deaf students. During the war, alongside his work at the Atfaluna kitchen, he administers a WhatsApp group and remains continuously present alongside Kuraz, monitoring political news and developments and helping pass information to the deaf community.
The problem extends beyond information sharing. Displacement has made it harder for deaf people to reach services, while many shelters, health facilities, and humanitarian responses are not designed around their communication needs.
“The challenge isn’t only reaching deaf people,” Kuraz says. “It’s that the services themselves are often not designed with them in mind.”
Access to hearing aids and their essential supplies has also been a persistent challenge. Atfaluna has previously reported that families of people with hearing disabilities struggled to obtain hearing-aid batteries and other necessary assistive equipment during periods of conflict. The challenge has continued amid Gaza’s wider shortages and disruption to essential services.
Measuring hearing loss
The scale of war-related hearing impairment in Gaza remains difficult to measure precisely — but the available data points to a crisis that is vast and largely invisible.
Before the war, approximately 20,000 people in Gaza were estimated to be living with hearing disabilities, according to data from rehabilitation centers and specialized associations cited by Al Jazeera. Field workers warn the number has risen sharply since October 2023, with estimates now reaching 30,000 to 40,000 people with hearing loss or impairment — many of them children.
The Global Protection Cluster’s July 2025 report estimated that over 35,000 people in Gaza have sustained significant hearing damage due to explosions. The same report noted that while comprehensive data on hearing and vision impairments resulting from hostilities is not consistently tracked, organizations working with people with sensory impairments report a substantial rise in the number of people with hearing and visual difficulties seeking services.
Atfaluna’s own assessments provide a further indication of the scale. Between December 2024 and August 2025, the organization screened 32,753 people and identified 2,500 children and adults with new hearing impairment as a direct consequence of the conflict.
That figure is not a total count, as it only reflects cases identified among those assessed. Gaza’s deaf community now includes people who were deaf before October 7, 2023, as well as people who developed hearing impairment during the attacks. Their communication needs are not always the same. Someone deaf from birth has usually developed sign language and a framework for navigating a world without sound. Someone who loses their hearing during a bombardment faces a sudden and disorienting loss, with no language to replace what sound once carried, and no established community to turn to.
On top of that, the organizations trying to help them face acute shortages themselves. Hearing devices, batteries, and cochlear implant parts remain severely restricted due to import limitations, according to Al Jazeera’s reporting. Many rehabilitation centers providing speech therapy and psychological and educational support have been damaged or destroyed.
For Kuraz, the work continues regardless. At the educational points, he helps teachers and students communicate despite displacement and repeated interruptions. And when the situation outside changes, the questions are often the same ones he heard from Murtaja at the start of the war:
What happened? Where should we go? What happens next?
Murtaja has not stopped asking them or helping others find the answers. In the WhatsApp group he runs, news circulates among deaf community members who would otherwise have no way of knowing what is happening around them. It is a small system, built from almost nothing, in the middle of a war.
“If they see fear on my face,” Kuraz said, “it will become theirs.”

China's zero-tariff treatment, enhanced RMB settlement to boost Africa-China trade: S. African banking executive
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
00:03:13 CST
01:03:13 KST

JOHANNESBURG, Sept. 2 (Xinhua) -- China's zero-tariff treatment is helping African businesses lower export costs, while growing renminbi (RMB) settlement capacity is further facilitating trade between Africa and China, a South African banking executive said Wednesday.
In a statement, Bill Blackie, chief executive of Business and Commercial Banking at Standard Bank Group, said that African exporters, including those from South Africa, Kenya, Zimbabwe and Nigeria, have begun to see tangible benefits from improved access to the Chinese market since China's zero-tariff treatment for 53 African countries with which it has diplomatic relations took effect on May 1.
"For many businesses, the emerging opportunity is not only to reduce landed costs, but to broaden export destinations, improve route-to-market resilience and reduce reliance on a narrow set of trading partners," he said.
The benefits of the zero-tariff treatment are already being felt across a range of African products entering the Chinese market, he said, citing South African apples as an example.
The first shipment of South African apples cleared through Shenzhen Bay Port under the framework following the removal of a previous 10 percent tariff, saving the importer about 20,000 yuan (about 2,976 U.S. dollars). Based on historical import volumes, the importer projected annual savings of more than 1.47 million dollars.
Kenyan coffee, Zimbabwean tobacco and Nigerian bovine bone products are among other African products benefiting from the zero-tariff framework, he added.
Beyond immediate tariff savings, Blackie said the policy is providing African businesses with opportunities to diversify export destinations and strengthen trade resilience amid growing uncertainties in the global trading environment.
Standard Bank's latest Africa Trade Barometer showed that 35 percent of businesses surveyed across 10 African markets identified Asian countries as their preferred trading partners, up from 24 percent in 2024, while China remains a major source of imported inputs for African businesses, cited by 67 percent of respondents.
Blackie also noted that improved RMB settlement and payment capabilities are helping businesses translate better market access into actual trade flows by reducing transaction friction and improving efficiency along the Africa-China trade corridor.
As Africa-China trade expands, greater use of the RMB in cross-border transactions could further lower trading costs and improve settlement efficiency, he said.
Standard Bank, in partnership with the Industrial and Commercial Bank of China, has developed an integrated ecosystem across payments, foreign exchange, trade finance and risk management for businesses trading between Africa and China, Blackie said.
Through its participation in China's Cross-Border Interbank Payment System, or CIPS, Standard Bank currently provides RMB payment connectivity in 10 African markets, enabling some cross-border payments to be settled within minutes rather than days, he added.
Blackie said the businesses that combine the tariff reduction with the settlement, payment and market-connectivity infrastructure required to make the corridor a stable and scalable part of their trade operations will stand to benefit most. ■

A press conference is held by the information office of the Xizang regional government to brief the rescue and relief efforts after a mudslide struck Gyirong Port on the China-Nepal border in the autonomous region, in Gyirong Town, southwest China's Xizang Autonomous Region, Sept. 2, 2026. (Xinhua/Tenzing Nima Qadhup)
GYIRONG, Xizang, Sept. 2 (Xinhua) -- Twenty-one people have been confirmed dead and 541 others remain missing as of Wednesday noon after a mudslide struck Gyirong Port on the China-Nepal border in southwest China's Xizang Autonomous Region on Aug. 26, according to the regional government's latest news briefing.
Rescuers have recovered 847 pieces of personal belongings, according to the news briefing. Local authorities have received 876 phone calls from the relatives of the victims and missing people, and have been promptly replying to their requests.
Caused by an ice-rock avalanche in Nepal, the deadly mudslide swept through the area and destroyed buildings, power supplies and a section of the G216 highway leading to Gyirong Port, which seriously hampered emergency response and rescue efforts.
Despite such difficulties, China has immediately mobilized helicopters, speedboats and rubber rafts to carry rescuers to the mudslide-hit port. Ground rescue teams have spent 12 hours traversing the steep mountain roads and reached the area on foot.
To date, some 2,300 rescue personnel, more than 400 search-and-rescue vehicles, over 8,000 sets of professional equipment, over 800 drone flights and 24 helicopter flights have been deployed. A total of 5.43 tonnes of materials and equipment have been airdropped to the area.
Telecom operators have restored 12 base stations in the port area, ensuring communications for emergency command, rescue operations and supply coordination.
At the core affected zone, some 336 rescuers have conducted multiple rounds of thorough and exhaustive search and rescue operations, covering a cumulative area of 1.591 million square meters.
Road access to the zone was basically restored at 10 a.m. Wednesday after days of round-the-clock repair work on the G216. Over 10 pieces of heavy machinery have entered the core area to aid on-site rescuers. ■

Asia-Pacific Community: Joint rescue efforts underscore enduring China-Nepal friendship amid deadly mudslide
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03

01:03:02 KST

KATHMANDU, Sept. 2 (Xinhua) -- Faced with the catastrophic mudslide disaster battering Nepal's border regions, China has stood firmly with its long-time neighbor with timely assistance and professional rescue support, turning bilateral friendship into tangible life-saving actions and showcasing the spirit of mutual assistance amid adversity.
A fast-moving chain mudslide, triggered by a high-altitude glacier collapse in Nepal, buried tunnels, destroyed roads, cut off transportation links, and left over 1,200 dead and more than 4,200 people missing by 6 p.m. local time Wednesday in Nepal.
The unprecedented scale of silt deposition and complex underground environments have posed unprecedented challenges to search and rescue operations, making the disaster far more difficult to tackle than conventional geological catastrophes.
"The situation in the mudslide-hit area has far exceeded expectations -- more severe than any disaster I have seen before," Pan Jiangyuan, who has been engaged in tunnel rescue for over 15 years, told Xinhua. "The tunnel is almost completely blocked by silt -- a situation that is unheard of and extremely rare in tunnel rescue."
Pan is one of the nine Chinese tunnel rescue experts sent to Nepal by the Chinese government, along with four DNA identification experts.
As a team member, Pan worked alongside Nepalese military rescue personnel for several consecutive days, conducting reconnaissance and search missions in designated rescue areas.
"We used a flotation device -- a raft -- with rescuers lying on it and moving forward bit by bit. We also used drones for reconnaissance," he said, explaining that in some areas the silt was so deep that personnel couldn't go in alone on foot.
Reshmi, the press officer at the Nepalese rescue command camp, said that the Chinese rescue team was one of the first international rescue teams that came to Nepal to assist in the search and rescue operations.
"We are working very closely together. This is a joint operation, and we are making joint efforts. We have also exchanged liaison officers to strengthen communication and coordination," he said.
As the relief operation unfolds in phases, China has continued to deliver multi-dimensional, all-round support to Nepal's disaster relief and post-disaster recovery. Since the disaster erupted, China has sent two batches of relief supplies to Nepal, continuously shared real-time meteorological and hydrological data, and provided professional technical consultations and early risk warnings to assist Nepal's risk assessment and emergency response.
Chinese social organizations, enterprises and overseas Chinese communities in Nepal have also actively joined the relief campaign.
The China Foundation for Rural Development has set up a forward operating base along the Trisuli River in Nuwakot, leveraging a local hospital as a comprehensive platform for material storage, personnel scheduling and follow-up medical support.
Zou Zhiqiang, director of the foundation's Nepal office, said that the relief work is being carried out in a scientific, phased manner tailored to evolving disaster needs. The current priority remains life-saving search and rescue. The subsequent stage will focus on recovering the deceased and relevant follow-up arrangements, while the third phase will center on resident resettlement, medical services and livelihood restoration.
"The foundation is preparing materials in advance according to the different needs of each phase. We plan to ship some 22 tonnes of relief supplies from China so that they can be put into use as soon as the follow-up work is fully launched," Zou said.
Huawei, together with local Nepalese operators, immediately launched communication network restoration work to ensure basic communication needs in the affected areas. The Nepal Overseas Chinese Association also initiated a fundraising campaign to aid affected residents.
"In this hour of national grief, PRC's prompt support once again reaffirms the enduring strength of our time-tested bilateral friendship," Nepali President Ram Chandra Poudel wrote on social media.
China's foreign ministry said Wednesday that the country is preparing a third batch of emergency relief supplies to Nepal, including Bailey bridges, epidemic prevention materials and emergency communications equipment, adding that China is ready to send a second group of DNA identification experts based on Nepal's needs.
"This is more than humanitarian assistance. It is a powerful expression of good neighbourliness, solidarity and the longstanding friendship between Nepal and China," Pushpa Raj Pradhan, editor-in-chief of People's Review, said. ■

According to UNICEF, intensifying droughts, extreme heat and severe flooding threaten children's nutrition, health, education, safety, and access to safe water and sanitation.
Etleva Kadilli, UNICEF regional director for eastern and southern Africa, warned that the threat from El Nino is accelerating and the risks to children are already clear, adding that forecasts provide a narrow yet critical window to act before the worst impacts materialize.
"Across the region, children are facing food and water insecurity, overstretched health services and disrupted learning. Further, major climate shocks will likely push children and the systems they rely on to breaking point," Kadilli said in a statement.
UNICEF assessments highlight compounding and immediate risks for children across Djibouti, Eritrea, Ethiopia, Kenya, Madagascar, Malawi, Mozambique, Somalia, South Sudan, Sudan, Uganda, Zambia, and Zimbabwe.
In Somalia, severe flooding could directly affect up to 2.5 million people, fueling displacement and disrupting access to food, healthcare, safe water and education, UNICEF said.
In Ethiopia, tens of thousands of children face heightened risks, particularly in regions already grappling with acute food insecurity and deep vulnerability.
Meanwhile, in South Sudan, a combination of drought, extreme heat and localized flooding threatens to exacerbate food insecurity and malnutrition, trigger disease outbreaks, and compound the risks of famine and large-scale displacement, it said.
Less than 1 percent of international humanitarian assistance is currently allocated to anticipatory action, a critical oversight given its vital role in saving lives, mitigating human suffering and safeguarding hard-won development gains, according to UNICEF.
It said early, flexible financing is essential to blunt the impact of El Nino before conditions deteriorate further.
To address these critical response gaps before impacts peak, UNICEF is calling for urgent investments to scale up nutrition services, including by pre-positioning life-saving supplies and expanding early screening and treatment.
It also called for stronger health systems, improved disease surveillance and vaccination campaigns, safe water access, and measures to keep children learning, including by reinforcing school infrastructure and establishing alternative learning spaces. ■

ENHANCING BILATERAL EXCHANGES, COOPERATION

In response, Namibia will adopt a phased elimination approach based on the intensity of transmission in different areas, according to Luvindao.
The ministry is also finalizing quality-assurance guidelines and strengthening the role of community health workers in malaria testing and treatment.
To reduce imported infections, Namibia plans to formalize cross-border surveillance, data sharing and joint response measures with neighboring Angola, Zambia and Botswana, Luvindao said. The ministry has described it as a key malaria prevention measure but said low household participation has weakened its effectiveness.

====================================================================================================

Maternal sleep latency during early pregnancy is linked to child intelligence scores
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
16:00:58 UTC
01:00:58 KST

Pregnant people often experience changes in their sleep patterns, but the long-term effects of these disruptions on the developing fetus are not fully understood. A recent study suggests that maternal sleep difficulties, particularly taking a long time to fall asleep, are associated with slightly lower intelligence scores in children at age four. The research, published in the Journal of Child Psychology and Psychiatry, also points to specific metabolic chemicals in the pregnant person’s blood that might link poor sleep to offspring brain development.
Nearly half of pregnant individuals report experiencing poor sleep quality. During pregnancy, hormonal, physical, and psychological shifts can dramatically alter a person’s sleep and wake cycles. Concurrently, fetal brain development occurs at a rapid pace.
Because the developing brain is highly adaptable, it is sensitive to the prenatal environment. Prior research has connected maternal sleep problems to adverse outcomes like preterm birth and low birth weight. Animal models have indicated that maternal sleep deprivation alters fetal brain structures, specifically areas involved in memory and learning.
Human studies have also hinted at a connection between prenatal sleep and a child’s cognitive outcomes. Most of these investigations assessed sleep at only one point in time. Pregnancy involves distinct phases of neural system development, meaning the timing of sleep disruptions could influence the brain differently. The basic architectural structures of the brain form rapidly during the first trimester. While the third trimester involves brain growth and maturation, the groundwork laid earlier makes early-pregnancy exposures particularly impactful.
Sleep is a foundational biological process that regulates metabolism. Disrupted sleep can alter glucose processing, increase inflammation, and change how the body breaks down nutrients. Researchers Yun Huang and Jun Zhang of the Shanghai Jiao Tong University School of Medicine wanted to track how sleep patterns throughout all three trimesters related to child intelligence. They also aimed to identify specific chemical markers, or metabolites, that might explain this biological connection.
The researchers analyzed data from 1,870 mother and child pairs enrolled in the Shanghai Birth Cohort. During their first, second, and third trimesters, the pregnant participants completed questionnaires detailing their sleep habits. These surveys asked about sleep duration, subjective sleep quality, and sleep latency. Sleep latency is the amount of time it takes to transition from full wakefulness to sleep.
When the children reached four years of age, trained staff evaluated their intelligence using a standardized assessment called the Wechsler Primary and Preschool Scale of Intelligence. This test measures a child’s full-scale intelligence quotient, or IQ, alongside specific cognitive abilities. Verbal comprehension measures a child’s ability to access and apply acquired word knowledge. Fluid reasoning evaluates the capacity to detect underlying conceptual relationships and use reasoning to solve novel problems.
The researchers used statistical models to compare the maternal sleep data from each trimester with the children’s test scores. They adjusted their calculations to account for maternal age, education, physical activity, and family history of mental disorders.
The analysis showed an association between taking longer to fall asleep and lower cognitive scores. Longer sleep latency in the first trimester was linked to lower full-scale IQ and lower verbal comprehension scores. In the second trimester, longer sleep latency was associated with lower fluid reasoning scores. Sleep difficulties in the third trimester did not yield statistically significant associations with the children’s test scores.
Next, the researchers evaluated how consistent sleep patterns across the entirety of pregnancy related to child brain development. They used a statistical technique to group participants based on how their sleep quality changed from the first trimester to the third. This longitudinal approach allowed the team to see the cumulative impact of sleep struggles. They found that individuals who consistently experienced longer sleep latency throughout their entire pregnancy had children with lower full-scale IQ, verbal comprehension, and fluid reasoning scores at age four.
To understand the biological mechanisms behind these observations, the researchers looked at metabolites. Metabolites are small molecules produced when the body breaks down food, chemicals, or its own tissue. The team analyzed fasting blood samples taken from 1,461 of the pregnant participants during their first trimester.
The researchers conducted untargeted metabolomic profiling. Instead of looking for a few specific chemicals, this technique scans the blood for hundreds of small molecules simultaneously, providing a broad snapshot of the body’s metabolic state. After identifying 413 metabolites in the maternal serum, they used a “meet-in-the-middle” analytical strategy. They first looked for metabolites linked to maternal sleep factors, then looked for metabolites linked to child test scores, and finally focused on the overlapping chemicals that connected the two endpoints.
Three specific molecules emerged as potential mediators: inositol, indoleacrylic acid, and 4-hydroxyquinoline. Inositol is a sugar that is synthesized by the body and found in common foods like fruits and beans. It is transferred across the placenta to the fetus, where it contributes to neurotransmitter signaling. The researchers observed an indirect path where maternal sleep duration was linked to child fluid reasoning through changes in maternal inositol levels.
Indoleacrylic acid and 4-hydroxyquinoline are byproducts of tryptophan, an amino acid involved in producing sleep-regulating hormones like serotonin and melatonin. Poor sleep can alter how the body breaks down tryptophan, increasing inflammatory pathways and changing the availability of serotonin, a hormone essential for neuronal growth. The researchers found that sleep disturbances influenced offspring verbal comprehension via alterations in these two tryptophan-related molecules.
The study relied on self-reported questionnaires to assess maternal sleep. These surveys capture a person’s subjective perception of their rest, which might differ from objective measurements like brainwave monitoring or movement tracking devices. The metabolic analysis only tested blood samples from the first trimester. A person’s metabolic profile can fluctuate due to diet and physical activity, meaning a single measurement might not capture the full biological environment across the entire pregnancy.
The large number of metabolites tested also increases the mathematical risk of identifying false associations, requiring future studies to validate these specific chemical links. Most participants in this sample had a college degree, meaning the findings might not generalize to populations with different educational or socioeconomic backgrounds. Because sleep disturbances are sometimes a symptom of underlying psychiatric conditions, residual genetic or environmental factors could still influence the outcomes.
The study, “Maternal sleep disturbance during pregnancy and child intelligence quotient: A metabolome-wide association study in the Shanghai Birth Cohort,” was authored by Yun Huang, Fei Luo, Guanghai Wang, Ting Zhang, Lin Zhang, Lichun Fan, and Jun Zhang.

A roll of 25 $1 coins was available for sale for $61 — a mark-up of 144 percent — with a 100-coin bag available for $154.50.
Households are limited to only two orders, the US Mint wrote, but that cap will lift at 2 pm Eastern time on Thursday.
The move to put Trump's countenance on a coin with monetary value runs counter to federal law that says no living president may appear on US currency. But in some circumstances, the treasury secretary does have authority to authorise the minting and issuance of special coins.
Calvin Coolidge was the first living US president to appear on a coin, featured on the front of the 1926 Sesquicentennial of American Independence Half Dollar.
$250 bill
The new coin features Trump's face on one side, with the words "Liberty" and "In God We Trust."
It also features the dates 1776-2026, marking 250 years of US independence.
The other side of the coin features a version of the US presidential seal, depicting an eagle clutching arrows and an olive branch while covered by a shield that says "250."
This is just the latest in Trump's campaign to put his face and name on US currency.
In May, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said his department was pursuing a plan to issue a new $250 bill with Trump's face on it.
He conceded that the move would require Congress to change the law barring living persons from appearing on currency.
In March, the Treasury announced that US paper money would soon bear Trump's signature — another first for a sitting US president.

How a quiz show and a dream took Azerbaijan's Sabah to the Champions League
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
15:55:35 UTC
00:55:35 KST

Azerbaijan’s Sabah Football Club have unexpectedly qualified for the UEFA Champions League, making it one of its most historic achievements to date.
"I think this story about the TV quiz is a little overrated," Valdas Dambrauskas told Euronews after he became the first Baltic coach to reach the Champions League main round, leading a club that did not exist nine years ago to fixtures against Arsenal, Manchester United and Barcelona.
In 2002, Dambrauskas won the prize money on the Lithuanian television show "Who Wants to Be a Millionaire?" and used it to move to England to fund his UEFA coaching badges.
He had no professional football background.
To pay for the courses, he worked as a babysitter, salesman and newspaper delivery man. He eventually got into the youth academies at Fulham, Brentford and Manchester United. Sabah FC in Baku is his 10th club.
"Sometimes it was difficult. I had to work hard, and sometimes to believe when myself and those around me were doubting," Dambrauskas recalled.
"I take this achievement as a milestone and believe that journey is more important. There are other dreams ahead and I really don't want to stop."
Sabah beat Hapoel Beer Sheva 5-2 last Tuesday — 6-4 on aggregate — to reach the Champions League main round, guaranteeing eight matches against European football's biggest clubs. Barcelona, Borussia Dortmund, Napoli and Slavia Prague will come to Baku.
Dambrauskas and his squad travel to Arsenal and Manchester United in England, then to Villarreal in Spain and Viking in Norway.
Dambrauskas was equally clear-eyed about what comes next.
"Everyone is speaking about the Champions League, but the Azerbaijan championship is what allows you to play there. It is very important we keep the focus and prepare for every game that we are going to play," he said.
"We have a fantastic international environment where a lot of times we select eleven different nationalities in the starting line-up. In this kind of environment the main word we base our philosophy on is respect."
'It is time to focus'
Sabah Futbol Klubu were founded in Baku in 2017. They won the Azerbaijan Cup in the 2024-25 season and the Azerbaijan Premier League title the following year, ending Qarabağ FK's domestic dominance.
Facing the likes of Barcelona and Arsenal came quickly in a rare footballing dream come true, and for Sabah right-back and right-winger Tellur Mutallimov, the scale of what lies ahead is a matter of focus, not thrills.
"Playing against clubs of this stature gives me a greater sense of responsibility and extra motivation rather than excitement," Mutallimov told Euronews.
"The celebrations are now behind us. It is time to focus all our attention on the important and difficult matches ahead."
Mutallimov paid tribute to supporters who had followed the club through the qualifying rounds.
"Even when we played far away from home in Denmark, England, Finland and Romania, we were not alone. We are grateful to our compatriots living abroad, who came to the stadiums and supported us during those matches."
Dambrauskas is assisted by Valerio Zuddas, a 37-year-old Italian who has worked across 10 countries and is responsible for the team's defensive organisation and analysis of European opponents.
"The biggest satisfaction for Valdas as head coach and for us as coaching staff is that we can clearly see how the players are into our team principles and how they believe in them," Zuddas told Euronews.
"Sometimes they find solutions by themselves inside our structure, their level of understanding of the game allows us to propose always different strategies and variations that help us to be more and more competitive," he said.
Dreaming differently about football
Club president Magsud Adigozalov said the route to the Champions League was built on analytics rather than spending.
"We could not compete financially with many established European clubs, so we had to find our own competitive advantages," Adigozalov told Euronews.
"We were inspired by the Moneyball philosophy, which demonstrated that intelligent use of data and recruitment can help a club compete far beyond what its financial size might suggest," he explained.
Yet to Adigozalov, the human factor always comes first.
"Footballers are people before they are assets or statistics. We try to provide players with excellent training and living conditions and treat them and their families with respect," Adigozalov said.
Sabah FC's total squad market value is estimated to be around €16.65 million, a far cry from Barcelona's €1.1 billion or Manchester United's €900 million.
Napoli centre-back Benoît Badiashile, who just transferred from Chelsea, is valued at roughly the same as the entire Azerbaijani squad.
Adigozalov remains undeterred and a firm believer in hard work above all.
"The Champions League is the result everyone can see today. What makes us especially proud is the system, the culture and the work behind it that people did not see for nine years."
Qualifying for the main round brings Sabah a base fee of millions of euros in direct UEFA distributions, alongside broadcasting rights income and new sponsorship opportunities.
Adigozalov said the longer-term impact will be on understanding that nothing is out of reach in sports like football.
"A young boy or girl sitting in the stadium and watching Barcelona or Borussia Dortmund play against Sabah may start dreaming differently about football," he said.
"If this achievement brings more children into football, more families into stadiums and creates greater belief in Azerbaijani football, then its impact will be much bigger than Sabah itself."

Reform UK bans three journalists who have investigated party from its conference
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
15:53:51 UTC
00:53:51 KST

Reform UK has banned at least three journalists from its annual conference who have reported critically on the party and Nigel Farage.
The Guardian’s City editor, Anna Isaac, the investigative reporter Peter Geoghegan and the broadcaster and biographer Michael Crick were told this week that their credentials to cover the event, which begins on Thursday, had been declined.
The party has billed its conference, which will take place at the National Exhibition Centre in Birmingham, as “the most talked about event of 2026”. Reform figures are hoping to use it as a reset after a difficult summer consumed by questions about an undeclared £5m gift Farage received shortly before he was elected in 2024.
A Reform spokesperson said Geoghegan and Crick were refused accreditation because the party viewed them as minor figures. They declined to comment on why Isaac was not given accreditation.
After the Guardian contacted Reform for comment, all three received emails saying their conference passes had been reinstated. However, when contacted again by the Guardian, a Reform spokesperson said this had been an administrative error and that they were still not accredited for the conference. They then received further emails confirming their exclusion.
Isaac broke the story that Farage had accepted an undeclared £5m gift from Christopher Harborne. Her reporting also revealed that a host of transactions involving Reform UK’s most senior figures and donations to the party caused bankers to report potential money-laundering concerns to the National Crime Agency.
The story has caused issues for Farage all summer and he has drastically reduced his time in front of the press. He also resigned as an MP over the furore, prompting a byelection which the other main parties boycotted, leaving Count Binface as his main opponent. Farage won, and was sworn back into parliament on Monday.
Geoghegan runs the Democracy for Sale newsletter on Substack and has written for the Guardian and the New York Times. He received the news he had been banned from the conference shortly after publishing a piece revealing negative comments the pro-Reform journalist Isabel Oakeshott allegedly made about Harborne. Oakeshott declined to comment about the allegations when the Guardian contacted her.
Geoghegan said: “Reform clearly wants press coverage but it doesn’t want the scrutiny and accountability that comes with it. Farage and co like to present themselves as the anti-establishment insurgents, but banning independent journalists like me from party conference isn’t anti-establishment. It’s the establishment playbook.”
Crick said: “I can understand why the Reform high command might not want me talking to ordinary party members.” He published an unflattering biography of Farage in 2022, including details of a letter a teacher once sent to the head of Dulwich college when Farage was proposed as a prefect, complaining about his “publicly professed racist and neo-fascist views”. Crick has also said he believes Farage “panders to racists”. He told the Telegraph this summer that Farage’s fatal flaw was that he was thin-skinned and purged people he disagreed with.
On the party’s apparent reinstatements and then U-turn, Crick said: “What cock-up merchants!”
A party spokesperson said: “Reform UK accepted 950 of about 1,000 media applications from a variety of outlets, including the entire Guardian lobby team.
“Mr Crick works for a university and Mr Geoghegan is a Substack blogger. Neither qualify for a media pass.”
The Reform spokesperson refused to give a reason for Isaac’s ban but said: “Anna will still be able to watch the conference proceedings on our livestream if she wishes.”
Laura Davison, NUJ general secretary, said: “Reports that Reform UK has chosen to ban journalists who have scrutinised the party from attending its conference are frustrating and concerning. A functioning democracy depends on a free press that can ask political parties difficult questions and hold those seeking power to account.”
Pointing to what she called “a wider pattern of intimidation and obstruction of journalists,” and noting that the Conservatives and Labour blocked or removed journalists from their conferences last year, Davison said: “We urge the government and all political parties to demonstrate their commitment to media freedom and uphold the public’s right to be informed. Reform UK should rethink its position and allow journalists full access to the conference.”
A Guardian spokesperson said: “Holding public figures to account is the role of a free press and an essential part of the democratic process. Our journalists should be able to ask questions in the public interest and not be deterred from doing their job.”

Dismissal of ex-US soldier Bergdahl’s conviction was invalid, court rules
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
15:53:33 UTC
00:53:33 KST

Dismissal of ex-US soldier Bergdahl’s conviction was invalid, court rules
Appeals panel says only military tribunals may assess court-martial convictions in blow to former Afghan war prisoner.
A federal judge had no authority to overturn former US Army soldier Bowe Bergdahl’s military conviction for deserting his post in Afghanistan before Taliban-allied forces captured him and held him for nearly five years, an appeals court has ruled.
A three-judge panel from the US Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit on Tuesday ordered the dismissal of Bergdahl’s claims in district court. The ruling essentially reinstates the ex-soldier’s conviction.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Mark Ruffalo comments spark pushback against anti-Semitism ‘smear campaign’
- list 2 of 3Massachusetts primary results: Key takeaways
- list 3 of 3What is Iran’s Castle Breaker missile, used against US bases?
The panel said District Judge Reggie Walton, sitting in Washington, DC, lacked the jurisdiction to vacate Bergdahl’s court-martial conviction and sentence in 2023.
Bergdahl had sued in civilian court in 2021, arguing that the military punishment violated his Fifth Amendment due-process rights. Walton ruled that military judge Jeffrey Nance created a potential conflict of interest by failing to disclose his application for a position as an immigration judge in the US Department of Justice.
But the appeals court concluded that only a court of appeals within the military justice system has the authority to overturn a court-martial judgement.
“Because Bergdahl seeks to have his court-martial conviction declared expunged and without effect due to violations of the Constitution and military rules, and its consequences reversed, he effectively asked the District Court to vacate the military judgment,” Circuit Judge Robert Wilkins wrote. “However, the authority to vacate a court-martial judgment belongs to tribunals exercising direct appellate review, not district courts conducting collateral review.”
Bergdahl, then a 23-year-old soldier from Hailey, Idaho, was stationed in eastern Afghanistan’s Paktika province in June 2009 when he left his post without permission. His defence team said he left to hike to headquarters to complain about what he viewed as poor leadership in his unit.
Bergdahl was captured by forces from the Taliban-affiliated Haqqani Network and repeatedly tortured before his release from captivity in 2014 as part of a prisoner swap under then-President Barack Obama.
The deal – which freed five Taliban prisoners from the Guantanamo Bay detention facility – was sharply criticised by some conservatives, including Donald Trump, who would be elected president two years later.
In 2015 during his campaign, Trump called for the death penalty for Bergdahl. He also criticised the decision to spare him jail time, calling it a “disgrace” to the country.
Several US service members were wounded during the search for Bergdahl, who was charged with desertion and misbehaviour before the enemy after his release from captivity. He pleaded guilty to both charges in 2017 and was dishonourably discharged. Prosecutors at his court martial had sought 14 years in prison.

The Logical End Point of AI Job Interviews Is Two Bots Talking to Each Other
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
15:51:46 UTC
00:51:46 KST

Christopher has become accustomed to jumping through the endless hoops of the modern job hunt. Like many government contractors, his work has dried up in the DOGE era. Over the past six months, he has applied to roughly 700 jobs; in the vast majority of cases, he’s heard nothing back.
Five of these applications have gone through “Riley,” an AI recruiter for the IT firm Everforth Apex Systems. The first time Riley reached out, Christopher was excited. It was June, and he had by then realized how difficult the job market was. (Christopher asked that WIRED use only his first name as his job hunt continues.) A text from Riley felt like a rare opportunity to pitch himself, even if his interlocutor was virtual.
During his first call with Riley, Christopher answered questions about his work authorization and his professional background. Riley promised that, if Christopher met the qualifications, someone would be in touch. But a human recruiter never reached out. Nor did the AI agent—until a little over a week later, when Riley texted Christopher about “another opportunity.”
Christopher hoped he could improve upon his original interview. So he set up another call with the AI agent. Then again for another job. And another. None of the interviews resulted in any follow-up conversations or emails; he never even received an automated rejection text.
By the fifth time Riley texted him, Christopher had had enough. If the company was going to use AI, he reasoned, why shouldn’t he do the same?
Christopher typed a handful of sentences of background information into ChatGPT Voice and told it to stand in as “Christopher.” Then, Christopher says, when Riley called, “I just put them next to each other, and they just hit it off.”
The call lasted 10 minutes. Riley told ChatGPT it was “great talking to you.” ChatGPT said it appreciated “how clear and straightforward the process was.” During one particularly entertaining sequence, the bots tried to nail down a potential start date and got trapped in a circular conversation about “standard onboarding and background checks.” Riley promised that a recruiter would reach out if the application met the company’s qualifications, just as she had the other four times. Again, a recruiter never materialized. It was, as Christopher calls it, a “slop flywheel.”
“This is one synthetic persona giving slop data to another synthetic persona,” he says. “And all of the data is going—where? Nowhere.” The exercise was a mix of “mischievous fun” and frustration, Christopher says, as well as “a dismissal of ever wanting to work” with this company.
Everforth Apex Systems did not respond to WIRED’s request for comment.
Though AI has seeped into every step of the job hunt for both applicants and recruiters, it has taken time to catch on in interviews. Voice AI is infamously tricky to pull off, as agents get tripped up by accents or “ums.” Behavior that would be second nature to a human—like not interrupting a candidate—turns into a “very, very difficult engineering problem,” according to Ophir Samson, the head of voice AI at recruitment platform Greenhouse. But recruiters, overwhelmed with the glut of applications, have increasingly turned to voice AI tools to screen candidates, with 63 percent of job seekers reporting they’ve encountered an AI interview, according to Greenhouse.
As recruiters turned to AI, so did applicants. Candidates using AI in the interview process has become so common that AI recruitment startups like Ribbon promise to help identify “overly scripted, AI-assisted, or coached” responses—just like those in Christopher’s experiment.
Now there are rumblings that bot-on-bot interviews aren’t duplicitous but a preview of things to come. In many ways, it’s the “next logical stage,” Mark Monaghan, vice president of organizational development at call center company IQor, tells WIRED.
That doesn’t mean he’s entirely happy about it. In Christopher’s case, Monaghan believes, the use of AI was more than justified.
“If you’re going to send a bot to me,” he says, “I’ll send a bot to you.”
After his fifth interview with no follow-up, Christopher decided to apply for one more Everforth Apex job. Perhaps, Christopher thought, the problem wasn’t AI. Maybe it was him. Maybe if Riley were able to speak to the company’s dream candidate, things would go differently. So he created a fake candidate, whom he called Don Dickner, packing a résumé to the brim with qualifications pulled from an open job posting.
After Christopher submitted the application, Riley immediately reached out. This time, the virtual recruiter spoke with ChatGPT—posing as Dickner—for 23 minutes. They discussed “sustainable operational improvement,” protecting “customer experience under volume pressure,” and refusing to let “tribal knowledge drift.” ChatGPT had an answer for every question, and a personal anecdote for every qualification. As the interview wrapped up, ChatGPT said it had a “few more questions I’d like answered.”
“I appreciate it,” Riley responded. “Upon carefully reviewing your application, we will assess your qualifications for the position. Should you meet our criteria, a recruiter from Everforth Apex will reach out to schedule a brief conversation.”
Christopher never heard from Riley again.

‘We have no interest in collapse of Gaza roadmap,’ senior Israeli official tells i24NEWS, says the plan must lead to Hamas’ disarmament
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
15:47:13 UTC
00:47:13 KST

- i24NEWS
- Israel
- Diplomacy & defense
- 'No interest in the collapse of the plan': Israel draws red lines for Gaza, Turkey and Syria
'No interest in the collapse of the plan': Israel draws red lines for Gaza, Turkey and Syria
Senior Israeli official says Jerusalem wants diplomacy to succeed while drawing firm red lines in Gaza and Syria amid growing regional tensions with Turkey
Israel remains committed to a diplomatic roadmap for Gaza but will not accept an agreement that allows Hamas to retain its weapons or gives Turkey and Qatar a role in the enclave’s future security, a senior Israeli official told i24NEWS, outlining Jerusalem’s position as negotiations increasingly intersect with wider regional tensions.
The official described a complex diplomatic landscape in which Israel is simultaneously pressing for Hamas’ disarmament, disputing elements of the Gaza framework with the Board of Peace, managing a deteriorating relationship with Turkey and maintaining cautious communication with Syria’s new leadership.
While emphasizing that Israel prefers diplomacy to renewed fighting, the official said Jerusalem would continue to defend what it considers its fundamental security interests in Gaza and along the Syrian frontier.
“We have no interest in the collapse of the plan. We have an interest in implementing it,” the official said. “In our view, implementing the plan means disarmament.”
According to the official, Israel believes the proposed 15-point Gaza roadmap does not fully correspond with US President Donald Trump’s 20-point peace plan.
“Our claim is that the 15-point plan does not align with the 20-point plan,” the official said.
Israel and the Board of Peace remain divided over aspects of the roadmap’s implementation, including the sequence linking Hamas’ disarmament to Gaza’s reconstruction. The official characterized those disagreements as legitimate but said they concern Israel’s most fundamental interests.
“There has unfortunately been no progress on disarmament,” the official said. “We stressed that Gaza’s reconstruction is linked to disarmament. The discussion on this continues.”
The official added that Israel seeks to achieve its objectives through diplomatic means whenever possible, rather than through continued military action.

No Turkish or Qatari security role in Gaza
Israel has ruled out the participation of Turkey and Qatar in the proposed International Stabilization Force, or ISF, and opposes granting either country influence over Gaza’s security arrangements.
“Qatar and Turkey will not be part of the ISF,” the official said. “When it comes to security matters, neither Turkey nor Qatar will have any standing.”
Both countries have played prominent regional roles during the Gaza conflict, but Israel has repeatedly questioned their relationships with Hamas and their suitability as security partners.
The official also acknowledged that proposals involving the large-scale departure of Palestinians from Gaza face a practical obstacle: No countries are prepared to receive them in significant numbers.
“In practice, there are no countries willing to absorb Gazans in any significant numbers,” the official said.
Israel seeks to contain tensions with Turkey
The official’s comments on Gaza came alongside a broader assessment of Israel’s strained relationship with Turkey, which has also emerged as a point of friction in Syria.
Israel has not designated Turkey an enemy state, the official said, but now considers Ankara an adversary in the economic and legal spheres.
“There is no rush to classify countries as enemy states,” the official said, noting that such a move would carry legal consequences.
Azerbaijan previously served as an intermediary for messages between Israel and Turkey, according to the official, although that channel has been used less frequently in recent months.
Despite the worsening relationship, Israel does not want tensions with Ankara to escalate into a direct military confrontation.
“I do not think that either side should reach a situation involving an exchange of fire — neither the Turks nor us,” the official said.
Turkish presence complicates Israel-Syria dialogue
Syria has become a central arena in the Israeli-Turkish dispute as both countries seek to protect their interests following the change of government in Damascus.
The official said Syrian President Ahmed al-Sharaa is open to dialogue and confirmed that Israel maintains communication channels with the Syrian authorities at several levels.

Israel and Syria held talks about a year ago in an effort to reach a security agreement, the official said, but the negotiations ultimately failed. Damascus became less motivated to reach an arrangement after some international sanctions were lifted, according to the Israeli assessment.
Israel also opposed withdrawing from the buffer zone as part of any potential agreement, with the official describing the area as a strategic security asset.
“In any case, there is always dialogue,” the official said. “Dialogue takes place at all kinds of levels.”
At the same time, Israel is closely monitoring Turkey’s military ambitions in Syria. The official said a recent point of contention involved a Turkish presence south of the existing lines and efforts to establish Turkish bases in areas Israel considers critical to its security.
The proposed bases were “against Israeli interests, and we are acting accordingly,” the official said.
Israel also remains cautious in its assessment of al-Sharaa, citing both his personal history and questions surrounding the political forces underpinning his leadership.
“I judge leaders based on their history, their record and good intelligence,” the official said. “We also need to see what al-Sharaa’s political base is — people with a worldview that is not necessarily moderate.”

No budget deal without new EU taxes, Costa warns
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
15:46:19 UTC
00:46:19 KST

European Council President António Costa speaks during the final press conference as part of the EU Summit at the EU headquarters in Brussels, on June 19, 2026. | Nicolas Tucat/AFP via Getty Images
European Council President António Costa is warning governments that they will be worse off if they fail to agree to new EU-wide taxes to finance the bloc’s next seven-year budget.
During a visit to Croatia on Wednesday, Costa urged EU leaders to soften their red lines ahead of an Oct. 15 summit, where he intends to narrow down several potential taxes that are acceptable to EU governments.
“Our priority is to try to fix already in October the basket of new own resources,” Costa said, speaking alongside the Croatian Prime Minister Andrej Plenković. “Then we can know how much we need to ask for each member state.”
Advertisement
Finding an agreement on new EU taxes — so-called own resources — is key to facilitating an overall budget deal in December before national elections in France, Spain and Italy in 2027 threaten the negotiations.
Costa is touring the EU’s 27 capitals to sound out their concerns and assess where there is room for compromise. The Portuguese politician plays a key role in the negotiations as he chairs leaders’ meetings and brokers compromises among different camps.
The issue of EU-wide taxes is among the thorniest in the discussions because national capitals are reluctant to hand more taxing powers to the European Commission and agree to new levies that would hit some countries harder than others.
Last year, the Commission proposed five new levies — targeting carbon imports, emissions, non-collected electronic waste, corporate profits and tobacco products — worth €66 billion per year to finance the budget. But most of the ideas have been met with resistance from governments, who must unanimously approve each new levy.
Tensions were on full display when Luxembourgish Prime Minister Luc Frieden rejected the proposed EU tobacco tax after a meeting with Costa earlier on Wednesday.
"We won’t accept proposals that impact [Luxembourg] in a disproportionate manner," he told reporters.
Advertisement
But in a warning to fellow leaders, Costa said that failure to agree on new taxes will either result in budget cuts or higher national contributions.
“We have only two ways: reduce our ambitions on security, defense, competitiveness, cohesion and agriculture …. and the other alternative is to increase national contributions which is also a problem for all member states.”
Either outcome would be unwelcome for the opposing camps in the negotiations. Northern countries led by Germany complain that their contributions to the EU cashpot are already too high, whereas Southern and Eastern countries are demanding more EU funds for agriculture and regional development.
Europe ministers will discuss the question of new taxes at a meeting in Brussels on Sept. 22.

every apartment gets an atlantic view in carlo ratti’s zig-zag west palm beach tower
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
15:45:40 UTC
00:45:40 KST

On a downtown block in West Palm Beach, Florida, CRA-Carlo Ratti Associati takes one of coastal real estate’s familiar hierarchies as the starting point for a 25-story housing tower: who gets the view. MiMar, developed with Jeff Greene under the states’s Live Local Act, brings affordable and market-rate apartments into the same building above the historic Datura Fire Station. Affordable housing makes up 40 percent of its residences, while the architecture works to give every home the same basic privilege, a view toward the Atlantic.
The tower achieves this through a zig-zag facade that repeatedly angles its residential modules toward the water. Each fold turns another apartment east, while alternating solid and open sections increase separation between neighboring balconies. CRA cites Miami’s Art Deco architecture as a reference, especially its relationship with coastal orientation, though the connection appears through geometry instead of applied ornament. From a distance, the building reads as a stack of shallow turns, each one directed toward the horizon.
The architects at CRA-Carlo Ratti Associati look to South Florida’s sun and prevailing winds to shape the MiMar Tower. This way, the folds take on an environmental role alongside their effect on the view. Balconies gradually deepen toward the upper floors, where exposure becomes stronger, and their overhangs shade the residences below. The face of the tower grows more protective with height and each change in depth is used to adjust the relationship between the interior and the coast.
MiMar also keeps the division between affordable and market-rate housing out of its circulation plan. Residents use the same entrance and elevators, with shared amenities gathered on a landscaped podium terrace. The ocean orientation continues across the building as well, so the architectural feature most easily turned into a premium upgrade becomes part of every apartment.
CRA angles MiMar’s residential modules toward the Atlantic so every home receives a sea view
DATURA FIRE STATION STAYS AT STREET LEVEL
At the base, the preserved frontage of the historic Datura Fire Station remains visible along the West Palm Beach streetscape. Retail spaces face Datura Street, while the residential entrance opens along South Dixie Highway. The new tower rises directly behind and above the older civic structure, keeping the fire station present within a block that will otherwise change considerably in scale.
Behind the facade, CRA proposes a hybrid mass timber and concrete structural system suited to Florida’s developing framework for tall timber construction. Parts of the building can be fabricated off site under controlled conditions before assembly on the downtown site, reducing construction time and disruption around the block. The system also lowers the embodied carbon associated with the tower compared with a conventional all-concrete approach.

The Lasting Economic Damage From the China-Nepal Flood
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
15:45:00 UTC
00:45:00 KST

Around 8:40 on the morning of August 26, a section of glacier collapsed on the north side of the Langtang range, near Nepal’s border with Tibet, three minutes after a magnitude 4.4 earthquake on the Chinese side. The impact registered as a magnitude 5.2 seismic event, which the U.S. Geological Survey initially logged as a separate earthquake before concluding it was the landslide itself. Scientists say warming likely helped trigger the glacier’s collapse.
The debris entered the Lhende Khola, a small river that crosses into Nepal. It blocked the river roughly 20 kilometers upstream from the China-Nepal border crossing at Rasuwagadhi. When the blockage eventually broke, water levels in the Trishuli River surged by as much as nine meters in just 30 minutes.
It is now the deadliest flood disaster on record in Nepal. The confirmed death toll stood at 987 in Nepal as of the morning of September 2, with 16 more dead in Tibet. Roughly 4,500 people remain missing on both sides of the border. Among them are hydropower workers, customs and immigration staff, security personnel, trekking guides, and some 700 foreign nationals, including pilgrims bound for Mount Kailash.
According to UNICEF, 17,000 children are affected, 18 schools were destroyed, and 20 more damaged. The government’s preliminary damage estimate is 200 billion rupees ($1.3 billion).
I was born in Nepal, and I study the economics of natural disasters, including floods in Nepal. All my experience and expertise suggests that these numbers – both deaths and damage – are going to keep going up.
But there is an aspect of the damage that isn’t being included in the counts: the opportunity cost of a broken trade connection.
On July 8, 2025, a supraglacial lake burst upstream in Tibet and sent a flood down the same river. It destroyed the Miteri Bridge linking Nepal and China, wrecked a dry port still under construction at Timure, and killed nine people. Before the flood, roughly a hundred container trucks crossed at Rasuwagadhi each day. Afterward, trade stopped entirely, and did not resume until the first day of 2026.
The closure from the flood lasted for almost six months, causing significant damage far beyond the cost of repairing the bridge. In the six months following the 2025 flood, trade through Rasuwagadhi fell 95 percent, from $302 million to $15 million, according to an analysis of Nepal’s own customs accounts by the Stimson Center. A fraction of that trade was redirected to Kora La, a crossing at roughly 4,650 meters of elevation in Upper Mustang that clears two or three cargo vehicles on a good day. Every dollar that arrived there came alongside roughly $3.30 lost at Rasuwa. The rest of Nepal’s trade went south, to India.
The bridge was eventually rebuilt, and the crossing reopened. But the trade was shut for half a year. Now it is destroyed again, along with the customs buildings on both sides, 19 road bridges and 40 kilometers of road. How long will take to resume trade this time?
Even worse, as of last month, before the August 26 flood, not one of Nepal’s three crossings with China was fully operational.
A trade route that shuts down for six months (or more) every year or two is not one an importer builds a business around, however good the bridge looks the day it reopens. And the cost of these repeated disruptions is being borne by the local community.
I saw this myself a few years ago. Studying a flood in Nepal’s southern plains, my co-authors and I found that the official damage assessment had missed most of what happened. Wages did not simply fall; they changed form, as employers with no cash began paying agricultural laborers in grain. Cash wages dropped 9 to 10 percent. Households borrowed more, taking on about 16,000 rupees each in new debt. All of this continued for roughly a year after the flood ended.
Nepal is a landlocked country with two neighbors, China and India – and the latter closed its border on Nepal in 2015. Ever since, Kathmandu has been working to develop infrastructure links with China, to provide a second option for trade.
The 2015 Gorkha earthquake effectively ended the old Tatopani route, and Rasuwagadhi became the main northern gateway almost by default. By 2024 the crossing at Gyirong – China’s side of the border with Rasuwa – was handling about $604 million in trade, close to a third of everything moving between Nepal and China.
Rasuwa was still rebuilding from that earthquake 11 years ago. Families it had displaced were resettled on the low banks of the Trishuli River; one such community of 250 households was swept away entirely last week.
The flood also destroyed the 111-megawatt Rasuwagadhi hydropower project outright and knocked more than 430 megawatts off Nepal’s grid – over a tenth of national capacity.
This doesn’t mean Nepal was wrong to build in the area. A landlocked country does not get to relocate its trade routes, and a country with Nepal’s rivers has every reason to build hydropower on them. But three of our assumptions need fixing
First, we can’t treat these recurring events as freak, one-off disasters. The same tributary has now produced a catastrophic flood twice in 14 months, and scientific evidence points out that 144 of 545 glacial lakes along the China-Nepal trade corridors are highly susceptible to outburst floods. Rebuilding to a hundred-year standard drawn from the old record is simply not good enough. The risks have changed.
Second, Nepal needs to build flood warning systems that watch for more than rain. Nepal’s meteorological service reported no significant rainfall in the area before the flood, as was true last July. But a warning was possible: German geoscientists even recorded the glacial collapse roughly seven minutes before floodwater reached the border. Sirens will not stop an avalanche, but they do help move people off a valley floor in the interval between the slope failing and the water arriving.
After the 2025 flood, Nepal and China agreed to share information on glacial lake risk across the Tibetan plateau. Clearly, there is work to be done linking upstream monitoring systems with warning mechanisms downstream.
Finally, Nepal keeps asking how to rebuild infrastructure when the question is how often it will close. The influx of aid in the wake of disasters like these is meant to rebuild a bridge, a customs building, a transmission line, or a school. While aid inflows can restore these assets, they do not instill confidence that they will stay open amid repeating disasters.
Until traders can buy insurance that will cover lost income during the months a border stays shut – not just for the goods a flood destroys – Nepal risks losing the trade along this corridor. Nepal will rebuild the bridges. What it cannot rebuild is the confidence that the road will stay open – and that is what trade is really built on.

China’s Xi urges new Middle East security framework during rare Egypt visit
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
15:42:01 UTC
00:42:01 KST

China’s Xi urges new Middle East security framework during rare Egypt visit
Chinese, Egyptian leaders discuss the US-Israel war on Iran, wich has prompted regional powers to rethink defence.
Chinese President Xi Jinping has called on Middle East countries to oppose external influence and consider reshaping the region’s security order.
Xi’s remarks on Wednesday to his Egyptian counterpart Abdel Fattah el-Sisi, on his first visit to Cairo in a decade, come as Beijing seeks to expand its influence in the region amid the United States-Israel war with Iran.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Can the Suez save Asian oil consumers after Houthis shut Bab al-Mandeb?
- list 2 of 3How US-Iran war may push Gulf countries to ‘diversify’ security alliances
- list 3 of 3How Pakistan mediated a US-Iran agreement after more than 100 days of war
“We must uphold the principle that the people of the Middle East are the masters of their own affairs, oppose external interference [and] support regional countries in strengthening dialogue on peace and security,” Xi said in a meeting with el-Sisi, according to Chinese state news agency Xinhua.
Xi was greeted by el-Sisi and a 21-gun salute for talks at the Ittihadiya presidential palace in the Egyptian capital.
The talks covered the six-month US-Israel war on Iran, with both presidents urging “diplomatic solutions” to reach a “comprehensive agreement to end the war”, according to a statement from el-Sisi’s spokesperson.
Sisi’s office also said the two countries signed an agreement to launch the third phase of the Egyptian-Chinese industrial zone at the Suez Canal, which officials say already hosts 200 companies and investments worth approximately $4bn.
The new investments – for which Egypt has not announced a figure – give Beijing even greater influence in the canal zone, a critical artery of global trade, as conflict in the region chokes traffic in the Strait of Hormuz, which passes between Oman and Iran, and the Bab al-Mandeb Strait, which separates Yemen and the Horn of Africa.
Xi said China “stands ready to work with countries in the region to safeguard the security of international shipping lanes, advance development cooperation … and eliminate the breeding grounds for conflict”.
A series of additional agreements were also signed, though Egyptian officials did not provide details.
Beijing seeks greater influence
Beijing is eyeing a greater foothold in the Middle East, at a time when “the United States looks like it can’t really make up its mind whether it wants to withdraw from the region or be more engaged”, Mirette Mabrouk, a senior fellow at the Washington-based Middle East Institute, told the AFP news agency.
China sees Egypt as a key partner and an entry point to more regional influence. For Egypt, closer ties with China are part of a broader effort to diversify partnerships rather than align with a single power, Mabrouk said.
The diplomatic campaign comes before an expected meeting between Xi and US President Donald Trump this month.
Cairo is one of the largest recipients of US military aid, receiving $1.3bn annually, and has historically served as a key Middle East mediator.
Xi’s visit also comes after Saudi Arabia, Turkiye and Pakistan last month signed the Mecca Defence Alliance. Experts have said the move demonstrates a desire by regional countries to diversify their security arrangements beyond Washington.
The US-Israel war with Iran has led several regional allies to question the dependability of the traditional US security guarantee. Washington has, in turn, called on Gulf partners to take greater charge of their own regional deterrence.
The pact contains a NATO-style Article 5 clause, meaning an armed attack on any of the three member states is considered an attack on all.
Officials in Turkiye, Pakistan and Saudi Arabia have stressed the pact is not meant to replace any pre-existing security deals.
Across Cairo, a megalopolis home to more than 26 million people, major streets were lined on Wednesday with Chinese and Egyptian flags, as well as billboards showing el-Sisi and Xi.
Xi is expected to head to the Grand Egyptian Museum overlooking the Giza Pyramids later on Wednesday.
