China’s Xi visits Egypt’s el-Sisi: Why it matters
Xi’s historic visit to Egypt aims to strengthen China-Egypt ties amid rising Middle East tensions.
Chinese President Xi Jinping is visiting Egypt for the first time in a decade, as Cairo looks to foster deeper economic and military ties with Beijing while maintaining its long-standing relationship with Washington.
The visit comes as the US-Israel war on Iran and resulting disruption to global trade have prompted US allies in the region to reassess their strategic relationships. Most recently, Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkiye announced the Mecca Joint Deterrence Agreement, a mutual defence pact.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3China’s Xi makes first visit to Egypt in a decade, amid regional turmoil
- list 2 of 3China’s Xi makes his first visit to Egypt in a decade
- list 3 of 3Xi, Modi and Putin attend SCO summit: What’s on the agenda?
Seeking closer ties with Beijing, therefore, is part of an effort to further what President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi has called Cairo’s “independent foreign policy”.
For China, Egypt offers an important foothold in the Middle East with its large economy, control of the Suez Canal and diplomatic influence across the Arab world and Africa.
Here is what you need to know:
What is the visit about?
Xi’s three-day visit, which began on Tuesday evening, includes talks with el-Sisi that are expected to focus on the regional conflict and its consequences for maritime trade security, as well as expanding Chinese investment in Egypt.
The two countries are expected to sign economic agreements covering areas including artificial intelligence (AI), transport and manufacturing.
The visit marks 70 years of diplomatic relations between Egypt and China. Egyptian state-run media reported that Xi has called for the two countries to “expand the scope of pragmatic collaboration”, while el-Sisi praised Chinese investment in Egypt and reiterated Cairo’s support for Beijing’s position on Taiwan, the island nation that China claims as part of its own territory.
Military cooperation is another increasingly important part of the relationship.
In August, Egypt and China held joint air exercises including Chinese J-16 fighter jets and Egypt’s French-made Rafale aircraft. It was the first time the J-16s had taken part in a combat exercise alongside the Rafales.
Why is this state visit important?
Xi’s visit highlights Beijing’s efforts to expand its influence in a region where the US has been the dominant military power for decades.
Egypt is a key Middle East ally for Washington, and the second-largest recipient of US military aid.
The meeting comes at a time of considerable geopolitical instability, with Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza, the US-Israel war with Iran, and disruption around the Red Sea caused by Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthis targeting Saudi-linked ships all raising questions about the durability of the existing US-led regional order, experts say.
Rob Geist Pinfold, a lecturer in international security at King’s College London, told Al Jazeera, “China is trying to position itself as an increasingly important economic and diplomatic actor in that environment, particularly as a counterweight to the US, as a more responsible and more hands-off regional actor.”
Egypt has a population of 110 million and is an important market for Chinese goods and investment. It is also particularly important to Beijing because it controls the Suez Canal, Pinfold said, adding that the waterway has become even more critical amid disruptions to shipping in the crucial Bab el-Mandeb and Hormuz straits.
Iran has effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz for the past six months in retaliation for US-Israeli strikes. Prior to the war, more than one-fifth of the world’s oil and petroleum products were shipped through the strait, which is the only sea route to the open ocean available to Gulf producers.
China offers Egypt opportunities to develop investment, infrastructure and technology, while bilateral ties have also expanded into areas including defence and artificial intelligence.
But the growing relationship should not be interpreted as Egypt pivoting away from the US entirely, Pinfold said, noting that “instead, el-Sisi’s approach is better understood as one of diversification and strategic autonomy”.
“In short,” Pinfold said, “as the Gulf states have done in recent years, he is trying to hedge without alienating or annoying Egypt’s indisputably most important ally, the US.”
How strong are Egypt-China relations?
Relations between Cairo and Beijing have deepened significantly since 2014, when el-Sisi visited China and the two countries signed a strategic partnership agreement.
China is now Egypt’s largest trading partner in non-petroleum goods, with bilateral trade reaching nearly $20.7bn by the end of 2025, according to Egypt’s State Information Service (SIS).
Data from the country’s Central Agency for Public Mobilization and Statistics (CAPMAS) shows a nearly 200 percent increase in Egyptian exports to China, at $840.8m in the first half of 2026, while imports stood at $10.4bn.
Beijing has also invested more than $10bn in Egypt, including in the New Administrative Capital east of Cairo and an electric rail line serving industry in the Nile Delta.
Chinese companies have also invested in container ports, green hydrogen, iron pipes, tyres and satellites.
Chinese investments in Egypt are focused mainly in the Suez Canal area and the China-Egypt TEDA cooperation zone in Ain Sokhna, part of Beijing’s Belt and Road Initiative, which hosts about 200 companies with investments exceeding $3.8bn, according to Egyptian state media.
In 2023, Egypt joined BRICS, the bloc of Global South nations including Brazil, Russia, India and China.

Best Pizza Cheese for Melting and Stretchiness
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
15:00:29 UTC
00:00:29 KST

Best Pizza Cheese for Melting and Stretchiness
When it comes to pizza, cheese is not just a topping; it is the foundation of texture, flavor, and visual appeal. The perfect pizza cheese should melt smoothly, stretch generously when sliced, and complement the crust and sauce. Achieving that iconic cheese pull depends on protein structure, moisture content, fat levels, and how the cheese is processed. Below is a detailed guide to the best cheeses for melting and stretchiness, along with why they work so well on pizza.
Mozzarella, The Gold Standard!
Mozzarella is widely considered the best pizza cheese for both melting and stretchiness, and for good reason. But why is it that good? Because it has high moisture and an elastic protein structure allow it to melt evenly, and Casein proteins form long strands when heated, creating the classic cheese pull. Also, Mild flavor lets the sauce and dough shine. Calindairy Mozzarella cheese is the best for American or Italian-style pizza.
Types of mozzarella
- Low-moisture mozzarella (whole milk): The most common choice for professional pizzerias. It melts smoothly, stretches well, and releases less water than fresh mozzarella.
- Low-moisture mozzarella (part-skim): Slightly less creamy but still very stretchy. Often used for cost efficiency.
- Fresh mozzarella: Soft and delicate with excellent melt, but high moisture can make pizza watery unless properly drained and baked at high temperatures.
Provolone, Stretch with Extra Flavor!
Provolone is a semi-hard Italian cheese that melts beautifully and stretches well, though slightly less than mozzarella. This cheese had a similar protein structure to mozzarella. Higher fat content adds richness, and more pronounced flavor enhances depth.
Best use of Provolone Cheese
- Blended with mozzarella for better flavor complexity.
- Excellent on Sicilian, Detroit-style, or pan pizzas.
Fior di Latte, Artisan-Level Stretch!
Fior di latte is a fresh mozzarella made from cow’s milk, commonly used in traditional Italian pizzas. Has exceptionally smooth melt, Clean, milky stretch with a soft bite, and Balanced moisture when baked properly.
Best use
- High-temperature ovens.
- Thin-crust pizzas where ingredient quality is the focus.
Oaxaca Cheese, Outstanding Stretch Alternative!
Oaxaca cheese, traditionally used in Mexican cuisine, is one of the stretchiest cheeses available, so you can use it in your next pizza recipe and enjoy the ultimate and extraordinary cheese pull. The pasta filata (stretched curd) process is similar to that of mozzarella. This cheese creates dramatic, long cheese pulls and has a mild flavor that works well with tomato-based sauces.
Normally Can be used for:
- Fusion-style pizzas.
- Home cooks seeking maximum stretch with minimal effort.
Monterey Jack, Smooth Melter with Elasticity!
Monterey Jack melts easily and smoothly, producing moderate stretch. The combination of Monterey Jack and mozzarella cheese is perfect for your signature in cooking a perfect pizza. If you want to have a perfect pizza that could never be found in another place, you should definitely try that combo! Monterey Jack has high moisture content, a soft texture that allows for even melting, and a creamy mouthfeel.
What is the usage of Monterey Jack?
- Blended with mozzarella for added creaminess.
- White pizzas or mild-flavored toppings.
Cheese Blends, Optimizing Melt and Stretch!
Many pizzerias use blends to balance stretch, melt, browning, and flavor.
Popular combinations:
- Mozzarella + Provolone: Improved stretch with deeper flavor.
- Mozzarella + Monterey Jack: Creamier melt with good elasticity.
- Mozzarella + Low amounts of Cheddar: Better browning and flavor, but limited stretch if overused.
Different fat and moisture levels create a more controlled melt and Enhanced flavor without sacrificing texture.
Cheeses to Use Sparingly or Avoid for Stretch!
Some cheeses melt well but do not stretch, while others resist melting altogether.
- Cheddar: Breaks into oil and solids when overheated. You can order cheese pizza and blend it with natural cheese to create a unique taste, and also avoid too much stretch.
- Parmesan: Adds flavor but no stretch.
- Feta and goat cheese: Softens but does not melt smoothly.
These are best used as secondary toppings rather than the main cheese.
Key Factors That Affect Cheese Stretch
If you want to have an ultimate cheese pull, remember the following information:
- Moisture: Moderate moisture allows proteins to loosen without releasing excess water.
- Fat content: Fat enhances meltability, but too much can reduce elasticity.
- Shredding method: Hand-shredded cheese melts better than pre-shredded cheese, which often contains anti-caking agents.
- Baking temperature: Higher heat promotes better stretch and faster melting.
For the best balance of melting and stretchiness, low-moisture whole milk mozzarella remains the top choice. For enhanced flavor and texture, blending it with provolone or Monterey Jack is ideal. If maximum stretch is the priority, Oaxaca cheese is a surprisingly excellent alternative. Choosing the right cheese and using it correctly can elevate pizza from good to unforgettable.

I was once ashamed to admit I’d been strangled nonconsensually during sex. Now I’m speaking up to save women’s lives | Hannah Ferguson
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
15:00:28 UTC
00:00:28 KST

Last week, a 16-year-old girl was found unresponsive in a home on Sydney’s northern beaches. She was airlifted to hospital and died two days later. New South Wales police are investigating her death as the result of a sexual strangulation act. Sources told the ABC the deceased may have experienced a seizure following asphyxiation, and that officers were told the sex was consensual.
While that investigation has yet to run its course, speaking generally, strangulation during sex is not a new phenomenon or conversation. Just a few years ago it was relatively taboo to criticise this normalisation of violence in sex – it was often framed as “anti-kink” to raise concern about this dangerous act that is increasingly depicted in mainstream pornography.
In 2024, Australian research affirmed the prevalence of sexual strangulation. The Archives of Sexual Behaviour published data revealing that 57% of Australians aged 18 to 35 had been strangled at least once during sex, and 51% said they had strangled a sexual partner.
Not only are reports of this act increasing, so are the reports of health impacts. Denele Crozier, the CEO of Women’s Health NSW, stated that since 2023 there had been a 123% increase in women presenting with concerns of a possible brain injury linked to strangulation.
I was previously ashamed to share my own experiences of being strangled during sex nonconsensually. Despite being an outspoken, progressive woman, I froze up and dissociated. Afterwards, I remember questioning whether my response was one of being in shock and afraid for my safety, or if I felt “prudish” if I spoke up and as if I’d be ruining the mood. For a long time, I was embarrassed to admit that while I intellectually knew something wasn’t right, I still failed to call it out in a moment of uncertainty.
That is exactly the concern I have for so many women who may be experiencing sexual strangulation. Affirmative consent is incredibly hard to achieve in these contexts; sexual strangulation is now commonplace and we are not equipped with the sophisticated sex education to match.
In 2022, consent advocate Chanel Contos wrote about this: “Another US study found that 58% of female college students have been choked during sex, further suggesting that this ‘kink’ is becoming increasingly common in younger age demographics. This study found that while many women enjoyed choking, others did it largely to please their sexual partner. This is the real kicker. The problem here is not only that women are being choked during sex without giving consent, but that a lot of the time they are ‘consenting’ not because they derive their own sexual pleasure from it, but because they think it turns the guy on.”
Violence against women and girls has been normalised to such an extent that pornography is convincing us it is normal to be strangled during intimacy, and that we are supposed to like it. I appreciate that messages from leaders like “talk to your kids” are made in good faith, but conversation cannot combat the nature and influence of sex content depicting violence as a standard part of sexual intercourse. We are teaching young men that perpetrating violent acts that have the potential to kill are erotic, and we are teaching women to endure having their lives threatened under the guise of pleasure.
There are people who engage with control of breath as part of particular kinks, but even in acknowledging these consensual engagements, it is important to reiterate that there is no safe way to engage in strangulation.
In response to this expanding dialogue, the social services minister, Tanya Plibersek, has shown her support for Australia to adopt legislation that was introduced to the UK in 2025, making it a criminal offence to possess or publish pornography depicting suffocation or strangulation. I want to add my voice to the many calling for the Albanese government to legislate this imminently.
The government is also, rightly, considering a second significant piece of reform proposed by Contos and her organisation Teach Us Consent. Contos has been campaigning for the government’s digital duty of care legislative drafting to adopt their “Fix Our Feeds” pitch, regulating big tech companies to ensure algorithms are an opt-in feature. This would introduce a consent-based model that allows users to have more control over the information these platforms are serving us, reducing the extremist material that so many are exposed to.
Our government has established that they are willing to take on the regulation of big tech. Australia was the first country in the world to legislate a social media ban for under-16s. We know we have the capability; now it’s time to introduce something that would actually be effective – and give power back to individual users.
These would be two significant steps from the government, after last week’s national cabinet meeting where the prime minister, Anthony Albanese, discussed violence against women and children with state and territory leaders. The subsequent announcements of frameworks and reviews were weak. We need politicians to meet the moment. The safety of women and girls depends on tangible action, now.

The head of Ukraine’s presidential office, has said courts should determine the significance of recordings that have raised questions about his involvement in an alleged $3.3 million money-laundering scheme aimed at securing bail for a former minister detained in a sprawling energy sector corruption probe.
Authorities have not publicly named Kyrylo Budanov and he has not been charged but court documents obtained by the Ukrainian news outlet hromadske appear to identify him participating in a conversation concerning the money laundering.
Responding to questions about the tapes, Budanov told hromadske that any determination regarding the recordings should be made by a judge. “Let the court figure out who appears where,” he said.

A separate but related investigation concerns the alleged laundering of funds through state-owned banking infrastructure to post bail for former Energy and Justice Minister Herman Halushchenko.
According to investigators, Mindich sought assistance to arrange Halushchenko’s release from custody. Budanov’s then-deputy, Iryna Mudra, was subsequently brought into the alleged scheme.
Prosecutors allege Mudra was tasked with legitimizing the bail money and recruited a former lawmaker who brought in several associates to route cash through bank accounts. In wiretaps cited by investigators, Mudra stated that Mindich had approached “Kyrylo” to take control of state-owned Sense Bank and its financial flows. Investigators allege the bank was later intended to be used in the money-laundering scheme.
The widening scandal has already reached the highest levels of government. President Volodymyr Zelensky dismissed Mudra earlier this month after anti-corruption authorities formally named her a suspect.
Mudra has denied wrongdoing, asserting that the wiretap recordings were released out of context and that she will defend her reputation in court. On Aug. 25, Ukraine’s High Anti-Corruption Court ordered her held in custody for 60 days, setting bail at 20 million hryvnias ($440,000).

Can Ukraine’s drones shut Russian airspace? What that means for airlines
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
14:55:16 UTC
23:55:16 KST

Can Ukraine’s drones shut Russian airspace? What that means for airlines
What happens if the airspace of the world’s largest country by land mass is out of bounds because of Ukrainian drones?
Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has warned that Russian airspace is effectively closed because of the volume of Ukrainian drones in the sky.
On Tuesday, he said that Russia, which began the war with the invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, is now “closing its own skies”.
While Kyiv is not threatening civil aviation, Zelenskyy said, “there will be drones in Russia’s skies and due notice must be taken” by airlines and insurance companies.
Russian President Vladimir Putin called Zelenskyy’s comments “a declaration of state terrorism”.
So, can Ukraine really shut down Russia’s airspace? And what happens if the airspace of the world’s largest country becomes inaccessible?
What has Zelenskyy said?
Ukrainian drones have increasingly threatened or disrupted air traffic at Russian airports in recent months.
As Russia has stepped up its use of ballistic missiles against Ukraine, Kyiv has struggled to intercept them due to a lack of ammunition for its air defence systems, particularly United States-made Patriot systems.
Ukraine has, instead, responded by striking Russian infrastructure, oil and port facilities, and even e-commerce warehouses, deep inside Russian territory.
“Today, we want to warn every airline that uses Russian airspace, every insurer and everyone who still uses Russia’s key airports: Russian airspace is becoming completely unsafe,” Zelenskyy said during his nightly address on Tuesday.
“Ukraine does not threaten civilian aviation as such – not a single civilian aircraft. There will simply be drones in Russia’s skies on a scale that has to be taken into account,” he said.
“Drone-infested skies are no place for civilian aviation,” Zelenskyy said on Tuesday. “The sky over Russia is currently for drones … as long as the war continues.”
“We in Ukraine do not want innocent lives to be lost. That is why we are warning our partners: The safe days in Russia’s skies are over,” Zelenskyy added.
How much of a threat do Ukrainian drones pose?
Unmanned drones, which Ukraine now mass-produces at low cost, have transformed the Ukraine-Russia war theatre, allowing Kyiv to take the fight hundreds of kilometres beyond the front line and increasingly into Russia’s major cities.
Analysts say that the distance they can reach is now more of a concern than the damage they can inflict as they are interfering with civilian aviation well inside Russia, including around Moscow.
As Ukraine has developed drone technology at an exponential rate since the start of the war, drones have become much longer-range. Ukraine says its deep-strike range has grown from about 630km (390 miles) in 2022 to 1,750km (1,090 miles) this year, with drones striking targets as far as Omsk, about 2,500km (1,550 miles) from Ukraine.
When they approach Russian cities, they trigger temporary restrictions in the airspace above, halting arrivals and departures at airports until the perceived threat passes, which can take several hours. Repeated drone alerts have forced temporary restrictions at Russian airports and are increasingly causing concern for general aircraft flying through Russian airspace.
“Ukraine has consistently launched more than 500 drones near daily, with multiple days exceeding 1,000 drones, according to figures released by the Russian [Ministry of Defence],” said Mark Brace, head of analysis at the aviation risk advisory firm Osprey Flight Solutions. This has caused frequent and extended airport closures and flight suspensions, he told Al Jazeera.
“Essentially, Zelenskyy is articulating publicly what Ukraine has been doing for months: systematically disrupting Russian airspace.”
According to data from Osprey, there has been an average of 30 Russian airport closures per day since the war began.
In an alert to its clients, Osprey Flight Solutions said that while the majority of Ukraine’s drone and missile strikes are likely to occur within 300km (186 miles) of the border between the two countries, daily attacks deeper inside Russia are likely to continue throughout the rest of 2026, including near Moscow and Saint Petersburg.
“It is assessed that miscalculation and/or misidentification is likely in areas related to the Ukraine conflict,” the alert said.
Last year, Putin told Azerbaijan’s President Ilham Aliyev that two Russian missiles had detonated beside an Azerbaijan Airlines plane in 2024 after Ukrainian drones entered Russian airspace, in an incident that killed 38 people.
How does this impact airlines and passengers?
“Russian airspace remains the single biggest structural distortion in global aviation,” Alex Macheras, an analyst based in the Middle East, said.
Before February 2022, flying over Russia was the shortest path between Europe and Northeast Asia, with more than 360,000 flights a year passing over Siberia, he told Al Jazeera. Since Russia invaded Ukraine, many European and US carriers have avoided this route.
As a result, many Europe-Northeast Asia routes now take two to four hours longer, Macheras said, while the Helsinki-Tokyo route has gone from nine hours to 13.
“It’s a cost now factored into ticket prices, operational overheads, crew rosters, and aircraft utilisation across the entire European long-haul network,” Macheras said.
Despite the ongoing war, some major airlines from countries such as China, Turkiye, the United Arab Emirates and other Gulf states have continued to use Russian airspace.
US airlines have complained that carriers still permitted to fly through Russian airspace, such as Chinese airlines, enjoy a competitive advantage with shorter routes and reduced operating costs. If Russian airspace does close to these operators, this competitive advantage will disappear.
Currently, Chinese carriers offer the fastest Europe-Asia and Asia-Europe connections by retaining Russian overflight rights. “Lose that, and their schedule advantage over Gulf and Turkish hubs narrows sharply,” Macheras said.
Meanwhile, Turkish Airlines has built “real strategic value from its neutral access to Russian airspace, positioning Istanbul as the natural connection point for traffic that Western carriers can no longer route directly,” the aviation analyst said.
He added that Indian carriers – Air India in particular – also rely on Russian airspace for efficient Delhi-London and Delhi-New York routings.
Gulf carriers, from airports in Doha, Dubai and Abu Dhabi, on the other hand, the analyst argued, do not depend on Russian airspace the way Istanbul does. “A broader closure would likely reinforce the Gulf hub model, rather than damage it, as long-haul traffic gets pushed further south through the Gulf rather than through the Caucasus corridor,” he added.
Is the aviation sector facing other pressures?
Conflicts in the Middle East have shaken the aviation industry over the past couple of years, compounding disruptions caused by the Russia-Ukraine war.
Osprey Flight Solutions’ Brace told Al Jazeera that “alternative routings through the Caucasus and Central Asia and the Middle East/Red Sea/Saudi Arabia/Gulf region are already congested due to the lack of availability of Russian airspace and the ongoing conflict in the Gulf region”.
Other regional factors, such as Indian carriers being restricted from using Pakistani airspace due to bilateral tensions in South Asia, have worsened that congestion.
“Despite some parts of the Middle East/Gulf airspace opening up during lulls in conflict activity in recent months, there has been no significant return to using Iraq/Iran airspace as corridors, for example,” Brace said, “primarily due to carrier risk assessments and regulators banning operators from these areas.”
The renewed fighting between the US and Iran this week will also “put further pressure on the alternative corridors”, Brace said.
Rising jet fuel prices have been another major concern for airlines. On Monday, China’s top three airlines posted losses for the first half of 2026. Meanwhile, Middle East airlines are expected collectively to fall into losses because of the war.
What happens when air traffic is disrupted?
Air traffic is similar to road traffic: When major roads and intersections are closed, cars, buses and cyclists are forced onto smaller neighbourhood streets and lanes, creating congestion and longer journeys. The same thing happens in the sky.
Azerbaijan, sandwiched between Russia to the north and Iran to the south, is an example.
Because of the conflicts involving both Russia and Iran, Azerbaijan has become a vital air corridor enabling airlines to operate between Europe and Asia.
Azerbaijan’s air traffic chief has noted that before Russia’s full-scale invasion in 2022, his country handled an average of 278 flights a day. By the end of 2025, that had risen to an average of 695 per day.
After the US and Israel attacked Iran in February this year, flights over Azerbaijan increased to a daily average of 810 during March. Azerbaijan handled a peak of 1,062 flights in a single day on May 9.
If Russian airspace becomes completely out of bounds, theoretically, analyst Macheras noted, “very little spare capacity exists” in already congested skies.
“The Caucasus corridor is barely 100 miles [161km] wide at its narrowest point, and it’s already handling detoured traffic from both the Russian closure and, more recently, Middle East disruptions tied to regional conflict,” he added. “Any further Russian airspace restriction would push still more volume onto a corridor that is already near saturation, driving fares and journey times higher across the board.”

Hans van de Ven on World War II and the Making of Modern Asia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
14:53:00 UTC
23:53:00 KST

In “Blood Dawn: World War II and the Making of Modern Asia,” Hans van de Ven, a professor of modern Chinese history at Cambridge University, provides a much-needed Asia-centric focus on World War II.
While Western histories of the global conflict center the European theater, and typically mark the war’s beginning with with Germany’s invasion of Poland in 1939, van de Ven starts with the reordering of Asia under European colonialism in the 19th century, the awakening of new political movements across the region in response, and Japan’s 1937 invasion of China.
World War II remade Asia, and the consequences thereof linger to this day.
“Many of today’s flashpoints – capable of sparking global conflict – are unresolved hangovers from this war,” van de Ven told The Diplomat’s Managing Editor Catherine Putz. From Kashmir and the India-Pakistan rivalry, to the status of Taiwan and the division of the Korean Peninsula, Asia’s flashpoints have their roots in the legacies of World War II.
“Blood Dawn: World War II and the Making of Modern Asia” will be published on September 8, 2026.
What changes in our understanding of World War II when we shift focus from the European theater to the Pacific?
The Second World War in Asia marked the end of British, French, and Dutch imperial rule and birthed a new Asia structured around the modern nation-state. In that sense, the transformations wrought by the war in Asia were as profound as those caused by the First World War in Europe.
The Asian theater was never just about defeating Japan – it was also about dismantling European imperialism and creating new national futures. Regional independence movements exploited Japan’s attempt to build an empire that rivaled Britain’s. Some built large followings and armies – like the Chinese Communists – while others sought independence by collaborating with the Japanese, as Sukarno did in Indonesia.
Another crucial shift was that the contest between Japan and the United States for control of the Pacific ended decisively in America’s favor. Following the Versailles Peace Treaty [that ended World War I], Japan gained control of the Mariana, Caroline, and Marshall Islands. During the war, the United States expended immense blood and treasure to conquer them. Today’s geopolitical contest between the U.S. and China is, in part, a continuation of this struggle for Pacific dominance. As an emerging superpower, China naturally wants to secure its vulnerable coastline – through which the British invaded in the 19th century and the Japanese in the 20th.
To what extent did the colonization of Asia by European powers set the stage for World War II in the region?
In three distinct ways.
First, prior to Europe’s colonization of Asia, the region was ruled by historic dynasties: the Mughals in India, the Manchus in China, the Tokugawa shogunate in Japan, the Joseon dynasty in Korea, and the Nguyễn dynasty in Vietnam. None survived the colonial regimes the Europeans built in the first part of the 19th century, and their collapses proved deeply destabilizing.
Second, Western military, technical, and scientific dominance created a severe crisis of confidence among Asian elites, who concluded that their own cultural and political traditions were backward. In the late 19th century, nationalist movements emerged that demanded radical political, cultural, and social change. Initially confined to elites, they gained mass followings in the 1920s after the Great Powers at Versailles rejected Asian demands for self-determination. Meanwhile, the 1917 October Revolution in Russia offered an inspiring new model of revolution. Communism provided an organizational framework for anti-imperialism and suggested that a backward country did not need decades of gradual development and industrialization but could through revolution jump to the forefront of history. In orthodox communism, feudalism is followed by capitalism before it finally reaches communism.
Finally, there was Japan. Before World War I, Japanese elites hoped to gain Western acceptance by “leaving” Asia and adopting Western models. However, the Western powers’ refusal to include a racial equality clause in the League of Nations covenant, combined with naval restrictions imposed on Japan at the Washington Conference, convinced Japanese leaders that Japan had to free Asia from European imperialism to achieve equal footing.
Many peg the start of World War II in Asia as the Marco Polo Bridge Incident in July 1937, two years before the war kicked off in Europe. What is most important to understand about that incident?
Chiang Kai-shek transformed a minor military clash near Beijing into an existential crisis involving the survival of China as a nation and civilization. Similar skirmishes had occurred before and were settled locally. However, Chiang insisted that any resolution be approved by China’s central government and demanded a full Japanese withdrawal from northern China.
When Japan refused, Chiang threw his elite troops against Japanese forces in Shanghai, stationed there by virtue of an earlier truce agreement. Chiang’s decision, which lacked unanimous support, ensured that the conflict threatened Western financial interests and received heavy global media coverage. China was quickly framed as a plucky underdog standing up to brutal Japanese militarism.
Equally important was the creation of a United Front between Chiang’s Nationalists and Mao Zedong’s Communists, who had been fighting each other since the mid-1920s. Chiang agreed to take on Japan partly because Joseph Stalin offered massive Soviet military aid and pressured Mao to join the alliance. Chiang hoped this United Front would absorb the Communists into the nationalist political order and end their efforts to overthrow him – a hope that ultimately proved to be a catastrophic miscalculation.
How did the twin forces of nationalism and anti-imperialism interact in World War II in Asia?
A really good question. We often equate Asia’s anti-imperialism with nationalism, but that oversimplifies reality. It was far from guaranteed that the nations of post-war Asia would be unitary states led by secular nationalists. For instance, there was massive support in Indonesia for establishing an Islamic state, which did not come to fruition largely through Sukarno’s personal charisma. Alternative visionaries imagined a Confucian East Asia or a vast federation of Islamic states spanning from Southeast Asia to the Middle East. Gandhi was a nationalist, of course, but he wanted a new Indian polity based on village councils. The Confucian leader Qian Mu wanted the same in China.
One core question driving my research was why China, India, and Indonesia rejected federalism, which, one could argue, would have suited their enormous internal diversity and for which there was support. First, federal structures were strongly associated with European “divide-and-rule” colonial tactics. Second, the war made it starkly obvious that only large, centralized powers possessed the strength to determine their own futures and to matter geopolitically.
“Blood Dawn” emphasizes how contingent these post-war outcomes really were. The 1947 partition of the Indian subcontinent into India and Pakistan is a prime example; neither Jawaharlal Nehru nor Muhammad Ali Jinnah originally desired a hard partition, but they exhausted each other and the British through endless negotiations. Similarly, as Mao Zedong later acknowledged to Japanese visitors in the 1950s, the Chinese Communists might never have emerged out of the hills of northwest Chia without the catalyst of WWII. Their ultimate victory was far from guaranteed until 1947 at the earliest.
Russia – at the time the Soviet Union – bridges all of Eurasia. How did Soviet leaders approach the conflict in East Asia at first and how did their approach evolve?
For Stalin, the ultimate nightmare was a two-front war requiring the USSR to fight Germany and Japan simultaneously across vast distances. To counter the rise of Hitler, Stalin advocated Popular Front alliances starting in 1932, encouraging communists to ally with all anti-fascists. This strategy shaped Léon Blum’s government in France, Manuel Azaña’s in Spain, and China’s United Front.
In 1939, Stalin reversed course. Japanese forces had become bogged down in China, and Soviet forces dealt a decisive blow to Japan’s Kwantung Army at the Battle of Khalkhin Gol. While that battle raged, Stalin negotiated simultaneously with Hitler’s Germany, which stood at the brink of invading Poland, as well as with Britain and France, who had guaranteed Poland’s security. Stalin ultimately chose a pact with Hitler. That and an armistice agreed with Japan meant that the Soviet Union did not have to fight either of its enemies for some time. To explain this awkward change, which left socialists and communists the world over confounded, Stalin declared that the new world war was not against fascism after all, but merely a contest between empires who could be left to slaughter each other.
Only in the summer of 1945, after Germany’s defeat, did Stalin enter the war against Japan by invading occupied Manchuria. Although Soviet troops eventually withdrew, the operation secured the USSR a major voice in post-war Asian affairs.
Finally, why do you think it is important to continue to revisit and reexamine the past – such as World War II writ large and in Asia, specifically?
For Asia, World War II was an axial moment. The modern states of Asia trace their origins directly to this period; the leaders of its independence movements remain central heroic figures, and wartime narratives still dominate national identity.
Furthermore, many of today’s flashpoints – capable of sparking global conflict – are unresolved hangovers from this war. These include Kashmir, the India-Pakistan rivalry, the status of Taiwan, and the standoff on the Korean Peninsula.
In the immediate post-war decades, Western observers often ignored Asia due to its poverty. That luxury is gone. China is now an emergent superpower, and Asia’s economies are driving global growth. Yet Western audiences remain strikingly ignorant of Asian history. While some Americans know a bit about China and some British know about India, very few people pay attention to Indonesia – which features prominently in “Blood Dawn.”

Lawmakers from the European People’s Party and Patriots for Europe are accusing Pedro Sánchez of abandoning the Spanish exclave, as a press report suggests the mass entry incident was guided by Moroccan security forces.
Around 500 people gathered in front of the European Parliament in Brussels on Wednesday to protest against the Spanish government’s handling of the crisis in Ceuta, where several thousand of more than 70,000 migrants who arrived in the exclave on 30 July remain.
MEPs and staffers from the centre-right European People’s Party and far-right Patriots for Europe gathered in the area in front of Parliament, waving the flags of Ceuta and Spain, and accusing Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez of failing to defend Spain’s territorial integrity and sovereignty.

Madrid has so far avoided publicly blaming Rabat for the incident. It generally considers Morocco a cooperative partner in migration management.
Spanish Interior Minister Fernando Grande-Marlaska asked police chief Francisco Pardo to verify the information, which CENIF reportedly sent to a judge gathering information on the incident, according to ministry sources.
Vox, the leading Spanish far-right party, claims Sánchez has “betrayed” his own country and is pushing to activate Article 102 of the Spanish Constitution, which would trigger a criminal trial against the prime minister and his cabinet.
“The situation is untenable. This government cannot continue to lead Spain,” Vox MEP Jorge Buxadé Villalba told reporters, claiming this is the “hardest hour” for the country since the Catalan attempted secession in 2017.
Vox’s MEPs also sent a letter to Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas and Home Affairs Commissioner Magnus Brunner.
They call for condemning and sanctioning Morocco, declaring the massive entry “an act of hybrid warfare” and immediately suspending all international agreements between the EU and Morocco, as well as the granting of visas to Moroccan citizens.
The European Commission told Euronews it will not comment on leaks and considers the ongoing investigation into Morocco’s involvement “a matter for the national authorities.”

Interstellar solar sails hit a strange problem at 75% of light speed
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
14:51:21 UTC
23:51:21 KST

Interstellar solar sails hit a strange problem at 75% of light speed
- Date:
- September 2, 2026
- Source:
- Universe Today
- Summary:
- Solar sails pushed by powerful lasers could reach incredible speeds, but relativity may eventually make the light itself work against them. At around 75% of the speed of light, scattered photons can begin creating drag, adding a surprising obstacle to interstellar travel.
- Share:
Reaching another star within a practical amount of time will require something far more capable than chemical rockets. One of the leading ideas is a solar sail, a large reflective structure that can be pushed by light. If extremely powerful lasers are aimed at such a sail, they could accelerate it to speeds well beyond what current propulsion systems can achieve.
But there may be an unexpected problem once a lightsail begins traveling at a significant fraction of the speed of light. According to a new paper on arXiv by Chao Shen and Jiaze Li of the Harbin Institute of Technology, the same light used to propel the sail could eventually produce a drag effect.
How Light Pushes a Solar Sail
The researchers separate the forces produced by photons striking a solar sail into three categories.
The strongest contribution comes from incident light (that raw momentum of the photons hitting the sail). Next is specular reflection (momentum imparted when photons bounce perfectly off the sail). The weakest contribution comes from diffuse scattering (momentum from photons that are absorbed by the sail then reemitted in random directions).
At relatively low speeds, these effects all contribute to pushing the sail forward. The situation becomes much more complicated once the spacecraft reaches relativistic velocities.
The Doppler Effect Weakens the Push
As the sail races away from the laser source, the light reaching it undergoes an increasingly strong Doppler shift. The frequency of the incoming light decreases, reducing the amount of thrust produced by all three components.
As a result, continued acceleration becomes progressively less efficient. The faster the sail travels, the harder it becomes for the laser to keep increasing its speed.
The situation changes even more dramatically once the lightsail reaches about 75% of the speed of light.
When Scattered Light Starts Creating Drag
At that speed, relativistic light aberration becomes important. From the viewpoint of a stationary observer on Earth, diffusely scattered light begins to be directed forward, toward the direction in which the sail is traveling.
Because every action has an equal and opposite reaction, that forward-directed radiation produces a force in the opposite direction. This means diffuse scattering (admittedly the weakest of the three forces) begins acting as drag once the sail passes roughly 75% of the speed of light.
The laser is still pushing the sail forward overall, so the total force does not become negative. However, the efficiency of the propulsion system drops substantially.
Real Solar Sails Would Face Even More Challenges
The study is focused specifically on radiative dynamics. It does not include nonradiative effects such as collisions and drag from interstellar gas or dust.
It also leaves out the thermal limits of real sail materials. A sail exposed to an extremely powerful laser could potentially overheat or even melt.
For simplicity, the researchers model the lightsail as an idealized mirror. Real spacecraft would likely use much more sophisticated materials.
Engineers are already investigating advanced metamaterials and photonic crystals designed for specific laser wavelengths. In principle, these materials might even take advantage of the aberration effects described in the study. They could help a lightsail automatically correct its orientation and stabilize its trajectory so that it remains centered within the laser beam.
The Long Road to Interstellar Flight
A fully operational interstellar solar sail is still far from becoming reality. Traveling across interstellar distances introduces many additional complications, including the curvature of spacetime, which the paper also simplifies out.
Even so, understanding these high-speed effects is an important part of determining how such spacecraft might eventually work. If humanity someday sends a probe to another star, engineers will need a detailed understanding of every force that could affect its journey.
Story Source:
Materials provided by Universe Today. Original written by Andy Tomaswick. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Chao Shen, Jiaze Li. Relativistic Lightsail Propulsion Dynamics. arXiv, 2 Jun 2026 DOI: 10.48550/arXiv.2606.04052

The US Arms Bottleneck Is Impacting Its East Asian Allies
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
14:49:00 UTC
23:49:00 KST

In May, Taiwan was offered no less than four different explanations for the delays in receiving a $14 billion arms package of Patriot PAC-3 interceptors and NASAMS air defense systems.
Acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao testified to senators that the United States was “doing a pause” on the arms sale to Taiwan “in order to make sure we have the munitions we need for Epic Fury,” the U.S. military operation in Iran. U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio then claimed that the sale was under review, not “paused.” Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth said it wasn’t about Iran at all: “our stockpiles are more than suited… both there [in Iran] and around the globe.” Meanwhile, U.S. President Donald Trump said the arms sales were “a very good negotiating chip” with China, suggesting a purely political motivation for the delay.
Beyond the problem of conflicting explanations, none of these statements provided the answer Taipei really wants: a delivery date.
Taiwan is not alone in waiting for promised U.S. weapons. The U.S. government informed Japan that delivery of 400 long-awaited Tomahawk cruise missiles would be delayed two years to meet drawdown demands from the current war in Iran.
The problem is obvious: the U.S. has finite supplies of these missiles, and a growing need. Taiwan and Japan are queuing up, in the same line, behind Ukraine and behind resupplies for the Iran war.
Lockheed Martin exceeded their production record with over 500 interceptors in 2024. But the U.S. military itself shot nearly 1,500 Patriot interceptors in the Iran war. In the fiscal budget for next year, the U.S. Army asked for over 2,700 interceptors, a large jump from the 357 it previously funded. Taiwan’s order of 102 interceptors sits somewhere within that request. Japan’s order does too.
The U.S. requirement for 2,700 interceptors merely scratches the surface of the problem. The United States is facing depleted assets of its own while also tasked with supporting vital allies through arms deliveries. If the United States spent 1,500 interceptors in a matter of months on Iran, what will Taiwan require to defend itself? Certainly, more than the 102 systems that currently only exist on paper.
In evaluating the strength of U.S. deterrence, Chinese military and political leaders will consider whether or not they can deplete U.S. and allied stocks more rapidly than they can replenish them. Beijing doesn’t have to guess if the United States can sustain a major war in the Indo-Pacific; the U.S. fiscal budget request, the contracts awarded, and the backlog of arms sales are all public information.
U.S. allies aren’t blind to this. Chen Yi-fan of Tamkang University wrote that even if the deal was opened up for bidding immediately it would take four to five years for a Patriot system to arrive in Taiwan – and that’s the exact timeframe during which American and Taiwan planners believe a crisis could occur.
Meanwhile, the AUKUS initiative was retooled in May due to the realization that the United States would be unable to produce new submarines for Australia. Allies know what that means.
You can’t ramp up factories, suppliers, machine shops, and skilled labor immediately. Even when Congress appropriates budgets, production capacity slotted to come online in 2030 isn’t going to deter Beijing in 2027. Funding the U.S. munitions supply chain is no longer the bottleneck. The challenge is accelerating the construction timeline for new production capacity.
The normal sequence is government demand first, then new capacity being developed. Contracts are awarded before firms invest in facilities, machines, and the people who will do the work. Flipping that model on its head could shorten the time between a shortage and the production to address it by years.
Some private firms are rapidly building capacity and production, before contracts are even awarded. They’re putting their own money where their mouths are and betting on guaranteed future demand. One of the leaders in that race is Hadrian, recently valued at nearly $8 billion in its latest funding round. In March, the private manufacturer opened Factory 4: a 2.2 million square foot machine shop in Cherokee, Alabama making parts for the Virginia- and Columbia-class submarines, the most relevant vessels to a potential war in the western Pacific. Under AUKUS, the United States was supposed to provide Australia with a new Virginia-class submarine before production constraints forced it to settle for in-service subs instead.
Hadrian’s move seeks to directly address one of the largest challenges facing the United States’ Navy and its Indo-Pacific presence. This approach is the one which should be replicated: they invested over $1.5 billion in private capital before receiving a roughly $900 million contract from the Navy.
The same model could expand the capabilities needed by Taiwan and Japan. In December, Lockheed Martin signed an MOU with Hadrian to co-locate a machine shop and inspection facility within Lockheed’s factory that produces the PAC-3 MSE and THAAD interceptors. To be clear: this is an arrangement, not a production deal. The company claims their Opus manufacturing system can have new production facilities operational in less than six months and new technicians operating at full productivity in 30 days.
These are not vetted performance metrics, just internal targets. That said, Hadrian has already been producing parts for Anduril’s autonomous weapons since 2023. Anduril says it has decreased delivery times up to 50 percent. Scaling up machine shops is no longer a pipe dream.
Part of the solution will also come from other countries. Japan currently produces PAC-3 interceptors under license at Mitsubishi Heavy Industries at a rate of about 30 interceptors per year, with the potential to double production. In November, Japan successfully exported its first domestically manufactured PAC-3 interceptors to the United States.
Production is bottlenecked by the Boeing seeker; the new seeker production lines won’t be running until 2027. However, Japan and the United States are negotiating joint production of the PAC-3 MSE. Japan could expand production of its own seekers, avoiding the bottleneck for itself but also for every other Patriot user in the area.
Taiwan cannot manufacture Patriots under license, but it can ramp up manufacturing for drones, naval mines, and shore-based missiles. These conversations might not make headlines, but they would contribute more to Japan and Taiwan’s defense than one more extended deterrence communique.
How quickly a country can replenish its arms is a key question of deterrence. Taken together, there’s a rough blueprint for quickly addressing production constraints. The United States can encourage the private-sector-first, public-sector-later approach Hadrian took to financing production, but only for already-approved suppliers on both sides of the Pacific.
Private firms taking action is the beginning of a solution, but without global engagement with allies, interceptor batteries will stay empty. Second, Washington should develop a surge production roadmap among allied industries: what U.S., Japanese, Australian, South Korean, and Taiwanese industries can ramp up or repurpose in six, twelve, or eighteen months, starting with seekers, rocket motors, and castings/forgings. National export controls are crucial for this, but I am advocating for selective industrial integration, not open and indiscriminate technology sharing.
Finally, Taiwan and Japan should demand to know, officially and on the record, how long their Patriot and other major arms systems will take to deliver once funded, and the Pentagon should provide those numbers. Taiwan’s 102 interceptors are lumped in with the U.S. Army’s 2,798, along with other allied requests, as well as the re-supply for each missile used over Iran. Japan’s Tomahawks are in that same queue. The United States can make a statement immediately, but what Taipei, Tokyo, and just as importantly, Beijing care about is the delivery at the pier.

Trump`s ‘Lightning Speed` Outpaces the Courts
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02

Trump ally defends Venezuela oil deal amid ‘gunpoint diplomacy’ criticism
Unknown

2026-09-02
14:44:39 UTC
23:44:39 KST

The US energy secretary, Chris Wright, has denied Washington is seeking to commandeer huge quantities of Venezuelan oil, amid growing criticism of Donald Trump’s energy deal with the country’s interim leaders.
“Absolutely not,” Wright replied when asked by a CNBC journalist if the US was engaged in a “heavy-handed” attempt to “take” Venezuelan oil in violation of the South American country’s constitution.
Wright landed in Venezuela’s capital, Caracas, on Tuesday night, four days after Trump announced what he called “the biggest oil deal in world history”.
“I think we are seeing an absolutely historic transformation of both Venezuela and the relations between Venezuela and the US,” Wright said of the deal, which Trump has claimed will give the US control of 65bn barrels of Venezuelan oil. “This is President Trump’s grand plan to replace conflict with commerce,” Wright said.
The White House says the deal will help secure US “energy dominance for the next century” as well as “purging foreign malign influence from our back yard” by excluding China and Russia from oilfields in the country with the world’s largest proven oil reserves. But there has been criticism from across the political spectrum.
The Wall Street Journal’s editorial board said Trump’s deal with Venezuela’s unelected interim president, Delcy Rodríguez, “looks less like a normal commercial transaction than it does the famous scene of US businessmen meeting with the Cuban strongman in The Godfather Part II”.
“The US government is essentially getting in bed with a foreign dictator and her favored capitalist,” the newspaper complained, in reference to Alejandro Betancourt, the Venezuelan tycoon at the centre of the deal.
The economist Francisco Rodríguez told Democracy Now: “It’s clear that this is not a deal that any Venezuelan government would have entered into unless this country had been subject to an invasion, and unless its authorities had been held at gunpoint. So I think we’ve replaced gunboat diplomacy now for gunpoint diplomacy.”
Delcy Rodríguez was installed as interim president on 5 January, two days after the president, Nicolás Maduro, was abducted by US special forces during a predawn raid on Caracas. Trump warned Rodríguez, who was Maduro’s vice-president, she would face an even worse fate if she did not toe the US line.
Since Maduro’s capture, Rodríguez has made a series of once unthinkable concessions to US officials who their nominally socialist political movement, Chavismo, had spent years denouncing as predatory imperialists bent on stealing Venezuela’s natural resources.
On Saturday, Rodríguez claimed the oil deal had “endless” benefits and would help produce more than $209bn in revenues that could be used to improve healthcare and education. “We are thinking of Venezuela’s future,” she said during a televised broadcast to the nation.
The deal has dealt a body blow to Venezuela’s political opposition, who fear Trump is unlikely to push for a democratic transition or fresh presidential elections given his lucrative arrangement with Rodríguez.
“This is a game between the Trump administration and Delcy and her people,” one opposition figure lamented after the deal was unveiled.
Speaking at a signing ceremony in the Miraflores presidential palace in Caracas on Wednesday, Rodríguez thanked the Trump administration for its part in what she called a “win-win deal”. She said: “I have faith in the future of Venezuela. What we are doing today represents the future and the hope of the people of Venezuela.”

AI-powered cyberattacks 'already happening' against critical infrastructure, Check Point chief says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
14:42:10 UTC
23:42:10 KST

AI-powered cyberattacks against critical infrastructure are no longer a future threat; they are already happening, Check Point Chief of Staff Gil Messing warned in an interview with 103FM on Monday.
Messing addressed a joint warning from major technology companies about the possibility that hostile actors could exploit artificial intelligence to attack critical infrastructure.
"The unusual call comes because more than 100 significant companies around the world, including us, have joined in saying that what has been happening cannot continue," Messing said. "It is becoming more dangerous, and it is not that this will happen soon; it is already happening."
According to Messing, the emergence of increasingly powerful artificial intelligence models has erased much of the gap that once separated major powers from smaller actors in mounting sophisticated cyberattacks.
"Since those significant models from OpenAI, Anthropic, and others were released, at levels we had never seen before, the gaps that previously existed between powers and actors that are not major powers in their ability to create cyberattacks have disappeared," he said.
"The models allow almost anyone with a little knowledge to create attacks and vulnerabilities that have never been seen before. This tool, which is like a weapon, is reaching everyone's hands, and that is at the heart of the approach of the new AI companies, so the attacks have become more sophisticated and more frequent."
Messing: Cyberattacks exploit software vulnerabilities, can lead to critical shutdowns
Messing said cyberattacks generally rely on exploiting vulnerabilities in software, with the consequences ranging from service disruptions to data theft, system crashes, encryption of information, and the shutdown of critical systems.
"The entire cyber world ultimately works on the fact that there is software with a vulnerability through which someone gets in, exploits it, and that becomes an attack," he said. "At the end of the process, what we see is something that does not work, something being shut down, information being stolen, a crash or encryption, and systems that stop functioning."
"The models make possible, although they should not make possible, attacks unlike anything we have seen before, without human involvement," Messing continued. "It has reached the point where the models sometimes attack on their own without a person controlling them and asking them to do it, and that gets out of control. There is an attempt to tell the world that there is something different here.
"Everyone needs to cooperate because this is not the world we knew before," he continued. "We are in a new era. What exists now is not good enough to stop it, and cooperation is needed."
Messing said addressing the threat would require action in three main areas, starting with ensuring organizations regularly update their software.
"There are three main components, and if we deal with them, we will deal with most of the problem," he said. "One is the issue of version updates, because organizations have to constantly update their versions. They do not know how to do this because they do not have enough manpower, so more personnel need to be trained to deal with it."
Trained professionals needed to deal with threat, Messing says
He added that trained professionals would need to operate those systems, while governments would have to establish appropriate regulation for the rapidly developing AI sector.
"There are the people who need to operate it, and there are governments that need to regulate what is happening now with AI models," Messing said. "If we do not deal with each of these components, we will not have the tools to deal with the attacks that are taking place. As the models continue to develop, if there is no effort to stop or confront this, then the warning from the companies is that we will face a world in which breaches will be significant and painful."

Senior Israeli official: Settler violence harming Israel, Syria security deal attempt failed
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
14:42:06 UTC
23:42:06 KST

Settler violence in the West Bank is causing diplomatic damage to Israel but has declined in recent months, while an Israeli attempt to reach a security agreement with Syria has failed, a senior Israeli diplomatic official said on Wednesday.
According to the official, the number of violent incidents involving settlers, including serious incidents, has fallen in recent months, while enforcement activity and arrests have increased.
The official described March as a "peak month," saying that both the overall number of incidents and the number of serious incidents declined between March and July. At the same time, enforcement increased.
"The phenomenon still exists. It needs to be dealt with," the official said. "We certainly see the damage caused as a result of it."
Foreign Ministry working to combat damage caused by West Bank settler violence
Israel is acting on several fronts to combat the phenomenon, the official said, ranging from deploying additional personnel and increasing enforcement on the ground to other measures aimed at addressing those behind the violence.
Amid international criticism, the Foreign Ministry is also working to present more clearly the steps Israeli authorities are taking against Israelis involved in violent incidents, the official added.
"We asked to show, not just tell, the enforcement actions," the official said. According to the official, this was also why footage of arrests and legal proceedings has been released recently. The goal is to demonstrate internationally that Israeli authorities are taking action against those involved in violence.
The official sought to distinguish the violence issue from the broader dispute between Israel and European countries over Israeli settlement in the West Bank. Israel rejects the European position regarding settlements, the official said, while at the same time continuing to act against Israelis involved in violence.
The official also noted that Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich had published an article opposing the phenomenon and addressed the relevant public on the issue.
Defense agreement falls through with Syria, Israeli official says
On Syria, the official confirmed that an attempt to reach a security agreement between Israel and the government in Damascus had failed.
"We tried to reach a security agreement. In the end, it did not succeed," the official said.
One development that complicated the talks was the easing of sanctions imposed on Syria, according to the official.
"Syrian motivation to move forward with such an agreement declined when certain sanctions on Syria were lifted," the official said.
Another central issue was the buffer zone. Israel was unwilling to accept an agreement that would require it to withdraw from the area.
"We did not think that, as part of a security arrangement or security agreement, we should withdraw from the buffer zone, which is a security asset," the official said.
Despite the failure to reach an agreement, communication channels with Damascus remain active.
"The State of Israel has communication channels with the Syrian regime," the official said.
The dialogue is taking place on several levels and concerns, among other things, security arrangements in southern Syria.
"I can't go into all the content, but there are channels in which dialogue is taking place. We try in this dialogue to preserve the interests of the State of Israel, the security interests," the official said.
Hamas disarmament stalls in Gaza, Israel working to keep diplomatic negotiations alive with the US
Regarding Gaza, the official said there had so far been no breakthrough on what Israel considers the central issue, the disarmament of Hamas.
"Unfortunately, there is no progress on the issue of disarmament," the official said.
Israel does not want the diplomatic track with the Americans and the Peace Council to collapse, the official said, but insists it include the conditions Israel believes were established in the original plan.
"Our basic argument was that the 15-point plan does not correspond with the 20-point plan," the official said. "We have no interest in the plan collapsing. We have an interest in the plan being implemented, but from our perspective, implementing the plan means implementing all of its conditions."
Two working groups are operating between Israel and the Peace Council, one dealing with the disarmament of Hamas and the other with humanitarian issues, according to the official.
Even if there is skepticism about the prospects of achieving all of Israel's objectives through the diplomatic track, Israel wants to exhaust that avenue as long as it offers an opportunity to achieve some of the goals of the war, the official said.
Israel also continues to link the disarmament of Hamas to the reconstruction of the Gaza Strip.
"We have always emphasized that the issue of reconstruction is linked to the issue of disarmament," the official said.
The international stabilization force, the ISF, has also not yet reached the implementation stage. According to the official, discussions on the issue are continuing with the Americans, and Morocco and Uganda are among the countries involved in the discussions.
The official said he had discussed the matter with the Moroccan foreign minister and said that "Israel's expectation is for a move connected to Hamas disarming."
On Lebanon, the official said Israel opposes the establishment of a "new UNIFIL." UNIFIL did not fulfill its role and had hindered Israeli activity over the years, the official said.
Jerusalem is not, however, ruling out other mechanisms, including training units of the Lebanese Armed Forces or establishing a verification mechanism.
Israel has raised the possibility that the US could train dedicated units in the Lebanese military that would be capable of effectively taking control of territory, the official said.
Israel also does not expect to object in principle to Italian participation in a verification mechanism if one is established.
The official estimated that the next round of talks between Israel, the US, and Lebanon would take place during September.
Regarding Turkey, the official said Israel does not define it as an "enemy state," but that it can be viewed as a rival because of steps Ankara has taken in recent years.
In earlier periods, the official said, messages were passed between Jerusalem and Ankara through Azerbaijan, but "that has been happening less recently."
The sides exchanged a few words during a meeting held as part of the Peace Council, the official said, but "there are no intensive exchanges."
Despite the escalation in rhetoric between the two countries, the official added that he did not believe either Israel or Turkey wanted to reach the point of a direct exchange of fire.

Nepal to rebuild early-warning system on China border after deadly flood, sources say
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
14:42:01 UTC
23:42:01 KST

Nepal plans to rebuild an early-warning system for landslides on part of its border with China, installing seismic sensors, cameras, and a satellite link, two Nepali government sources told Reuters, a week after a glacial flood killed more than 1,000.
The equipment is being set up at Timure, a border settlement in Nepal's Rasuwa district on the same river corridor along the border with China where a collapsing glacier sent a gigantic wall of mud, water and rock hurtling through mountain valleys.
At least 1,114 people have died in both countries, the vast majority in Nepal, and nearly 4,000 are still missing.
The stretch of border where the instruments will be placed lies in one of the most sensitive parts of Nepal's frontier with China's Tibet region, a high-altitude area closely watched by Kathmandu, Beijing, and New Delhi.
Nepal has not formally announced the plans, and the two sources spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to discuss the issue.
The officials said there was a sense of urgency to act.
"The landscape is adjusting after the mega event, so [it] could trigger a few more landslides," one of the sources said.
Officials survey locations for warning system placement
Central to the plan is a satellite system known as Very Small Aperture Terminal (VSAT), meant to keep monitoring posts connected even when mobile networks go down, so they can spot fresh hazards and issue warnings quickly, both sources said.
Such a blackout occurred when last week's flood knocked out at least four gauging stations near the border.
"We had sensors and monitoring stations, but they were not being monitored extensively," the source said, describing a previous early warning system that would send a message every few minutes but was swept away by Wednesday's floods.
"Because we were unaware, we couldn't check when they failed."
For now, cameras, sensors and the VSAT will be installed at a single site by Nepal's National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority (NDRRMA) and more would follow, the second source said, adding that officials have already surveyed the area by helicopter to assess their placement.
An NDRRMA spokesperson did not immediately respond to Reuters emails and messages seeking comment.
China's foreign minister and the country's embassy in Nepal also did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Since the disaster, China has said imagery of the affected areas, satellite and hydrological data, as well as early-warning information on upstream barrier lakes, have been shared with Nepal.
Previous system only provided a few minutes of warning
The immediate danger from two barrier lakes near the border - formed after the glacial collapse - has passed after they drained. But the terrain remains unstable and is being closely watched, one source said.
An early-warning system for any landslide-triggered events would give authorities only a few minutes to alert downstream communities of another flood, a brief window that could still prove critical.
Last week's flood struck a border crossing at 8:32 a.m., but a public alert was not issued until 9:13 a.m., Reuters has reported.
Nepal had pressed China for more detailed, real-time sharing of data on glacier movements and water levels in the months before the disaster, and Nepali officials now plan to deepen their cooperation.

USS Abraham Lincoln docks in Thailand after record-breaking 286-day deployment
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
14:41:50 UTC
23:41:50 KST

US Navy aircraft carrier Abraham Lincoln arrived in port in eastern Thailand on Wednesday after 286 days at sea, including a lengthy deployment in the Middle East, amid reports of mental health concerns and deteriorating conditions on board.
The nuclear-powered Lincoln, with roughly 5,000 personnel, was involved in the US naval blockade and combat operations in the war with Iran and - according to Democratic lawmakers - set a modern-day record for consecutive days at sea.
Accompanied by other US naval vessels, the Lincoln arrived early Wednesday in Thailand, the United States' only treaty partner in mainland Southeast Asia, for rest and recuperation during a visit that Thai officials said would last five days.
By afternoon, busloads of sailors and Marines wearing civilian clothes, many smiling and waving, started arriving at a hotel in the resort city of Pattaya, about 150 km southeast of Bangkok.
Strike group achieved 'truly historical' accomplishments
"Our arrival in Laem Chabang provides a well-deserved opportunity for our Sailors and Marines to rest and recharge," the commander of Carrier Strike Group 3, Rear Admiral Robert E. Loughran, said in a statement.
"What this strike group has accomplished is truly historic. I could not be prouder of the exceptional professionalism and expertise demonstrated by every member of this team during our operations."
The Lincoln was deployed last November. Typically naval deployments are for between six and nine months, but those can be extended during times of conflict.
Eastern Thailand is long accustomed to port visits by the US Navy and has a relationship going back to the Vietnam War, when Pattaya was a sleepy beach town close to a naval base and an airfield used by US bombers, with thousands of US personnel based in the area.
Thailand became a US treaty ally in 1954 before being designated a major non-NATO ally in 2003. The two countries' militaries maintain strong ties and hold joint exercises every year.
The Lincoln, its broad flight deck packed with helicopters and warplanes, including the latest F-35 fighter jets, arrived in Laem Chabang early on Wednesday, and the guided-missile destroyer USS Frank E. Petersen Jr. docked in nearby Sri Racha.
Both vessels were streaked with rust and showed mottled paint along the waterlines. A third ship, the guided-missile cruiser USS Robert Smalls, arrived in the port of Map Tha Phut.
Port visit raises hopes of economic boost for Pattaya
The port visit has raised hopes of an economic boost for Pattaya, which also has a long-standing reputation as a sex tourism destination.
The city's mayor, Poramase Ngampiches, met the commander of the Lincoln on Wednesday and said US officials had placed restrictions on the crew's activities during the stay, including on water sports and visiting certain entertainment zones after sunset, which he said could present a negative image.
Police will deploy additional patrols around Pattaya's main beachfront and nightlife district, following raids over the weekend and the arrest of 40 to 50 people for suspected prostitution.
Although illegal in Thailand, the sex industry operates openly in tourism hubs, including in Bangkok, Phuket and Pattaya, despite occasional crackdowns.
On the eve of the Lincoln's arrival, Pattaya street vendors near the city's infamous "Walking Street" nightlife zone were excited by the prospect of a boost in sales.
