Feature: When robot picks up Chinese calligraphy brush at Venice Biennale
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
21:29:41 CST
22:29:41 KST

VENICE, Italy, Sept. 2 (Xinhua) -- Dozens of visitors lined up at the China pavilion of the Venice Biennale, waiting for their turn to see something unusual: a robot slowly moved its mechanical arm, guiding a traditional Chinese calligraphy brush across a sheet of paper.
Stroke by stroke, the brush wrote two Chinese characters which mean "Dream" and "Stream" respectively.
The scene was unfolding recently at the China pavilion of the 61st International Art Exhibition of La Biennale di Venezia in Venice, Italy. "Dream Stream," inspired by Dream Stream Essays, an encyclopedia written by Shen Kuo in China's Song Dynasty, is the theme of this year's China pavilion exhibition.
As the 83rd Venice International Film Festival opens on Wednesday, Venice is welcoming visitors from around the world, with the Biennale also seeing a surge in visitors. At the China pavilion, the blend of traditional Chinese culture, contemporary art and modern technology has drawn many curious visitors.
"It is the first time I have seen a robot writing," Andrea, a visitor from Austria, told Xinhua. "What makes it even more special is that it is writing Chinese calligraphy with a traditional brush," she said.
Visiting the pavilion with her daughter, Andrea said they both enjoyed experiencing the combination of traditional Chinese culture and modern technology. "We were really surprised by what we saw here," she said.
Another attraction for visitors is a playable section featuring scenes from the globally acclaimed Chinese video game "Black Myth: Wukong".
A giant widescreen unfolds before visitors, creating an immersive experience that brings them into a world inspired by traditional Chinese mythology. Beside the screen stands a sculpture of "the Destined One", the game's iconic protagonist.
After playing for several minutes, Thomas, a visitor from Germany, said he was impressed by the game's beautiful visuals and smooth controls.
He asked how to download the game, saying he hoped to experience the full version and learn more about the traditional Chinese mythology behind it.
According to the organizers, the exhibition combines calligraphy, video, digital art, multimedia installations and robot display to present Chinese tradition in new forms.
Works such as "Liangzhu Highlight" and "Kinetic Droplet Instrument" transform diverse Chinese cultural elements into experiences that can be seen, felt and interacted with, creating a space for dialogues between the ancient and the contemporary, while highlighting cultural exchanges and mutual learning between China and other parts of the world, according to the organizers.
At the opening ceremony of the China pavilion in May, Curator Yu Xuhong, also president of the China Academy of Art, said the theme "Dream Stream" draws on the Eastern wisdom embodied in Dream Stream Essays, particularly its spirit of exploring the principles of things and seeking harmony between humanity and nature.
Through the integration of tradition and innovation, as well as art and science and technology, the exhibition seeks to create an immersive and perceptible Eastern visual system and a distinctive way of understanding the world, said Yu.
For visitors, that vision comes to life through the artworks and interactive experiences on display. Eszter Nagy and Adam Lendvai, visitors from Hungary, told Xinhua that the exhibition offered a glimpse into the intersection of Chinese culture and digital technology.
"What we saw here was just a small part of each. We believe there is still so much more to explore," they said, adding that they would be interested in seeing more and perhaps visiting China one day to experience its culture firsthand.
This year's China pavilion exhibition will run through Nov. 22. ■

China Focus: China's manufacturing powerhouse blends research, industry to fuel innovation
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
21:29:38 CST
22:29:38 KST

HANGZHOU, Sept. 2 (Xinhua) -- Holding up a small vial of fine white powder, Su Hongjiu said it took his company only 14 months to turn a laboratory sample of the ultrapure nanosilica abrasive, a key chip-polishing consumable, into China's first mass-produced version.
"Overseas companies once held more than 90 percent of the market. Now we can make this type of abrasive ourselves," said Su, founder of Ningbo GSi Electronic Materials Co., Ltd.
Incubated by Yongjiang Laboratory (Y-LAB), a government-approved materials research institution in Ningbo city, GSi is among a crop of startups emerging in Zhejiang, a province that was home to 2,167 national 'little giant' enterprises by the end of 2025 -- about 12 percent of the country's total.
The title is a government designation for top-tier small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) that excel in niche markets with strong innovation capabilities and core technologies.
Thanks to established mechanisms connecting researchers and manufacturers, and bridging lab-factory gaps, Zhejiang has grown from a manufacturing powerhouse to a fertile ground for innovative enterprises.
CO-BUILDERS, NOT TAKERS
Y-LAB has established joint innovation centers with local tech companies, with a clear division of labor: the lab provides technology and talent, while the companies offer application scenarios and market access.
Some enterprises want even closer ties, giving rise to the role of "part-time technology vice president" -- a title for university or research institution researchers who take part-time executive posts at companies.
They help identify technical problems, coordinate joint research and strengthen in-house innovation. By July, 2,017 such appointments had been made across the province.
Zhang Ruihua, a professor at Lishui University, was paired with Zhejiang Lishui Jiexiang Technology, a leading domestic maker of rolling functional components.
Zhang brought students onto the shop floor, mapped production bottlenecks, and focused on the automated assembly of guideway blocks, a hurdle for domestic high-end machine tools.
The resulting equipment works six to eight times faster than manual labor, and 11 enterprises now use multiple sets of the intelligent equipment developed by the team.
The company-university partnership has since expanded into a joint provincial engineering research center and a master's program, with 15 graduate students whose research topics all come from factory production.
Other companies team up with researchers even earlier. Ningbo Yongxin Optics Co. hired a Zhejiang University professor as its technology vice president, to steer pilot projects.
The partnership resulted in the firm's four-color laser confocal microscope which broke a decades-long foreign monopoly.
"You can't wait until a paper is published or a prototype is built -- by then the technical route is set," said Cui Zhiying, a company technician in the joint team.
"We want to be co-builders of original innovation, not takers of hand-me-down technology," Cui said.
FROM MARKET FRONTIER TO UNIVERSITY CLASSROOMS
Wang Xingxing, founder of the world's leading robot maker Unitree Robotics headquartered in Hangzhou, capital of Zhejiang province, also serves as an "industry professor" at his alma mater, Zhejiang Sci-Tech University, with the standard academic requirements waived.
"We have long cooperated with Unitree, but the company and the school were still disconnected. With Wang Xingxing as our industry professor, we can go all out in both student training and research," said Chen Gang, a professor at the university.
To bridge the gap between fast-moving industry and university education, and to make up for students' lack of firsthand, real-world experience, senior technical professionals were introduced into Zhejiang's universities for such part-time positions.
So far, Zhejiang has appointed 973 of them.
In Ningbo, Jing Ge, chief engineer of a local new-energy subsidiary of CRRC, the world's top supplier of rail transit equipment, wears a second hat as an industry professor at Zhejiang Wanli University, where he helps set up the discipline, from which courses to offer to what they should cover.
Jing was also a key contributor to a project on ultra-high-power supercapacitors that won the 2025 national sci-tech award.
Citywide, more than 70 percent of Ningbo's industry professors have helped design academic programs, co-written 74 textbooks, developed 178 courses, and mentored more than 660 students.
FROM SCIENTISTS TO CEOs
When Zhejiang University professor Li Jingbo set out to build a company around his team's new silicon carbide chip, investors pushed back. A production line could cost hundreds of millions of yuan, and they were not ready to bet on a lab-born technology.
The hurdle Li faced is common. Researchers-turned-founders need more than scientific expertise -- they must pick a market, assemble a team and raise capital for technologies that can take years to mature.
Li found a partner in the Hangzhou Institute of Optics and Fine Mechanics, or SIOM-H, founded in 2019. It is among China's first "excellent-level" technology business incubators, built to help researchers clear exactly those barriers.
Qi Hongji, head of SIOM-H, calls the institute an "entrepreneurial partner." Its professional team fills gaps scientists often face in product development, marketing, team building and financing.
SIOM-H stepped into Li's project with 15 million yuan (about 2.2 million U.S. dollars) in angel investment, followed by other investors.
"It enabled us to make a start," said Li, chairman of startup Zhejiang XinKe Semiconductor.
Within months, SIOM-H helped attract nearly 50 million yuan from market investors, enough for second-hand equipment. In 2023, it helped secure hundreds of millions more, allowing Li to upgrade the production line.
Li's story is not an exception. As of July, SIOM-H had incubated more than 70 companies and attracted over 5 billion yuan in external capital, with the incubated firms' combined valuation exceeding 50 billion yuan.
"With stamina, passion and a team, we can take a company to the global forefront," Qi said. ■

Simple thigh ultrasound may help predict heart surgery risks: study
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
21:29:21 CST
22:29:21 KST

CANBERRA, Sept. 2 (Xinhua) -- A simple, low-cost bedside ultrasound scan of the thigh could help predict which heart surgery patients are most at risk of serious lung complications, new Australian research shows.
The study, led by Australia's Calvary Adelaide Hospital (CAH) in partnership with Adelaide University, is exploring whether a quick, non-invasive ultrasound of the thigh can flag early signs of post-operative decline in cardiac patients, according to a university statement released Wednesday.
Researchers will assess whether measuring the rectus femoris muscle, a major thigh muscle, can predict complications following major heart surgery. If successful, it could provide the first objectively verified bedside method to identify cardiac patients at higher risk of pulmonary complications, the statement said.
Around 10-25 percent of post-operative cardiac patients develop pulmonary complications, which can lead to rapid deconditioning, delayed mobilization and longer hospital stays, the researchers noted.
The project will be piloted over 12 months in South Australia, focusing on rural and remote populations where unique barriers affect access and continuity of care. ■

Moscow vows to avoid airspace disruption despite Zelenskiy's aviation warning
Unknown

Moscow vows to avoid airspace disruption despite Zelenskiy's warning
MOSCOW/LONDON/DUBAI, Sept 2 - Russia vowed to head off any disruption to civil aviation on Wednesday after a warning by Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy that its drones had made Russian airspace dangerous to use.
Zelenskiy warned airlines and insurance firms on Tuesday that the presence of Ukrainian drones as Ukraine responded to Russian attacks meant "the war started by Russia is closing its own skies". He said he was not targeting civil aviation.
Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said on Wednesday Ukraine had also officially notified the International Civil Aviation Organization that Russian airspace was not safe.
While European and U.S. carriers do not fly over Russia due to the war that erupted when Russia invaded Ukraine in February 2022, the airspace is used by airlines from countries such as China, Turkey, the United Arab Emirates and other Gulf states.
Andrei Nikitin, Russia's transport minister, was quoted as saying by the Interfax news agency: "We are constantly improving flight safety and airport security requirements, and we have solutions for all of this."
"We are working in close contact with the Ministry of Defence and the Russian National Guard. And I believe that we will not allow any significant disruption to civil aviation,” he said.
Russia's civil aviation authority, Rosaviatsia said in a statement that Ukrainian approaches to international aviation bodies "have no legal force and violate the Convention on International Civil Aviation".
"Russia's air transport and its ground infrastructure continue to operate according to plan, handling arrivals and departures, including flights by foreign airlines," it said.
SOME FLIGHTS CANCELLED
Flightradar24 data showed disruptions on Wednesday at Moscow's main airport, while some airlines cancelled flights though they did not specify the reason for doing so.
"We continue to closely monitor the evolving situation in the region and adjust our flight schedules and routings as necessary," airline flydubai said in a statement.
"As the situation remains dynamic, our teams are continuously assessing operational requirements. We recognise that some delays and diversions may occur ... The safety of our customers and crew remains our highest priority."
Turkish carrier Pegasus Airlines said it had cancelled some flights to Russia for "technical and operational" reasons, without giving further details.
RUSSIAN ATTACKS ON KYIV
Moscow's Sheremetyevo International Airport showed 21 cancelled flights and 235 delays, while the city's Vnukovo airport had 22 cancelled flights and 94 delays, according to Flightradar24.
Vnukovo airport said Pegasus Airlines had cancelled six arriving and six departing flights at the hub on Tuesday. The carrier said overnight flights into Wednesday were impacted, but other ongoing flights were "operating as scheduled".
Other carriers that fly regularly to and over Russia, including Turkish Airlines, Qatar, Etihad and Emirates, did not respond to Reuters requests for comment.
Zelenskiy in his nightly video address on Wednesday said that a number of airlines were not flying into Russia, describing such decisions as "the right and entirely logical response to everything that is happening".
Aviation risk advisory firm Osprey Flight Solutions has said in an alert to clients that while the majority of Ukraine's drone and missile strikes were likely to occur within 300 km (185 miles) of the border, daily attacks deeper inside Russia were likely through 2026, including near Moscow and St Petersburg.
Russia has stepped up its air attacks on Kyiv and other cities in recent weeks, with residents enduring the seventh day of intense assaults on the Ukrainian capital on Wednesday.
Ukraine has responded with frequent drone strikes on Russian targets, many associated with the country's oil industry as well as retail sites. REUTERS

From Partnership to Penalty: US Tariffs Shadow India Trade Deal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
13:26:00 UTC
22:26:00 KST

U.S. Ambassador to India Sergio Gor recently claimed that the India-U.S. trade agreement is on the verge of finalization and that “almost everything” about the agreement was done “in principle.”
However, even as Gor was exuding confidence regarding the deal, two initiatives taken in Washington in just over a month have brought yet another round of the tariff war to India’s doorstep. These initiatives have the potential of increasing friction between the two countries, and could even torpedo the deal.
The most egregious of these developments is the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026, a bipartisan bill proposed in the U.S. Senate, which has the backing of the U.S. President Donald Trump.
The second development is Trump’s proposal to impose 100 percent tariffs on generic medicines from 2028, unless the firms exporting these medicines do not reshore their operations to the U.S. This proposal could significantly affect India’s pharmaceutical industry since the U.S. is its largest export market.
The bipartisan Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026, named after the late Republican senator, who was the bill’s strongest proponent, was overwhelmingly voted by the Senate (86-11) in early August. The House of Representatives will take up the bill for consideration after it reconvenes in early September, and could push for its early adoption.
The primary objective of the bill is to tighten the economic sanctions on Russia for its continued war on Ukraine. The bill proposes 500 percent tariffs on all goods imported into the U.S. from Russia. It also proposes 100 percent tariffs on all goods imported into the U.S. from the five largest importers of crude oil or natural gas, by total volume, originating in the Russian Federation. As one of the largest importers of Russian-origin crude oil, India also faces penal tariffs for facilitating Russia’s sanctions evasion.
Market analysts put India as the second-largest buyer of Russian crude oil in July 2026, valued at over $7.3 billion, or about 37 percent of Russia’s global exports.
According to Indian government data, India’s dependence on Russian crude oil increased from 30 percent to nearly 43 percent of its total imports between January and June 2026. In February 2026, after the U.S. and India reached a framework for an interim agreement as a step toward finalizing the trade deal, Trump announced that the 25 percent tariffs imposed on India in August 2025 for importing Russian crude oil was withdrawn.
India, according to Trump, had “committed to stop directly or indirectly importing Russian Federation oil, has represented that it will purchase United States energy products from the United States.”
However, after the conflict in West Asia, India’s dependence on Russian crude increased to record levels, and simultaneously, its imports from the U.S. dropped from 13 percent in April 2025 to three percent in June 2026. Trump would surely have viewed this development as a trigger for action against India.
India’s generic pharmaceutical industry faces uncertain times following Trump’s post on Truth Social announcing his decision to impose a 100 percent tariff on all generic medicines from 2028, and increased to 200 percent a year by 2029. The objective of this proposed increase in tariffs is to “Reshore Generic Pharmaceutical Production into America, with a penalty to those Companies that decide not to build Plant and Equipment within the stated period of time given to them.”
This announcement followed an earlier decision by Trump to impose a 100 percent tariff on patented pharmaceuticals and associated pharmaceutical ingredients from July 31, 2026, if the companies exporting them do not declare plans to start producing in the US. Thus, Trump has put in place an expansive plan to control the global pharmaceutical industry.
Pharmaceuticals are the second largest products in India’s export basket to the U.S., accounting for about 13 percent of total exports in 2025-26. More importantly, the U.S. is the largest export market for all major Indian pharmaceutical companies.
The U.S. accounted for about a third of the total sales of most companies, but two Indian pharma companies — Dr. Reddy’s Laboratories and Zydus Life Sciences — are considerably more dependent on the US market: their shares of sales to the US were close to 50 percent in 2023-24.
Besides, all the top Indian companies have invested in production capacities in the U.S. through their subsidiaries, with the largest company, Sun Pharmaceutical Industries having 21 subsidiaries in 2025-26.
Trump’s insistence that the generic pharmaceutical companies must invest in the US to escape 100 percent tariff in 2028 has had its desired effect as Indian companies, including pharmaceutical companies have already announced their plans to invest over $19.1 billion to increase their production capacities in the US.
Only time will tell whether these investments will result in diversion of India’s domestic pharmaceutical production to the U.S., and the implication this could have on the availability of medicines in India.

A coffee-table-size scorpion roamed Earth before forests existed
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
13:23:16 UTC
22:23:16 KST

A coffee-table-size scorpion roamed Earth before forests existed
- Date:
- September 2, 2026
- Source:
- University of Manchester
- Summary:
- A meter-long scorpion with massive pincers stalked ancient Britain 415 million years ago, long before forests and the better-known age of giant insects. Its surprising size and possible semi-aquatic lifestyle could reshape ideas about how early arthropods became giants.
- Share:
A newly analyzed fossil predator from what is now England and Wales has been identified as the largest scorpion known to science. Researchers from The University of Manchester and the Natural History Museum reached the conclusion after revisiting fossils that had remained in museum collections for more than 150 years.
The animal, Praearcturus gigas, reached roughly one meter in length and carried pincers more than 16 centimeters long. Around 415 million years ago, it would have been an imposing predator in the floodplain environments of the Early Devonian.
A study published in Palaeontology used modern analytical methods and comparisons with more recently described fossil species to determine that Praearcturus was a scorpion and represented a distinct species.
A Giant From Before the Age of Trees
Dr. Richard J. Howard, Curator of Fossil Arthropods at the Natural History Museum, London, and lead author of the study, said: "When we think of giant arthropods, people often picture Carboniferous rainforests with giant millipedes or dragonfly-like insects from later in Earth's history. But Praearcturus lived at least 50 million years earlier, well before the evolution of trees, when life on land was only just getting started.
"Confirming that this animal is a scorpion fundamentally changes our understanding of how and when these creatures evolved to such extraordinary sizes."
The discovery pushes the story of giant arthropods much further back in time than the period usually associated with enormous insects and other invertebrates.
Dr. Russell Garwood, Paleontologist at The University of Manchester, added: "Praearcturus has puzzled us paleontologists for more than a century. By bringing together material from several collections and using cutting-edge imaging techniques, we've been able to build a clearer picture of the animal than was previously possible, which is really exciting.
"What makes Praearcturus so interesting is that it became enormous at a time when life on land was otherwise very small. But it was a world that could somehow support a giant predator. To try and better understand this ancient world, we compared the size of fossil scorpions with other animals alive at the time. To reach such extraordinary sizes, and conclude that perhaps it lived in water, where life was bigger."
Why Did This Scorpion Grow So Large?
Praearcturus gigas lived during the Early Devonian, when terrestrial ecosystems were still in their infancy. Small plants and fungi had only recently begun spreading across the landscape, while forests and other complex land ecosystems had not yet developed.
That timing is important because Praearcturus lived before the high atmospheric oxygen levels associated with the later rise of forests. Those oxygen-rich conditions have often been linked to the enormous size of some later arthropods.
Instead, the researchers suggest that ecological opportunity may help explain the animal's extraordinary size. With few other large predators competing for resources, Praearcturus may have been able to dominate its environment in a way that became much harder once terrestrial ecosystems grew more crowded and complex.
A Scorpion That May Have Lived in Water
The fossils also provide clues that Praearcturus may have spent part of its life in aquatic environments. Some specimens preserve flap-like structures on the abdomen resembling features seen in modern crustaceans such as lobsters, raising the possibility that the giant scorpion could move between water and land.
An analysis of the broader arachnid fossil record, led by Dr. Garwood and the team, also found that scorpions are unusually common in rocks from this period compared with other arachnids. That pattern supports the possibility that some early scorpions occupied freshwater environments, where their remains would have had a greater chance of being preserved as fossils.
This places Praearcturus at an especially important stage in Earth's history, when animals were beginning to explore habitats beyond the oceans.
This places Praearcturus at a pivotal moment in Earth's history when animals were first experimenting with life outside the oceans.
Dr. Greg Edgecombe, Merit Researcher at the Natural History Museum, London, and co-author of the study, said: "The boundary between land and sea was much less defined at this time. Praearcturus gives us a fascinating glimpse into how early animals adapted to these changing environments.
"It may even represent a lineage that returned to the water after earlier ancestors had already begun living on land."
A 150 Year Fossil Mystery
Scientists first described Praearcturus gigas in 1871, but at the time it was interpreted as a giant crustacean resembling a woodlouse. The fossils were incomplete and lacked important anatomical features, including a tail, which made confident identification difficult for more than a century.
The new interpretation became possible after researchers compared the historic specimens with better preserved fossils discovered more recently. Those newer remains revealed anatomical traits found specifically in scorpions, giving scientists the evidence needed to reassess Praearcturus.
The finding also demonstrates how older museum specimens can continue to produce major discoveries long after they were first collected.
Dr. Howard added: "Specimens collected over a century ago can still hold entirely new insights. By revisiting them with modern techniques, we can uncover discoveries that reshape our understanding of life on Earth."
Rethinking Prehistoric Arthropod Gigantism
Finding such an enormous scorpion so early in the history of terrestrial life challenges traditional ideas about why prehistoric arthropods sometimes evolved to gigantic sizes.
The results suggest that high oxygen levels and other environmental conditions may not have been the only factors involved. Ecological opportunity, particularly the absence of competing large predators, may also have allowed animals such as Praearcturus to reach remarkable sizes.
Story Source:
Materials provided by University of Manchester. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Richard J. Howard, Russell J. Garwood, Gregory D. Edgecombe, David A. Legg. A revision of Praearcturus gigas: a giant scorpion from the Lower Devonian (Lochkovian) of Britain. Palaeontology, 2026; 69 (3) DOI: 10.1111/pala.70064

Tumbler Ridge mass shooting victims file 30 new lawsuits against OpenAI
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
13:22:57 UTC
22:22:57 KST

OpenAI faces 30 new lawsuits filed on behalf of victims of the Tumbler Ridge mass shooting.
The suits, filed on Wednesday, allege the company’s ChatGPT chatbot induced the shooter to carry out the attack in rural Canada in February, in which eight people were killed and dozens more wounded – most of them children.
“These were people who really endured just total hell that day,” Jay Edelson, the lead lawyer representing the plaintiffs, said in an interview. “Young kids who watched their teachers die, watched friends die and thought they were going to get shot and killed.”
These new lawsuits, filed in federal court for the northern district of California, come after Edelson filed seven initial suits in April – bringing the total number of cases against OpenAI for the Tumbler Ridge shooting to 37. All of the suits allege that the violent intentions of the shooter, identified as 18-year-old Jesse Van Rootselaar, were well-known to the senior leadership of OpenAI, which failed to report her to the authorities.
Employees on the company’s safety team had flagged the shooter’s account to executives eight months before the attack, describing her in internal messages as “a credible and specific threat of gun violence against real people”, according to court filings. OpenAI banned her account, but she was able to quickly create a new one, the suits claim.
The lawsuits accuse OpenAI and its CEO, Sam Altman, of negligence, aiding and abetting a mass shooting and product liability.
Jason Kwon, OpenAI’s chief strategy officer, said in a statement that he thinks about what happened at Tumbler Ridge every day and that the company works hard to create standards for reporting cases to law enforcement.
“The professionals working on these teams choose to do this incredibly difficult work because they care so deeply about keeping people safe,” Kwon said. “They come to work every day knowing that they may have to make a decision that they’ll think about for the rest of their lives.”
A groundswell of cases have been brought against OpenAI and other tech companies alleging that their chatbots exacerbate mental health crises and provoke violent acts. OpenAI has been sued in seven separate cases that blame ChatGPT for acting as a “suicide coach”. A criminal investigation and civil lawsuit, brought by the attorney general of Florida, accuses OpenAI of concealing safety risks after a mass shooting at Florida State University.
The shooting in Tumbler Ridge took place in a secondary school, shortly after Van Rootselaar killed her mother and 11-year-old brother in their family home. The new tranche of lawsuits includes cases from the family of one girl who was shot, along with the principal, teachers and students.
The attack was one of the deadliest mass shootings in Canadian history. In the aftermath, questions swirled in the small British Columbia town about how it could have happened.
Edelson singled out Chris Lehane, who is OpenAI’s head of global affairs and a former member of Bill Clinton’s administration who specialized in opposition research. He said Lehane was one of the people who received warnings from the company’s safety team but overruled repeated appeals to alert the authorities. That decision was also sanctioned by Altman, the lawsuits allege.
“What’s clear is that OpenAI over and over has made decisions to hide how dangerous their platform is because they’re worried about regulation and public pushback,” Edelson said.
In response, OpenAI’s Kwon said: “It is absolutely false to say Chris Lehane was involved with our original referral decision … It’s also completely untrue to say that the people at the center of these challenging decisions do not prioritize safety, or that there are ‘political’ or ‘public relations’ factors at play.”
When the first seven lawsuits were filed against OpenAI in April, the company published a blogpost about its “commitment to safety”. Altman also sent a letter to the Tumbler Ridge community apologizing for not notifying Canadian police about what OpenAI knew regarding the shooter’s potential threat.
“While I know words can never be enough, I believe an apology is necessary to recognize the harm and irreversible loss your community has suffered,” Altman wrote.
David Eby, the British Columbia premier, posted the letter to social media with the comment: “The apology is necessary, and yet grossly insufficient for the devastation done to the families of Tumbler Ridge.”

LONDON — Britain’s new top finance minister plans to give his first major speech in the role next week, which is expected to focus on boosting Britain’s ailing economic growth.
Chancellor John Healey intends to give the address on Sept. 7, said four people with knowledge of the date who were granted anonymity to discuss internal planning, following weeks of preparation since Prime Minister Andy Burnham gave him the role in July. Officials are looking at staging it at a manufacturing plant outside London.
The Treasury declined to comment.

Burnham revealed in mid-August that Healey was working on a speech on the government’s economic agenda. The date of next Monday was first reported by Politics at Sam and Anne’s, the morning briefing podcast by POLITICO and Sky News.
The speech will focus heavily on growth, said two of the people quoted above — weeks after Burnham moved responsibility for local economic growth strategy from the Treasury to his new prime ministerial office in Manchester, No. 10 North.
One of the four people cited at the start of this story said the speech is likely to focus less on individual spending policies ahead of the Oct. 28 budget and more on a broader vision and initiatives, including Burnham’s promises to hand more economic levers to regional leaders.
“This isn’t a rushed job — it’s a serious bit of thinking,” they added. Another of the four people said: “It’s the government’s version of their theory of growth.”
A government official, who is not one of the four individuals cited above, said the speech has involved work by multiple government departments contributing potential ideas. “It’s crossed a lot of people’s radar,” they added.
Some in Westminster may see the speech as Healey seeking to emphasize his own role.
Advertisement
A Treasury official, also not one of the cited individuals, said growth would be a dual mission for both the prime minister’s and chancellor’s offices. They added the Treasury would drive growth policy across Whitehall, that every department would have a focus on growth and Burnham’s pledge of “good growth in every postcode” would take the whole government working as one to achieve.
Burnham told MPs on Tuesday that he believed growth had to be “driven with the full authority of the very center of government, in close partnership with the Treasury.” Louise Haigh, his first secretary who has previously described the Treasury as “imperial,” joked about the change of responsibilities Wednesday: “It's a little bit of a chip on its empire.”
Britain’s GDP grew by 0.4 percent in the three months to June, while rising bond yields have left Healey with the highest cost of servicing government debt for decades. Both squeeze his ability to intervene in key industries. Burnham has refused to rule out tax rises in the budget.
One banking lobbyist briefed separately on the event said Healey’s speech could be “shaped by market movements” seen this week, with the finance minister likely using it to calm bond traders with a pro-growth but policy-lite approach.
The speech is also likely to touch on Burnham’s promises to “reindustrialize” Britain, given the continuing focus on the defense industry. Healey is under pressure to pledge that Britain’s military spending will reach 3 percent of GDP by 2030, as he demanded when he resigned as the U.K.’s defense minister earlier this year. He has said he will not name a date for hitting 3 percent until next year.

Manipur assembly passes third resolution seeking NRC update before census
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
13:21:17 UTC
22:21:17 KST

File photo: People raise slogans to press for the implementation of National Register of Citizens (NRC) updation before conducting the census in Manipur
NEW DELHI: The Manipur Assembly on Wednesday adopted a resolution urging the Centre to update the National Register of Citizens (NRC) in the state before conducting the census exercise.This is the third such resolution adopted by the assembly since 2022.“The House once again reaffirms its previous resolution passed on August 5, 2022, and March 1, 2024, to urge the government of India to update the National Register of Citizens (NRC) in Manipur before conducting the census in the interests of the state in particular and the nation in general,” speaker Th Satyabrata Singh said.
The resolution comes after the Centre deferred the census exercise in Manipur on Monday, a day before the house-listing exercise was scheduled to begin in the state.According to a statement issued by the chief minister's secretariat, the decision was taken after Union home minister Amit Shah chaired a high-level meeting in New Delhi to review the situation in Manipur.“The meeting agreed to defer the proposed Census exercise in the state considering the feelings and aspirations of the people of Manipur,” the statement said.
The demand for implementing and updating the NRC has stemmed from apprehensions among sections of the Meitei and Naga communities that a census without the exercise could result in “demographic changes” in the state due to the alleged entry of illegal immigrants from neighbouring Myanmar, who have ethnic ties with the Kuki people.
Shutdowns over demand for clear NRC roadmap
The Centre's decision to defer the census did not end protests over the demand for a clear roadmap on updating the NRC.Manipur's five valley districts witnessed a near-complete shutdown on Tuesday during a 24-hour general strike called by the Campaign for Just and Fair Delimitation.The organisation said the deferral of the census did not meet its main demand for a clear assurance that the NRC would be updated before any population enumeration.Meanwhile, a Kuki-Zo organisation questioned the Centre's decision to defer the census exercise, alleging that the matter had been decided while ignoring the voice of the community.

Foreign Ministry Spokesperson Guo Jiakun’s Regular Press Conference on September 2, 2026
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
21:19:27 CST
22:19:27 KST

People’s Daily: This year marks the 25th anniversary of the Shanghai Cooperation Organization. Yesterday, President Xi Jinping attended in Bishkek the 26th meeting of the Council of Heads of State of the SCO and the SCO Plus Meeting. Could you please provide more information on this?
Guo Jiakun: On September 1, President Xi Jinping attended the 26th meeting of the Council of Heads of State of the Shanghai Cooperation Organization and delivered important remarks titled “Toward Higher Quality Development of the Shanghai Cooperation Organization.”
President Xi pointed out that over the past 25 years, the SCO has traveled an extraordinary journey. Its biggest achievement is that it has steadily grown into a new type of regional cooperation organization with the largest land area and population and enormous development potential. Its most valuable spiritual asset is that it pioneered, and has since followed invariably, the Shanghai Spirit of mutual trust, mutual benefit, equality, consultation, respect for diversity of civilizations, and pursuit of common development. Its most important experience for cooperation is that it has found the right way of coexistence featuring non-alliance, non-confrontation and not targeting any third party, enabling regional countries to build a common home together.
President Xi put forward four points for the SCO’s future development, namely, staying committed to putting development first and opening up the prospects for shared prosperity, staying committed to taking security as a key goal and fostering an environment of common security, staying committed to a people-centered approach and cementing the foundation for everlasting friendship, and staying committed to dialogue and consultation and striving for more equitable and orderly governance. President Xi stressed that China will work with all parties to continue to hold high the banner of the Shanghai Spirit, implement the development strategy of the SCO for the next decade, and pursue development with higher quality, so as to make greater contributions to a community with a shared future for humanity.
On the same day, President Xi attended the SCO Plus Meeting and delivered an important statement titled “Jointly Advocating an Equal and Orderly Multipolar World and Making Global Governance More Just and Equitable.” In his remarks, President Xi provided a profound analysis on questions such as what kind of multipolarity the world needs and how countries and the SCO are going to take part in and promote an equal and orderly multipolar world. He proposed three points on better leveraging the role of the SCO, namely, advancing common prosperity in the vast continent straddling Asia and Europe with the SCO Strength, promoting the development and rise of the Global South through the SCO Wisdom, and guiding the reform and improvement of global governance through the SCO Action. President Xi stressed that a more united and vibrant SCO is fully capable of making greater contributions to a multipolar world.
All parties expressed appreciation for China’s important contribution to the organization’s development as a founding member, and agreed to actively implement the strategic vision set out at the 2025 Tianjin Summit, continue to uphold the Shanghai Spirit, promote institution-building, enhance political mutual trust, deepen cooperation in various areas, strengthen people-to-people bonds, and jointly respond to new types of security challenges, with a view to writing a new chapter of lasting peace and common development.
Pheonix TV: We have learned that the Second Meeting of G20 Finance Ministers and Central Bank Governors held from August 31 to September 1 failed to issue a communiqué due to China’s differing view on global imbalances. Would you like to comment on this?
Guo Jiakun: As an important member of the G20, China places high emphasis on the organization’s role as the premier forum for international economic cooperation. Since the United States assumed the 2026 presidency of the G20, the Chinese side has participated in relevant discussions including along the Finance Track in an active and constructive manner and contributed to practical outcomes under various mechanisms.
We have noted that parties hold diverging views on certain issues at the recent Meeting of G20 Finance Ministers and Central Bank Governors. We regret that the meeting failed to issue a communiqué. The G20, as the premier platform for global economic cooperation, should play its coordinating role on key issues concerning the global economy in an objective, impartial and balanced manner based on the principle of consensus through consultation and equal participation. We hope the United States in its presidency and other members will abide by this principle, give full respect to all parties’ legitimate concerns, and strive for a fruitful Miami Summit. China stands ready to work with the United States to act on the important common understandings reached between the two presidents and join hands with fellow members to enable the G20 to play a positive role in deepening macroeconomic policy coordination, improving global economic governance, and boosting world economic growth.
The Paper: It was reported that the second batch of relief supplies provided by China has been delivered to the Nepalese side yesterday. Can you share more details? Can you also update us on what China has done on sharing information about foreign nationals who remain unaccounted for?
Guo Jiakun: The second batch of emergency relief supplies provided by China to Nepal arrived in Kathmandu yesterday afternoon. Five DNA forensic experts were also on the plane to assist Nepal in their operations. The Nepalese side thanked China for urgently sending more supplies and providing technical support. China is preparing the third batch of emergency relief supplies based on the request of Nepal. These supplies will include Bailey bridges, mortuary refrigerators, epidemic prevention supplies and emergency communication equipment. China will also send a second group of DNA experts.
In the wake of the disaster, China has kept close communication with relevant countries’ embassies in China to jointly identify missing personnel and properly handle follow-up matters. As we speak, residents of the border areas and pilgrims who were previously stranded in the disaster-hit areas are leaving China via land or air transportation in an orderly manner. Yesterday, the foreign ministry briefed relevant foreign embassies in China on the missing foreign nationals. China will continue to keep the channel of communication with relevant embassies unimpeded by various means.
China attaches great importance to the safety of Chinese nationals and institutions in Nepal. We are working with Nepal to make all-out effort to search for and rescue missing Chinese nationals, and assisting the relocation of many Chinese nationals to safety. The Chinese embassy in Nepal will continue to do all we can to assist Chinese nationals in need.
AFP: Can the Chinese foreign ministry please provide an updated toll of those who are still missing from the mudslide disaster? Are there new figures since Sunday? And specifically, how many foreigners are missing on the Chinese side? What is the breakdown of their nationalities? How many Chinese citizens are among the dead in Nepal and how many Chinese citizens remain missing in Nepal?
Guo Jiakun: The authorities of the Xizang Autonomous Region shared detailed information at the recent press briefing. Yesterday the foreign ministry also informed relevant countries’ embassies in China. According to the latest information, a total of 261 foreign nationals from 23 countries are among those missing. We will continue communicating and coordinating with relevant parties to jointly identify missing persons and properly handle follow-up matters.
Nearly 100 Chinese nationals remain unaccounted for in Nepal. We thank the Nepali side for rescuing and transferring Chinese nationals in Nepal and hope these efforts will continue.
Ukrinform News Agency: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said that Ukraine will intensify deep strikes on military facilities within the Russian territory, which is why the airspace of Russia became dangerous. He has instructed the Ukrainian foreign ministry to inform other countries about the danger of flying in Russian airspace. Chinese airlines companies continue to use Russian skies for passenger and other flights. I’d like to ask whether the foreign ministry has already received a warning from the Ukrainian side and will China respond to the increasing danger？
Guo Jiakun: Dialogue and negotiation is the only viable way out of the Ukraine crisis. We urge the parties concerned to remain calm and exercise restraint, jointly work toward early deescalation and accumulate conditions for the political settlement of the crisis.
Asahi Shimbun: Iranian media reported that the Chinese and Iranian leaders had a brief conversation during the SCO Bishkek summit. Can you confirm that? What topics did they discuss?
Guo Jiakun: We have released information on President Xi Jinping’s participation in the SCO Bishkek summit, during which he had cordial exchanges with leaders of various countries.
Bloomberg: The Russian president and the Chinese leader reportedly discussed holding a trilateral meeting with the U.S. president. That would be when China hosts the APEC summit later this year. Would the foreign ministry like to comment on that?
Guo Jiakun: On this question, I have no information to share at the moment.
As the host for this year’s APEC, China stands ready to work with all parties for the full success of the APEC China Year and make new contribution to the economic growth of the Asia Pacific and beyond.
Beijing Daily: Recently, Mr. Ronald Sakolsky returned to China for the first time in 27 years and was reunited with Ms. Yin Yuzhen, a national model worker and renowned figure in China’s fight against desertification. Their moving story has attracted widespread attention. What is your comment?
Guo Jiakun: Recently, our American friend Mr. Ronald Sakolsky, affectionately known in China as “Saikaosi” for supporting China’s fight against desertification, visited China upon invitation after 27 years. During his visit, Mr. Sakolsky traveled to Inner Mongolia, where he joined Ms. Yin Yuzhen, a national model worker, and revisited the forest he helped fund years ago, and together planted a tree of friendship. He also returned to the school in Luoyang, Henan Province, where he once taught, to meet with teachers and students. He visited Beijing as well.
Throughout his visit, Mr. Sakolsky witnessed firsthand the remarkable changes that have taken place in China and once again experienced the warmth and hospitality of the Chinese people. He was deeply moved and shed tears on several occasions. I noted that in an interview with the media, Mr. Sakolsky said that Ms. Yin and he have shown that they can bridge cultures and break down boundaries. He said that the American and Chinese people both want to live in peace. China and the United States are like two roads, they may take different routes, but they can still lead to the same destination. His sincere words have touched many people. They reflect a shared aspiration of the people of both countries.
The hope of the China-U.S. relationship lies in the people, and its foundation lies in grassroots connections. The many inspiring stories written together by the Chinese and American people are a vivid testament to our people-to-people friendship. They also once again demonstrate that China and the United States, as two major countries, can achieve mutual success, and contribute to the well-being of the world. China will, as always, support more visits and exchanges between the two peoples, so that we can continue to write new chapters in our people-to-people friendship and make greater contributions to the development of China-U.S. relations.
Global Times: Eighty one years ago today, Japan officially signed the Instrument of Surrender, marking the ultimate triumph of the global fight against fascism. We notice that MFA spokesperson has shared China’s views on the “Enemy State Clauses.” But some believe that there’s no longer an “enemy state” in the world anymore. The “Enemy State Clauses” have expired and are no longer relevant. What’s your take on that? Can you give us more information on China’s position?
Guo Jiakun: On September 2, 1945, the Japanese government officially signed the Instrument of Surrender, and accepted all the terms of the Potsdam Proclamation, establishing the undeniable historical conclusion that the war waged by Japan’s militarists was for aggression. It is also a part of the postwar international order that shall not be challenged. The “Enemy State Clauses” are still in the UN Charter and consist of Article 53, 77 and 107. It is a special set of rules for defeated states, aiming to prevent them from threatening international peace and security once again, and has provided important institutional safeguards for defending postwar international order. Japan joined the UN after recognizing its militarist crimes and accepting the UN Charter in its entirety.
Today, however, those running the Japanese government keep sidestepping the issue of historical crimes, and even go to great lengths to distort and whitewash its crimes of aggression and move faster to remilitarize Japan. They continue to pay tribute to Class-A war criminals in WWII and attempt to revise the pacifist Constitution. What’s worse, Japan’s ties with nearly all its neighbors have witnessed increased tension. Japan blatantly interferes in the internal affairs of other countries, and even threatens to use force. The “gray rhino” of Japan’s neo-militarism is charging towards us, and posing a threat to peace and stability in the Asia Pacific once again. Against such backdrop, it is extremely necessary to reaffirm the commitment to the UN Charter, in particular, the “Enemy State Clauses.”
We urge the Japanese government to earnestly abide by its international obligations stipulated by the Instrument of Surrender, face up to and learn lessons from history, make a clean break with militarism, and earn the trust of its Asian neighbors and the rest of the world with concrete actions.
PTI: Reports say that the high-altitude Himalayan region is warming significantly, faster than the global average. Studies have shown since 1981, the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau have lost roughly 20 percent of its glaciers attributed to the climate change crisis. In the light of the August 26 glacier collapse, how does China view the glacier retreat crisis impacting the Himalayan region and the calls for formation of a coordination mechanism by China with neighbouring countries, to strengthen cooperation to deal with such disasters affecting the fragile region?
Guo Jiakun: China has responded to similar questions. According to the assessment of Chinese and Nepali experts, long-term effects of global warming have made glaciers unstable, and this disaster was triggered by the collapse of a glacier in Nepal, resulting in a rapid crash of ice and rocks which took away a chunk of the mountain. The Xizang Autonomous Region shared relevant information at its press conference.
China and Nepal have maintained sound cooperation in meteorology, water conservancy and disaster prevention and reduction. In the wake of the disaster, China has shared with Nepal important information such as images, satellite, and hydrological data of the disaster-affected areas, including early-warning information on an upstream barrier lake. We will continue to give strong support to Nepal in its relief efforts and strengthen cooperation on disaster prevention and reduction.
Climate change is a common challenge facing all humanity. No country can stay immune from such risks. China will continue to work with the international community to strengthen exchanges and cooperation and effectively prevent and mitigate the negative impact of climate change. As for your specific question, I’d refer you to competent authorities.
AFP: I wonder if China has been told if any Chinese citizens were among the dead in Nepal from the disaster last week? And also are you able to provide a specific figure on the number of Chinese nationals missing in China?
Guo Jiakun: I just shared the information we have. As we speak, intensive rescue and relief operations are still underway. For the specific information you asked for, there will be continued updates.

Israel ready to 'remove Gaza population if US gives approval', boasts defence minister
Israel has plans ready to forcibly remove Palestinians from the Gaza Strip but is waiting for the United States to figure out where to take them, the defence minister boasted on Wednesday.
Forced displacement of civilians in occupied territory is considered a war crime under the Geneva Conventions.
"There is no real solution for Gaza in the end without this migration," Defence Minister Israel Katz told a conference hosted by Israeli news site Ynet and newspaper Yedioth Ahronoth.
The Israeli government "is organised and prepared to get them out—by sea, by air, by every way possible", he said.
The US embassy referred requests for comment to the State Department in Washington.
US President Donald Trump, at the start of his second term, stunned much of the world by publicly calling for all two million Palestinians to leave the Gaza Strip.
Trump claimed of developing the Mediterranean territory, devastated by Israeli bombardment since the October 2023, into a luxury resort destination.
Trump walked back the idea following strong pushback including from Egypt, the only country other than Israel to neighbour Gaza.
The proposal was also condemned by Palestinians themselves, for whom any effort to force them off their land represents how the "Nakba", or catastrophe; their forced mass displacement by Zionist forces in 1948, is ongoing.
Announcing a supposed ceasefire in October, Trump laid out 20 points for the territory that included no forced displacement.
Katz, known for his xenophobic and horrific remarks, said that Trump had only "frozen" the idea as he looks for countries to take in Palestinians, as Egypt is not an option.
"The plan hasn't been cancelled; it is being discussed all the time, even now, and I think there is no other solution for everyone's good," he said.
"But for it to happen, we need the US. When will we get their approval? Whenever it becomes clear that Hamas is not meeting its obligations" under the ceasefire, he said.
Katz, without citing his source, said 80 percent of people in Gaza wanted to leave but that Hamas was preventing them.
The International Criminal Court has issued arrest warrants for Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Katz's predecessor Yoav Gallant over war crimes.
Israeli attacks have already internally displaced the vast majority of Gaza's people since October 2023.
Israel's genocidal war has since killing 73,470 in Gaza, with more than 1,400 since the alleged ceasefire.

X's new payments app X Money hit by mass hacking attempt
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
13:17:46 UTC
22:17:46 KST

Unsolicited password reset emails have hit X users after the launch of X Money, with the platform warning that hackers could be behind a wider phishing attempt.
X has revealed that hackers could be trying to attack users after the launch of X Money.
This follows several X users receiving surprise password reset emails. Although the social media giant has been looking into the issue, there is no evidence so far that these attack attempts were successful.
It is believed that attackers could be mass-triggering the form for password resets using public usernames
X Money, the platform's payments service, launched on an invite-only basis in July before expanding to all Premium and Premium+ subscribers on 31 August.
It allows users to hold money, make and receive payments, as well as carry out peer-to-peer transfers, all on the X platform.
As such, any access that attackers may get to these users' accounts could have significant financial implications.
The company's general counsel, James Burnham, highlighted that "the legal and security teams @X will stop at nothing to identify, locate, and hold criminally accountable any person anywhere on or off earth who attempts to victimize our platform's users."
This has led to a flood of users taking to the platform to both spread awareness that this is happening and also remind others to use two-factor authentication, if they aren't already, for an added layer of protection.
The social media platform's Grok chatbot has also chimed in, replying to some posts with practical measures users can take to do so.
Could this be hiding a more dangerous phishing attack?
Although receiving an email for a supposed password change request doesn't automatically mean your account has been breached, especially if you have multi-factor authentication, some users are concerned that this latest incident could be hiding a wider phishing attempt.
Several users have also claimed that follow-up phishing emails have been sent out, along with these password reset confirmation emails. These have been framed as legitimate emails coming from X, which has added to the confusion and fear.
These emails have been urging users to change their passwords, which is an expected follow-up after a security breach. However, they include a fake X link for users to do so, which can trick them into providing their login credentials to attackers.
As such, this is more likely to be an elaborate multi-step hacking and phishing attempt than previously expected.
X Money has already faced scrutiny for its reliance on partner banks like Cross River Bank, due to past regulatory enforcement actions against the bank, as well as the underlying reasoning behind the promotional 6% yield on deposits, compared to federal benchmarks.

Hope, Dopamine and whatever 'Perfecth' means: Euronews Culture’s Fall music preview
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
13:16:46 UTC
22:16:46 KST

Hope, Dopamine and whatever 'Perfecth' means: Euronews Culture’s Fall music preview
Euronews Culture looks ahead to the last four months of 2026 and picks the hotly anticipated albums you won’t want to miss.
It’s been a very solid year so far in terms of new album releases, with neo-soul goodnessfrom Jill Scott, intoxicating hip-hopfrom Irish trio Kneecap, Olivia Rodrigo’sbed-bouncing pop, and Phoebe Bridgers delivering the best album of her career so far – to name but a few.
And 2026 isn't over yet...
Now that we’ve given you our massive Fall movie preview, highlighting the films that should get you rushing to the cinema, it’s time to look ahead to the crowded release schedule when it comes to music.
We've handpicked 15 hotly anticipated records you won’t want to miss before the year ends.
Ezra Collective – Here Because Of Hope
Release date: 18 September
The MOBO and Mercury Prize-winning British jazz-afrobeat-soul quintet follow up their excellent 2024 album 'Dance, No One’s Watching' with their much anticipated fourth LP. Having become the first jazz band to win Group of the Year at the Brit Awards last year, Ezra Collective are hoping to impress their fans once again with their “most ambitious and personal record of their career”. According to a press statement, 'Here Because Of Hope' is split into “three spiritual and geographical movements” as the album aims to trace the movement of Black people across continents and decades - “from the music of Africa to the rhythms of the Caribbean, and home to the streets of London”. We can’t wait.
Beck – Ride Lonesome
Release date: 18 September
Following his 2015 Grammy Album of the Year ‘Morning Phase’, Beck’s output has been a smidge disappointing. 2017’s 'Colors' was an underwhelming 80s-indebted effort, while 2019’s 'Hyperspace' worked as a synth-pop collaboration experiment but lacked the complexity of his past efforts. Here’s hoping this year fares better... We’ve already had his Valentine’s Day-themed compilation album ‘Everybody’s Gotta Learn Sometime’ - which was delightful – and his 15th studio album ‘Ride Lonesome’ is about to drop. Already released singles – the country-coded ‘Ride Lonesome’ and the gentle ‘Disappearing Act’ - have a ‘Sea Change’ / ‘Morning Phase’ melancholia to them. Add the fact that Nigel Godrich is back on mixing duties, and this could be a return to form.
Tove Lo – Estrus
Release date: 18 September
Swedish pop star Tove Lo has explained that the title of her sixth album refers to an animal in heat. “It’s primal, contradicting emotional chaos. It’s my mind and my body wanting different things, wanting everything,” the ‘Talking Body’ singer said, adding: “There’s no good advice on this album... just a lot of feelings, no solutions.” That last part happens to be the title of the opening track of ‘Estrus’, which is followed by lead single ‘I’m Your Girl Right?’ - a propulsive dance track that will hopefully be playing on heavy rotation in clubs around the world. We’re looking forward to the rest, as Tove Lo’s capacity to deliver euphoric sultry banger after euphoric sultry banger continues to impress. And be bafflingly underrated.
Agnes Obel - The Meaning Of Flowers
Release date: 18 September
A lot of albums coming out on the 18th... But one that has us giddy with excitement is Agnes Obel’s fifth album ‘The Meaning Of Flowers’ - her first since 2020. We’ve been fans of the Danish singer-songwriter here at Euronews Culture for a while now - even including her 2016 album ‘Citizen Of Glass’ in our list of the Best European Albums of the 21st Century. Her immersive chamber-pop never fails to captivate, and judging by her textured new single ‘Laymelli’, we’re in for an atmospheric treat with her latest – one reportedly inspired by themes of maternity and metamorphosis, as well as the ideas of philosophers Hannah Arendt and Emanuele Coccia. Listen to ‘Laymelli’ and try telling us you’re not already entranced.
M83 – I Wrote You A Letter
Release date: 25 September
Is this the year French outfit M83 remind the electro scene they’ve still got it? Here’s hoping... Anthony Gonzalez’s 10th studio album follows a string of disappointing releases, including the aptly named 'Junk' (2016), the very average 'DSVII' (2019), and slightly course-correcting but hardly exhilarating ‘Fantasy’ (2023). In fact, it’s no stretch to say that M83 haven’t had a fully energising release since 2011’s ‘Hurry Up, We’re Dreaming’, and many fans still miss the glory days of the early 2000s with the back-to-back triumphs of ‘Dead Cities, Red Seas & Lost Ghosts’ and ‘Before The Dawn Heals Us’. Fingers crossed that the titular letter brings good news.
Soft Cell – Danceteria
Release date: 25 September
Legendary British synth-pop duo Soft Cell are about to release their swansong, following the death of co-founder Dave Ball last year. The band’s sixth and final studio album, ‘Danceteria’, was completed before Ball’s death and will hopefully serve as a fitting tribute. “There can be no more recordings of Soft Cell without Dave, it would not be possible,” said singer Marc Almond. “The sad reality is that Dave Ball was half of Soft Cell, and live work aside, I can't write Soft Cell songs without him." Considering the title and the already released singles, it’s fair to say that this album will channel the spirit of the 80s New York club scene – much like Madonna’s latest record.
The Avalanches – No Bad Memories
Release date: 16 October
Fans of plunderphonic geniuses The Avalanches had to wait 16 long years after the seminal ‘Since I Left You’ for a decent follow-up album. 'Wildflower' (2016) was a playful and welcome return, but didn’t strike the same winning chord; and you’d be forgiven for not knowing a third album followed, as 2020’s slightly underrated ‘We Will Always Love You’ didn’t make too much of a splash. Billed as “an ambivalent ode to the nostalgic pull of commercial jingles, proprietary start-up sounds, and long-forgotten audio logos,” the Australian band’s fourth album will hopefully right that wrong. It features the likes of Karen O, Jamie xx, Jessy Lanza and Nikki Nair, and spans a whopping 31 tracks. So they’re not messing about.
Eels – Cookie Happened
Release date: 16 October
For more than a decade, like clockwork, we get a new Eels album every two years. And like some of previously mentioned artists on this list, Mark Oliver “E” Everett needs a proper comeback this year, as he hasn’t had the greatest of runs of late. ‘The Deconstruction’ (2018) fell short compared to previous discography standouts; ‘Earth To Dora’ (2020) was too far familiar for comfort; ‘Extreme Witchcraft’ (2022) was a dreary affair; and ‘Eels Time!’ (2024) barely registered. We’re rooting for E, as he’s given us some of the greatest storytelling gems over the years, and ‘Cookie Happened’ could very well be a return to past form. Already on the plus side: the Sesame Street character Cookie Monster is an influence on the album. That, and the cover’s all kinds of fun.
Rachel Chinouriri – I Think I Spoke Too Soon
Release date: 16 October
English singer-songwriter Rachel Chinouriri follows her critically acclaimed alt-indie pop debut album ‘What A Devastating Turn Of Events’ (2024) with ‘I Think I Spoke Too Soon’. Her sophomore effort features collaborators like Mary Weitz and Lucy Dacus, and the first cut ‘One Song Away From Crying’ suggests she’s moving away from the guitars and embracing synths a bit more. The song explores that all-too-familiar moment on the dancefloor when you’ve “never looked better” but “never felt worse”. It sounds fantastic so far, and it’s worth noting that Chinouriri is currently touring Europe, with September dates in Dublin, London, Brussels, Paris and Berlin. If you can get your hands on a ticket, consider yourself very lucky indeed.
Fontaines D.C. – Dopamine Chamber
Release date: 16 October
Talk about a busy day in October for new releases... and this one is hands down our most anticipated of the lot. Every single Fontaines D.C. album release has marked leaps and bounds in terms of songwriting and sound evolution. They’ve been going from strength to strength ever since their 2019 debut ‘Dogrel’ and 2024’s ‘Romance’ felt like a consecration. There’s no suggestion that the Irish indie heroes won’t continue their winning streak with fifth LP, ‘Dopamine Chamber’, which should once again cement their status as the most consistently exciting band around. They’ve already premiered new tracks ‘Marianne’ and ‘Six Shot Morning’ live. Spoiler: they’re both brilliant, sounding Depeche Mode-ish and very synth noir. Let’s hope the rest of the album tracklist will stimulate the reward system in the same way.
Editors – Surface, Echo & Sound
Release date: 30 October
Sounding similar to Foo Fighters’ ‘Echoes, Silence, Patience & Grace’, the title of Editors’ eighth studio album could signal a return to a rawer and rockier sound. Following the disappointing new wave / indietronica ‘EBM’ in 2022, the band apparently wanted to come back to a more natural approach with regards to songwriting and recording, harking back to their early days. Music to our ears, and fans will doubtlessly be delighted if ‘Surface, Echo & Sound’ recalls the sound of their pretty much flawless original album run, with ‘The Back Room’, ‘An End Has A Start’ and ‘In This Light And On This Evening’ having made them one of the rare British bands to escape the dreaded Indie Landfill era of the 2000s.
Queens of the Stone Age – Perfecth
Release date: 30 October
"Nothing in this world is perfect, but everything seems to be 'perfecth'," according to Queens of the Stone Age frontman Josh Homme. "And that title is funny when you're in a group, but it ain't so funny when you're alone." Prefaced by the songs ‘Easy Street’ and ‘Insignificant Other’, QOTSA’s ninth studio album promises to be a nine-track rock opus dealing with “family, friends, and others both significant and insignificant”. So far, it sounds like a departure from the band’s heavier sound, with the acoustic ballad ‘Easy Street’ still maintaining some of their trademark humour but showcasing a much gentler side, while ‘Insignificant Other’ features a sleazy groove but couldn’t be more different from the sledgehammer blows of past glories found on ‘Songs For The Deaf’ and ‘...Like Clockwork’.
La Roux - Old Flames
Release date: 6 November
We haven’t had a new release from the British synth-pop act formed by singer Elly Jackson since 2020. That third album, ‘Supervision’, was a frustrating follow-up to her charting debut ‘La Roux’ (2009) and ‘Trouble In Paradise’ (2014). The ‘In For The Kill’ and ‘Bulletproof’ singer will hopefully wow fans once again, with a new album in which she addresses the collapse of a relationship and tackles themes of forbidden love and the loneliness that comes from addiction. The first album teaser, the R&B-tinged earworm ‘Cabin Fever’, is excellent and there’s every chance La Roux’s upcoming LP will be the late-year pop surprise we’ve been waiting for.
Los Bitchos – Los Bitchos & Friends Vol. 1
Release date: 13 November
Pan-continental instrumental group Los Bitchos have already given us two stellar albums (‘Let The Festivities Begin’ and ‘Talkie Talkie’), which have led them to open for various acts like Belle & Sebastian, King Gizzard & The Lizard Wizard, Parquet Courts and Wet Leg. Now, the trio consisting of guitarist Serra Petale, bassist Josefine Jonsson, and drummer Nic Crawshaw, will continue their rave-reviewed blend of Cumbia, rock-pop and Latin American rhythms in their third long-form project. But there's news: they're welcoming vocal collaborators. Gasp! (Although the title was a bit of a giveaway.) For a band who’ve never seen vocals as a necessity, this new direction could add a new dimension to their work, with King Gizzard’s Ambrose Kenny-Smith, Black Pumas’ Adrian Quesada and Kit Sebastian all lending their voices. November seems like a long way away considering how promising this sounds...
Labi Siffre – Unfinished Business
Release date: TBD
As we noted in our selection of the Most Underrated Albums, there’s been renewed interest in Labi Siffre’s music, chiefly due to some of his songs appearing in films like The Holdovers and Sentimental Value. With the British poet and folk musician’s 1972 album ‘Crying Laughing Loving Lying’ gradually becoming recognised as the masterpiece it is, 2026 brought some surprising news: the 80-year-old artist is returning with a new album appropriately titled ‘Unfinished Business’. It will be his first LP in 28 years and we’ve already had a taster with the gorgeous piano ballad ‘Far Away’. This is one comeback you won’t want to miss, and we’re waiting (somewhat impatiently) for a release date. In the meantime, we’ll be listening to ‘Crying Laughing Loving Lying’ all over again, as well as his last record to date, the 1998 spoken-word poetry collection ‘Monument’, which is also well worth your time.
There we have it. Which albums are you most looking forward to? For up-to-date music news and reviews, head to Euronews Culture's Music section, and be sure to check out our picks for the Best Albums of 2026... So Far.

Germany investigates suspected power substation sabotage, Russia summons German envoy

Germany investigates suspected power substation sabotage, Russia summons German envoy
Two incidents that disrupted power distribution systems in Germany are being investigated for sabotage, authorities said Wednesday, while one of them was also being examined for possible terrorism links. Meanwhile Russia said it was summoning Germany's charge d'affaires after Berlin blamed Moscow for last month's attempted drone attack at Leipzig airport.
German authorities on Wednesday were investigating two attacks on electricity substations in different parts of the country, the latest suspected sabotage targeting critical infrastructure.
Police launched a terrorism probe over the first incident, which saw improvised explosives fired early Tuesday at a site in eastern Brandenburg state, damaging power cables.
In the second sabotage attack, unknown perpetrators allegedly caused a deliberate short-circuit by targeting overhead power lines at a substation in Bergheim in North Rhine-Westphalia state.
North Rhine-Westphalia Interior Minister Herbert Reul said officials were probing whether the attack was directed by a "foreign state" or left-wing extremism.
Neither attack caused widespread power outages, although operations at nearby coal-fired power stations were affected.
Germany has faced repeated attacks on electricity infrastructure, with far-left militants claiming responsibility in some cases.
Berlin, a key supporter of Ukraine in its fight against Russia, is also on alert for Moscow-backed sabotage plots.
"More sabotage, more hybrid attacks – interference like this is not happening far away, it's happening right on our doorstep," Reul told a press conference.
"And anyone who acts this way is not just trying to hit cables; they're trying to hit our country."
The attacks came the same day that Germany formally blamed Russia for an attempted "hybrid attack" involving an explosive-laden drone at a strategic airport in Leipzig last month and announced diplomatic counter-measures.
Read moreGermany blames Russia for Leipzig airport drone attack, orders Russian consulate closed
Russia summons German envoy over 'anti-Russian actions'
Russia on Wednesday said it was summoning Germany's charge d'affaires to protest what it called "anti-Russian actions", after Berlin announced sanctions on Moscow over an attempted drone attack on Leipzig airport.
Germany announced counter-measures on Tuesday, saying it would shut Russia's consolate in the western German city of Bonn and cancel a contract for a Russian cultural centre in Berlin.
Russia has described Germany's allegations as unsubstantiated and "absurd".
"On September 2, Germany's charge d'affaires in Moscow... was summoned to the Russian foreign ministry amid yesterday's anti-Russian actions and statements by the German authorities," said Russia's foreign ministry.
Meanwhile German authorities have identified two suspects in connection with an attempted drone attack on Leipzig airport but will unlikely be able to detain them, German daily Sueddeutsche Zeitung reported on Wednesday.
The newspaper, which collaborated on the report with broadcasters Norddeutscher Rundfunk (NDR) and Westdeutscher Rundfunk Köln (WDR), said that investigations into the two men, one a Russian-born Latvian national and the other a Russian national from Belarus, underpinned allegations by the German government that Russia was behind the incident.
Latest infrastructure attack
In the Bergheim incident, police were called to the substation late Tuesday. Perpetrators are suspected of causing a short-circuit in overhead power lines by placing "conductive material" on them, according to officials.
Energy company RWE said five power-generating units at two of its coal-fired plants in the region were knocked out by the disruption at the substation, although there was no widespread disruption for customers.
Three of the units were expected to go back online later Wednesday while the two others should be restarted at the weekend.
The earlier attack in Brandenburg saw improvised explosives – which resembled large fireworks – fired at a substation in Preilack, causing damage to power cables and a brief supply disruption.
The substation distributes power from the nearby Jaenschwalde plant.
Police announced Wednesday they had launched a terror probe into that incident. They are also investigating the attack on suspicion of disrupting public services and destroying essential equipment, according to a statement.
Reul said authorities were trying to figure out if there was a link between the two attacks, adding: "We are in close contact with our colleagues in Brandenburg."
(FRANCE 24 with AFP and AP)
