Can the US deport you for what you say? A federal judge says no
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
13:09:00 UTC
22:09:00 KST

A federal judge in California has ruled that immigration provisions used by the US administration to target non-citizens over political speech are unconstitutional, delivering one of the strongest legal challenges yet to its use of immigration law against pro-Palestinian activists.
US District Judge Noel Wise ruled on August 28 that the government's application of the provisions to revoke visas and pursue deportations over protected speech violated the First and Fifth Amendments.
The case emerged from a fear already taking hold on university campuses: that an international student's words could put their legal status at risk.
The Stanford Daily, Stanford University's student newspaper, and an anonymous F-1 visa holder identified as Jane Doe challenged the policy, arguing that it pushed international students to delete posts, avoid political activity, and think twice before reporting on Gaza.
Wise's 90-page decision sided with the plaintiffs on six of eight claims. It also challenged the breadth of the government's claimed authority, finding that its application of the provisions to constitutionally protected speech amounted to viewpoint- and content-based restrictions.
Too many brave and principled pro-Palestinian voices have become collateral damage due to Washington’s attempts to suppress criticism of the genocidal Israeli state, according to human rights lawyer and writer Maria Kari.
"I cannot think of anything more profoundly un-American than silencing students and activists for voicing opposition to the US government funding genocide, war crimes and the murder of thousands of babies and for that reason Judge Wise's ruling is a very welcome and significant victory," Kari tells TRT World.
Kari has represented several people targeted by the administration's immigration crackdown, including Momodou Taal, Yaakub Ira Vijandre and Mahmoud Khalil.
“...Constitutional rights are inalienable and belong to the people and that the free speech rights of noncitizens are not any less than citizens," she adds.
An undefined line
At the centre of the dispute are the provisions of the Immigration and Nationality Act of 1952, which US administration invoked to revoke visas and pursue the removal of non-citizens whose presence and activities were deemed to have potentially serious foreign policy consequences for the United States.
Under the administration's interpretation, Secretary of State Marco Rubio had broad discretion to determine when a non-citizen's presence threatened a compelling US foreign policy interest.
The judge rejected that logic. The government cannot punish protected speech simply because it objects to the viewpoint behind it, she wrote.
Rubio's own arguments showed just how far the provision could reach.
He suggested that protests over something as mundane as paper straws could theoretically fall under the same authority, even as his department was using it against people whose speech concerned Gaza.
"If you're complaining about paper straws, then we're obviously not going to yank a visa over that," he said.
The ruling, which cites the founding fathers of the US, Benjamin Franklin and James Madison at length, therefore goes beyond the fate of the students named in the lawsuit, putting a constitutional limit on a strategy Washington has increasingly used against non-citizens whose political speech it considers objectionable.
However, when it comes to the practical, beneficial impact this ruling can have, Kari believes the answer is, unfortunately, not much.
"This ruling is declaratory and not injunctive which means it does not stop the Secretary of State from future visa revocations nor does it free those in ICE prison currently facing detention and deportation.”
From Columbia to Stanford
By the time the Stanford Daily case reached the courts, the policy's consequences were already evident on university campuses.
In March 2025, Mahmoud Khalil, a Columbia University graduate and legal permanent resident, was detained by ICE for his role in pro-Palestinian campus organising.
Weeks later, federal agents detained Rumeysa Ozturk, a doctoral student at Tufts University, after she co-wrote an op-ed criticising her university's response to the Israeli genocide in Gaza.
Their cases were followed by those of Cornell University student Momodou Taal and Columbia student Mohsen Mahdawi, turning a series of individual immigration actions into a wider fight over whether political activism could become grounds for removal.
In a January 2025 executive order, the US administration directed federal agencies to identify and remove non-citizen students and faculty whose political activity was deemed contrary to US foreign policy.
Now, with Wise's ruling on the books, the administration faces a choice. According to Kari, the US government will most certainly appeal, and has sixty days to do so.
"When something is on appeal it means that other judges in other jurisdictions are more likely to say, 'that case is on appeal, I don't have to rely on it'.”
But these plaintiffs have an advantage on appeal, because the court that will hear it, the Ninth Circuit, has already ruled that free speech protections apply to noncitizens too, she adds.
Colliding with constitutional limits
The Stanford Daily's lawsuit took that policy beyond individual activists and into the newsroom itself.
The newspaper argued that international students were deleting pro-Palestinian posts, avoiding political activity and steering away from stories critical of Israel because they feared what speaking out could mean for their immigration status.
The result was a form of censorship that did not require the government to silence every student directly, as the possibility of deportation was enough to make some students think twice.
"I think Judge Wise's decision does a brilliant job of laying out the pattern we've seen unfold since March 2025 when the foreign policy grounds provision was invoked after three decades of non-use with Mahmoud Khalil's request," Kari says.
"Since then… campuses are quiet, protests for Palestine have died down and people - citizens and noncitizens alike - are scared.”
Wise's decision follows a similar ruling last year in Massachusetts in AAUP v. Rubio. In September 2025, US District Judge William Young found that the US administration's policy of arresting, detaining and seeking to deport non-citizen students and faculty for pro-Palestinian advocacy violated the First Amendment. A remedial order followed in January 2026.
Together, the cases reinforce a principle the Supreme Court recognised decades ago: constitutional free-speech protections do not disappear at the border or depend on US citizenship.
The ruling does not undo what Mahmoud Khalil, Rumeysa Ozturk, Momodou Taal, Mohsen Mahdawi and others went through, and the administration is expected to appeal.
Kari says what is most alarming now is how the provision is being weaponised against people targeted purely for their family ties, regardless of anything they've said or done.
"All the cases discussed in the Stanford Daily case involved people who were targeted by the government for their political speech."
"Now, ICE is going after people not because of something they said or did but who they're related to. This is the new and terrifying frontier that's opened up," Kari says.
"I predict the legality of using the foreign policy grounds provision in this way will be tested in the courts next," she adds.

Bardella’s international blitz hints at new role for French far-right leader
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
13:05:37 UTC
22:05:37 KST

President of French far-right party Rassemblement National Jordan Bardella reacts as he speaks to the press during a visit to the agricultural fair in Châlons-en-Champagne on August 29, 2026. | Sameer Al-Doumy/AFP via Getty Images
PARIS — French far-right leader Jordan Bardella is taking on more international responsibilities for his party, the National Rally, as part of a push to reassure international markets worried about the cost of Marine Le Pen’s populist platform.
An aide to Bardella told reporters that the National Rally president’s Friday speech at the Reform UK party congress in Birmingham and visit to the Ambrosetti Forum in Italy on Saturday are the beginning of a concerted campaign to strategically deploy the 30-year-old.
Bardella is also slated to give 10 interviews to international media outlets in the coming days.
Advertisement
“Bardella has always been attached to the international credibility of the National Rally,” said the aide, who was granted anonymity to share details of Bardella’s plans. “He will give great attention to the international press during the campaign.”
Since shooting up the National Rally’s ranks in his twenties, Bardella has brought a polished professionalism to a party that long struggled to run a tight ship. He led the party to impressive victories in the 2019 and 2024 European elections and is now the head of the Patriots group in the European Parliament. The party is now more popular than ever, and Le Pen is the front-runner to win next year’s presidential election.
But when it looked like an embezzlement conviction would doom Le Pen’s chances at running for the presidency, Bardella, as the National Rally’s presumptive candidate, tried to woo more fiscally conservative voters — including France’s business elite — by flirting with a more market-friendly platform than his mentor.
But Bardella has been adjusting to a secondary role since an appeals court cleared a path for Le Pen to run as the party’s presidential nominee — and she has made clear that fiscal discipline won’t come at the expense of the promises she has made to her core voters. That includes her pledge to lower the retirement age for most workers to 62 at a cost of €9 billion per year.
Bardella is now eyeing a role similar to the one Giorgia Meloni held before she became Italian prime minister in 2022.
Bardella “watched with great interest the campaign of Giorgia Meloni, who flooded the international press to reassure institutions and the financial markets,” the aide said.
Advertisement
The carving up of roles between Bardella and Le Pen also makes sense given Le Pen’s spotty track record of international trips — notably her reported failed attempt to meet U.S. President Donald Trump — and the difficulties in shedding the toxic baggage linked to her name. Her father, party founder Jean-Marie, was notorious for downplaying the Holocaust and was convicted of hate speech multiple times.

Angola takes delivery of six Swiss-made HT-100 drones
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
13:05:18 UTC
22:05:18 KST

- ANAVIA completed customer acceptance of six HT-100 Naval unmanned helicopters for the Angolan Navy, to be deployed two per ship across three new BR71 MK II corvettes.
- The HT-100 Naval features an autonomous radar-guided deck landing system and a six-hour flight endurance, part of a roughly $1.1 billion Angolan naval modernization program.
Swiss manufacturer ANAVIA completed on-site customer acceptance of six HT-100 Naval unmanned helicopters purchased by the Angolan Navy, the company said, following individual flight tests and sign-offs for each aircraft delivered.
The acceptance was conducted jointly with ADSB, a partner involved in the delivery. ANAVIA said each of the six aircraft underwent its own flight test and verification process rather than a single blanket acceptance for the batch, with the customer verifying each system firsthand.
“This milestone shows our ability to deliver a complete system, closely aligned with our customer’s operational requirements,” said Ishan Sahgal, founder and co-CEO of ANAVIA.
The delivered package includes electro-optical and infrared sensors, maritime control stations, and the helicopters themselves, all tested together on site as an integrated system rather than as separate components. The six aircraft will be split two per ship across three new BR71 MK II-class corvettes the Angolan Navy is bringing into service, extending each vessel’s reconnaissance reach.
The HT-100 Naval is a maritime variant of ANAVIA’s HT-100 unmanned helicopter, built around a Flettner intermeshing rotor system, two counter-rotating main rotors that eliminate the need for a tail rotor. ANAVIA says that design sends roughly 30 percent more of the aircraft’s power into useful lift rather than countering torque, resulting in longer endurance and higher payload capacity compared with a conventional single-rotor design. The aircraft has a maximum takeoff weight of 120 kilograms (265 pounds), a payload capacity of 60 kilograms (132 pounds), and a flight endurance of six hours, powered by a 15-kilowatt turbine engine that burns roughly 9 liters (2.4 gallons) of Jet A-1 fuel per hour. The HT-100 has a maximum mission range of 600 kilometers (373 miles).
For shipboard use, the Naval variant adds a fully autonomous, radar-guided deck landing system that measures the aircraft’s position, velocity and attitude relative to the moving vessel independent of GPS, allowing it to land without a human operator steering the approach, even in conditions up to Sea State 3. The airframe uses a corrosion-resistant carbon composite structure with sealed electronics rated for continuous saltwater exposure, along with emergency equipment including a harpoon deck-securing system, flotation gear and an emergency locator transmitter.
The three BR71 MK II-class corvettes form part of a roughly €1 billion ($1.16 billion) naval modernization program for Angola. The first of the three vessels, the NRA Ekuikui II, was launched in Cherbourg, France, on March 4, 2026. ANAVIA is a Swiss company headquartered in Bilten, with additional operations in nearby Näfels; the UAE-based EDGE Group acquired a 52 percent majority stake in the company in late 2023.

Fact check: How inaccurate and conflicting claims may have affected Iceland's EU referendum
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
13:02:52 UTC
22:02:52 KST

The Icelandic EU referendum raised a number of important issues for voters, but also a series of unclear claims.
Uncertainty over fishing quotas may have made many Icelandic voters reluctant to embark on an EU membership pathway.
The country voted no on 29 August on resuming negotiations with Brussels by 52.8%, with the talks between the two on hold since 2013.
The campaign was fierce and, as with many crucial public votes in recent years, was also marked by inaccurate claims circulating online and among media channels.
One of them involved the referendum's main sticking point: fisheries.
A few media outlets reported on talks between Iceland's foreign affairs minister Þorgerður Katrín Gunnarsdóttir and Dutch Prime Minister Rob Jetten about a special exemption from the EU's Common Fisheries Policy.
They said that Gunnarsdóttir claimed that such exemptions were discussed and that the Dutch government strongly denied her version of events.
However, Gunnarsdóttir later rejected those claims, prompting the press to admit the story had been largely misreported.
Yet it touched a sensitive nerve: control over fishing grounds is fiercely guarded in Iceland, so much so that it led to a series of confrontations between Iceland and the UK in the 1950s and the 1970s — known as the Cod Wars.
Joining the EU would likely mean giving up part of its quota, under the Common Fisheries Policy, although there is no consensus on how much exactly Iceland would have to give up.
Some experts argue the quota would be minimal, mainly involving pelagic fish species (i.e. herrings, sardines, mackerel) that migrate across the sea and so are not stationed permanently in Icelandic waters.
However, failing to address this sensitive issue early on may have dulled voters' enthusiasm for EU membership, according to international relations expert Arno Minasian.
"Iceland didn't get to negotiate fisheries and agriculture in 2009, either," he told Euronews' fact-checking team, The Cube. "The EU and Iceland never actually got to those chapters, which is concerning, because those are the really big, important chapters for Iceland."
Some 4% of Iceland's workforce is employed in fisheries, and the sector accounts for around 8% of its GDP. "So fisheries have a lot of economic and political weight," Minasian added.
"If Iceland and the EU cannot negotiate this in the first place, it's quite unrealistic that Icelanders would agree on imposing these quotas through the Common Fisheries Policy," he said.
All of the obligations, none of the benefits?
Another misleading claim was about Iceland's EU-related rights as a non-EU member.
Some, such as former Prime Minister Sigmundur Davíð Gunnlaugsson, said that, since Iceland is already part of the European Economic Area, it already enjoys all the benefits of EU membership.
Gunnlaugsson, who is now leader of the Centre Party, added that joining the EU would mean taking on just downsides and obligations, rather than any extra benefits.
While it is true that, as a member of the European Economic Area, Reykjavík is already playing by much of the EU's economic playbook, by not being a member of the EU itself, it has no seat at the table when the rules are defined.
Iceland does not have votes in the European Parliament, nor a role in the European Commission. It also misses out on certain EU subsidies and funds, to name just a few.
When it comes to the cost of accessing the EU, the opposing camps cited drastically different numbers.
The "No" front set the figure as high as €1 billion a year, while prominent pro-EU figures said it would be just over €50 million.
The latter seems much closer to the truth, according to a study by the independent think tank Evropustraumar, which claimed Iceland's net EU membership cost would be around €60 million a year.

- Over 10,000 migrants remain stranded in Ceuta, causing tension and near-daily protests calling for their return or redistribution.
- Political deadlock persists between Spain's government and opposition, with increased but insufficient resources to manage the crisis effectively.

CEUTA, Spain – Residents of Spain's North African enclave of Ceuta took to the streets on Sept 2 to protest the handling by Madrid of a migration crisis caused by a deadly border surge in July when at least 72,000 people crossed from Morocco.
Thousands of people marched through the streets of the city of about 80,000 residents in a protest that coincided with the annual Ceuta Day. Waving Spanish flags and blowing whistles, they chanted: “Ceuta is not for sale, Ceuta must be defended.”
One placard read, “SOS. Europe, save us from our traitor government”, while some demanded that the authorities should “expel the invaders”. Others called for Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez to resign as demonstrations also took place in other cities across Spain, including Madrid, Barcelona and Bilbao.
Nearly five weeks after the surge, over 10,000 migrants, including unaccompanied minors, remain stranded in makeshift camps or scattered across streets and beaches in the enclave, according to Ceuta’s authorities.
Their presence has triggered near-daily protests by locals against the Spanish government’s management of the crisis, with demonstrators calling for the migrants to be sent back to their countries of origin or redistributed across Spain.
“The response has been inadequate, late and, to top it all, has involved a complete dereliction of duty on the part of the government. We cannot be second-class citizens, and our border must not be sidelined,” said David Hernandez, a 45-year-old teacher.
Recent protests featured sporadic attacks against a makeshift migrant camp at El Trampolin beach and arrests of Moroccan citizens who lobbed stones and bottles at army patrols.
Political deadlock hampers solution
The Sept 2 Spain-wide protests were called by the FEMP federation of municipalities, dominated by the main opposition conservative People’s Party (PP).
Spain’s leftist government distanced itself from the initiative, accusing the right of exploiting the crisis for political benefit.
“This is not about defending Ceuta and the Ceutans, it is about attacking the government,” Territorial Policy Minister Angel Victor Torres told radio station RNE.
A manifesto by citizens’ initiative “Por Ceuta” (For Ceuta), which calls for respect for residents’ and migrants’ human rights, the orderly return of those without the right to remain and more security reinforcements, has garnered nearly 65,000 signatures. The initiative says it has no political affiliation.
Left-wing collectives and unions organised counter-gatherings in several cities, including Madrid, to condemn “racist and Islamophobic persecutions and attacks” against migrants in Ceuta since the rush.
Negotiations between local and central government on how to handle the crisis are deadlocked, with the PP, which governs most regions, some in coalition with the far-right Vox, calling for all those remaining, including minors, to be deported.
The government has increased capacity at temporary accommodation centres to more than 3,400 places from about 500, and deployed over 1,600 police.
But local groups and political leaders say this still falls far short of what is needed to keep citizens and migrants safe.
“The central government needs to provide funds and the local government needs to provide space... that’s the battle we’re in,” said Juan Miguel Morales, director of Sur Acoge charity. “The response has lacked agility: that much is clear.” REUTERS

Heavy ChatGPT use linked to intellectual laziness and social isolation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
13:00:52 UTC
22:00:52 KST

Artificial intelligence has woven its way into everyday life, prompting questions about how reliance on generative tools affects the human mind. A recent small study published in Applied Cognitive Psychology suggests that leaning heavily on ChatGPT can reduce critical thinking, diminish memory, and lead to social isolation. However, users who engage with the software intentionally can also harness it to boost their creativity and reasoning skills.
Over the last few years, tools that generate human-like text have become wildly popular. ChatGPT reached one million users within a week of its launch and currently boasts over 180 million active users. People use the program for everything from writing emails to solving programming problems.
As these programs become a regular part of daily workflows, researchers are trying to understand the psychological and cognitive costs. Zeineb Farhat, a researcher at ISC Paris, initiated the research to investigate what happens when habitual use turns into dependence. Much of the early research on generative software has focused on its benefits in education and the workplace.
Farhat wanted to document the potential downsides of outsourcing mental effort and emotional needs to a machine. The research draws on established ideas in psychology regarding how people manage mental effort and motivation. One concept is cognitive offloading, which happens when individuals use external tools, like calculators or search engines, to reduce the amount of information they need to process or remember.
Another core idea involves the psychological needs for autonomy, competence, and social connection. When people feel capable and in control of their actions, they are generally more motivated. Farhat set out to see how constant access to an intelligent digital assistant might alter these processes.
The researcher wanted to know if offloading cognitive tasks to an algorithm would compromise a user’s ability to think independently. To explore these dynamics, Farhat conducted a small study involving 45 young adults in France. The participants, aged 18 to 25, were all regular users who interacted with ChatGPT daily.
The researcher conducted semi-structured interviews with each participant, either face-to-face or via video call. These interviews lasted between 45 and 60 minutes. The conversations covered how the participants used the software, how it affected their study or work habits, and how it made them feel.
Farhat then analyzed the interview transcripts to identify recurring themes in the users’ experiences. The analysis revealed that heavy reliance on the software often discouraged independent thought. Participants reported that having instant answers at their fingertips made them less likely to analyze problems deeply or evaluate sources.
Some described experiencing intellectual laziness, noting that their attention spans felt shorter. Users also reported trouble retaining information. They were externalizing their memory by relying on the chatbot to retrieve facts rather than practicing active recall.
“I used to take notes and actively review materials, but now I just ask ChatGPT whenever I need something,” one student noted in the study. “The problem is, I don’t retain much. I feel like my memory has become weaker because I rely on ChatGPT instead of trying to recall things on my own.”
Psychologically, the interviews indicated that heavy use eroded the participants’ sense of autonomy and self-trust. Many users started second-guessing their own judgment. They began seeking the software’s validation for simple decisions, like choosing the right words for a basic email.
The ease of getting quick answers also lowered their intrinsic motivation to learn new things. Without the struggle normally required to master a topic, the learning process felt less rewarding. Some participants even reported anxiety and a sense of paralysis when the software was offline for maintenance.
One participant recalled a time when the system went down, bringing their workflow to a complete halt. “I needed it for a work project, and I felt completely paralyzed without it,” the user shared. “It’s like my safety net is gone.”
The study also uncovered shifts in social behavior. Participants frequently chose to interact with the software instead of discussing ideas with peers or teachers. This preference sometimes led to feelings of social isolation, as users lost the habit of engaging in deep conversations with other people.
A few participants began to treat the text generator as a companion, projecting human traits onto it. “ChatGPT has become my friend; it knows everything about me,” one participant stated. “It’s always there, always ready to listen, and it feels like it understands me better than most people do.”
While this offered temporary comfort, it substituted genuine human connection with a machine response. Relying on an algorithm for emotional support risks blurring the line between technological mediation and true social interaction. Over time, this dynamic can weaken interpersonal skills and empathy.
Despite these negative reports, the study identified a pattern of constructive use. Some users treated the software as a collaborative tool rather than a replacement for their own brains. By allowing the program to handle tedious tasks like structuring data or summarizing dense text, these individuals freed up mental energy for complex reasoning.
They used the tool to brainstorm or overcome writer’s block. Instead of copying what the program generated, they used the output as a starting point to think differently. When used reflectively, the software actually increased users’ confidence and reduced their anxiety about challenging tasks.
Because the research relies on qualitative interviews with a small group of young adults in France, the findings reflect a specific demographic and cannot be broadly generalized. People from older generations or different cultural backgrounds might interact with the software differently. The study also captures user experiences at a single point in time.
It remains unknown whether these cognitive and social habits change over years of use. Future research will need to track larger and more diverse groups over longer periods to see if these patterns persist. Additional studies could also explore how to best train people to use these tools adaptively rather than dependently.
The study, “When AI Thinks for Us: Unveiling the Cognitive and Social Toll of ChatGPT Over-Reliance,” was authored by Zeineb Farhat.

How horse milk ‘kymyz’ became a drink still in demand thousands of years later
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
13:00:43 UTC
22:00:43 KST

Fermented horse milk, known as kymyz, is a traditional Central Asian drink with thousands of years of history. In Kazakhstan, it remains an important part of nomadic heritage, cuisine and hospitality.
Kymyz is a traditional drink made from mare's milk and drunk in many countries across Central Asia. Peoples ranging from northern Han Chinese to Kazakhs, Bashkirs, Kalmyks, Kyrgyz, Mongols and Yakuts say their ancestors have been drinking kymyz since time immemorial.
The earliest Western text that mentions it is by Herodotus, who, in his 5th-century BC Histories, describes the Scythians’ processing of mare's milk.
Kazakhstan holds a special place in kymyz production. In the Copper Age necropolis of the Botai culture, located in modern-day Kazakhstan, archaeologists found evidence of the world’s earliest horse domestication. They also found traces of horse milk on pottery.
Kymyz also provided energy to nomadic warriors during wartime. Rich in vitamins and nutrients, kymyz is attracting scientific interest as researchers explore its potential benefits.
Gaukhar Konuspayeva, a professor of food biotechnology, has spent the past 26 years studying camel and horse milk. She says there is still much more to learn about the potential of kymyz.
“According to our research, mare’s milk is very rich in vitamins A, B1, B2, B5 and B6. But what makes kymyz unique is its fatty acid composition and the presence of prebiotic bacteria,” she added.
Kymyz was not forgotten during the Soviet era, when many of the peoples with a tradition of drinking it lived within the Soviet Union. Soviet state farms in the region kept hundreds of thousands of mares for their milk and dairy products, including kymyz.
Inside the tradition of kymyz making
There are different types of kymyz. Its taste depends not only on the region where the horse grazes and the grass it eats, but also on how the drink is prepared.
Every farmer has their own recipe, but the freshest mare’s milk, known as saumal, is considered the most valuable. You won’t find it in supermarkets, as it stays fresh for only a few hours. To try it, you usually have to go to the countryside.
In the village of Zhanaarka in the Ulytau Region, Aiman Kutzhanova showed us how she milks her mares. She works as a deputy principal at a local school and also raises horses with her husband.
There is a traditional way of milking a mare. First, the foal is allowed to feed, and only then is the milk collected.
Unlike cows, mares need to be milked every one to two hours, and they can produce only about a litre of milk a day.
“Horses are sacred animals. They choose the person who milks them. For example, my mares won’t let anyone else milk them. Even if I come wearing different clothes, they won’t let me milk them,” says Aiman Kutzhanova.
After milking, the milk should either be drunk fresh (saumal) or used to make kymyz. To prepare it, the milk is stirred in deep wooden vessels called ‘kubi’. The inside of the vessel is traditionally coated with butter before the milk is added.
In the past, leather sacks filled with mare’s milk were hung from the top of the yurt or attached to a saddle, allowing the milk to be shaken throughout the day.
Today, there are also many different varieties of kymyz, including versions made with honey, smoked flavours, herbs and even horse meat.
The celebration of mare milking
For centuries, Kazakhs lived as nomads, moving between winter and summer pastures with their herds. The start of the mare-milking season coincided with the move to the summer pastures, where families would set up their yurts(portable homes used by nomadic families).
The first milking of the season marked the beginning of a new season and was celebrated as a big event. The tradition is known as ‘Kymyz Muryndyk’, which refers to the first kymyz of the season.
This tradition is still alive today. Festivals dedicated to Kymyz Muryndyk are held in two regions of Kazakhstan: Ulytau and Almaty, often far from the cities and close to the steppe.
The celebrations bring together local families, farmers and visitors.
The BaiKymyz festival
Every year, Astana also hosts the BaiKymyz Festival, where producers compete to find the best kymyz. The festival brings together farmers and kymyz producers from across the country.
The festival was created by Zhumazhan Kaltayev, who drew inspiration from Germany’s Oktoberfest and adapted the idea to Kazakhstan, putting kymyz and nomadic culture at the heart of the event.
“I went to Oktoberfest in Munich in 2020. I saw that it was a family celebration, and I also saw how much it could contribute to the local economy. We didn’t have anything like that in Kazakhstan,” Zhumazhan Kaltayev said.
“People really liked our festival because it is not just about the drink. It represents our national identity, our culture, our spirit and our history.”
The competition is not only about taste. This year, producers also competed for the title of kymyz with the best nutritional composition, with experts examining the quality and characteristics of the drink.
“The total prize fund this year is 45 million tenge. The main prize, the Grand Prix, is a car,” Kaltayev added.
The new life of kymyz
In Kazakhstan, the drink has become part of everyday life. You can now find bottled kymyz in supermarkets and order it in cafes and restaurants.
For a drink with centuries of history, kymyz is finding surprisingly modern ways to reach a new generation.
One of the latest trends is the rise of kymyz houses (kymyz-khana). Here, visitors can try different types of kymyz, including traditional varieties as well as versions made with honey, herbs and other ingredients.
Kymyz is also reaching international markets. Dried mare’s milk and other kymyz products are exported to countries such as China, Russia and Germany.

Swedish minister defends strict post-Brexit removals of Britons
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
12:59:23 UTC
21:59:23 KST

The Swedish government has doubled down on its position on removing and deporting British citizens on the grounds they were late to apply for permission to stay after Brexit.
The migration minister, Johan Forssell, issued a robust defence of the Swedish migration agency’s implementation of the Brexit withdrawal agreement on Wednesday in response to a question from an MP about the case of Joyce Thomas, a 78-year-old British widow who has been ordered to leave the country after 21 years.
Forssell said the European Commission, which is legally mandated to ensure EU member states implement the withdrawal agreement correctly, was onboard with Sweden’s approach.
“The migration board has followed up on the application of the withdrawal agreement and the assessment is that Sweden has fulfilled its commitments. This assessment is shared by the commission,” he said.
There has been growing controversy over removal orders issued to British citizens who did not know that Sweden was one of 13 countries in the EU that required formal applications to stay in the country post-Brexit.
In another case, a 34-year-old British man, John Sellers, has been deported despite having lived in Sweden since he was 10.
Thomas’s local MP, Häkan Svenneling, of the Left party, told the Guardian: “It seems to me that the Swedish government thinks everything is fine even though British citizens are being deported from Sweden right now. Not acting is also an action in this situation. What Sweden needs is a new government and a new migration minister who stops deporting people with strong connections to Sweden.”
In his written answer to Svenneling, Forssell offered British citizens facing deportation a sliver of hope. He said: “The relationship with the UK is very important to Sweden and the government will continue to safeguard the correct implementation of the withdrawal agreement. As part of this, the government is investigating whether further measures can be taken to facilitate the process in the future.”
Thomas has been told she must remove herself from Sweden by Tuesday 8 September or face deportation and a potential ban from the Schengen area.
She is one of several British citizens who have been faced with removal orders after the migration agency rejected their late applications to stay.
The UK Foreign Office has raised Sweden’s approach to late applications for post-Brexit residency a number of times in the specialised committee on citizens’ rights, a structure set up to ensure the withdrawal agreement is implemented properly.
David Milstead, who runs the grassroots organisation Brits in Sweden, said the Swedish response was not a surprise. “The government was hardly going to disown the decisions of [the migration agency] or the Swedish courts. The real question is whether Sweden’s approach is consistent with EU law and the [withdrawal agreement],” he said.
He pointed out that under the agreement, the UK was obliged to set up a statutory body, the Independent Monitoring Authority (IMA), to independently ensure the Home Office implemented the Brexit deal correctly, while the European Commission performed the correspondent role for EU member states.
“The IMA has taken a much more robust approach. It is hard to imagine it not challenging the UK had it operated a policy like Sweden’s, which would have put the rights of around a quarter of a million successful late applicants [in the UK] at risk,” Milstead said.
“Sweden’s approach now needs either to be tested before the European court of justice or addressed through measures that remedy the problem. The government’s response leaves open the possibility of change, and that must include fixing unjust deportation decisions.”
The European Commission has been approached for comment.
According to Eurostat data, between 2021 and 2025 a total of 2,490 UK nationals were ordered to leave Sweden. Analysis by the Foreign Office found this was 32.9% of the 7,565 UK nationals ordered to leave the 27 EU member states over this period. Although it is not possible to determine exactly how many were in Sweden prior to the end of the UK-EU transition period, it is likely that the majority will have been.
Thomas has been in Sweden for 21 years and says her late husband inquired about the impact of Brexit and was told by the authorities there was nothing they needed to do to remain in the country legally.
The couple moved to the country to be close to their son and grandchildren, and Thomas said she had been left feeling sick with worry after receiving the removal order.

Drone incident in Germany has ‘hallmarks of state-sponsored terrorism’, EU's Kallas says
Last month's incident involving an explosive-laden drone at Leipzig airport bears "all the hallmarks of state-sponsored terrorism," EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said Wednesday. Germany has blamed Russia for the "hybrid attack". The EU has summoned the Russian envoy, and member states were doing the same, Kallas said.
EU countries on Wednesday summoned Russia's envoys and discussed fresh sanctions after a drone incident in Germany that the bloc's foreign policy chief said bore the marks of "state-sponsored terrorism".
The incident involving an explosive-laden drone at Leipzig airport has heightened fears over a sabotage campaign that the EU and NATO say is a Russian attempt to destabilise Ukraine's backers.
"It is clear that it has all the hallmarks of state-sponsored terrorism," EU High Representative for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy, Kaja Kallas said at a meeting of the bloc's foreign ministers in Ireland.
"The question is, what do we do about this?"
Kallas said the EU had summoned the Russian envoy, and member states were doing the same.
"We will not let an act of such gravity go unpunished," France's Minister for Europe and Foreign Affairs Jean-Noël Barrot said, adding he had called in Russia's envoy in Paris.
Kallas said that EU foreign ministers agreed to keep working on a proposal to impose sanctions on 1,600 individuals and entities linked to Russia's military industry in the hope of adopting them next month.
"Seeing these hybrid attacks across Europe, I think these are also wake-up calls for the countries who have not been so strong, maybe on this," she said.
"If we want to end this war, we all have to focus our efforts. Take it to a new level."
Germany blamed Moscow for the Leipzig incident on Tuesday and said it was shutting a Russian consulate and ending the contract for a cultural centre in Berlin.
Read moreGermany investigates suspected power substation sabotage, Russia summons German envoy
Russia's President Vladimir Putin in televised comments later branded those moves "another mistake, a serious one", saying it "clearly runs counter to the interests of the German people".
'Live with the consequences'
Germany's Federal Minister for Foreign Affairs Johann Wadephul said there was a "large number of people who can now be sanctioned in addition".
"Russia has escalated, Russia has carried out this hybrid attack, and now Russia must live with the consequences," he said, speaking from Ireland.
President of the European Commission Ursula von der Leyen said the Leipzig incident marked "a new escalation" in Europe.
"This was an attack using military-grade material carried out by Russian operatives on European Union soil," she said after talks with NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte, adding: "We will not tolerate it."
But von der Leyen also warned such incidents had become a "new normal" for Europe, as Russia steps up destabilising activities.
"We do not seek conflict with Russia, but Russia seems to be at hybrid war with us," said Poland's Minister of Foreign Affairs, Radoslaw Sikorski.
"We are no longer in regular peacetime."
While the level of rhetoric is being ramped up, some said that Europe's response has failed to match its strong words.
Lithuania's Minister of Foreign Affairs Kestutis Budrys called for more to be done to punish Moscow for its actions.
"We have to consider what options we have in our hands and respond, because it is obvious Russia does not see the political cost of the hybrid activities against us," he said.
Kallas said that there was "broad consensus" to continue work on a proposal to ban visas for Russians who fought in Ukraine and increase restrictions for tourists.
She added without giving details, that there had also been new pledges of desperately-needed air defence missiles for Ukraine.
Discussion has resurfaced on whether the bloc should tap some 200 billion euros ($235 billion) of frozen Russian central bank assets to fund Ukraine.
"I think this is a fair approach to start serious discussion on how we could use immobilised frozen assets," said Ukraine's Minister of Foreign Affairs Andriy Sybiga.
The EU last year failed to agree a plan to employ the Russian funds, and instead came up with a 90 billion euro loan off its own back.
But there is already a sense that the loan will not be enough for the two years it was intended to keep Kyiv afloat.

Putin and Zelenskyy issue threats as strikes rock Ukraine, Russia
Putin accuses Zelenskyy of ‘terrorism’, while Ukraine warns foreign airlines against using Russian airspace.
Russian drone attacks across Ukraine have killed at least one person and wounded more than a dozen others, as Volodymyr Zelenskyy and Vladimir Putin threatened to escalate the conflict.
Between Tuesday and Wednesday, Ukrainian authorities reported attacks in the capital, Kyiv, in the southern city of Odesa and in eastern Dnipro, where the body of a man was retrieved from under rubble.
The air war between Russia and Ukraine has intensified as the conflict stretches into its fifth year following Moscow’s invasion of its neighbour. The front line in eastern and southern Ukraine remains largely deadlocked, and US efforts to negotiate a peace settlement have yet to produce a path to peace.
Russian President Vladimir Putin and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy exchanged threats late on Tuesday over what their next steps might be.
Zelenskyy warned foreign airlines that the skies over Russia are not safe for flights due to Ukrainian long-range drone attacks, saying that “Russian airspace will effectively be closing”. He said Ukrainian military pressure aims to compel Russia to accept peace negotiations.
Putin accused Zelenskyy of “state terrorism” and said: “We don’t negotiate with terrorists.”
At a late-night news conference on the sidelines of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation summit in Kyrgyzstan, Putin also addressed reports that the Ukrainian military had used British-made drones to strike targets inside Russia.
Asked whether Russia would strike British military facilities if the UK government continues to provide Ukraine with weaponry, Putin declined to rule it out. With a small smile, he told reporters it was “a military secret”.
China and North Korea, meanwhile, have provided military support for Russia, as has Iran in previous years.
The Russian and Ukrainian leaders’ comments came as European officials weigh their response to the latest in what they say is Moscow’s campaign of continental sabotage and disruption aimed at weakening European support for Ukraine. Germany on Tuesday blamed Russia for an attempted attack at Leipzig/Halle airport last month using a drone laden with explosives.
Odesa power outage
Russia fired 174 attack drones, about half of them jet-powered drones that are hard to stop and are increasingly being deployed by Moscow, as well as two ballistic missiles and two plane-launched missiles at Ukraine overnight, according to the Ukrainian Air Force.
Officials in the southern Ukraine region of Odesa reported that the attack damaged a 24-storey residential building, destroying apartments on several floors and wounding eight people, including a child.
Odesa office buildings and two educational facilities were also damaged, Serhiy Lysak, head of the Odesa city military administration, said. The barrage also caused a power outage that halted electric-powered public transport, the city council said.
A man and a woman were wounded by shrapnel in morning attacks on the Kyiv region, according to Tymur Tkachenko, head of the regional military administration.
It was the seventh straight day Kyiv came under attack, although the latest barrage wasn’t as heavy as in previous days. The assault started a fire at a warehouse, officials said. Russian forces have targeted civilian facilities in what Ukrainian officials say is an effort to disrupt daily life and sap public morale.
A fire broke out at an educational facility and a medical practice was also damaged, the Kyiv city military administration said.
Meanwhile in Russia, air defences destroyed 130 Ukrainian drones overnight, the Defence Ministry said on Wednesday. The drones were shot down over 11 Russian regions, as well as the annexed Ukrainian peninsula of Crimea and the Black Sea, it said.
Ukrainian drone attacks killed two people in Russia’s Belgorod border region and wounded 16 more, acting governor Aleksand Shuvaev said. Ukrainian forces hit the region 140 times over the course of 24 hours, he said.
Ukraine’s domestically developed long-range drones have repeatedly targeted Russia’s oil sector, hoping to dent the economy and the warehouses of online retailers to make the Russian public feel the effects of war.

Rheinmetall to supply turret parts for U.S. Marines’ new combat vehicles
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
12:55:03 UTC
21:55:03 KST

- American Rheinmetall won a $710,000 subcontract from Kongsberg to produce MCT-30 turret components for the Marine Corps' ACV-30 vehicle.
- The award is the first Kongsberg contract for the company's Michigan facilities, with deliveries running through 2026 and 2027.
American Rheinmetall has won a $710,000 subcontract from Kongsberg Defence & Aerospace to produce machined components for the MCT-30 turret used on the U.S. Marine Corps’ ACV-30, the amphibious combat vehicle variant equipped with a medium-caliber gun.
The work will be performed at American Rheinmetall’s Lapeer and Lansing, Michigan facilities, with deliveries scheduled throughout 2026 and 2027. American Rheinmetall is serving as a subcontractor to Kongsberg, which builds the MCT-30 turret system.
The award marks the first contract Kongsberg has placed with American Rheinmetall’s Michigan operations. The company said the deal builds on an existing relationship with Kongsberg centered on its facility in Maine, which has supported the CROWS remote weapon station program.
“The opportunity to support Kongsberg on the ACV-30 program reflects our expanding partnership and strengthens American Rheinmetall’s role in delivering high-quality components for critical U.S. military platforms,” said Tom McDonnell, Senior Vice President of Sales and Marketing at American Rheinmetall. “We’re proud that our Michigan facilities will contribute to the Marine Corps’ modernization priorities as it evolves into a more mobile and capable force.”
The ACV-30 is a variant of the Marine Corps’ Amphibious Combat Vehicle, fitted with the MCT-30 turret to add a 30mm cannon and improved firepower compared with the base ACV personnel carrier configuration. The Amphibious Combat Vehicle program overall is intended to replace the Marine Corps’ aging Assault Amphibious Vehicle fleet, which has been in service since the 1970s.
American Rheinmetall’s Michigan facilities are also involved in the company’s Lynx XM30 program, which delivered its first prototype to the U.S. Army last week as part of the competition to replace the Bradley Infantry Fighting Vehicle. The Kongsberg award adds a separate Marine Corps-linked customer relationship to the company’s Michigan operations, alongside that Army-focused work.
American Rheinmetall said the award reflects its continued growth within the Tier 1 defense industry supplier base as the company expands both its manufacturing capabilities and its customer base across U.S. military branches.

====================================================================================================

Prioritizing Social Stability Over Democratic Reforms: Uzbekistan Announces New Development Programs
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
12:50:00 UTC
21:50:00 KST

As Uzbekistan celebrated its 35th independence anniversary this week, President Shavkat Mirziyoyev announced seven national programs for the years ahead. The programs focus on socio-economic development and conspicuously omit any reform related to political pluralism, press freedom, freedom of conscience, or other democratic elements.
Mirziyoyev has prioritized areas viewed as critical to retaining popular support for his government. The first is improving public education, with a special focus on extending compulsory education to age six, supporting private kindergartens, and having at least ten universities ranked in the top 1,000 higher education institutions in the world. Uzbekistan has one of the highest numbers of schoolchildren in the region, with 6.8 million students and 600,000 teachers in public mandatory schools alone.
The next few national programs announced by Mirziyoyev also concern socio-economic well-being: improving public health and increasing longevity; transitioning to a high technology economy, and ensuring high labor productivity as well as changing public attitudes toward the environment and addressing environmental challenges.
The fifth national program is set to ensure judicial independence and the rule of law. The Diplomat recently reported that one of the country’s new laws allows the president’s daughter, who heads the presidential administration, to be directly involved in shaping the judicial system while having lifetime legal immunity for her actions with no accountability. A few areas – cybercrime, drug trafficking, and human trafficking – are singled out for additional attention but concrete steps in this regard have not been outlined.
The sixth program Mirziyoyev announced identified mahallas as the “‘main customer (or commissioner)’ of development.” This program basically aims to further empower mahallas along with slightly altering the district budgeting system. Mahallas are unique self-governing institutions established at the neighborhood level. Each household is part of a mahalla. As of 2021, there were 9,251 mahallas across the country.
“The mood of our people, the well-being of families, the dreams and aspirations of young people, and the initiative of entrepreneurs are first and foremost reflected in the neighborhood,” Mirziyoyev said in his speech. “Mood” is an odd word to pick – not financial stability, safety, employment or other aspects of socio-economic life. It reflects mahallas’ role as an observer of citizens’ sentiment (and hopefully their needs too).
Historically, mahalla institutions have played a distributing role rather than a commissioning one, carrying government policies down and out to the people rather than gathering and feeding social sentiments upward into the system. Mirziyoyev is now saying that mahallas ought to be “the main customer (commissioner) of social development.” While this is, in one sense, a form of decentralization where citizens might participate in some degree of decision-making, it is not a genuine political decentralization. It appears that mahallas will report upward the social and financial needs on the ground and the budget allocation will be made accordingly. The president’s announcement noted, “District budgets, investment programs, and infrastructure projects are developed based on the needs of neighborhoods.”
But mahallas still will not have a final say in anything. They will not receive full control over their own budgets. Ultimate decisions on budget allocations will remain at the hands of the central government. The proposed change, if implemented, will result in participatory or needs-based local governance, but does not grant fiscal independence.
The last area of development focuses on a peaceful foreign policy and economic diplomacy.
The proposed national development programs place emphasis on socio-economic areas. These are safe areas wherein changes, minor or even radical, will not threaten or challenge the political regime. Instead, increased attention to these spheres will increase Mirziyoyev’s popularity and thus further consolidate power in the existing government.
The programs as outlined do not address areas in which Mirziyoyev initially promised reforms, particularly freedom of expression. His early promises on supporting journalists and allowing the press to become a true watchdog has undergone a clear backslide. The Diplomat has continuously reported on waves of arrests of local bloggers, including popular religious scholar and blogger, Mubashshir Ahmad. Not only journalists or bloggers, but ordinary citizens are also regularly charged with crimes and sentenced to prison for expressing their personal religious views, sharing religious songs online that are not approved by the government or for saying anything negative about the president or his family. The recent law that expanded the authority of the presidential administration, headed by Mirziyoyev’s first daughter, Saida Mirziyoyeva, also prohibits “insulting the honor and dignity” of its officials. The law does not explicitly differentiate between healthy criticism and insult.
The Mirziyoyev administration’s priorities are clear in its announced programs: to keep average people happy by ensuring their basic needs are covered. Anything else, particularly those related to freedom of speech, mobilization, or independent teaching and practice of religion that can eventually challenge the status quo, has been swept under the carpet.

- General Dynamics Land Systems, Ford and Ricardo are teaming up to compete for the UK's Light Mobility Vehicle program, based on the Ford Ranger platform.
- The LMV requirement is part of the UK's broader Land Mobility Programme, valued at more than £4.8 billion over its first decade, aimed at replacing the Land Rover and Pinzgauer fleets by 2030.
General Dynamics Land Systems has teamed up with Ford Motor Company and Ricardo to compete for the UK Ministry of Defence’s Light Mobility Vehicle program, the companies announced.
The team’s proposal is built on the Ford Ranger platform, which General Dynamics UK described as Europe’s best-selling pickup truck for 11 consecutive years.
“Combining the strengths of three industry leaders, the team will deliver a proven, scalable, and cost-effective solution built on the Ford Ranger platform,” General Dynamics UK said. “Together, General Dynamics Land Systems, Ford and Ricardo bring a credible, low-risk and highly scalable proposition that meets the British Army’s needs while creating significant export opportunities and maximising value for the UK taxpayer.”
The Light Mobility Vehicle program is intended to replace the British Army’s aging Land Rover and Pinzgauer utility vehicle fleets, both of which are due to leave service by 2030. The LMV requirement forms one strand of the UK’s wider Land Mobility Programme, a modernization effort covering more than 11,000 vehicles across multiple weight classes that the Ministry of Defence launched to consolidate a patchwork of legacy fleets built up over decades, some dating back to operations in Iraq and Afghanistan.
The Land Mobility Programme is structured around several vehicle categories. The Light Mobility Vehicle segment alone is expected to cover roughly 2,500 vehicles, part of a broader program the Ministry of Defence has said could exceed £4.8 billion ($6.1 billion) in total value across its first decade. The program also includes a Light Protected Mobility category for vehicles up to 10,000 kilograms (22,046 pounds), and a Heavy Protected Mobility requirement covering platforms in the 20 to 30 tonne range, which replaced an earlier “medium” category the Ministry of Defence dropped from the program’s structure in January.
The Ministry of Defence first sought industry input on the LMV requirement through a Request for Information issued in January 2025, seeking a wheeled utility platform built on a common base to modernize roles currently filled by the Land Rover and Pinzgauer. That process specifically explored the potential for an off-the-shelf solution, rather than a bespoke design, to meet the requirement quickly. A formal tender notice for the LMV competition was expected imminently as of late July, according to trade publication Army Technology, with vehicle trials tentatively planned to run from October 2026 through January 2027.
General Dynamics Land Systems joins a competitive field for the LMV requirement that has already drawn interest from other established suppliers, including UK vehicle maker Supacat, which unveiled its own tactical Light Mobility Vehicle in late 2024 aimed at high-readiness units such as the Royal Marines’ 3 Commando Brigade and the British Army’s Ranger Regiment.
The wider Land Mobility Programme has separately seen the UK select Patria and Babcock’s Common Armoured Vehicle System for elements of its heavier vehicle requirements, a decision announced in September 2025 that also brought Norway into that program.

Euroclear back in the spotlight: 4 countries eager to use €193 billion in Russian assets after all
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
12:45:33 UTC
21:45:33 KST

The Netherlands, Poland, Spain and Sweden are asking the European Commission, the EU’s executive, to devise a solution that would allow the frozen Russian assets held at Euroclear, the European securities depository, to be used to support Ukraine after all. This brings a matter that seemed to have been settled last December back onto the European negotiating table and puts Belgium back in the grinder.
Euroclear back in the spotlight: 4 countries eager to use €193 billion in Russian assets after all
The four countries raised this request last Thursday in a letter to the Commission. The fact that it is these countries in particular comes as little surprise. The Netherlands, Poland and Sweden were already in favour of this last year. In the Netherlands, the use of the frozen funds is even included in the Jetten government’s coalition agreement.
“These are countries that provide a great deal of support to Ukraine from their own budgets – more than the average,” says VRT’s EU correspondent Rob Heirbaut. “In fact, they would prefer not to have to do so any longer, which is why they are eying those Russian assets.”
It is notable, however, that Spain is on also board. “Spain has always kept a low profile on this issue until now and is certainly no champion when it comes to financial support for Ukraine,” says Heirbaut.
The issue is back on the table, just nine months after European leaders decided not to release the frozen funds. Belgian Prime Minister Bart De Wever (Flemish nationalist) stood his ground at the time. The EU chose instead to borrow 90 billion euros on the capital markets and pass this on to Ukraine as an interest-free loan. That was supposed to suffice for 2026 and 2027.
“That appears not to be the case. That much is already clear,” says Heirbaut. “The war is only intensifying. Moreover, Europe had hoped that non-EU countries such as Canada and Japan would also contribute, but they have contributed less than promised.”
What does this mean for Belgium?
The request from the four countries is not addressed to Belgium, but to the European Commission. They are explicitly asking for a proposal that takes Belgian concerns into account, whereby the risk is spread across all EU Member States. At present, that risk lies largely with Belgium, as the majority of the frozen Russian assets are held at Euroclear in Brussels.
In August, three former senior officials put forward a proposal to this end: Annegret Kramp-Karrenbauer, the former German Defence Minister; Nathalie Loiseau, the former French European Affairs Minister, and Daleep Singh, who served as Deputy National Security Adviser under President Joe Biden.
‘They say: we can use a European decision to remove that money from Euroclear and transfer it to the EU, and also remove all liability from Belgium,’ explains Heirbaut. ‘They say that is legally possible. I assume those four countries are also in favour of this.’
Meanwhile, the Belgian position remains unchanged. Belgium does not want to bear the burden of legal claims and potential Russian countermeasures alone. It is therefore demanding unlimited solidarity from the other Member States. “At this stage, that is only to be expected,” says Heirbaut. “There isn’t a single proposal on paper yet, so countries are staking out their positions.”
The Belgian government’s hardline stance is partly due to recent developments in Moscow. A Russian court ordered Euroclear to pay damages of over 200 billion euros and upheld that ruling on appeal in July.
Euroclear does not recognise the jurisdiction of that court and has taken the matter to the Commercial Court in Brussels. Belgian PM De Wever fears harsher reprisals if the assets are actually seized.
According to VRT’s Rob Heirbaut, Belgium’s allies are the same countries as in December. France, where several banks also hold Russian assets, and Italy supported Belgium then and continues to do so.
“Who I find to be conspicuously silent is Germany,” says Heirbaut. Last year, Chancellor Friedrich Merz made a complete U-turn by suddenly advocating the use of the assets. “At the moment, Germany is remaining conspicuously silent.”
What next?
According to Heirbaut, the European Commission is not yet working on a concrete plan. Last year, Commission President Ursula von der Leyen announced that the assets would be used, but she now seems more cautious. “Apparently, they would rather wait until the heads of government have discussed the matter.”
That won’t happen until October, at the European summit. The agenda will include both support for Ukraine and the European multiannual budget. If it proves impossible to find funds for Ukraine through that budget, the Russian assets will once again come in focus.
What is at issue?
Euroclear is a Brussels-based financial institution that holds shares and bonds on behalf of banks and central banks and handles the settlement of stock market transactions. Since the Russian invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, the Russian central bank’s reserves there have been frozen.
Across the EU, this amounts to approximately 210 billion euros in frozen Russian funds. The bulk of this, around 193 billion euros, is held by Euroclear. Russia cannot access these securities, but the money remains legally owned by Russia. Consequently, it cannot simply be seized.
The interest and dividends generated by these assets are paid into a blocked account. Euroclear uses them for reinvestment. The majority of the interest revenue is transferred to the European support fund for Ukraine. In total, Ukraine has already received 6.6 billion euros in interest income.

Israeli Defense Minister Katz refuses to say there was no betrayal from within on Oct. 7: 'I only comment on what I know'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
12:42:14 UTC
21:42:14 KST

Israeli Defense Minister Israel Katz refused on Wednesday to say there was no betrayal from inside Israel involved in Hamas' surprise attack on October 7, 2023. Speaking at a conference sponsored by the Ynet website and the Yedioth Aharonoth daily, Katz was asked about comments made this week by Sara Netanyahu, the prime minister's wife, about the chairman of Israel's Democrats party, Yair Golan, in which she hinted that he must have known about the attack in advance.
When asked about the issue on Wednesday, Katz, who is a affiliated with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's Likud party, said that he doesn't "consume the media" and "can only comment on what I know." Katz said that Hamas officials had coordinated their attack with Hezbollah in Lebanon and with Iran and had applied a Hamas military plan dubbed Jericho Wall to overwhelm the Israeli army's Gaza Division on the border, a plan that Katz said Israel's political leadership had not been informed about in advance.
"What I know from the material I saw is that the failure is deep enough to explain what happened there." But he explicitly refused to say there was no betrayal. The defense minister also claimed that in its war with Iran in June of last year, Israel destroyed the Iranian nuclear program and said that it has not been revived since. He had praise for the Israel Defense Forces and said that the IDF is prepared to attack Iran. "If they attack us, we will respond with great force, without depending on anyone," he added, in an apparent reference to the United States.
On Monday, in an interview on Channel 14, the prime minister's wife, Sara, hinted that Yair Golan, who is a former IDF deputy chief of staff, was part of a conspiracy on the morning of the Hamas attack, which began just before 6:30 A.M.
"You're a military man of such high rank, claiming to be a fighter on October 7. You were there early in the morning, already dressed and ready, at a very, very early hour, when others, such as the prime minister, didn't know," she said. When asked if there was a betrayal on October 7, she said she didn't want to speak." But she added that she "is not a party to any theories" and "does not know."
She also demanded the establishment of a "real commission of inquiry" into the events of October 7. The Netanyahu government has resisted the convening of a formal state commission of inquiry appointed by the president of the Supreme Court.
The day after the interview was broadcast, Yair Golan sent Sara Netanyahu a warning letter demanding that she apologize within 24 hours and pay compensation to be donated to the survivors of the Nova music festival, where hundreds were killed on October 7 in the Hamas attack. If she failed to do so, Golan's letter stated, he would sue her for 2.5 million shekels (about $833,000). Mrs. Netanyahu has refused to apologize.
Her husband, the prime minister, subsequently denied that there had been any "internal betrayal" on October 7.

Taiwan Tourism Administration warns travel agencies of China risks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
12:40:17 UTC
21:40:17 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) – The Tourism Administration recently reminded travel agencies to file reports about groups traveling to China or face fines of up to NT$50,000 (US$1,500), reports said Wednesday.
The warning level for travel to China issued by the Mainland Affairs Council stands at orange, advising against non-essential travel to China. The government recently pointed out the case of a former Amnesty International staffer facing hours of questioning by immigration after his arrival in Shanghai on a business trip.
Despite an official ban on Taiwanese tour groups heading to China, they have been assisting travelers and forming groups, supposedly for research or exchange purposes, per Liberty Times. Even in the event of individuals forming groups to travel in China, Hong Kong, and Macau, the details of the itinerary should be registered, the government said.
New immigration regulations China plans to implement on Sept. 15 will increase the risks of travel to China, according to MAC. Registration before the trip will allow the government to assist in the case of emergencies.
The Tourism Administration sent letters to travel agencies telling them to register groups from Sept. 1. The tour operators also need to remind travelers of the risks.
The administration said it had asked travel associations to tell member agencies about the rules, and the possibility of fines ranging from NT$10,000 to NT$50,000 if they failed to comply, Liberty Times reported.

19 killed in overnight U.S. attacks on Iran as Tehran retaliates across region
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
20:38:41 CST
21:38:41 KST

TEHRAN/KUWAIT CITY, Sept. 2 (Xinhua) -- At least 19 people, including military personnel and civilians, were killed in overnight U.S. strikes across several provinces in Iran, as the country's armed forces retaliated by attacking U.S. bases and assets in the region, Iranian media reported Wednesday.
The U.S. attacks on Iran's southwestern Khuzestan province killed seven people and wounded eight others, the semi-official Mehr news agency cited Valiollah Hayati, Khuzestan's deputy governor for security and law enforcement affairs, as saying.
The report said U.S. strikes on southern Lavan Island killed three members of the Basij volunteer force of Iran's Islamic Revolution Guard Corps (IRGC), while four members of the IRGC's Aerospace division were killed in strikes on the western province of Kermanshah.
A commando, identified as Malek Mousavi-Tabar, was killed Wednesday morning during operations to counter the movements of an invading drone in Bahmai County in the western Kohgiluyeh and Boyer-Ahmad province, it added.
It also cited provincial authorities as saying that four people were killed and 68 others wounded in a U.S. attack targeting a wedding ceremony in Sirik County in southern Hormozgan province. The victims included one four-year-old child, a teenager and two women.
In a post on social media platform X earlier in the day, U.S. Central Command said its forces had "successfully completed a wave of strikes against Iranian military targets," citing "recent attempted attacks by the IRGC against commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz and against American service members."
In retaliation for the U.S. strikes, Iran's IRGC and army announced that they targeted U.S. bases and assets in Jordan, Kuwait, Bahrain, Iraq's semi-autonomous Kurdistan region and the United Arab Emirates (UAE).
In statements published on its official news outlet Sepah News, the IRGC said its forces shot down a "hostile" U.S. MQ-9 Reaper drone and launched ballistic missiles toward Camp Titin in Jordan, reportedly killing "a large number of" U.S. troops and destroying several key facilities and combat helicopters.
The IRGC said its aerospace forces struck with ballistic missiles the hangars of U.S. RQ-4 Global Hawk and MQ-9 Reaper drones at the Prince Hassan Air Base in Jordan, destroying a number of the aircraft and setting the technical infrastructure facilities on fire.
It noted that its ground forces targeted with drones and missiles the headquarters and accommodation of the U.S. commander at the Ali Al Salem Air Base in Kuwait, setting on fire a hangar of U.S. drones and a drone deployment ramp and destroying several unmanned aerial vehicles.
Its ground forces also launched a hybrid missile-drone strike on U.S. bases in Erbil, capital of Iraq's Kurdistan region, destroying a maintenance center, technical-equipment warehouses, and a system for guiding espionage balloons, all belonging to the U.S. Army, the IRGC added.
In statements published on its website, Iran's Army said its drone attacks targeted U.S. bases in Bahrain and the UAE.
It said it struck with kamikaze drones U.S. troops and radar facilities at the Shaikh Isa Air Base in Bahrain as well as the Al Minhad and Al Dhafra Air Bases in the UAE.
In a statement carried by Iranian media earlier in the day, Iran's main military command, Khatam al-Anbiya Central Headquarters, warned that continued U.S. "malicious" acts in the region would draw "heavier, more extensive and more devastating" responses.

CAPE TOWN, Sept. 2 (Xinhua) -- South Africa could face its hottest year on record in 2027 amid an intensifying strong El Nino event, the South African Weather Service (SAWS) has said.
In a statement on Tuesday, SAWS said a strong El Nino had formed in the Pacific Ocean and was likely to intensify during the Southern Hemisphere spring.
"The latest predictions are indicative that the El Nino will likely intensify further to become the strongest event in living memory," it said.
The latest weekly averaged sea surface temperature anomalies in the eastern central tropical Pacific Ocean have already exceeded the threshold for a very strong El Nino, SAWS said.
A strong El Nino is defined as sea surface temperatures more than 1.5 degrees Celsius above normal, while a very strong event exceeds 2 degrees.
According to SAWS, current forecasts indicate that the anomaly could surpass 3 degrees Celsius.
"Most El Nino events bring conditions of below-normal rainfall and above-normal temperatures to the southern African region," SAWS said, while noting that not every El Nino event results in drought.
The weather service's October to December 2026 forecast indicates below-normal rainfall and above-normal temperatures over most of South Africa, with similar conditions expected from November 2026 to January 2027.
"It should be noted that the expected very strong El Nino of 2026/27, in combination with global warming, will likely result in 2027 being the warmest year ever recorded," it said.
SAWS said the 2015/16 El Nino brought unprecedented heatwaves to southern Africa and warned that, if the expected below-normal rainfall occurs, a high frequency of potentially severe heatwaves could accompany the current event.
The agency said uncertainty remained over the eventual strength and regional impacts of the El Nino and that it would closely monitor risks including heatwaves and water scarcity. ■
