World News in Brief: US-Iran war intensifies, aid for Myanmar, casualties in Ukraine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
12:00:00 UTC
21:00:00 KST

World News in Brief: US-Iran war intensifies, aid for Myanmar, casualties in Ukraine
Fighting between the United States and Iran has sharply escalated after a month-long lull, with the two sides exchanging strikes as fears grow over further civilian casualties.
The US military struck rocket launchers on an island in the Strait of Hormuz over the weekend, days after US President Donald Trump announced that American forces had cleared all mines from the crucial trade route.
The US said the weekend strikes were aimed at preventing Iran from laying new mines.
After Iranian missiles launched towards Jordan in retaliation were intercepted, the US struck targets it claims were linked to the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps.
According to Iranian authorities, US strikes hit a wedding party in Kuhestak on Wednesday, killing at least four and injuring 68 more.
The US military said it is investigating the incident and that it never targets civilians.
The latest exchange marks a major escalation in the conflict that began in February, when the US and Israel launched military operations against Iran.
Condemnation from Guterres
UN Secretary-General António Guterres expressed grave concern over the escalation and reported rise in civilian casualties, including at the wedding party.
“The Secretary-General condemns all attacks against civilians,” UN Spokesperson Stéphane Dujarric said.
“He recalls that all parties must respect their obligations under international humanitarian law, including the principles of distinction, proportionality and precautions.”
Mr. Guterres strongly encouraged the US and Iran to return to diplomacy to avoid the “devastating consequences” further escalation would have on civilians across the Middle East.
UN launches aid transport service in Myanmar
The UN’s World Food Programme (WFP) has launched an emergency cargo transport service to help humanitarian partners in Myanmar deliver lifesaving assistance to flood-stricken areas.
The logistics service – free for UN partners to use – is initially focusing on the towns of Lemyethna, Yegyi and Ngathaingchaung, which have been hit hard by floods in the past few months that have displaced thousands of families.
“When floodwaters isolate entire communities, logistics becomes the difference between success and failure of an operation,” WFP Myanmar Country Director Michael Dunford said.
“Beyond delivering our own food assistance, WFP is serving as the logistics provider for the wider humanitarian response.”
Collective effort
For at least two weeks, WFP will transport food and nutrition assistance; water, sanitation and hygiene supplies; medicines; and emergency shelter materials to civilians in hard-to-reach areas.
“By opening our transport lines to our partners, we can collectively ensure that food, medicine, and shelter materials swiftly and safely reach those who need them most,” Mr. Dunford said.
WFP has also launched an emergency food response in Myanmar’s Sagaing Region, which was hit especially hard by an earthquake earlier this year and already faces conflict, widespread restrictions to access and connectivity challenges.
The agency has already reached 15,000 people with emergency rations in the Ayeyarwady and Sagaing regions.
Russian attacks kill more civilians in Ukraine
Russian attacks on Ukraine between Tuesday and Wednesday morning killed at least 12 civilians and injured more than 65 others, causing casualties across six regions, according to the UN’s humanitarian aid office (OCHA).
The attacks damaged homes, schools, a shopping centre and a postal hub. Strikes on energy facilities caused power outages in several regions.
Power generation equipment at a utility plant in Kherson was destroyed, raising fears that families unable to move to safer regions could lack heat and electricity in the coming winter.
“This escalation inflicts a devastating and growing toll on civilians by destroying livelihoods, worsening the psychological burden and disrupting daily life,” said Matthias Schmale, the UN’s humanitarian coordinator in Ukraine. “We must never normalise this.”
Meanwhile, German officials have accused Russia of authorising an attempted explosive drone attack at Leipzig Airport on 4 August. Russian officials have denied any involvement.
Humanitarian facilities destroyed
A humanitarian warehouse contracted by the UN Children’s Fund (UNICEF) was destroyed in a Russian attack on 27 August in Chubynske, Kyiv region, destroying lifesaving supplies intended for children and families.
“This impedes the delivery of vital support to the most vulnerable, especially as another harsh winter approaches,” UNICEF said.
In recent days, a missile strike also destroyed the humanitarian warehouses and vehicles of a UN-partnered NGO in Sumy, and another strike damaged an NGO-operated evacuation bus in Donetsk.
These attacks are part of a wider pattern of Russian strikes. At least six warehouses belonging to humanitarian organizations – including UN agencies, the Ukrainian Red Cross Society and NGOs – were impacted by Russian attacks in August.
“Our partners continue to provide medical and psychological aid, hot meals and shelter materials to support the humanitarian response,” Mr. Dujarric said.

A humanitarian warehouse contracted by the UN Children’s Fund (UNICEF) was destroyed in a Russian attack on 27 August in Chubynske, Kyiv region, destroying lifesaving supplies intended for children and families.
“This impedes the delivery of vital support to the most vulnerable, especially as another harsh winter approaches,” UNICEF said.
In recent days, a missile strike also destroyed the humanitarian warehouses and vehicles of a UN-partnered NGO in Sumy, and another strike damaged an NGO-operated evacuation bus in Donetsk.
These attacks are part of a wider pattern of Russian strikes. At least six warehouses belonging to humanitarian organizations – including UN agencies, the Ukrainian Red Cross Society and NGOs – were impacted by Russian attacks in August.
“Our partners continue to provide medical and psychological aid, hot meals and shelter materials to support the humanitarian response,” Mr. Dujarric said.

20:56:00 KST

Iran has accused the US of a war crime after a missile blast killed at least four people and injured 68 who were attending a wedding at a private home in a coastal city of southern Iran, as the fresh exchange of strikes prompted fears of a wider renewal of hostilities.
Iranian media said that the wedding ceremony was being held in a home in the city of Kuhestak, Hormozgan province, late on Tuesday when a US missile struck, with shrapnel and debris from the strike killing and injuring people.
Among the dead was a four-year-old child, Amir-Ali Karimi, and a 16-year-old, Mohammad Mollahi.
“It’s a terrible thing. I’m extremely worried and upset about what happened – really upset,” Ali Mollahi, the father of the bride, told Mehr News.
A video of the aftermath shows colourful wedding streamers and decorations strewn across the ground, and shoes abandoned in the rush to escape the attack.
“You wicked people have attacked people’s homes and turned their wedding ceremony into a funeral,” said a man filming the aftermath of the strike, shared by Fars news agency.
The deputy of the provincial government, Ahmad Nafisi, said first responders had headed immediately to the scene and transferred the wounded to the hospitals.
Iran’s foreign ministry spokesperson called the US attack a “war crime” and said Iran “will respond to these savage crimes with firmness”.
The chief Iranian negotiator, Mohammad Baqer Ghalibaf, said the attack had killed families with children, and called the US the “great Satan”.
“If a power acts like Satan, picks targets like Satan and kills like Satan, it’s Satan. Shields a junior Satan that does the same? It’s THE Great Satan,” Ghalibaf said in a post on X.
The US attacks followed strikes on Sunday, ending a month-long uneasy truce between the US and Iran, and appeared to signal a resumption of another cycle of escalation. US Central Command (Centcom) said the overnight strikes focused on Iranian military targets, including air defence sites, radars and maritime assets.
Iran responded by launching drones and missiles on US bases across the Middle East, including in Bahrain, Kuwait and the UAE. Iran’s military spokesperson, Lt Col Ebrahim Zolfaghari, vowed “heavier, broader, and more crushing and devastating” retaliation.
Videos of the aftermath of the strike show a caved-in roof, blown-out windows and ground riddled with debris, as well as walls pockmarked with what appeared to be holes from shrapnel. Footage from a nearby hospital showed women in wedding attire watching as injured children were being treated.
“When we arrived there, an explosion occurred. It was very intense. Bricks, stones and cement hit me in the face and head, and many others were injured,” a child who was injured at the wedding told the state-affiliated Fars news agency.
A woman with her hands decorated in henna for the nuptials posted a video on Instagram after the attack, saying “my hands and feet are still shaking”.
A spokesperson for Centcom, Tim Hawkins, said the US was aware of reports of civilian casualties, but the “US military never targets civilians, unlike the [Iranian Revolutionary Guards Corps]”.
In February, a strike on an elementary school killed at least 156 people, including more than 120 schoolchildren. Independent investigations concluded that the US likely carried out the strike with the assistance of AI, though the US government said the incident remained under investigation.
Pictures of shrapnel collected at the site of Tuesday’s attack were published on Iranian state media, and appeared to show the internal components of US munitions. Trevor Ball, an independent weapons analyst, identified some of the remnants as belonging to the Standoff Land Attack Missile-Expanded Response (Slam-Er) missile, which is made by the US weapons company Boeing. The Slam-Er is a 1,500-pound, GPS-guided missile touted by Boeing to be “extremely accurate”.
It was unclear if the home where the wedding was being held was struck directly, or if a missile hit close to the home and debris from the strike hit the home and its occupants. CCTV footage captured at least six strikes in the area within a minute. A separate strike appeared to hit a communications tower about 150 metres away from the home.
Authorities said that several “telecommunications and internet towers and sites were also seriously damaged in the latest strikes”.
The US has been targeting communications and radar infrastructure along Iran’s coast to try to stop its blockade on the strait of Hormuz, a chokepoint which prior to the US-Iran war was a transit point for at least 20% of the world’s oil supply.
Iran has virtually closed the strait since the start of the Iran war, frustrating the US president, Donald Trump, who is facing a midterm election with expensive gas prices and knock-on inflation across the board.
In recent weeks, the US has focused on trying to degrade Iran’s capacity to strike ships transiting the strait to reopen the waterway for traffic.

From infrastructure to military drills, China deepens footprint in Egypt as Xi visits Cairo
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
11:53:49 UTC
20:53:49 KST

Chinese President Xi Jinping’s return to Cairo comes as Egypt and China push their relationship beyond infrastructure and trade into technology, defence and a broader strategic partnership with regional implications.
Chinese President Xi Jinping arrived in Egypt on Tuesday for his first visit since 2016, as the two countries mark 70 years of diplomatic ties and push their relationship into new areas in what Beijing has described as a "comprehensive strategic partnership".
Since his last visit, some of Beijing's megaprojects have become part of Egypt’s landscape.
Chinese companies have helped build the central business district of Egypt’s New Administrative Capital. Built by China State Construction Engineering Corporation, it consists of 20 skyscrapers.
At its centre stands the 385.8-metre Iconic Tower, Africa's tallest building.
A light rail system built with Chinese involvement connects Cairo’s eastern outskirts with new urban centres, and a China-Egypt industrial zone near the Suez Canal now hosts more than 200 companies.
The industrial zone created more than 10,000 direct jobs, according to Chinese figures. Chinese reporting puts total investment at more than $4.7 billion (€4.05bn).
The scope is now widening.
AI, advanced manufacturing and technology transfer are increasingly part of the economic agenda, while Chinese and Egyptian fighter aircraft have been training together in the second joint air force exercise between the two countries.
Trade grows, but so does the imbalance
Bilateral trade reached $11.3 billion (€9.75bn) in the first six months of 2026, up 21.5% year on year, according to Egypt's Central Agency for Public Mobilisation and Statistics.
Egyptian exports to China almost tripled to $840.8 million (€725.4m), driven by fuel, mineral oil, fruit, vegetables and cotton.
But imports from China reached $10.4 billion (€8.97bn) over the same period — machinery and electrical equipment alone accounting for $4.1 billion (€3.5bn), followed by vehicles, iron and steel, plastics and chemicals.
Egypt wants Chinese investment and technology, but also wants more Chinese companies to manufacture inside Egypt and greater access for Egyptian goods to the Chinese market.
A five-year programme agreed for 2024-2028 calls for local production and technology transfer in electric vehicles, electronics, solar panels, chemicals and modern agricultural technology, with artificial intelligence also listed as a priority.
El-Sisi said ahead of the visit that Egypt wanted to attract Chinese investment in EVs, battery storage, renewable energy and shipbuilding, while expanding technology transfer in telecommunications, AI and space sciences.
Military ties move into view
Defence links are also becoming more visible. China and Egypt are holding the second edition of their Eagles of Civilisation joint air force exercise, running from mid-August into early September at Egyptian air bases. The first was held only last year.
Chinese officials said the 2026 drills would include air combat tactics, air superiority operations, combat search and rescue and joint force deployment.
The US remains Cairo's key longstanding security partner, providing large-scale military assistance and supplying a significant part of Egypt's diversely sourced military equipment.
Washington has not publicly commented on the Chinese exercises. The Pentagon has previously flagged concerns about Chinese military engagement with US partners across the Middle East and Africa.
The exercises fit Egypt's wider policy of diversifying its defence partnerships, a deliberate balancing act that also encompasses its involvement in BRICS, the New Development Bank and the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation alongside continued reliance on Western economic and security support.
Next phase of relations crucial
Ahead of the visit, Xi described the country as an important link between the Arab world and Africa and called for deeper China-Arab and China-Africa cooperation through Egypt.
For China, Egypt combines a market of more than 100 million people with a strategic position on the Suez Canal and political weight across the Arab world and Africa.
The two governments have also taken similar positions on several regional issues, including support for a Palestinian state, while Egypt maintains its One China policy.
Egypt was the first Arab and African country to establish diplomatic relations with the People's Republic of China in 1956.
El-Sisi has travelled to China eight times since taking office in 2014, most recently in May 2024.
The agreements announced during Xi's visit are expected to provide more detail on newer areas of cooperation, particularly technology transfer and advanced manufacturing, where Egypt has pushed hardest to move beyond the construction and infrastructure model that defined the relationship's first decade.

The president said the state and all other relevant bodies are running the process with care in a bid not to give any room for those who want to ruin it.

‘Not democratically elected’: SC says Manan Kumar Mishra only ‘pro tem’ BCI chairman till fresh election
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
11:51:35 UTC
20:51:35 KST

BCI chief Manan Kumar Mishra only ‘pro tem’ till fresh election, Supreme Court says
NEW DELHI: The Supreme Court on Wednesday said Bar Council of India (BCI) chairperson Manan Kumar Mishra was only a “pro tem Chairman” until a freshly constituted BCI elects its office-bearers, and directed that major policy decisions be taken in consultation with the Attorney General for India and the Solicitor General, who are permanent ex-officio BCI members.A bench headed by Chief Justice Surya Kant and comprising Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana said Mishra could oversee the BCI's day-to-day functioning but could not be treated as a democratically elected office-bearer once the newly elected state bar councils complete the process of constituting a fresh BCI.
“You should also bear in mind that you are like a pro tem chairman till a fresh election of the Bar Council of India, pursuant to the elections already conducted in the state bar councils, takes place,” Justice Bagchi told senior advocate Guru Krishnakumar, appearing for the BCI chairman, according to LiveLaw.“So, it is not a situation where he is democratically elected and continues to be so. His term is co-terminus with the elections which are imminent,” the judge said.The court said the existing arrangement could continue for routine administrative work but stressed that institutional checks would apply to policy decisions.“In such situations, day-to-day functioning can be left to the existing arrangement. However, when a policy decision is taken, the participation of a permanent ex officio member acting independently, such as the Attorney General, is necessary,” Justice Bagchi remarked orally, PTI said.
The bench also said it was not endorsing Mishra's continued tenure.“We are not placing any stamp of approval upon the existing arrangement. It is apparent that the present chairperson can continue only until a fresh election to the Bar Council of India takes place pursuant to the state bar council elections already conducted,” it said.The observations came while the court heard pleas challenging Mishra's continued occupation of the BCI chairperson's post and the legal basis for extending his tenure until 2030.Senior advocate Madhavi Divan, appearing for the petitioners, said Mishra was unanimously elected chairman for a term from April 17, 2025 to April 16, 2030. She also challenged a resolution extending the tenure of the chairman and vice-chairman from three years to five years despite rules prescribing a two-year term.
Senior advocate Gopal Sankaranarayanan, appearing for one of the petitioners, questioned the creation of the Bar Council of India Trust for Promotion of Education, Legal and Professional Reforms and Improvement in Research.Sankaranarayanan alleged that its deed made 11 managing trustees “original and permanent trustees”. The bench questioned how elected members could appoint themselves as perpetual trustees.“The Bar Council of India is a juristic entity. That entity has created a trust from its assets through the elected members who constituted the Council. Can those elected members make themselves permanent trustees of those assets when the composition of the corporate entity that settled the trust is itself determined through elections?” it asked.The court directed the newly constituted state bar councils to elect their office-bearers and representatives to the BCI within three weeks of notification of their composition. The matter will be heard next on September 23.

US strikes wedding party in southern Iran: What we know so far
Iran accused the United States of striking a wedding gathering in the country’s south, killing five people, including a child, and injuring dozens more in an attack on a residential area near the Strait of Hormuz in Kuhestak, in Sirik county of Hormozgan province, on Tuesday night.
The Red Crescent said shrapnel from a US missile struck the residential property, killing five people and injuring more than 50. Six-year-old Amir Mohammad Karimi was among those killed, it said, adding that those wounded had been transferred to hospital in the nearby city of Minab.
Earlier, Reza Shahidiyan, the governor of Sirik county, told the IRIB state broadcaster that 63 people had been injured, including 50 women and children. Other Iranian reporting has cited as many as 68 wounded.
Videos circulated by Iranian rescue workers showed debris scattered across the site and extensive damage to several buildings, including blown-out walls and windows. Another video posted by the Red Crescent showed a large whole on the roof of a residential building, supposedly from the site of the impact.
Kuhestak lies in Sirik county, on Iran’s southern coast along the strategic Strait of Hormuz, through which roughly a fifth of global seaborne oil trade passes. The attack came during a large new wave of US strikes across Iran, following more than a month without a direct exchange of fire between Washington and Tehran.
US Central Command (CENTCOM) said its forces had launched strikes against targets linked to Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, citing what it called recent attempted attacks on commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz and on US personnel in the region.
But Washington has not publicly identified the precise target near the wedding site, disclosed the weapon used, or explained how a missile strike came to send lethal shrapnel into a home packed with civilians celebrating a wedding. Earlier reports suggested a telecommunications tower in the Kuhestak area may have been among the targets.
US response
The US did not deny carrying out strikes in the area. Asked about reports of civilian casualties, CENTCOM spokesperson Capt. Tim Hawkins said: "We’re aware of the reports, which originated from Iranian state media," claiming that "The US military never targets civilians, unlike the IRGC."
The statement does not address whether the strike hit a civilian residence, whether US planners knew a wedding was under way, whether the house was within the expected blast radius of an intended target, or whether CENTCOM is investigating the deaths and injuries reported by emergency workers and local officials.
The US assertion that it does not target civilians sits uneasily alongside mounting reports of civilian harm from its campaign in Iran. On 28 February, a strike on a girls’ school in Minab, also in Hormozgan province, killed more than 150 people, most of them children, according to Iranian authorities and rights groups.
Washington has yet to publicly accept responsibility or release a final account of that attack. However, a preliminary US military assessment concluded that US forces were likely responsible and that the school was not the intended target. The reported explanation was that outdated intelligence had wrongly classified the site, or the surrounding area, as associated with an Iranian military installation.
Iranian condemnation
Iranian officials condemned the Sirik attack as an assault on civilians and said the country would respond.
Foreign ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei said Tehran would respond "with firmness", while Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, Iran’s top negotiator and parliamentary speaker, described the United States as the "Great Satan" and linked the wedding deaths to what he called a broader pattern of US attacks on civilians.
The head of the Iranian Red Crescent Society sent a letter to the Prosecutor of the International Criminal Court on Wednesday regarding the wedding attack, assuring prosecutors that the organisation was documenting the effects of the attack in order to "collect and record (them) for follow-up through legal and international channels," calling for an independent investigation into Tuesday's deadly incident.
Iranian officials also said electricity and telephone services had been disrupted in the area, amid reports that US strikes had targeted telecommunications infrastructure in Hormozgan province. Restoration work was under way, according to Iran’s health ministry.
The strike was followed by Iranian missile and drone attacks directed towards US-linked targets and allies across the region, including Bahrain, Kuwait, the United Arab Emirates and Jordan. The exchange marked one of the sharpest escalations in weeks in the six-month conflict.

20:48:48 KST

At Pattaya’s Hard Rock Cafe and hotel, the city’s mayor and police officials, along with women in traditional Thai dress, waited to greet the sailors who were arriving in civilian clothes, bags slung over their shoulders, off the buses.
The USS Abraham Lincoln’s crew of 5,000 had not been on shore for nearly nine months, a record-setting uninterrupted time at sea.
Crew appeared to have been told not to speak to the gathered journalists about the reportedly deteriorating living conditions onboard but said they were looking forward to being on dry land, sleeping and going home.
One sailor, Breese, who did not want to give his surname, said “it’s a fever dream right now” and he was looking forward to trying Thai food for the first time and meeting new people.
Once a quiet fishing village, Pattaya was transformed during the Vietnam war into one of the most infamous red light districts in the world with the arrival of American troops using military bases in Thailand.
At its peak, tens of thousands of US military personnel came through each year, said Pipatpong Fakfare, an associate professor specialising in tourism at Bangkok University. “In my opinion, it’s really the founding influence for the town. The US military turned a quiet fishing village into a global destination for an international nightlife and entertainment hub in about 15 years,” he said.
Although the American troops left by the mid-70s, the sex industry infrastructure continued to grow, with European tourists taking their place, and more recently waves of Chinese and Russian visitors, Pipatpong said.
The Hard Rock hotel is around the corner from the Soi 6 alley, known for its go-go bars, one of the many areas that contribute to Pattaya’s sex tourism industry. Soi 6 and the neighbouring area would be off-limits for crew after sunset, said Pattaya’s mayor, Poramet Ngampichet.
However, Walking Street, the town’s other entertainment and red light district, was displaying a massive neon sign at its entrance saying: “Pattaya City is pleased to welcome USS Abraham Lincoln carrier and its personnel.”
The sailors were being released in staggered groups, so not everyone was out. Shakeira Fairfax, who had travelled all the way from New Jersey, had to wait one more day to be reunited with her sailor daughter, Jada Fairfax.
Fairfax said she was mostly excited. “I just want to pick her up and spin her around. She’s my baby always,” but, she said, “I don’t know who I’m welcoming home.”
Jada finished her basic training last October and was shipped out a month later, two months before the US and Israel launched their war on Iran. Jada celebrated her 25th birthday onboard in June.
Fairfax said there was an “abrupt” stop to communication when the war broke out, but she had since been able to check in with her intermittently and send care packages.
The ship’s captain, Dan Keeler, acknowledged to the media that the carrier “looks like a dirty car in a parking lot”. As for the reports of the conditions onboard, he said: “I don’t know how to say it other than there’s a disconnect between reporting back home and what’s happening on the ship.”
Keeler added: “First-time sailors are going to complain about the food, the living conditions, similar to sending kids off to college for the first time. We did get caught up in an election cycle and got thrown around like a football.”
Keeler said there was plenty of food on the ship but admitted it became hard to get fresh fruit and vegetables, which stopped being served. “I am looking forward to a fresh salad.” They also had to be careful with supplies of soap and toothpaste to ensure every sailor could receive some, he added.
Asked about the reports of attempted suicides onboard the ship, Keeler did not answer, saying there was an open investigation. As for comments from Donald Trump, which included claims that the 270-day deployment was “not nearly long enough”, Keeler told the Guardian: “The president speaks for himself.”
Crew from the USS Higgins also arrived at the Hard Rock hotel. When asked about the conditions onboard the two vessels, Ethan Johnson, a cook on the Higgins, said: “We joined the military, it’s not a cruise ship.”
Johnson said there was plenty of meat and vegetables onboard the Higgins.
As well as being prohibited from entering certain areas, sailors are also being prevented from doing any water sports in the area, owing to the potential danger.
They will also not be allowed to visit pharmacies as Thai authorities do not want sailors accessing medicines that do not require a prescription in Thailand but may need a prescription in the US, Poramet said.
Kristopher Robinson, a naval attache with the US embassy, said Pattaya was chosen as the destination for rest and relaxation because the “people of Thailand have a history of being wonderful hosts not just to US sailors but people from all around”.
Robinson said the crew would take as much opportunity for rest as possible and conduct themselves in accordance with US and local laws. “Sailors here, like all tourists, they’re going to enjoy Pattaya’s great food and wonderful culture,” he said.

The Book of Damascus: Stories from a city haunted by its past
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
11:48:46 UTC
20:48:46 KST

Breadcrumb
The Book of Damascus: A journey through a city transformed by war, repression and exile
One of the functions of literature is to capture historical moments from the inside, to describe their social and experiential reality rather than merely listing the external facts. That function is admirably performed by The Book of Damascus – the latest in Comma Press's excellent Reading the City series.
Khaled Khalifa, the greatest Syrian novelist of his generation and a fixture of Damascus literary life, wrote the Preface: "It is true we live in a forsaken land, afraid of the future and the past, afraid of being arrested and 'disappeared', afraid of all forms of annihilation."
Khaled wrote those words – and the contributors wrote their stories – before the collapse of the Assad regime after 14 years of war and more than half a century of tyranny.
His point about annihilation and disappearance still holds, given that sectarian massacres and detentions without due process continue to characterise Syrian political life, albeit on a smaller scale than before.
It's also still true that Damascus is "a city that lives on invisible layers of endless sorrow." But it's no longer true that "What exists today is merely a remnant of a country waiting to breathe its last so it can be buried." That country no longer exists. It was buried on 8 December 2024, when militiamen trained in Idlib arrived in the capital, when the prison gates opened, and when statues of Assad were toppled.
Khaled Khalifa also no longer exists. He died, aged only 59, on 30 September 2023, in the city he loved and refused to leave, whatever horrors it produced. He missed the liberation, the death of the old and the birth of a violently contested new world, with new winners and new victims, a new type of identity politics and a new authoritarianism, and new enthusiasms and possibilities too.
The stories here study that strange extended period when the Assad regime had already died but – its corpse propped up by foreign powers – refused to lie down. They record the city during that long limbo, expressing what it felt like to walk its streets and suffocate in its crushing fear.
Damascus, in this battered but not quite defeated state, is seen through a range of perspectives and filtered through a variety of genres.
Haseeb al-Zainy's The Blacklist is a Kafkaesque story from the depths of the counter-revolutionary war, when the city was characterised by "the sounds of military helicopters overhead, and patriotic songs glorifying the leader blasting" on "a breeze mingled with the smell of car exhausts, gunpowder and burnt corpses."
The narrator does his best to deal with a grotesquely lecherous intelligence officer, but the nightmarishly surreal situation refuses to be so easily dealt with.
In a very different way, The Seven-Gated Girl-Lady by Rasha Abbas recounts nightmares on the way to the shrine of Ruqqayah, stopping at each of the city’s seven gates, each one associated with a planet.
Omar al-Jbaai's brief, sad story In the First Hour of Traffic describes the end of a Damascene type, Mr Kaleh (Kaleh means ‘faded’), whose worn grey suit was purchased with a government voucher, and who won a prize in the 1980s for being "the most productive worker in the public sector."
Odai al-Zoubi's Bitter Hymns is narrated by characters entangled in adultery, deception, and sectarian prejudice. Fares al-Zahaby’s The Curse of Eid Eve, set in Rukn ed-Din, is a tale of haram money and generalised corruption.
Salwa Zakzak's Butterflies in the Sky of Damascus captures the war-ravaged, cannibalised city as experienced by some of its weakest, most overlooked inhabitants: those "silent, terrified girls, searching through rubbish for anything that can be sold or traded, or put to personal use, like childish joy."
There's no room for romanticism in this tale with its simultaneously grim and prosaic ending. Nor in Rawaa Sonbol's A Storyteller for Our Times, whose hero's attempt to supplement his income by reviving a Damascene tradition ends in humiliation and in a deadening and dangerous rather than creative and entertaining form of storytelling.
Some of the stories portray the city from a greater distance, as seen by provincials.
Zaher Omareen's What Only the Chickens and the Donkey Know, for instance, is the story of a conscript from "the open cemetery" of Hama who is first obliged to attend military camp at Dumayr, and then goes looking for debauched delights in Merjeh Square.
The undying tragedy of the 1982 Hama massacre overhangs this otherwise comic tale. In addition to being a contributor, Omareen is also the editor of this collection.
The eponymous Abu Hajal of Abu Hajal and the Magic Lamp is from Deir ez-Zor, but is residing in the capital's Adra Prison on a drug charge.
Abu Hajal’s brother Khalil, a poet, visits the city’s literary hang-outs, like the Rawda and Havana cafés, when he isn’t visiting lawyers and intermediaries on his brother's behalf.
Aboud Saeed, the author of this compact but wide-ranging story, became renowned for his irreverent, tragicomic Facebook updates during the revolution. His book, The Smartest Guy on Facebook, is highly recommended.
The city is seen from the distance of exile too, as so many have been forced to see it.
Alaa Rashidi's Marvellous Musical Memory offers the distanced Damascene a nostalgic tour of the city's musical spots, from the nightclubs of Rabweh to classical performances in Khan Asa'd Pasha, from Sufi chanting at Kaftarou's mosque to the protest songs of Abdul Baset Sarout, not forgetting the Hawasli pirated cassette shop on Sharia al-Hamra.
The narrator once composed his own 'Ultimate Song of Romance and Social Justice', he tells us, his own 'Grand Unification of World Scales', and his own 'Definitive Spirituality-Sensuality Mix'.
He wished to "reconcile" his "completely contradictory tastes in music" but – and this becomes a refrain – "I was displaced," and so "I lost all of my recordings." There’s a powerful metaphor at work here.
In general, there's a lot of power packed into the slim volume of The Book of Damascus, a worthy addition to Comma Press's excellent series, which includes The Book of Cairo, The Book of Khartoum, and The Book of Gaza, among others.
My only complaint is the absence of stories set in the suburbs, in places like Harasta, Muadamiya and Jaramana, that have either been reduced to rubble or crammed with people displaced from elsewhere. But this is less a criticism than a call for another collection of stories – The Book of the Damascus Countryside, perhaps.
Robin Yassin-Kassab co-wrote Burning Country: Syrians in Revolution and War and is the English editor at the ISIS Prisons Museum. His latest book is The Blood Between Us: Syria After the Fall of Assad
Follow him on X: @qunfuz2

SINGAPORE, Sept. 2 (Xinhua) -- Singapore's economy is expected to grow 5 percent this year, up from the 3.5 percent forecast in the previous survey, with most sectors receiving upgrades, according to the Monetary Authority of Singapore's latest survey of professional forecasters released on Wednesday.
The most likely outcome is for the Singapore economy to grow by 5 percent to 5.4 percent, with an average probability of 37 percent, the survey showed.
The most frequently cited downside risks were an escalation or prolonged conflict in the Middle East and a bursting of the artificial intelligence (AI) bubble, which could trigger spillovers to financial markets.
On the upside, all respondents identified a sustained AI-driven upturn in the technology cycle as a key support for Singapore's economic outlook. Other upside risks included a de-escalation or resolution of the Middle East conflict and stronger-than-expected global growth.
Singapore's economy expanded 5.9 percent year-on-year in the second quarter of 2026, significantly exceeding the respondents' median forecast of 4.3 percent in the previous survey.
For the third quarter, respondents expect gross domestic product growth to moderate to 4.6 percent year-on-year. The median forecast for Singapore's economic growth in 2027 is 3.1 percent. ■

Economic Watch: Strong earnings of listed firms show resilience of Chinese economy
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
19:45:53 CST
20:45:53 KST

BEIJING, Sept. 2 (Xinhua) -- Listed companies in China reported a combined net profit of 3.58 trillion yuan (about 527.95 billion U.S. dollars) in the first half (H1) of 2026, up 19.5 percent year on year, according to a report by the China Association for Public Companies (CAPCO).
With the H1 figure surpassing 3.5 trillion yuan for the first time, the improving profitability of these companies, as the micro-level embodiment of the real economy, offers direct evidence of the resilience and vitality of the world's second-largest economy.
About three quarters of the 5,557 companies that had published H1 reports remained profitable. Growth also accelerated through the period, with second-quarter revenue and net profit both rising markedly faster than in the first quarter of 2026.
This earnings improvement mirrors the broader economic picture. Profits of China's industrial enterprises above the designated size rose 18.7 percent in the first half, while the overall economy expanded 4.7 percent during this period.
The recovery is structurally driven, with growth concentrated in new-economy sectors. Companies listed on the STAR Market, home to many of China's tech innovators, saw net profits soaring 4.4-fold year on year on revenue growth of nearly 40 percent, while those on the ChiNext board reported a 32.7-percent increase in net profits, with revenue up 22.3 percent. Private companies reported net profit growth of 29.6 percent in the first six months.
These gains were powered by hard-tech sectors, with net profits of integrated circuits growing 2.4-fold, according to the CAPCO report. The biopharmaceutical industry saw a net profit increase of 9.9 percent as domestically developed innovative drugs entered a commercialization window, and high-end equipment manufacturing reported revenue and net profit growth of 13.1 percent and 16.7 percent, respectively. More broadly, 10 of the 19 major industry categories reported simultaneous growth in both revenue and profit.
Behind these aggregate numbers are standout performers riding the artificial intelligence (AI) boom. CXMT, China's leading memory chip maker that listed on the STAR Market in July, reported H1 net profit of 77.6 billion yuan, recovering from a loss of 2.3 billion yuan a year earlier, with revenue surging 873.6 percent.
Foxconn Industrial Internet, a major AI server manufacturer, saw its net profit rise by 96 percent in H1. Zhongji Innolight, a leading optical module supplier with products essential to AI data centers, posted a net profit of 13.65 billion yuan, up 241.7 percent, while Cambricon, a homegrown AI chip designer, saw its net profit surge by 122.6 percent.
Gains extend beyond the tech sector. CATL, a world-leading electric vehicle battery maker, posted a net profit of 43.3 billion yuan in H1, up 42 percent. In the pharmaceutical sector, Zelgen Biopharmaceuticals reported an H1 net profit of 640 million yuan, its first profitable half-year, with revenue up 220.9 percent, as China's innovative drug industry matures.
The quality of earnings also improved. Research and development spending by listed companies totaled 847.3 billion yuan in the first half, up 3 percent year on year, with overall R&D intensity at 2.24 percent, according to the report. On the STAR Market, R&D intensity has exceeded 10 percent of revenue for several years.
Overseas revenue of 3,196 companies totaled 6.06 trillion yuan in H1, an increase of 22.9 percent, the CAPCO report noted, with 553 companies generating more than half of their revenue overseas.
The report also showed that 872 companies announced interim cash dividends totaling 740.3 billion yuan, while 1,051 companies planned share buybacks worth over 220 billion yuan, thus providing returns to investors.
Analysts expect this momentum to continue. Li Xunlei, chief economist at Zhongtai Financial International Limited, said the A-share market posted "steady revenue growth and notable earnings improvement" in H1, with corporate profitability rising steadily and business vitality being released.
He attributed this surge in profits across semiconductors, communications and electronics to the AI computing boom, a pattern he described as "one superpower with multiple strong players."
Stressing that the AI boom is "by no means a short-term bubble but a confirmation of a long-term industrial upgrade trend," with earnings spilling over from upstream to the broader real economy, Li forecast an increase of 12 to 15 percent in non-financial corporate earnings for the full year.
Ruan Xiaoqin, head of the policy research office at SWS Research, noted that A-share listed companies saw growth in both revenue and net profits, presenting a sound picture of overall recovery, structural improvement and renewed growth momentum. "Structural improvement was another keyword, with profit, industrial and market value structures all upgraded," she said.
She also said that non-financial manufacturing and hard-tech growth industries have become the main contributors to profit growth, adding that large-cap companies on the main board remain broadly stable, and that many small and mid-cap companies on the STAR Market and ChiNext have demonstrated growth potential.
Looking ahead, she said that with growth-stabilizing policies being implemented and domestic demand steadily recovering, the economy remains resilient and A-share earnings are expected to keep improving. ■

China Focus: Retired American teacher weaves new thread in China-U.S. friendship tapestry
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
19:45:45 CST
20:45:45 KST

BEIJING, Sept. 2 (Xinhua) -- "Stories never end."
At a Beijing airport on Tuesday, retired American teacher Ronald Sakolsky embraced his longtime Chinese friend Yin Yuzhen, a pioneering desertification fighter, before boarding a flight home. Both were in tears.
Twenty-six years earlier, Sakolsky had supported Yin with her efforts to turn the sands of Inner Mongolia green. Upon his return this time, he found not only trees stretching across the dunes, but also a friendship that had quietly endured across the decades.
A NEW SAPLING, 26 YEARS ON
The long-awaited reunion took them back to the very place where Sakolsky and Yin's friendship first took root -- the Maowusu Sandy Land.
Back in 1999, Sakolsky was teaching in China when he caught a television report about Yin and her tireless efforts to plant trees in the sandy land. Moved by her determination, he contacted more than a dozen organizations across the United States and eventually raised 5,000 U.S. dollars to support her cause. Yin used the money to buy more than 50,000 saplings and plant them in the sand.
When Sakolsky first set foot on this patch of sand in north China's Inner Mongolia Autonomous Region in 2000, the saplings were so fragile that he doubted they would survive. "This is impossible," he had told Yin then.
Yet on Aug. 24, 2026, as Sakolsky visited the Maowusu again, rows of poplar, pine and cypress rose from the dunes as far as the eye could see. The barren sands he remembered had become an ecological oasis.
Walking towards a poplar he had planted with Yin 26 years ago, Sakolsky couldn't believe his eyes. "That tree? Oh, my goodness. When I planted this tree, I never expected it would grow this tall."
Later, in front of the forest, they planted a new sapling together. "Plant a Tree of Friendship in Inner Mongolia," read a sign nearby. Sakolsky signed his name on the sign while the sea of green behind them embraced the young tree. "It's like a newborn baby," he said.
So far, including the trees funded by Sakolsky's efforts, Yin and her family have planted trees across 70,000 mu, an area roughly the size of 6,500 standard soccer pitches. Poplars, oriental arborvitaes, spruce and Mongolian Scots pines now rustle in the wind as birds chirp.
Official figures show that about 85 percent of the Maowusu has been restored. Between 2021 and 2025, China accounted for roughly one-quarter of the world's increase in green vegetation and rehabilitated approximately 152 million mu (over 10 million hectares) of sandified land.
RETURN TO THE CLASSROOM
Sakolsky's kindness in planting green was but one chapter of his time in the country. His real stage, back then, was the classroom of a school in central China's Henan province.
On Aug. 29, he returned to Luoyang Foreign Language Junior Middle School. On a classroom blackboard were the words: "Welcome home, S." Seeing his former students before him, Sakolsky's eyes welled up. He pointed to the "NEVER" printed across his T-shirt and said, "I have never forgotten you."
In 1999, during a one-year teaching exchange program, Sakolsky first came to this school. Some of his former students have since become teachers themselves.
"A teacher teaches a student, the student becomes a teacher, and more people learn education," he said. "In this unit I plant a seed, it becomes a tree, more trees become a forest."
Over the years, through the program, more than 300 Chinese teachers have traveled to the United States to teach in primary and secondary schools. Meanwhile, over 100 U.S. educators have come to China for teaching exchanges.
At a China-U.S. teacher exchange event on Monday in Beijing, Sakolsky met representatives from both sides of the program.
Zhou Xiangli, a teacher from Peking Academy High School, remembered staying with Sakolsky's family during her U.S. exchange. "They welcomed me without reservation and called me their 'fifth daughter,'" she said.
With Sakolsky's support, she visited more than 20 local schools during her time in the U.S., sharing a real, multi-dimensional picture of China with American children.
These exchanges, small as they may seem, are part of a much larger story. They have added another thread to the long history of goodwill between the people of China and the United States -- from the American volunteer pilots who fought alongside Chinese forces during World War II to the historic visit of a U.S. table tennis team to China in 1971 and, more recently, the Philadelphia Orchestra's decades of performances in the country.
"The Chinese people opened their arms to me," Sakolsky said. "What ties us all together is the love they have given me." ■

Asia diversifies beyond dollar as digital finance expands: AMRO
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
19:45:32 CST
20:45:32 KST

SINGAPORE, Sept. 2 (Xinhua) -- Asia's economies are gradually reducing their reliance on the U.S. dollar for regional trade and finance as geopolitical fragmentation and digital innovation accelerate the shift towards local currencies and alternative payment networks, according to the ASEAN+3 Macroeconomic Research Office (AMRO).
Local currency settlement arrangements and digital payment platforms will assume a larger role in trade and supply-chain integration, AMRO said in a commentary on Wednesday.
It noted that events ranging from the tariffs imposed by the U.S. administration to conflict in the Middle East have driven the switches.
"When uncertainty originates elsewhere, investors seek safety in dollar-denominated assets. But when questions arise about the stability or predictability of U.S. policies and institutions, concerns inevitably emerge about the dollar's reliability as the anchor of the international monetary system," it said.
It sees that greater use of local currencies in intra-regional trade could further reduce currency mismatches and lessen Asian economies' exposure to U.S. monetary policy. ■

Heatwaves, drought to shave 0.1 percentage point off French GDP growth in 2026
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
19:45:18 CST
20:45:18 KST

PARIS, Sept. 2 (Xinhua) -- Heatwaves and drought in France are expected to shave 0.1 percentage point off France's gross domestic product (GDP) growth in 2026 due to lower agricultural production, France's Ministry of Economy and Finance said Wednesday.
The estimate was presented by the French Treasury within the ministry during a hearing at the National Assembly on Wednesday as part of an information mission examining the economic cost of heatwaves.
According to preliminary data, the 2026 heatwaves and drought "have considerably affected certain agricultural production," particularly corn, with output expected to fall by 35 percent in 2026 from 2025, the ministry said.
The impact of heatwaves on agriculture has been compounded by the conflict in the Middle East, which has affected the agricultural sector through higher gas prices that have increased the cost of nitrogen fertilizers, as well as disruptions to global fertilizer trade, the ministry said.
Meanwhile, France's GDP growth was revised down to zero quarter-on- quarter in the second quarter of 2026, from a preliminary estimate of 0.2-percent growth, according to revised data released last Friday by France's National Institute of Statistics and Economic Studies (INSEE).
INSEE said the revision reflected a further deterioration in agricultural production, compared with the information available at the end of July.
At a crisis meeting devoted to drought on Aug. 12, French Minister for Ecological Transition Monique Barbut said this summer's heatwaves could cost the French economy between 10 billion and 15 billion euros (11.6 billion to 17.5 billion U.S. dollars). ■

China cracks down on AI misuse, removes 5.6 million pieces of unlawful, rule-violating content
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
19:45:11 CST
20:45:11 KST

BEIJING, Sept. 2 (Xinhua) -- Cyberspace authorities across China have removed more than 5.61 million pieces of unlawful or rule-violating content and taken action against over 49,000 accounts as part of a nationwide campaign targeting misuse of artificial intelligence tools.
The campaign against irregularities in AI applications has also dealt with more than 2,400 websites and apps found in violation of the rules, according to the Cyberspace Administration of China (CAC).
It is targeting the fabrication and spread of false information using AI, the production of violent or vulgar content, AI-enabled impersonation of real people, and content that infringes on the rights of minors.
The latest move comes as China continues to refine its regulatory framework for generative AI, following rules that took effect in August 2023 requiring providers of generative AI services to fulfill personal information protection obligations, and content-labeling regulations, effective from September 2025, that require AI-generated text, images, audio and video to carry visible or embedded identifiers.
Regional authorities have adopted differing enforcement approaches, the CAC said. In Beijing, authorities have directed platforms to upgrade content-review systems to better detect new variants of banned material, while Shanghai regulators have pushed platforms to conduct internal audits and issued public-facing materials explaining AI-related risks.
Major Chinese online platforms, including Douyin, Kuaishou, Weibo, Tencent, Baidu, Bilibili, Xiaohongshu, Zhihu, Douban and Taobao, have strengthened multimodal detection systems and expanded databases used to identify manipulated faces, cloned voices and known violation samples, according to the CAC.
AI chatbot and content-generation services, including ByteDance's Doubao, Tencent's Yuanbao, Alibaba's Qwen and Baidu's Ernie Bot, have tightened review of training and output content and stepped up compliance with the AI-labeling requirements, the regulator said. Smartphone app stores run by Huawei, Xiaomi, OPPO and Vivo have also introduced stricter vetting standards for app developers, including rechecking apps already listed on their platforms.
The CAC published examples of accounts and applications that had been penalized, including social media accounts using AI face- and voice-swapping tools to impersonate public figures, and websites and platforms hosting AI agents whose cover images, profile descriptions or generated dialogue contained sexually explicit material or other content harmful to minors.
The regulator said it would continue to monitor emerging risks tied to AI-generated content and take further steps to curb misuse of the technology, while stating a parallel goal of fostering healthy and orderly development of AI applications in China. ■

WFP releases July report on Iran
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
11:45:11 UTC
20:45:11 KST

WFP releases July report on Iran
TEHRAN – The World Food Program (WFP) has released a report, expounding on activities in Iran over the month of July.
In July, WFP food assistance reached 35,611 beneficiaries, including Afghan and Iraqi refugees, through a hybrid combination of in-kind food and cash-based transfers (CBT).
Refugees are assisted with a staple food basket, which includes fortified wheat flour (a ration of 9 kg per person, reduced from 12 Kg since the month of November 2025 due to funding shortfalls).
Under CBT modality, WFP continued to provide cash assistance to support the essential living costs of vulnerable refugees. The transfer is IRR 8 million (USD 5.3) for households headed by men and IRR 9 million (USD 6) for households headed by women.
Following the resolution in late July of technical issues caused by June 13 cyberattacks on Tejarat Bank, WFP financial service providers, June and July cash transfers were completed on July 21 and 22.
By July, WFP Iran helped ease the financial burden associated with the gluten-free dietary needs of 58 refugee celiac patients from WFP’s beneficiaries by providing them with an extra cash amount of IRR 9.7 million (USD 6.5) per person as a replacement for their usual food entitlement.
WFP supported 409 refugees with disabilities across eleven settlements, each receiving an additional monthly cash support of IRR 3 million (USD 2), on top of their regular aid. Initially launched in two provinces, the initiative was gradually expanded to cover 11 settlements in Saveh, Semnan, Bani Najar, Sarvestan, Bezileh, Abazar, Rafsanjan, Bardsir, Jahrom, Meybod, and Torbat-e-jam.
The school feeding program and education incentives are currently suspended due to summer holidays, and will resume with the start of the new academic year.
In July, WFP supported 29 income-generating projects in 18 settlements to improve economic resilience and self-sufficiency for 303 refugees, 38 percent of whom were women, and the remainder were youth. These activities included welding, tailoring, baking, farming, and other trades, providing opportunities for women and youth to develop practical skills, strengthen social connections, and actively engage with their communities.
In 2025, WFP sustained food assistance to some 33,300 vulnerable refugees living in 20 settlements across 13 provinces, including 404 refugees with disabilities (40 percent women) who received monthly cash top-ups. About 183 women and 190 men received WFP livelihood support.
WFP doubled cash transfer values since January 2025, safeguarding access to food amid price volatility and protecting the most vulnerable households.
Assistance remained uninterrupted, with targeted adjustments: wheat flour entitlements reduced from 12 kg to 9 kg (Nov-Dec) and school snacks paused (Oct-Dec) to stretch limited resources.
To promote girls’ education and reduce barriers to attendance, approximately 2,629 girl students received cash incentives as part of WFP’s commitment to empowering young women. Some 9,261 boys and girls and their teachers benefitted from WFP school snacks.
For more than four decades, the Islamic Republic of Iran has hosted Afghans fleeing conflict and hardship. In 2025, WFP remained essential to protecting the food security of vulnerable refugees residing in 20 settlements, where households rely on shelter, education and primary health care by the Government and other humanitarian actors, complemented by WFP’s monthly food assistance (through cash and in-kind modalities).
The program’s focus is on maintaining a dignified minimum basic needs while prioritizing those with the highest vulnerability, including households headed by women and persons with disabilities.
Operations are implemented in close collaboration and coordination with the Center for Alien and Foreign Immigrant Affairs (CAFIA), WFP’s primary governmental counterpart, and with International Non-Governmental Organizations (INGO) and UN agencies, mainly the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR), to ensure coherent refugee support and referral pathways.
Despite a complex year, marked by economic volatility and temporary operational risks, WFP sustained core assistance to settlement refugees. To safeguard purchasing power, WFP increased cash-based transfer values by 100 percent in January 2025 following the recommendation of a settlement-specific Minimum Expenditure Basket (MEB) assessment; this was complemented by a one-time cash top-up to cushion households during market instability and reduced income after the Iran-Israel 12-day conflict.
Targeted adjustments preserved program continuity: wheat flour entitlements were reduced from 12 kg to 9 kg per person for November-December, and the school snacks program was suspended for October to December.
These measures limit service disruptions while protecting life-saving transfers for the most vulnerable. Livelihood activities were scaled down given funding shortfalls and corporate efficiency measures, with WFP continuing to explore cost-effective, resilience-building options that can be re-activated as resources allow.
By December 2025, Iran continued to be one of the world’s largest refugee-hosting countries, sheltering approximately 2.5 million Afghans, including 773,000 individuals with official refugee status. Among them, around 35,000 critically vulnerable refugees reside in 20 settlements across 13 provinces.

Sanitation services, safe water restored in war-affected provinces
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
11:43:43 UTC
20:43:43 KST

Sanitation services, safe water restored in war-affected provinces
TEHRAN – The United Nations Children’s Fund (UNICEF), in cooperation with national and local authorities and partners, has supported the delivery of essential water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH) equipment and emergency supplies to nine provinces affected by the recently imposed US-Israeli war against the country.
The effort helps maintain and restore safe water and sanitation services in Sistan-Baluchestan, Hormozgan, Khuzestan, Bushehr, Kordestan, Lorestan, Fars, Markazi and Ilam provinces, UNICEF website announced in a press release in August.
The support is helping keep safe water flowing, restore disrupted services and manage wastewater safely for more than one million children and family members.
The supplies include 26 solar-powered water disinfection and chlorination systems to help keep drinking water safe during power disruptions, four portable water-quality monitoring sets, and 17 submersible sludge pumps for wastewater management.
A further 10 tonnes of calcium hypochlorite have been distributed for water disinfection. The equipment and supplies have reached affected areas.
Protecting access to safe water during emergencies
When conflict damages or disrupts water and sanitation systems, the consequences for children can be immediate. Reduced access to safe drinking water and functioning sanitation increases the risk of disease and can leave families without services they depend on every day.
Keeping water disinfected, monitoring its quality and ensuring wastewater systems continue to function are critical to protecting public health and preventing further disruption to essential services. Through the distributed equipment and supplies, UNICEF, together with national authorities and partners, is helping sustain essential WASH services for more than one million children and their family members, while strengthening the capacity to respond quickly when water and sanitation systems are damaged or disrupted.
Preparing to respond when services are disrupted
Keeping emergency WASH equipment and supplies ready for rapid deployment can help reduce delays when water and sanitation services are damaged or disrupted. UNICEF works closely with national partners to strengthen emergency preparedness and maintain critical supplies that can support water disinfection, water-quality monitoring and wastewater management during emergencies.
This preparedness helps ensure that critical WASH support can reach affected communities quickly, allowing UNICEF and its partners to help protect children’s and families’ access to safe water and sanitation when they need it most.
WASH FIT to help health facilities improve services
Funded by the Government of the Republic of Korea, UNICEF and the World Health Organization (WHO) are supporting the Ministry of Health and Medical Education to strengthen water, sanitation and hygiene services in health facilities nationwide.
The initiative supports introducing and institutionalizing the Water and Sanitation for Health Facility Improvement Tool, known as WASH FIT, across Iran’s health system. The tool helps health facilities identify risks and plan practical improvements in areas such as safe water, sanitation, hygiene, waste management, environmental cleaning, workforce, management, and energy and environment, UNICEF’s website announced in a press release on July 17.
Children and families across Iran will benefit from efforts to make health care facilities more resilient and hygienic and better equipped to prevent infections.
Building national capacity
The initiative began with a national workshop held in Tehran in October 2025, which brought together 40 environmental health experts from Universities of Medical Sciences from 25 provinces.
The workshop prepared participants to support health facilities in assessing their water, sanitation and hygiene conditions and identifying priority areas for improvement. It built on an earlier national assessment of health facilities and a roadmap developed by WHO to strengthen these essential services across the country.
Expanding training across the country
Following the national workshop, a series of provincial cascade training workshops has started from April 2026. Environmental health experts from hospitals and urban and rural health centers take part in the trainings.
Participants learn how to assess conditions in health facilities, identify risks, and prepare action plans based on the needs of each facility. These skills will help health workers improve hygiene standards, reduce the risk of infections, and provide safer services for patients, including children and mothers.
UNICEF and WHO are also working with the Ministry of Health and Medical Education to integrate WASH FIT into the national health system, ensuring its sustainable implementation and scale-up.
By strengthening the skills of health professionals and supporting a consistent approach across the country, the initiative aims to improve the quality and safety of health services for children, families, patients and health workers.

====================================================================================================

The US is gobbling up Venezuelan oil, but will it lower fuel prices?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
11:43:31 UTC
20:43:31 KST

The US is gobbling up Venezuelan oil, but will it lower fuel prices?
Analysts say Venezuelan crude is hard to extract and refine, and likely can’t replace oil supplies stuck in the Strait of Hormuz.
When United States President Donald Trump announced “the biggest oil deal in world history” with Venezuela on August 28, he claimed it would “more than double” US oil reserves and “substantially lower gas prices for all Americans”.
Venezuela is home to the world’s largest proven oil reserves – an estimated 303 billion barrels, or about 17 percent of the global total, according to the US Energy Information Administration. But the country’s oil is heavy, sour crude and extracting and refining it is costly.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Venezuela’s Maduro shares first photos from US detention
- list 2 of 3Vance says Trump ‘sending a message’ to Iran with AI-generated video
- list 3 of 3White House unveils more details of Trump’s Venezuela oil deal
While US Gulf Coast refineries are able to process this type of oil from Venezuela, analysts have warned that, in reality, Washington’s deal with Caracas will not lower crude prices in the US in the near term.
What is in the US-Venezuela oil deal, and will it lower fuel prices in the US – or elsewhere?
Here’s what we know:
What’s in the new oil deal between the US and Venezuela?
Last week, the Trump administration announced a deal that would give the US control of more than 65 billion barrels of Venezuela’s proven oil reserves. That is more than one-fifth of all of Venezuela’s known oil.
To do this, a White House fact sheet has revealed, the US is creating a private joint venture with North American Blue Energy Partners (NABEP), which is owned by billionaire Venezuelan businessman Alejandro Betancourt, an ex-ally of Hugo Chavez, the former socialist president.
NABEP is already the second-largest operator in Venezuela after US oil giant Chevron, which is also expected to expand its oil operations in Venezuela.
The deal will give the Pentagon’s Office of Strategic Capital a 35 percent stake in NABEP, which will “have reputable US auditors, lawyers, and advisors”, the White House said.
The White House said that “millions of barrels of new Venezuelan output will be processed through US refineries and pumped with American rigs and infrastructure, supporting billions in investment in the United States and thousands of jobs here at home”. The US will be guaranteed a right to buy 20 percent of the output at cost.
The joint venture with NABEP has capacity to produce about 200,000 barrels of crude oil per day, increasing US production as Iran’s blockade of the Strait of Hormuz has spiked global oil prices, including in the US.
Venezuela’s interim President Delcy Rodriguez welcomed the oil deal, which is also expected to add much-needed funds to the state’s treasury.
The creation of the joint venture will make it easier for NABEP to operate from Venezuela, which remains under US sanctions.
The US has been importing large amounts of Venezuelan oil since President Nicolas Maduro was captured in a US military operation in January this year. Maduro was flown to the US to stand trial on guns-and-drugs charges, while his vice president, Rodriguez, was left as interim leader. She has since facilitated US access to Venezuela’s oil industry and the US has lifted personal sanctions against her.
In August, US Under Secretary of Energy Kyle Haustveit said more than 500,000 barrels per day (bpd) is now moving from Venezuela to the US – some 40 percent of the country’s national output of 1.25 million bpd.
Have US crude prices fallen since the deal was announced?
According to analysts, US crude prices have actually risen since Trump announced the latest deal.
Johannes Rauball, a senior crude oil analyst at Kpler, the global trade intelligence agency, noted that before Washington’s agreement with Caracas, US West Texas Intermediate (WTI) crude was trading about $83-$86 per barrel, while Brent crude – the global benchmark for oil prices – was hovering between $85-$88 per barrel.
“Since then, prices have moved even higher – with WTI pushing past $90 and Brent topping $95 per barrel – driven up primarily by heightened geopolitical risks and acute Middle East supply disruptions around the Strait of Hormuz,” he told Al Jazeera.
On Thursday morning (06:00 GMT), WTI crude futures had climbed by 61 cents, or 0.7 percent, to $90.83.
Why aren’t US crude or gas prices coming down?
According to Rauball, while the US-Venezuela deal may improve supply and, therefore, market sentiment in the longer term, near-term prices are unlikely to be impacted because of the practical difficulties of extracting oil from the ground in Venezuela.
“It will take years for this deal to result in a meaningful ramp-up in production due to Venezuela’s severe physical bottlenecks and ageing infrastructure – most notably degraded pipeline gathering systems, insufficient electrical grid support, and a lack of specialised crude upgraders,” he said.
As far as US fuel prices are concerned, he added, US refiners are already operating at maximum capacity to meet demand both domestically and abroad, leaving little room to scale up further.
“While access to heavier Venezuelan crude supplies offers the specific feedstocks US Gulf Coast refiners require, it will not translate into near-term price relief at the pump given these refining throughput constraints and ongoing operational delays,” he said.
Tracy Shuchart, senior economist at futures trading platform NinjaTrader, wrote in a post on X on August 29: “Everyone cheering the Venezuela deal thinks a flood of cheap oil is about to hit and pull gas prices down. It isn’t.
“Venezuela pumps about 1.2M bpd right now, up from just under a million. That gain came mostly from Chevron ramping up existing wells after sanctions were lifted, not from new drilling. The easy barrels are already back. The reserve number is a stock that will take decades to convert to flow,” she said.
What does this deal mean for global oil prices?
Iran’s closure of the strait, through which more than 20 percent of global oil and natural gas is shipped in peacetime, has upended global energy markets.
Shortly after the strait was closed in early March, the price of Brent crude oil rose above $100 per barrel. Before the war, it was trading at about $66 per barrel. On Thursday, Brent crude rose $1.03, or 1.1 percent, to $95.68 a barrel at 06:05 GMT.
According to Kpler’s Rauball, the immediate impact of the US-Venezuela oil deal on global crude prices remains “neutral” as current markets remain focused on short-term geopolitical supply shortages caused primarily by the closure of the Strait of Hormuz.
“Over the longer term, a successful ramp-up [of production] will gradually increase the overall availability of Venezuelan crude in the global market. This added volume will help increase crude supply globally over time, ultimately exerting persistent downward pressure on global oil prices further down the line,” he said.
But there are several reasons why an increased supply of Venezuelan oil ultimately cannot make up for the reduced supply of oil from Gulf producers which used to be shipped through the Strait of Hormuz.
Frederic Schneider, a nonresident senior fellow at the Middle East Council on Global Affairs, said: “The US-Israeli war on Iran took at least 10million barrels a day off the market through Hormuz. Venezuela cannot replace that, also partly because it is a different grade, namely, heavy, sour crude which competes with other heavy imports (mostly Canadian and some Mexican) rather than substituting for the lighter Gulf oil.”
Hamad Hussain, a climate and commodities economist at the United Kingdom-based firm Capital Economics, also told Al Jazeera that developing oilfields in Venezuela requires significant amounts of investment and time before more crude could be produced and sold to global markets.
“Even in the long term, the potential for political instability and high costs involved could make investors wary of committing to oilfield projects in Venezuela. This could hold back the extent to which oil supply in Venezuela increases and, in turn, limit the downward pressure on crude oil prices over the coming years,” he told Al Jazeera.
Furthermore, only a few countries have refineries capable of processing the very heavy oil which Venezuela produces. These are primarily the US, China and India.
“Refineries in Europe are geared towards refining lighter grades of crude, so there would be little interest in importing oil from Venezuela there,” Hussain said.
“The heaviness of Venezuelan crude would be a bigger problem for President Trump’s stated aim to refill the US Strategic Petroleum Reserve (SPR) with crude from Venezuela. This is because storing oil from Venezuela in the SPR could cause damage to the underground caverns.
Global crude prices will, therefore, also continue to depend heavily on how the US and Israel’s war on Iran, which has paralysed the Strait of Hormuz, plays out.
So who will really benefit from this deal?
US oil companies are likely to earn the biggest gains from this deal. After the deal was announced late on Friday, shares in Chevron, currently the only big US oil company active in Venezuela, rose 2.2 percent to $206.20 on the Dow Jones index of publicly listed companies.
On Tuesday, US Energy Secretary Chris Wright said several oil companies from the US and other countries are also expected to sign oil deals in Caracas this week, which will increase Venezuela’s crude oil production. These are expected to include Chevron, Italy’s Eni, India’s ONGC, Colombia’s GeoPark and the US’s GE Vernova.
Venezuelan oil production peaked above 3 million bpd in the late 1990s but plummeted after that due to lack of investment, mismanagement and US sanctions. In recent months it has been about 1.1 million to 1.2 million bpd, rising slightly since President Nicolas Maduro was abducted by US forces in January.
Wright claimed that gas prices will fall for US consumers as and when US oil companies increase their investments in Venezuela.
“The investment in these deals will massively grow available oil production, which will give downward pressure on oil prices, but the biggest kink right now in gasoline and diesel prices is refining capacity,” Wright told reporters in Venezuela, without giving any details about how refining capacity would be increased.
However, Schneider said he did not envisage many other oil companies rushing to invest in Venezuela’s oil industry. “The more fundamental problem is that the high-price shock earlier in the war has destroyed demand, which has put pressure on WTI,” he told Al Jazeera. “With a highly uncertain demand forecast and Gulf oil coming back online at some point, no company wants to put $100bn into a country as risky as Venezuela,” he added.

Islamic World Science and Technology Exchange Office unveiled
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
