A Prop 65 Crash Course: What You Need to Know (2026)
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
09:32:00 UTC
18:32:00 KST

My first encounter with a Prop 65 warning was on the back of my TV.
I was selling it on Facebook Marketplace, and when the buyer arrived to pick it up, he spotted a warning I had never noticed. “California Proposition 65 Warning: This product contains chemicals known to the state of California to cause cancer and birth defects or reproductive harm.” Neither of us had seen such a label before, and for a moment, he didn’t want the TV anymore. We did what anyone would do in this situation: We Googled it. He ended up taking the TV. I kept Googling.
California’s Proposition 65, officially called the Safe Drinking Water and Toxic Enforcement Act, applies to a dizzying range of products, from food and cosmetics to electronics and household goods. Passed in 1986, the law turns 40 this year, yet that ominous little label still confuses the average consumer.
So, should you steer clear of all products with a Prop 65 warning? Not necessarily. Here’s what you need to know before you panic-buy a new TV.
Proposition 65, Explained
In November 1986, California voters approved Proposition 65 by a landslide margin of about 63 percent to 37 percent. It’s a right-to-know law, meant to inform Californians about potential exposure to chemicals that may cause cancer or reproductive harm over a lifetime.
It doesn’t ban those chemicals; instead, it requires businesses to provide a warning when their products could expose people to a listed chemical at levels above specific thresholds.
“At that time, it was part of a broader effort to address a growing concern that the public had about toxic chemical exposure,” says Megan Schwarzman, environmental health scientist at UC Berkeley’s School of Public Health.
The idea is that consumers can use that information to make their own decisions. A warning might prompt someone to choose an alternative, use a product less frequently, or take other steps to reduce their exposure. Prop 65 also gives businesses an incentive to reformulate products or change manufacturing practices to avoid issuing a warning that may deter customers.
And because California is such a massive consumer market, products often need to comply with Prop 65 requirements even when they’re manufactured or sold by companies elsewhere. Some large retailers, such as Target and Amazon, also require their vendors to comply with Prop 65 warning requirements.
Prop 65 Is Everywhere
Prop 65 covers a broad range of products and potential exposures. You can find warnings on fortified foods, smartphones, and appliances. The law is concerned with exposure, not simply whether the chemical is detectable. California's Office of Environmental Health Hazard Assessment (OEHHA) establishes the so-called safe-harbor levels for many listed chemicals. Generally speaking, a warning is required when anticipated exposure exceeds these levels.
The Prop 65 list contains both naturally occurring and synthetic chemicals that California has determined are known to cause cancer or reproductive harm. Supplements, for example, can contain trace amounts of naturally occurring or environmental contaminants, including lead, cadmium, and arsenic. The list is updated at least annually, and chemicals can also be removed from the list as scientific evidence evolves.
Chemicals can be added to the Prop 65 list through four mechanisms: through California’s Labor Code; through evaluations from California’s Carcinogen Identification Committee (CIC) or Developmental and Reproductive Toxicant Identification Committee (DARTIC); through identification by certain authoritative bodies, like the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA); or through identification by a state or federal agency.
Mariana C. Stern, cancer epidemiologist and member of the CIC, says the committee includes epidemiologists, toxicologists, molecular biologists, and cancer scientists who review the available literature before deciding whether a chemical belongs on the list.
“We may spend the whole day trying to dissect one chemical,” Stern says. “It’s not uncommon that we end up deciding we don’t have enough evidence to add this compound to the list.”
But seeing a warning doesn’t necessarily mean a product contains a dangerous amount of a chemical, or even that the product itself has been tested. According to Schwarzman, “some companies have opted to warn rather than test or reformulate, but from our research, I believe that is much less common than when companies post a warning because of the actual presence of the chemical above a certain threshold.”
From a consumer standpoint, the ubiquity of Prop 65 labels also means that it can be harder to prioritize which ones actually warrant attention. “We definitely have a concern with over-warning,” says Tina Cox, section chief of the OEHHA’s Proposition 65 Implementation Program. “Any unnecessary warnings do make it difficult for consumers to identify where the real exposures are, and it does dilute the value of Prop 65 warnings.”
As a result, California has started trying to make them more useful by requiring short-form warnings to name at least one chemical, rather than relying on the generic “may cause cancer or reproductive harm” language. Businesses have until January 2028 to fully comply with the new requirement. The state is also conducting more outreach to help companies understand when a warning is required and when it is not.
The Warning Isn’t a Verdict
Prop 65 was meant to inform consumers, not to tell them which products to buy. By the same token, a product without a warning isn’t necessarily free of hazardous chemicals.
“You’re never going to be zero exposure, even if you avoid all Prop 65 labels,” says air pollution scientist Shahir Fouad Masri. “If you have a product that doesn’t have a label, it’s one of two things: It was tested and it didn’t exceed Prop 65, and therefore it’s safe, or simply nobody ever sent it to the lab.”
That said, a Prop 65 warning is still useful information, and there are ways to reduce your exposure to these harmful chemicals. “Everybody has different risk tolerances and different priorities,” says Schwarzman. Consider how frequently you use the product and at what dose.
“Exposure from that one product, in many cases, is not going to cause cancer,” adds Cox, “but maybe over a lifetime of exposure, or exposure to similar products that have the same chemical, will increase your risk for cancer or reproductive toxicity.”
One example is holiday lights. Flexible plastic components can contain phthalates, which are added to PVC (polyvinyl chloride) to make it more pliable. Those chemicals migrate out of the plastic and come into contact with your hands or enter household dust. “My own choice around that is to handle them briefly and wash my hands,” says Schwarzman. “I don’t have my kids handle them, and I do make a different decision about that than something I’d be consuming on a daily basis.”
On a similar note, if you’re concerned about a warning on a tool, Masri suggests wearing gloves to reduce direct skin contact. There’s also a difference in dermal absorption rate. The skin on your hands, for example, is generally thicker and more calloused than the skin on your face, which means less absorption. So you might think differently about a screwdriver you occasionally handle with gloves than an LED mask you put directly on your face every day, where the potential for absorption is higher.
TL;DR
If you’re considering a product with a Prop 65 warning, don’t fret. Instead, look for more information.
- Determine what chemical triggered the warning, if identified.
- Check whether the manufacturer provides testing or contaminant information. Look for credible third-party certification, where appropriate.
- Consider how frequently you’re using the product and how extensively. Occasional exposure is different from using something every day.
- Don’t assume the absence of a Prop 65 label means the product is free of contaminants.
- For consumers who want to dig deeper, P65warnings.ca.gov has information about individual chemicals and ways to reduce exposure. There’s also a dedicated Help Desk for Prop 65, along with an email and phone line for specific inquiries.
- If you’re pregnant, trying to become pregnant, taking medications, or managing a medical condition, talk to a qualified health professional.
Prop 65 is a right-to-know law meant to raise awareness and ensure that we, as consumers, have an impact on the type of products we’re exposed to in our daily lives. As Schwarzman puts it, “I want to encourage us all not to feel like the toxic things are inevitable, and there’s nothing we can do, because there often is something we can do.”
Meet the Experts
- Tina Cox, senior environmental scientist (supervisory) and section chief of the Proposition 65 Implementation Program at the Office of Environmental Health Hazard Assessment (OEHHA)
- Mariana C. Stern, PhD, a cancer epidemiologist and professor of preventive medicine and urology at the University of Southern California, Keck School of Medicine
- Megan Schwarzman, MD, a physician and environmental health scientist at UC Berkeley’s School of Public Health
- Shahir Fouad Masri, ScD, an air pollution scientist at the University of California, Irvine

EU's Kallas says Leipzig attack had hallmarks of state-sponsored terrorism

Unknown Publisher

EU's Kallas says Leipzig attack had hallmarks of state-sponsored terrorism
WICKLOW, Ireland, Sept 2 - The attempted attack in Leipzig had all the hallmarks of state-sponsored terrorism, the European Union's foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said on Wednesday, adding that Europe needs to coordinate on what more can be done given the escalation of Russia's attacks on Ukraine.
The German government said on Tuesday that it had concluded that Russia was responsible for the attempted drone attack last month.
Speaking ahead of an informal gathering of European foreign ministers in Ireland, Kallas also said that work is ongoing on 1,600 sanctions listings related to Russia's military complex and "maybe there are more to be added".
Ministers arriving at the meeting said the bloc needs to look for more ways to put pressure on Moscow.
"I think we need to now really explore all the options on the table in terms of tightening the sanctions," Finnish Foreign Minister Elina Valtonen told reporters.
Lithuania's Foreign Minister Kestutis Budrys said Europeans need to consider their options and respond.
"It is obvious Russia does not see the political cost of its hybrid activities against us. So for them, this is the cheap way to make tensions in our society," he said, adding that "our goal is to show that these activities will neither intimidate us nor prevent us from supporting Ukraine and maintaining our pressure on Russia".
German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul said the EU will work on imposing further sanctions on Russian individuals in the coming weeks.
"Pressure on Russia is being stepped up and support for Ukraine also remains at a high level. That is the unity we are demonstrating at this time," he said.
'CLOSE THE UKRAINIAN SKY'
Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha told reporters that Ukrainians are suffering daily attacks and that Kyiv is working with European countries who have interceptors in storage.
"I hope that we will have additional strong decisions to close the Ukrainian sky," he said.
Some European ministers pointed to risks stemming from Russia's activities following the Leipzig incident.
"We are lucky that nothing happened, but we see what happened in Romania, what happened in so many countries," Luxembourg's Foreign Minister Xavier Bettel said when arriving for the talks.
"We see that there is no will from the Russian side to de-escalate. It’s my neighbouring country so the danger is coming closer," he added.
Romania has reported repeated breaches of its airspace by Russian drones over the past four years, as well as mines floating in the Black Sea across key trade and energy routes.
The Netherlands, Poland, Spain and Sweden called last week for the EU to reopen discussion on using Russia's frozen assets, an idea some ministers reiterated on Wednesday.
But it remained unclear whether Europe would once again seriously consider using the frozen assets.
EU countries immobilised some €210 billion of Russian central bank assets after Moscow invaded Ukraine in February 2022. Around €185 billion of this is held in Brussels-based central securities depository Euroclear.
The European Commission proposed last year to use Russian cash for a loan to Ukraine, but Belgium rejected the plan, saying it did not provide sufficient guarantees that it would not be left alone to deal with potential lawsuits and demands of damages from Russia. REUTERS

UK yet to decide CASEVAC helicopter mix after 2027
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
10:30:37 BST
18:30:37 KST

The Ministry of Defence has identified Chinook, Merlin Mk4/4A, Wildcat AH Mk1 and Jupiter HC Mk2 as the helicopter fleets currently able to support casualty evacuation tasks, while stopping short of confirming exactly which platforms will perform the role between 2027 and 2030.
The position was set out in a written parliamentary answer to Liberal Democrat MP James MacCleary, who asked which helicopter platforms would be available to the Armed Forces to perform casualty evacuation between 2027 and 2030. Armed Forces Minister Louise Sandher-Jones said Defence does not treat casualty evacuation, or CASEVAC, as a capability tied to a single aircraft type.
She said: “The Ministry of Defence continually reviews platform capabilities to ensure that current and future Defence requirements are met. Casualty evacuation (CASEVAC) is a military task rather than a capability delivered by a single helicopter type, and Defence maintains a range of rotary-wing platforms that can be employed to support casualty evacuation as required.”
Sandher-Jones then identified the aircraft currently available for the task, saying: “At present, CASEVAC capability is provided by the Chinook, Merlin Mk4/4A, Wildcat AH Mk1 and Jupiter HC Mk2 helicopter fleets. As announced in the Defence Investment Plan, Wildcat AH Mk1 is planned to be withdrawn from service from 2027.”
The answer means the Army’s Wildcat AH Mk1 remains part of the current CASEVAC mix, but is not planned to remain in service across the full period covered by MacCleary’s question. The MOD did not identify a direct replacement platform for Wildcat in the casualty evacuation task, instead saying future decisions would depend on operational and capability requirements.
Sandher-Jones said: “Decisions on the helicopter platforms that will be available to perform the CASEVAC role between 2027 and 2030 will be taken in accordance with Defence capability requirements and operational needs, which are kept under regular review.”
The Chinook fleet provides heavy-lift helicopter support to the Armed Forces, while Merlin Mk4 and Mk4A aircraft are operated by the Commando Helicopter Force in support of Royal Marines and wider maritime operations. Wildcat AH Mk1 is operated by the Army Air Corps, and Jupiter HC Mk2 is used within the military helicopter training system.
The MOD also declined to provide a fixed figure for the number of helicopters that could be made available for casualty evacuation at any one time. Sandher-Jones said availability would depend on the wider demands placed on individual fleets, including maintenance and training as well as operational commitments.
She said: “The number of helicopters available to undertake a CASEVAC task at any given time is not fixed and will vary according to operational commitments, maintenance requirements, training activity and force readiness levels.”
The minister added that more detailed readiness information would not be released publicly, saying: “The Department does not disclose detailed readiness or availability information, as doing so could prejudice the operational effectiveness and security of the Armed Forces.”

The Federation of Public Housing Estates noted on Wednesday that recent cuts to administration fees for the Mandatory Provident Fund (MPF) – the city’s compulsory retirement scheme – would generate higher savings for its 4.8 million members, making this an ideal time to relax withdrawal restrictions.

Leung noted that Singapore allowed residents to withdraw a proportion of their pension to buy homes under certain conditions, while requiring them to refund their accounts if they sell their properties.

Working Limburg windmill opens as guesthouse
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
09:25:55 UTC
18:25:55 KST

Starting this week, guests can check in for a night spent in the historic De Hoop windmill in Elen (Dilsen-Stokkem - Limburg). The windmill, which is still used to grind grain to this day, will now also serve as a guesthouse. The people behind the project explain the accommodation is needed to ensure this gem of Limburg heritage can be preserved for the future.
Windmill De Hoop was built in 1870 and remained in use until 1968. The mill is now a listed building and has been fully restored. A young miller recently resumed flour production, whilst guests are now given the chance to stay overnight at the mill.
“People are increasingly looking for a unique overnight experience,” says Stef van Boekel of Specialstays. “This mill has a rich history, and we’ve reflected that in the interior, with carefully chosen colours and materials.”
Every Saturday afternoon, work at the mill is in full swing. That’s when a miller grinds grain into flour here. “He’s a passionate 23-year-old, the youngest miller in Flanders,” explains Van Boekel. “Among other things, he produces and sells bread and cake flour.”
Guests staying at the mill or in one of the other rooms on this site can watch the entire milling process up close. “That’s what makes a stay here truly special,” explains Van Boekel. “Not only do guests sleep in a unique location, but they also experience a piece of living heritage.”
Guaranteeing a future for Mill De Hoop
The people behind the project say the provision of accommodation gives Mill De Hoop new prospects for the future. “These days, it’s very difficult for a mill to survive financially on the sale of flour alone,” says Van Boekel.
“By combining it with accommodation, we’re creating a sustainable model that helps the mill to survive. That’s not only important for the mill itself, but also for the village. In this way, the familiar silhouette that has defined the local landscape for over a century will be preserved.”

Charlie Kirk’s Murder Case Heads to Trial As Judge Rules Defendant Could Face Death Penalty
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
09:25:18 UTC
18:25:18 KST

Almost a year after the killing of right-wing activist Charlie Kirk at a Utah college campus, the case against the suspect accused of fatally shooting him is headed for trial.
On Tuesday, Tyler Robinson, 23, pleaded not guilty to aggravated murder and six other charges related to the shooting of Kirk at Utah Valley University on Sept. 10, 2025.
But Utah District Judge Tony Graf ruled that Robinson should stand trial, siding with prosecutors who argued there was “a mountain of evidence” against the defendant.
Graf also ruled that prosecutors can continue seeking the death penalty against Robinson, which the defense team has tried to remove as an option. Graf said the court found probable cause for an aggravating circumstance involving the alleged risk to other people at the crowded campus event, making Robinson eligible for capital punishment.
The hearing on Tuesday followed prosecutors’ presentation of evidence during a five-day hearing in July. No trial date has been set, but a pretrial conference is scheduled for Oct. 23.
Kirk’s death worsened fears of political violence spreading across the U.S., and prompted condemnation from allies, including President Donald Trump.
In a statement, Kirk’s widow Erika called the ruling “an important step in our family’s pursuit of justice”.
“Every step in this process carries the weight of all that Charlie’s murder has taken from his family, especially his children who will grow up without their father,” the statement added.
Erika Kirk and the defendant were both in court on Tuesday for the hearing in the city of Provo.
Why capital punishment is an option
According to Utah law, aggravated murder can become a capital felony if prosecutors file notice that they intend to seek the death penalty, which prosecutors have earlier done in Robinson’s case.
Graf bound over Robinson on one count of aggravated murder, one count of felony discharge of a firearm causing serious injury, two counts of obstruction of justice, two counts of witness tampering, and one count of committing a violent offense in front of a child.
The judge could have sent the case to trial on a lesser charge of murder, which has a sentence of at least 15 years and a maximum of life imprisonment. But Graf said in his ruling that it was reasonable to infer that shooting Kirk from a distance, while surrounded by a crowd of thousands of people, exposed at least one other individual at great risk, meriting the aggravated murder charge.
Kirk, 31, was sitting under a tent when he was shot in the neck while speaking at an event at the university in Orem.
Ryan McBride, a prosecutor with the Utah County Attorney’s Office, said in closing arguments to the court that the four rounds found in the alleged murder weapon—a bolt-action rifle—explain that Robinson knew there was an increased risk to others since it showed the suspect was prepared to fire more bullets if he had missed.
Robinson was lying on a rooftop around 400 ft away when he fired at Kirk, and the prosecutors argued that a shot merely a degree off could have a considerable difference in distance and endangered others’ lives.
“There is a mountain of evidence that proves he is the shooter,” McBride told the court.
But Staci Visser, representing Robinson, argued the state failed to prove the shooter “knowingly” risked people’s lives and said the prosecutors were trying to force the aggravated murder charge.
“There is one shot. There is one bullet. There is one victim,” Visser said. “There was no evidence that would suggest that anyone else was threatened.”
Other factors could affect sentencing
Besides the risk to others, prosecutors also alleged that Robinson targeted Kirk for his political expression and that he fired in the presence of children. If prosecutors prove this at trial, it could affect his sentencing.
Kirk and the organization he co-founded, Turning Point USA, were central to the growing young conservative movement that helped elect Trump.
Kirk was also critical of same-sex marriage and transgender rights. Earlier this year, prosecutors alleged that the political commentator’s stances on these issues drove Robinson to target him. “It’s not difficult to understand the motive here,” McBride said.

It’s a great honor to be Iran’s flag-bearer: Atrachali
TEHRAN - Fazel Atrachali, the male flag-bearer for Iran’s delegation at the Nagoya Asian Games, says he is proud to have been given the honor and hopes the national team can also claim the gold medal at the continental event.
Iran, one of the leading kabaddi powers in Asia and the world, will compete in Nagoya with high ambitions. India, meanwhile, will be looking to once again demonstrate their dominance over Iran and the rest of Asia.
Atrachali spoke exclusively to Tehran Times about his own preparations and Iran’s prospects at the Asian Games.
“Given the special circumstances currently facing our country, carrying the national flag can be a symbol of strength and authority, which makes this responsibility particularly significant,” Atrachali said.
“Of course, it is a very heavy responsibility. The name of our delegation is The Children of Minab, and that makes me feel an even greater sense of responsibility.”
He added: “It is a great honor to be the flag-bearer of the national team at the opening ceremony, especially when great champions such as Arian Salimi and our wrestlers are also part of this delegation. I am proud to represent these famous athletes,” the kabaddi captain explained.
Asked about his expectations for Iran’s performance at the Asian Games, the national team captain said Iran cannot afford to underestimate any opponent.
“All the countries will come to these Games at full strength. For example, in previous competitions, Malaysia emerged as a very strong team, even though we did not expect them to perform at such a high level,” he said.
“Teams such as South Korea, Sri Lanka, Pakistan and Chinese Taipei have also performed very well in recent years. So, it would be wrong to think that India are our only serious rival. All the teams are strong, although India remain our traditional and long-standing rival.”
At the previous Asian Games in Hangzhou, the match between Iran and India was halted for a prolonged period because of refereeing issues. Eventually, contrary to expectations that the officials would rule in Iran’s favor and allow the match to continue, that did not happen.
Reflecting on the controversial incident, Atrachali said: “The match was stopped for 70 minutes, but in the end we saw that the Indians had more influence when it came to the refereeing decisions, and they won the match. Of course, I have played alongside several Indian players and know them very well.”
“On paper and statistically, their players may be better than ours, but when it comes to teamwork, we have always been stronger.
“In terms of facilities, technique and tactics, perhaps we have only 10 percent of what they have, but 90 percent comes down to belief and mentality. We will step onto the court aiming for the gold medal — whether our opponent are India or Pakistan,” Atrachali concluded.

Arab American Institute highlights growing anti-Latino attacks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
09:21:30 UTC
18:21:30 KST

Breadcrumb
Arab American Institute highlights growing anti-Latino attacks after FBI report
The US Federal Bureau of Investigation’s 2025 hate crime report shows a record number of attacks on Latinos amid a heightened climate of fear in immigrant communities.
While the report doesn’t show an overall increase in hate crime, the current political climate raises questions about underreporting bias incidents at a time when many people, particularly from marginialised communities, do not feel comfortable reporting crime to law enforcement.
"While the overall number of reported hate crimes declined in 2025, this data should not be mistaken for a decline in hate across our communities," said Maya Berry, executive director of the Arab American Institute, in a public statement in response to the FBI report.
"The increase in anti-Latino hate crimes is particularly alarming, reaching the highest level ever recorded as the Trump Administration targets immigrant and Latino communities with bigoted rhetoric and policy," she said.
The report showed that 10,881 incidents were reported in 2025, the lowest level of hate crime reported in five years. There is a nine percent decrease compared with 2024. There have, however, been changes to reporting practices, placing potential limitations on data collection.
Berry also noted that national hate crime statistics reflect what is reported from state and local authorities, meaning that the politicisation of law enforcement could account for underreporting of bias incidents. The FBI’s report found that while hate crime incidents against Muslims and Jews had declined by over 20 percent between 2024 and 2025, incidents against Christians had increased.
"Hate crime data also reflects only what's reported to law enforcement and passed on to the FBI. Chronic underreporting, uneven participation across jurisdictions, and the politicisation of government data all limit our ability to see the full scope of hate in America," said Berry.
"We would prefer to take comfort in a decline in reported incidents but worry the loss of confidence in government institutions under this administration has become yet another barrier to accurate hate crime reporting," she said, noting that the current administration has gutted the civil rights division of the Department of Justice.
In addition, even with an official decline in hate crime, advocates note that the numbers are still significant and show that minorities remain vulnerable.
"Hate crime data is an essential tool for identifying gaps in protections and holding institutions accountable. A decline in reported incidents that still top 10,000 annually is not a reason to look away—it's an urgent call to strengthen reporting and confront the policies and policymakers that let hate flourish," said Berry.

Guinea-Bissau voters approve new constitution expanding presidential powers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
09:20:55 UTC
18:20:55 KST

Guinea-Bissau voters have approved a new constitution, which critics say will undermine democracy, that significantly expands presidential powers ahead of elections due in December.
According to provisional results, 70% of voters approved sweeping changes in the tiny west African state’s first constitutional amendment since revisions that ended the one-party socialist state more than three decades ago.
The turnout for Sunday’s referendum was reportedly over 55%, amounting to an estimated 544,060 people.
The new constitution will reduce the number of seats in parliament from 102 to 65 and cut electoral constituencies from 29 to 12. New provisions will require presidential candidates to have lived continuously in the country for at least five years before the vote, which is believed to target diaspora-based politicians with significant followings.
The referendum’s outcome is expected to pave the way for December’s elections, which many hope will steady the political landscape in Guinea-Bissau, which has been through a series of politically turbulent periods since its declaration of independence from Portugal was globally recognised in 1974. Since then it has had at least 10 coup attempts, half of which have been successful.
The most recent came after last November’s disputed presidential elections. Both candidates declared themselves winners, citing electoral malpractice by the other’s camp. The military forcefully intervened, setting up a transitional ruling council headed by Gen Horta Inta-A Na Man, a former military chief of general staff.
Na Man said: “What we want after this referendum is to allow whoever wins the elections to see out their mandate without hindrance.”
Nelson Moreira, the second vice-president of the transitional council, said the outgoing constitution, which came into effect in 1993, had often been cited as “the cause of instability in Guinea”.
The leading opposition party, the African Party for the Independence of Guinea and Cape Verde (PAIGC), which was barred from fielding a presidential candidate in the 2025 election, had asked its supporters to boycott the referendum, which it called a democratic farce.
“What will happen on 30 August is the continuation of the coup d’état carried out on 26 November,” its leader, Domingos Simões Pereira, had said.

Taiwan's Tongtai brings machine tool capabilities to wafer processing
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
09:20:26 UTC
18:20:26 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Tongtai Machine & Tool Co. is expanding its presence in the semiconductor industry by bringing together its electronics equipment and machine tool businesses, CTEE reported Wednesday.
The move targets both the wafer industry and the semiconductor equipment supply chain. The company’s electronics unit focuses on wafer processing and advanced packaging, while its machine tool business makes precision-machined components used in semiconductor manufacturing.
In wafer processing, Tongtai offers machinery for grinding and flattening wafers. They are used at multiple production stages, including manufacturing, packaging, and recycling.
Grinding thins wafers and removes minor surface defects from earlier processing. Flattening creates a more uniform surface and reduces the likelihood of particles adhering to the wafer, according to Good Technology and a thesis by National Taiwan University’s Tu Chi-hsu (凃岐旭).
The company has also developed ductile grinding for harder materials such as silicon carbide. The process removes nanometer-scale amounts of material, minimizing damage and reducing the number of steps required in conventional wafer processing.
On the machine tool side, Tongtai uses high-precision turning and milling combined with ultrasonic processing to manufacture components for semiconductor production machinery. These include gas-control systems, wafer carriers used to hold wafers during processing, and chambers where wafers undergo manufacturing processes.
The company is also supplying laser-processing equipment for advanced packaging. Its systems have been used on advanced packaging production lines to process multilayer composite structures, forming micro-holes and openings while limiting the area affected by heat and minimizing damage to surrounding materials.
Tongtai primarily manufactures and sells machine tools, or industrial machinery used to process metal and other materials. Its revenue totaled NT$665 million (US$20.9 million) in July, up 57.06% from the same month a year earlier, according to Sinotrade.

Chelpis showcases post-quantum security solutions at Semicon Taiwan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
09:20:12 UTC
18:20:12 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taiwan cybersecurity company Chelpis is showcasing post-quantum cryptography technologies spanning semiconductor chips, firmware, communications, and autonomous systems at Semicon Taiwan.
The global technology industry is preparing for the transition to security standards designed to withstand attacks from quantum computers. To assist with this transition, the company is presenting an array of technologies aimed at semiconductor and financial systems, AI data centers, drones, and autonomous robots, per a press release.
Chelpis is exhibiting on the fourth floor in Hall 1 at the Taipei Nangang Exhibition Center until Friday. The company said the semiconductor industry's long product lifecycles make it increasingly important to incorporate quantum-resistant security at the chip-design stage rather than treating it as a software upgrade later.
Chelpis Founder and CEO Chih Ming-yang (池明洋) said the shift toward post-quantum security represents both a new technical requirement and a business opportunity for the semiconductor supply chain.
“Quantum-safe security is no longer just a future consideration,” the company said, describing its technology as designed to protect systems against both current and future cryptographic threats.
Security closer to the chip
One of Chelpis' main exhibits is its Quantum-Safe Root of Trust (QoT) technology, which incorporates a hardware-based PQC Secure Enclave into chip and system-on-chip architectures. The company said the technology combines protected PQC cryptographic processing cores with dedicated memory, allowing manufacturers to incorporate quantum-safe security into products from the earliest stages of chip design.
Chelpis said the approach is particularly relevant to products with long operating lifecycles, including automotive electronics, industrial control systems, defense technology, edge AI devices, and other smart devices.
The company also promotes the technology as a defense against so-called “harvest now, decrypt later” attacks, in which encrypted data is collected today with the expectation that future advances in quantum computing could eventually make it possible to decrypt the information.
The US National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) finalized its first three PQC standards in 2024 — FIPS 203, FIPS 204 and FIPS 205. The standards cover key establishment and digital signatures designed to resist attacks by quantum computers.
NIST has continued expanding its PQC work. In March 2025, it selected the HQC algorithm as a backup encryption algorithm to ML-KEM, while advising organizations to continue migrating to the standards finalized in 2024.
PQC for drones and robots
Chelpis is also demonstrating applications for autonomous unmanned systems, including drones, quadruped robots and other autonomous machines. The company said the security challenge for such systems extends beyond protecting stored data. Command authority, device identity, control instructions, and real-time video transmissions also need protection against interception or manipulation.
Its PQ-SDN, PQConnect, and PQTunnel technologies are designed to establish post-quantum-secure communications across multiple network protocols, including distributed and mesh-network environments. Chelpis said its PQC technology has already been deployed in the nation’s drone industry to encrypt communications between flight controllers and ground control stations, protecting flight-control commands and video data.
Chelpis will present “Quantum-Safe in Autonomous Robots" at Semicon Taiwan's TechXPOT stage at 2:40 p.m. Friday in Area L on the fourth floor of TaiNEX 1. The presentation will examine how PQC can be incorporated into autonomous robots' devices, communications, and control architectures, as well as how semiconductor suppliers can prepare for the global transition to quantum-safe security, per the press release.
The company said it is also working on PQC migration services covering cryptographic asset inventories, risk assessments, migration planning, and deployment. Chelpis describes its product portfolio as covering three areas: PQ-IC for quantum-safe chip technologies, PQ-UxV for unmanned vehicles, and PQ-AI data center technologies for AI infrastructure.
Chelpis said it was the first company in Taiwan to receive certification under NIST's Cryptographic Algorithm Validation Program and that it has integrated NIST-standardized PQC algorithms into chip intellectual property and firmware-protection solutions.

Meta settlement could clear the way for new AI product launches, Morgan Stanley says

Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
09:19:25 UTC
18:19:25 KST

Meta's $18 billion social media settlement lifts a legal overhang that some analysts say could clear the way for a wave of new AI product launches.
The tech giant went to trial in August after a lawsuit filed by 29 U.S. state attorneys general alleged that its platforms, Instagram and Facebook, had design features that posed harms to younger users.
In week two of the trial, Meta and the states agreed to a settlement in which Meta said it would make core changes to its platforms for users under 18. These range from a two-hour daily usage limit to disabling extreme makeup and cosmetic surgery filters and introducing tighter age verification measures.
The outcome raised investor concerns about reduced advertising revenue, and analysts at Morgan Stanley said that substantial lawsuits often drive tech giants to release innovative new products and offerings.
"We see multiple new products in the pipeline from Meta (MetaClaw/a better MetaAI, a full suite of agentic ad tooling for small to medium-sized businesses, upcoming rollout of new subscription offerings, a robust API offering, neocloud optionality and more)," they said in a Saturday note. They added that they're not claiming Meta's products are ready for launch.
Meta is reportedly set to release its consumer AI agent Hatch in early September, which will run inside its platforms WhatsApp and Instagram, and can perform autonomous tasks including online purchases and restaurant bookings, according to an internal memo seen by Business Insider.
A "slew of successful new product and model launches" followed the Department of Justice's decision to rule against a forced sale of Google's key assets last year, the Morgan Stanley analysts said. Those product launches included "Gemini 3 and broader rollout of search tools including AI Mode/AI Overviews," which also lifted its valuation.
"There are certainly signals, in our view, that Meta's product pipeline could start flowing following this legal clearing event… just like Google's last year," they added.
Investment bank Needham maintained its "hold" rating on Meta stock after the settlement.
It noted Meta's costly "strategy diffusion," which includes expanding simultaneously into custom chips, data center infrastructure, enterprise AI software, business agents, model APIs, compute sales, advertising tools, consumer assistants, smart glasses and other hardware.
"By not concentrating its capital and free cash flow on the highest-return products and services, it raises the risk that management attention, engineering talent and shareholder capital are spread across too many things, and lowers the likelihood that Meta succeeds at any of them, we believe," the Needham analysts added in Aug. 27 note.
Morgan Stanley: Teens make up only 1% of Meta's revenue
Meta will pay out the billion-dollar settlement in the social media case over ten years, and said it's booking a $10 billion legal charge in its third quarter this year following the outcome of the trial.
The guidance the company provided in July otherwise remains unchanged, following the settlement.
One of the conditions of paying out the full settlement is that rivals YouTube and TikTok make similar changes to their apps for younger users.
Enforcing youth engagement ceilings may pose a "larger long-term headwind" for YouTube than for Meta, as youth adoption of YouTube is higher than for Facebook or Instagram, the Morgan Stanley analysts said.
"We also believe revenue from teens represents only ~1% of META revenue," they added.
However, the Needham analysts pointed out that "the timing of payments couldn't be worse," as Meta expects up to $145 billion of capital expenditure in 2026 as it races to come out on top in the AI buildout.
The settlement and compliance costs could add to the company's growing cost pressures.

Serco wins RAF Fylingdales radar support contract
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
10:17:22 BST
18:17:22 KST

Serco has been awarded a five-year Ministry of Defence contract to continue operating, maintaining and sustaining the early warning radar at RAF Fylingdales in North Yorkshire, according to the company.
The contract, awarded by the National Armaments Director Group, covers the Solid State Phased Array Radar, or SSPAR, which forms part of the UK and US governments’ Upgraded Early Warning Radar network.
The new agreement will begin in April 2027 and includes an option for a further two-year extension.
RAF Fylingdales provides missile warning and space surveillance functions, with the radar designed to detect and track missiles as part of the US Missile Defence ground-based radar network. Serco provides continuous support at the site 24 hours a day, 365 days a year. Under the new contract it will remain responsible for radar hardware, systems operation and maintenance, alongside analytical and training activities.
The company said the Fylingdales team is also involved in tracking objects in Low Earth Orbit. During 2025, the SSPAR completed more than 5.9 million tracks of satellites in Low Earth Orbit, with Serco personnel providing real-time analysis of satellite break-ups, re-entries, new launches and manoeuvres.
Anthony Kirby, Serco Group Chief Executive, said: “We are immensely proud of our dedicated team at RAF Fylingdales who are entrusted to seamlessly deliver this continuous service, helping to defend the nation and protect our skies.”
He added: “We have a long history over sixty years supporting the UK Space Command, US Space Force and the Royal Air Force at RAF Fylingdales, with our people at the heart of this critical infrastructure asset.”
Kirby said: “Our success in securing this contract reflects the strength of our expertise and growing capabilities in defence and builds on our recent strong momentum.”
The contract will also introduce a new Serco-developed analytical system known as the Enhanced Spacetrack Processor, or ESP. The software will be used to analyse large volumes of tracking data to determine the position, orbit and size of objects in Low Earth Orbit. Serco developed ESP with the Royal Air Force and UK Space Command. It will replace the United Kingdom Spacetrack Processor, another Serco-developed system which has been used for more than three decades.
The company will also provide apprenticeships during the contract period. These will include Level 3 opportunities for school and college leavers and Level 5 and 6 apprenticeships for existing employees. Serco has partnered with Teesside University and Redcar & Cleveland College to develop an apprenticeship specifically for RAF Fylingdales, covering skills and qualifications relevant to work at the site.

China cracks down on AI ‘slop’, clearing out clutter from WeChat, RedNote, Douyin
Clampdown sweeps across 2,400 websites and apps as cyberspace watchdog escalates fight against generative tech abuse
1-MIN READ1-MIN
 Listen
Ben Jiangin Beijing
China is cracking down on artificial intelligence-generated “slop” – low-grade, mass-produced synthetic content cluttering social media and news feeds – as part of a sweeping campaign against the abuse of the generative technology, the country’s top internet watchdog said on Wednesday.
In a statement posted to its website, the Cyberspace Administration of China (CAC) said it had scrubbed more than 5.61 million pieces of harmful or illegal content and removed some 49,000 accounts during its latest enforcement drive.
The clampdown swept up 2,400 websites and apps, targeting some of China’s biggest digital spaces, including TikTok’s sister app Douyin and rival Kuaishou, as well as RedNote and Tencent Holdings’ WeChat.
Authorities focused on reining in AI-driven fake news, explicit and violent material, impersonation and safety violations involving minors.
The response underscores Beijing’s growing concerns over the accessibility of generative AI. As tools become cheaper and more sophisticated, creators can produce convincing deepfakes and clickbait in seconds, challenging existing moderation systems.
The CAC said creators on Douyin, Kuaishou and WeChat used AI to turn literary classics such as Romance of the Three Kingdoms and Journey to the West into sensationalised, low-grade “digital swill” to attract traffic.

RAF receives Saab Giraffe 1X radars for drone defence
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
10:13:55 BST
18:13:55 KST

Saab UK has delivered Giraffe 1X radar systems to the Royal Air Force for use in counter-drone operations, with the equipment intended to support the detection and tracking of uncrewed aerial systems on deployed operations.
The delivery follows what Saab described as an urgent operational requirement from the RAF and builds on previous work between the company and the service on counter-UAS capability. Saab said the radars have now become part of the RAF’s wider counter-drone architecture, supporting the detection, tracking and engagement of airborne threats alongside other systems used to protect personnel and facilities.
A Royal Air Force spokesperson said: “As the customer, we have been impressed with how Saab were able to mobilise their global production capacity to rapidly satisfy our Giraffe 1X requirement in support of Counter Drone operations on deployed operations. This equipment is critical in mitigating the risk to life posed by the drone threat. Saab gave delivery quickly and innovatively, working with the MOD team to satisfy this contract.”
Saab said the procurement was driven by an operational requirement and involved cooperation between its UK operations and the company’s wider production network. The company did not give the number of Giraffe 1X systems delivered, the value of the procurement or the precise locations at which the radars will be operated.
The Giraffe 1X is a compact three-dimensional radar designed for short-range surveillance and the detection of small airborne targets. Saab markets the system for roles including counter-UAS, ground-based air defence and battlefield surveillance, with the radar designed to be deployed from fixed positions or integrated onto vehicles and other mobile platforms.
Andy Fraser, Group Managing Director at Saab UK, said: “This delivery showcases the dedication and expertise of teams across Saab, from our UK manufacturing operations through to colleagues across the wider business, who worked together to support delivery of this capability. It demonstrates the strength of Saab’s industrial footprint in the UK and our ability to bring together the right resources to support our customers’ requirements. We are proud to provide British and coalition forces with the capabilities they need to carry out their mission and to keep people and society safe.”
Giraffe 1X is the smallest member of Saab’s Giraffe radar family. According to Saab, the system is designed to detect small, low and slow-moving targets while remaining sufficiently compact for rapid deployment. The radar can also contribute tracking data to wider command-and-control and air defence systems rather than operating as a standalone counter-drone weapon.

World Food Programme halves food assistance to West Bank due to funding shortages
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
09:12:51 UTC
18:12:51 KST

The UN’s World Food Program (WFP) is cutting in half the number of Palestinians it can support with food assistance in the West Bank due to funding shortfalls.
The WFP made the announcement on Tuesday. Despite reducing the service, the WFP shared that food needs have doubled since 2023, and an estimated 900,000 people are experiencing food insecurity in Palestinian territory, and up until now the WFP has only been able to support 400,000 of those in need.
While not mentioned by the WFP, after Hamas’s October 7 attacks on southern Israel, the Israeli work permits of 140,000 Palestinians were revoked.
WFP’s latest quarterly food security analysis found that 76% of households in the West Bank have experienced a significant decline in income, and food and fuel prices remain among the highest in the Middle East. These prices, the WFP claimed, have forced many families to sell assets and reduce the number and quality of their meals to survive.
Notably, according to the Palestinian Central Bureau of Statistics, the unemployment rate among those aged 15 and above stood at 27.9%, and the average daily wage stands at only NIS 134.3, just over half of Israel’s minimum daily wage of NIS 257.75.
One-third of West Bank Palestinian families cannot afford nutritious diet
The WFP’s analysis also noted that around 12% of Palestinians in the West Bank have poor food consumption and around a third of families cannot afford a nutritious diet, especially those living in rural areas and in the southern West Bank.
“Families who were once thriving and earning a living from their land are now unable to afford enough food,” said Shaun Hughes, WFP country director for the Palestinian territories. “At a time when WFP should be scaling up assistance to reach more people, we are being forced to make difficult decisions, prioritizing the most vulnerable while cutting assistance to others despite widespread needs. We urge the international community to act immediately and step up support for Palestinians.”
Operations in Gaza are also being affected by the funding shortfall. In July, the WFP reduced by 40% the cash value of its assistance for 375,000 people.

Former IDF soldier charged for affiliating himself with ISIS, watching terror training videos
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
09:12:34 UTC
18:12:34 KST

A former IDF soldier from northern Israel was charged on Wednesday with training for terrorist purposes after prosecutors alleged that he prepared himself to join ISIS and fight for the organization in Syria or Africa.
Khamis Su’ad, 30, an Arab-Israeli resident of Huseiniya in the Galilee, was arrested on August 2 following a joint investigation by the Shin Bet (Israel Security Agency) and Israel Police.
The prosecution filed the indictment in Haifa Magistrate’s Court alongside a request to keep Su’ad in custody until the proceedings conclude.
According to the indictment, Su’ad served in the IDF from 2017 to 2019. Beginning in 2023, he allegedly developed a growing interest in ISIS and came to identify with its activities, values, and objectives.
Prosecutors said he regularly visited websites and viewed social-media content associated with the terrorist organization.
In 2024, Su’ad allegedly decided to travel to Syria or Africa and fight for ISIS against those the organization considers infidels. According to the indictment, he then began preparing to carry out that plan.
Suspect allegedly watched ISIS killing videos, religious lessons
Prosecutors divided the alleged preparations into three areas.
Su’ad watched videos showing killings and beheadings to prepare himself psychologically, studied weapons use and combat methods, and watched religious lessons delivered by senior ISIS figures. He also began saving money for the planned journey.
During 2026, he allegedly downloaded manuals and watched videos explaining how to produce missiles and drones, use sniper rifles and other weapons associated with ISIS, and employ military tactics.
Su’ad was charged with receiving training or instruction in operational methods and weapons for the purpose of advancing the activities of a terrorist organization or carrying out a terrorist act.
The charge does not require prosecutors to prove that he completed his alleged plan to travel abroad. They must, however, prove that the material amounted to training or instruction and that he received it for a terrorist purpose.
In the accompanying detention request, prosecutors said Su’ad admitted the conduct attributed to him during questioning. They also said investigators found videos and manuals on his phones that supported the allegations.
Prosecutors argued that Su’ad would pose a danger to the public and state security if released and that there was also a risk he could obstruct or evade the proceedings. They said no release conditions would adequately address that risk.
The detention request also states that Su’ad has no previous convictions.
Israel sees spate of ISIS-linked planned attacks
Su’ad’s indictment follows at least two other ISIS-linked cases publicized by Israeli authorities in August.
On August 18, prosecutors charged Abdullah Gergawi, 20, from Segev Shalom, with allegedly planning to attack Beersheba’s Forum nightclub using a vehicle rigged with explosives.
Police said he had communicated with ISIS supporters and intended to join the organization in Syria.
On August 28, police and the Shin Bet announced that prosecutors would file indictments against a 16-year-old Galilee resident and Ibrahim Kaabiyya, a 19-year-old Haifa resident.
Authorities alleged that the minor intended to attack Jewish police officers and soldiers on the Temple Mount, while Kaabiyya planned an attack against an IDF base in northern Israel.
Kaabiyya’s attorney denied that he had planned an attack and said his interest in ISIS material stemmed from curiosity.
Unlike those cases, the indictment against Su’ad does not identify a planned attack inside Israel. It rather concerns his alleged online training and preparations to travel abroad and fight for ISIS.
The court must now consider the prosecution’s request to detain him through the trial. That decision is separate from the question of guilt and determines only where Su’ad will remain while the criminal proceedings continue.

The Democratic Republic of the Congo’s Ebola outbreak has killed more than 3,000 people out of more than 6,100 confirmed cases, according to the latest government data released on Wednesday, as the disease continues to spread rapidly.

There are currently no approved vaccines or treatments for the Bundibugyo strain.
The outbreak has intensified since it was first declared, while weak health infrastructure, community resistance, instability and protests by response workers have hampered efforts to identify and contain cases.

10 missing as Turkish cargo ship sinks after collision with vessel off Istanbul
- A Turkish cargo ship, Tugberk Imamoglu, sank quickly after colliding with the empty oil tanker ALSU near Istanbul's Marmara Sea.
- Ten crew members are missing; search and rescue efforts involve 14 vessels and a helicopter but no survivors have been found so far.
- The cargo ship carried 4,200 tons of rolled steel, and the incident happened just days after another deadly ferry accident in the region.
AI generated
ISTANBUL – A Turkish cargo ship sank in the Marmara Sea near Istanbul after colliding with a second vessel, with rescuers searching for its 10 crew members, Turkish officials said on Sept 2.
The incident occurred before dawn when the Alsu, an empty oil tanker, collided with the Tugberk Imamoglu, a cargo ship carrying rolled steel, which sank shortly after, the transport ministry’s maritime directorate said on X.
“Due to the Tugberk Imamoglu not responding to any calls and the crew not answering their mobile phones... it is believed the dry cargo ship has sunk,” it said.
The collision occurred 18 nautical miles off Silivri district on the western edge of Istanbul province, with Transport Minister Abdulkadir Uraloglu telling journalists the damaged vessel had sunk “very quickly”.
“We received the emergency call at 3.26am. If we accept the captain’s reported time of 3.15am, we can say the sinking occurred very rapidly, within just 11 minutes.
“We spotted life buoys and a lifeboat but it was empty. Unfortunately, no survivors have been found so far,” he said, indicating that search and rescue operations were ongoing.
He said there were 10 people on board: the captain and nine crew members, all of them Turkish nationals.
The cargo ship went down in waters that were approximately 900m deep, with 14 vessels and a helicopter involved in search and rescue efforts, the maritime directorate said.
“Life-saving equipment, including a lifeboat belonging to the Tugberk Imamoglu which had 10 crew members on board, has been found at sea. Unfortunately, the crew members were not inside,” it said.
The Alsu, which was damaged in the collision, was also participating in search and rescue efforts, it said.
Human error?
What caused the collision was not immediately clear but experts said it was likely human error.
“The Sea of Marmara is a heavily trafficked and closely monitored area, it has all the characteristics of a maritime highway,” maritime engineer Sabri Gokhan told the private NTV broadcaster.
“Ships don’t sink easily there. It was likely a mistake by the crew,” he said.
According to the VesselFinder tracking website, the Tugberk Imamoglu is a Turkish-flagged cargo ship built in 1990 which is 90m long.
At the time of the collision, it was carrying 4,200 tons of rolled sheet metal and rebar, the authorities said.
The maritime directorate initially said the Alsu was carrying 3,000 tonnes of motor oil, but later said the tanker was empty in a detail confirmed by the governorate.
The incident took place three days after a deadly ferry accident off Northern Cyprus in which eight Turkish nationals died, with rescuers still hunting for another 20 people listed as missing.
The last fatal shipwreck in the area occurred in September 2018 when a ferry that left Bandirma on the southern shores of the Sea of Marmara – which lies between the Black Sea and the Aegean Sea – sank, leaving one person dead and four missing. AFP

From Sushant Singh Rajput 'link' to CBI probe: The Disha Salian case so far
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
09:10:45 UTC
18:10:45 KST

The Bombay High Court on Wednesday ordered a CBI investigation into Disha Salian’s death, citing concerns over the prolonged police probe and failure to register an FIR
NEW DELHI: The Bombay High Court on Wednesday ordered the Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI) to register an FIR and take over the investigation into the death of Disha Salian, former manager of actor Sushant Singh Rajput, who died in June 2020.A bench of Justices Sarang Kotwal and Ranjitsinha Raja Bhonsale directed Mumbai Police to hand over all case records to the CBI and ordered that the probe be conducted by a suitably experienced and senior officer.The court also pulled up Mumbai Police over the manner and duration of its investigation, saying it had continued for about six years without an FIR being registered. The bench observed that the police investigation “raises more questions than it answers” and said a CBI probe was necessary.
The 44-page judgment said there were “glaring discrepancies” in the police investigation and called for a “proper and substantive” probe.“In this case, we are of the opinion that the police had sufficient opportunity to investigate the offence, but they have not registered the FIR and have not carried out the investigation of a cognisable offence,” the court said.Reacting to the order, Salian’s father Satish Salian, who has pursued the case for six years and alleged that his daughter was murdered, said he felt “relieved” but had no reason to celebrate after losing his daughter.
“I have been waiting for this for 6 years. There is no reason to be happy. I have lost my daughter. I feel relieved today. That's all,” he told reporters, adding that he had folded his hands and thanked the judge.
What is the case?
Disha Salian was found dead on June 8, 2020, after falling from the 14th floor of a residential building in Mumbai’s Malad area. Mumbai Police registered an Accidental Death Report (ADR) and, after an inquiry, maintained that she had died by suicide.Salian’s father challenged the police’s handling of the case and approached the Bombay High Court, alleging that his daughter had been gang-raped and murdered.He also alleged a politically orchestrated cover-up to protect influential people and sought registration of an FIR and a CBI investigation, including into allegations against Shiv Sena (UBT) MLA Aaditya Thackeray.The high court, however, made it clear that it was not expressing any opinion on the allegations against any individual. It said the CBI would have to determine whether the evidence gathered during its investigation warranted treating anyone as an accused.The court pointed to several aspects of the investigation that it said required closer examination. One issue was the spot panchnama, or the record of the scene where Salian’s body was found, which the court noted had been conducted belatedly.The bench also questioned the absence of blood at the spot. It raised doubts about whether the injuries recorded in the case were consistent with a fall from such a height.“If the deceased had fallen on her face from the 12th floor, then it is difficult to accept that there was only one injury on the chin of the body. Not a single facial bone was fractured. We find this difficult to accept,” the court said, as quoted by PTI.During an earlier hearing, the court had also questioned how a fall from such height could result in such limited injuries. The prosecution had argued that Salian suffered severe facial, skull and rib fractures and that rain could have washed away blood from the spot. The court noted that the rain cited by the prosecution had occurred several hours after the incident.The bench also noted an apparent discrepancy concerning Salian’s clothing. It observed that while the panchnama and post-mortem report stated that her body had no clothes, photographs from the hospital and morgue appeared to show her wearing clothes.“There is room for reasonable doubt in all these aspects. However, we are not drawing any conclusion at this stage,” the court said.The court had also earlier questioned why Mumbai Police had registered only an ADR despite the allegations raised by Salian’s family. It noted that copies of the post-mortem report and ADR had not been provided to the family even years after her death.Salian’s lawyer Nilesh Ojha had alleged discrepancies in the post-mortem report and argued that an FIR should have been registered on the basis of the allegations and material placed before the authorities.
What has the HC ordered?
The High Court directed the CBI to record Satish Salian’s statement and register an FIR. Mumbai Police was ordered to hand over all papers and records relating to the case to the central agency “forthwith”.The CBI has been asked to appoint a suitably experienced and senior officer to investigate the case.The court also imposed an important safeguard: no individual can be treated as an accused merely on the basis of the allegations made before the court.“Nobody shall be treated as an accused unless in the opinion of the investigating officer there are sufficient grounds to raise reasonable suspicion against him depending on the material collected during the investigation,” the court said.The bench also said that if the investigation finds that no criminal case is made out, the CBI must file an appropriate summary report before the competent court.“In case the investigation reveals that no case is made out, then the CBI shall file the appropriate summary report before the court concerned,” it said.Satish Salian will be free to challenge such a report and file objections before the court.The high court described Salian as an “unfortunate” father who had lost his young daughter in “tragic circumstances” and said the matter required a substantive investigation. At the same time, it refrained from commenting on the allegations made against specific individuals.Satish Salian’s petition sought an FIR and investigation into allegations against Shiv Sena (UBT) leader Aaditya Thackeray, son of former Maharashtra chief minister Uddhav Thackeray.The court however did not make any adverse finding against Thackeray and said it was for the investigating agency to examine the evidence.Thackeray had separately approached the high court seeking to intervene in the proceedings. In his application, he described Satish Salian’s petition as “false, frivolous and motivated” and sought an opportunity to be heard before any order was passed.
The case has also drawn attention because Salian had briefly worked as a manager for actor Sushant Singh Rajput.Rajput was found dead at his Bandra residence on June 14, 2020, six days after Salian’s death. The proximity of the two deaths led to widespread speculation, although the cases were investigated separately.
A CBI probe was also ordered into Rajput’s death. The agency subsequently filed a closure report stating that he died by suicide; the concerned court is yet to decide on the report.The latest order does not establish that Salian was murdered or that the allegations made by her family are true. It instead directs a fresh investigation by the CBI after finding that the police probe contained issues that, in the court’s view, warranted further examination.

18:08:23 KST

Range Rover has launched its first electric vehicle – a year later than planned – offering a greener option for fans of gargantuan British-made SUVs who are also conscious about the climate crisis.
Due to be built in Solihull, the home of the marque since 1970, the vehicle comes with an eye-watering price tag, starting at £154,070.
However, the delayed launch marks a milestone departure from cars powered by fossil fuels for Jaguar Land Rover (JLR), which is owned by India’s Tata Motors but headquartered in Coventry in the UK.
It also provides a much-needed moment of positivity for JLR, which reported falling profits earlier this year as it counted the cost of Donald Trump’s tariff wars and supply chain disruption after a crippling cyber-attack last year.
JLR said it had given extra training to 10,500 staff working on the project and that the car had undergone testing equivalent to 38 trips around the world, more than any other Range Rover.
The company said the luxury vehicle, which can reach 60mph in 4.3 seconds, heralded “a new era of enhanced refinement and capability”.
While the model’s electric powertrain will limit its impact on the environment compared with JLR’s petrol and diesel models, SUVs of its size are consistently linked to higher numbers of road deaths in accidents involving pedestrians.
However, Range Rover’s bespoke commissioning service does mean that buyers have an “extended choice of near limitless paint colours and finishes, elevated materials, tailored colour combinations and personalisation details including unique embroidery”.
Martin Limpert, the managing director of Range Rover, said the vehicle was the end product of a “decade of considered engineering and technological development”.
Production at Solihull will be supported by the automaker’s propulsion manufacturing centre, in Wolverhampton, which makes battery packs and electric drive units, as well as traditional internal combustion engines.

====================================================================================================

Chinese researchers crack tough challenge of low-grade iron ore utilization
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
17:06:02 CST
18:06:02 KST

BEIJING, Sept. 2 (Xinhua) -- For decades, billions of tonnes of iron-bearing mine tailings in China lay largely unused. Zhu Qingshan, a researcher at the Institute of Process Engineering (IPE) under the Chinese Academy of Sciences, once said: "Turning this 'sleeping wealth' into usable high-grade resources is key to solving the country's iron ore supply problem."
That vision has now become reality. On Tuesday, the world's largest iron ore magnetization roasting project, with an annual capacity of 5.56 million tonnes, passed official acceptance tests in Anshan, northeast China's Liaoning Province. It has been operating stably at full capacity, with key performance indicators exceeding design targets. The project marks a major breakthrough in the industrial use of low-grade iron ore.
According to the IPE, the technology is the world's first solution for large-scale industrial processing of ultra-low-grade iron tailings. It can turn tailings with an iron content of just 11 percent into concentrate with a grade of 65 percent.
This breakthrough is expected to enable efficient and green development and utilization of nearly 30 billion tonnes of refractory iron ore and almost 10 billion tonnes of iron-bearing tailings in China, the IPE said.
HALF-CENTURY QUEST
China consumes more than half of the world's iron ore. Although domestic reserves are abundant, most of the country's deposits are low-grade and hard to process with conventional methods. Over the past decade, China has imported 11.3 billion tonnes of iron ore. Tapping underused domestic resources has driven generations of researchers to tackle this long-standing technical challenge.
In the 1950s, the Institute of Chemical Metallurgy, the IPE's predecessor, began exploring ways to make efficient use of low-grade iron ore. Chemical engineer Mooson Kwauk pioneered fluidized-bed magnetizing roasting techniques to convert poor-quality iron minerals into recoverable magnetite.
Although the technology showed promise, its industrialization was interrupted due to the country's weak industrial base and the historical conditions at the time. Researcher Zhu Qingshan later took up the unfinished mission.
In 2004, Zhu began devoting himself to research on refractory iron ore. At that time, the technology still faced major hurdles to industrialization: conventional magnetizing roasting suffered from low reaction efficiency, high energy consumption and costs, and poor operational stability. Zhu's team introduced innovative technical approaches to address these issues and lay the groundwork for practical application.
FROM LAB TO INDUSTRIAL SCALE
For Zhu, successful basic research was not the end, but the starting point for industrial application. To turn research into usable technology, Zhu and his team developed a complete system for fluidized-bed magnetizing roasting, including key equipment and supporting technologies.
The team secured a partner in southwest China's Yunnan Province for a project with an annual capacity of 100,000 tonnes. However, the project stalled in 2008 amid the global financial crisis due to funding shortages. With support from various levels of government, the researchers spent more than a year troubleshooting on site, and the plant achieved continuous stable operation in December 2012.
This experience also exposed new limitations in the technology, prompting the team to further improve the roasting process and energy efficiency. They developed a second-generation magnetizing roasting process with more precise control of particle residence time, which was later introduced to Ansteel Group, one of China's major steelmakers.
At Ansteel, the technology has achieved a 98-percent conversion rate for iron minerals, delivering significant economic benefits. Eleven licensing agreements now cover a combined annual processing capacity of more than 15 million tonnes. The team is also advancing overseas projects, including a limonite upgrading initiative in Laos. Looking ahead, researchers plan to extend the technology to other mineral processing and solid-waste recycling applications. ■

China issues new national safety standard for large-scale fireworks displays
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
17:05:28 CST
18:05:28 KST

BEIJING, Sept. 2 (Xinhua) -- China has issued a revised mandatory national standard for the safe operation of large-scale fireworks displays, with the new rules set to take effect on Sept. 1, 2027, the State Administration for Market Regulation disclosed on Wednesday.
The standard, GB 24824-2026, was revised under the organization of the Ministry of Public Security and sets unified safety requirements for the design, operation and management of large fireworks displays used at major celebrations and cultural and tourism events.
The revised standard introduces a five-tier classification system for large fireworks displays, from Level I to Level V, based on the size and quantity of aerial shells and other professional fireworks used. Each level is matched with corresponding qualifications for operators and technical personnel, making clear who is responsible for the display.
It also specifies minimum spectator safety distances and tightens operating procedures, adding technical requirements for the fixing and installation angles of launch tubes, as well as rules covering installation, wiring checks and ignition.
Emergency provisions are also strengthened. Displays must be suspended or terminated in conditions including winds above Force 6, sudden heavy rain or thunderstorms, or accidents such as shell explosions inside launch tubes or overturned launch equipment.
Temporary storage sites must be staffed around the clock, and personnel may only enter the display area for cleanup 30 minutes after the show ends, according to the new standard.
The market regulator said it will work with the Ministry of Public Security to promote implementation of the standard and regularly assess its effectiveness.
China is the world's largest producer and consumer of fireworks and firecrackers. The revision comes as large-scale fireworks displays are increasingly used at major celebrations, tourism festivals and nighttime cultural events across China, raising demand for more standardized safety management at crowded public venues.
It also reflects a broader push to strengthen safety governance for large public events, with clearer operator qualifications, risk assessment requirements and emergency procedures aimed at reducing accidents and clarifying accountability. ■

Threatened freshwater fish face multiple extinction risks in Australia's Wet Tropics: study
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
17:05:23 CST
18:05:23 KST

SYDNEY, Sept. 2 (Xinhua) -- A study of Australia's Tropical North Queensland freshwater fish has found numerous species face severe risks of extinction from multiple threats, including habitat loss, invasive species, and warmer waters.
Led by Griffith University's Australian Rivers Institute, the assessment identified the Daintree rainbowfish, found only in small rainforest streams in the Daintree region of Far North Queensland, as the species facing the highest risk, with up to 10 unique threats to its population, according to a university statement released Wednesday.
"Freshwater fish are also important components of stream ecosystems and are indicators of ecosystem health. Their decline signals broader environmental deterioration," said lead author Kaitlyn O'Mara, research fellow at the Australian Rivers Institute.
"Many are found nowhere else on Earth. If they are lost from the Wet Tropics, they become globally extinct," O'Mara said.
The study, published in Pacific Conservation Biology, assessed 24 threats, including climate change, invasive species, water extraction, habitat degradation and hybridization.
Researchers found invasive species, climate-driven changes to temperature and hydrology, habitat and water quality degradation, and hybridization with translocated native fishes were among the most severe threats, particularly for narrowly distributed rainbowfish and migratory cling gobies.
They called for urgent conservation actions including habitat restoration, invasive species control, improved riparian management and captive breeding. ■

Chinese researchers design AI-driven platform to empower marine materials innovation
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
17:05:19 CST
18:05:19 KST

BEIJING, Sept. 2 (Xinhua) -- A group of Chinese researchers has unveiled the Robotic Marine Materials Scientist Platform, an intelligent fabrication system that dramatically improves materials research and development efficiency over conventional approaches.
Traditional materials research faces two long-standing bottlenecks: valuable marine experimental data from failed trials are often lost, hindering artificial intelligence (AI) model training, while repetitive manual operations consume time and introduce errors.
To address these challenges, researchers at the Ningbo Institute of Materials Technology and Engineering of the Chinese Academy of Sciences developed the Robotic Marine Materials Scientist Platform for severe marine environments: high temperature, high pressure, high speed, high salinity, and high humidity.
The platform, covering a 400-square-meter intelligent laboratory, automates the entire workflow from design and preparation to testing and feedback. Robots act as "materials scientists" and carry out these tasks autonomously, significantly accelerating the material innovation cycle.
Working in synergy with the "MarineMat AI" assistant, the platform creates a closed-loop R&D system spanning AI-driven design, automated fabrication, characterization, and data feedback. The platform automatically records and structures all experimental parameters for model iteration, with AI prediction accuracy exceeding 90 percent.
Using this platform, the researchers have developed a novel multi-component cermet composite with excellent temperature and wear resistance, achieving over 30 percent improvement in mechanical and tribological performance over conventional ternary materials.
The screw drills made from this material have been deployed in the Chuanke-1 scientific exploration well in south China's Shenzhen at depths of 7,500 to 10,000 meters. ■
