Across China: Revived wetland breathes new life into north China's green "city of future"
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
17:05:11 CST
18:05:11 KST

SHIJIAZHUANG, Sept. 2 (Xinhua) -- On a calm autumn evening, families paddled across Huizhi Lake in Xiong'an New Area's central green valley park, where waterbirds skimmed over reeds and trees lined the shore.
The lake lies within the Baiyangdian wetland in north China's Hebei Province. Once known as the "Pearl of North China" for its vast waterways, the area is now becoming an integral part of a modern city taking shape nearby.
"In many cities, paddleboarding is usually offered on the outskirts, because suitable waters are hard to find in the urban core," said Li Nan, head of a local paddleboarding club. "Here, people can enjoy nature right on their doorstep."
The club opened at Huizhi Lake in June. On peak weekend days, it receives more than 100 visitors, drawn by the sport's low entry barrier and the chance to get close to nature without leaving the city.
The central green valley is also just a short walk from the headquarters of several centrally administered state-owned enterprises. For their employees, the water offers an easy escape from the office.
"Paddleboarding is becoming a new way for some Xiong'an residents to relax and socialize," said Li.
For Xiong'an, often dubbed a "city of the future" being built from the ground up, such easy access to clean water and greenery is more than just a recreational amenity. It reflects an approach to urban development that places the natural landscape at the heart of the city's design.
On April 1, 2017, China announced plans to establish Xiong'an New Area to relieve Beijing of functions non-essential to its role as the national capital and advance the coordinated development of the Beijing-Tianjin-Hebei region.
The master plan for Xiong'an calls for green development, controlled development intensity and systematic ecological restoration, with Baiyangdian a key focus. Waterways, wetlands and green spaces are being woven into the urban fabric from the outset.
Since the establishment of Xiong'an New Area, Baiyangdian has undergone the largest systematic ecological restoration in its history, bringing a major leap forward in water quality.
In 2021, Baiyangdian's water quality improved to Grade III under China's national surface-water quality standards, a level it has maintained for five consecutive years. The wetland is now among China's lakes classified as having good overall water quality.
The restored landscape also opens new opportunities for local industries and breathes new life into cultural traditions.
Cattails, once abundant in Baiyangdian, had come to be seen as a nuisance. They could overgrow waterways and required labor-intensive removal, while the traditional craft of weaving cattails had gradually declined.
In 2024, Yangzhuangzi Village in Anxin County opened a workshop offering free cattail-weaving training to villagers. The initiative has helped turn a once-neglected craft into a source of employment and income.
"Water quality has improved in Baiyangdian in recent years, and the cattails have grown stronger and more resilient, making them better suited for handicrafts," said Yang Zhiliang, Party chief of Yangzhuangzi Village.
After visiting other regions to learn from their experience, the village decided to revive this craft.
Zhao Fengrong, 61, was among the workshop's first trainees. In her hands, ordinary cattails are transformed into baskets and other objects of various shapes.
"We used to weave cattails for our own use. We never imagined we could make money from the craft," Zhao said.
The workshop has helped more than 2,000 people in the village and surrounding areas find employment.
Xiong'an is also developing local brands around its cattail and reed weaving handicrafts, while short-video platforms, livestreaming and online stores are helping traditional products reach customers far beyond the wetland.
Revival, however, is not limited to livelihoods.
For generations, Baiyangdian has also inspired Chinese writers and poets. Its waterways, villages and wetlands have left a distinctive mark on local culture and helped nurture a notable community of poets.
At the Baiyangdian Poetry Culture Park in Anxin County, modern buildings blend with pathways and landscaped spaces. Poems are engraved on walls, steps and walkways, turning the park into an open-air cultural landscape.
In May, an exhibition hall for local poetry opened at the park, providing a venue for exhibitions, reading and cultural exchanges.
"Ecological restoration has given culture the soil it needs to thrive," said Ling Zhiqing, director of the exhibition hall and a native of the area.
Poet Lin Mang said the ecological environment of Baiyangdian has helped nurture the local poetry community. Since the establishment of Xiong'an New Area, he said, the landscape had undergone significant changes.
"Urban development and ecological protection can reinforce each other, allowing local culture, the spirit of poetry and the heritage of the water town to live on and flourish," Lin added. ■

Cambodia launches 10-year policy to eliminate landmines, cluster bombs, other ERWs by 2035
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
17:05:10 CST
18:05:10 KST

PHNOM PENH, Sept. 2 (Xinhua) -- Cambodia officially launched the National Mine Action Policy 2026-2035 on Wednesday, establishing a comprehensive 10-year roadmap aimed at eliminating all identified landmines, cluster bombs, and other explosive remnants of war (ERWs) across the country.
Under the policy document, the Southeast Asian nation aims to clear all identified landmines by 2030, and all identified cluster munitions and priority areas containing ERWs by 2035.
According to the policy document, Cambodia cleared 3,541 square kilometers of contaminated land between the start of humanitarian mine action in 1992 and 2025. Over those 33 years, deminers located and destroyed more than 1.2 million anti-personnel mines, 26,700 anti-tank mines, and 3.24 million ERWs.
Despite these significant achievements, critical challenges remain, the policy document said.
A total of 1,749 square kilometers of land is still contaminated, it said, adding that this includes approximately 557 square kilometers contaminated by landmines, 663 square kilometers affected by cluster munitions, and 529 square kilometers by other ERWs.
Ly Thuch, a senior minister and first vice president of the Cambodian Mine Action and Victim Assistance Authority (CMAA), emphasized that the policy provides a definitive roadmap to eradicate all explosive ordnance by 2035.
Cambodia remains one of the world's most severely affected nations regarding landmines and ERWs. According to the CMAA, landmine and ERW explosions claimed 19,852 lives and injured or amputated 45,301 others between 1979 and June 2026. ■

The sides noted that these agreements establish a solid legal and institutional framework for scientific and educational cooperation, facilitate academic mobility, open up new opportunities for the training of highly qualified specialists and deepen expert level interaction, which will become a key driver for mutual goodwill and strengthening people to people interactions.
The leaders noted with satisfaction the establishment of the Kyrgyz-Pakistan Joint Working Group on Tourism and instructed it to identify specific areas of cooperation, including the joint promotion of tourism products, exchange of experience and development of interaction between representatives of the tourism industries of the two States.
The sides welcomed the signing of the Treaty between the Kyrgyz Republic and the Islamic Republic of Pakistan on Extradition, the Agreement on Mutual Legal Assistance in Criminal Matters, as well as Memorandum of Understanding between the Ministry of Internal Affairs of the Kyrgyz Republic and the Ministry of Interior and Narcotics Control of the Islamic Republic of Pakistan on Cooperation in Combating Illicit Trafficking of Narcotic Drugs, Psychotropic Substances, new Psychoactive Substances, their Precursor Chemicals and Related Issues, particularly emphasizing the fundamental importance of this set of documents for strengthening cooperation in these areas. No eggs, no potatoes but ‘a lot of imagination’: how Spain cooked in war’s hunger years
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
09:00:27 UTC
18:00:27 KST

Few dishes are simpler to prepare than Spain’s signature dish of tortilla de patatas, which – aside from disputes about onions – requires nothing more than two basic ingredients and a pinch of salt. But where to begin if you have neither eggs nor potatoes?
That is the question the chef and food writer Berta Álvarez Acal sets out to answer in Recetas de Guerra (Wartime Recipes), a compilation of recipes covering the years of hunger after the end of the Spanish civil war in 1939.
In the case of the tortilla de patatas, the absent eggs and potatoes were substituted by moistened bread and onion to try to simulate the texture of an omelette.
“There was a formula using water, bicarbonate of soda and a bit of oil which simulated an egg perfectly and the potatoes are substituted by bread to make a tortilla that really is delicious,” Álvarez said.
In the recipe for “fried squid without squid”, deep-fried onion rings masquerade as squid while the “wartime hake” is instead salt cod.
As for the “wartime and postwar breakfast”, this consists of “coffee” made from a blend of barley, malt and chicory.
“I got the idea for the book when I came across one of my great-aunt’s handwritten recipe books and I noticed that some of the recipes were marked ‘wartime’,” Álvarez said. “That led me to research recipes from other sources such as Ignacio Doménech, who wrote a book during the war about how to substitute ingredients and how to make the most of leftovers.”
She added: “Doménech showed us hundreds of examples of how, with a lot of imagination, we could survive those terrible days of starvation.”
Some of Doménech’s recipes, although born of privation, could well find themselves on the menu of an upmarket restaurant today, such as his rose petals with milk and honey.
Álvarez did not just compile the recipes. “We recreated them and shared them with friends and family,” she said. “Some dishes, although they were prepared from scraps, surprised us as they were real gems, others were not so great.”
The recipes in the book span the period from the founding of the second republic in 1931 to the phasing out of ration cards in 1952. In between, starvation stalked the land, especially in areas that supported the losing republican side in the civil war.
According to Miguel Ángel del Arco Blanco, a historian at the University of Granada, between 1939 and 1942 about 200,000 people died of starvation in Spain.
While people in the countryside could to some extent subsist on olives and whatever they could grow, Álvarez said “the hunger in Madrid, Barcelona and Valencia was horrific”.
“It may seem implausible,” she said. “But for far too long, food in the postwar period was far worse than during the war.”
Produce previously fed to livestock such as beetroot and turnips found its way to the table while the shortage of protein meant pets, cats in particular, were at risk.
“They were dangerous years for cats,” Álvarez said. “People used to put notices up in the hallway saying ‘please respect your neighbour’s cat’. But the cats lived on rats and were not good to eat.”
Álvarez said that what she learned while researching the book was to make the most of every kind of produce, adding that the book was also a homage to the generation that lived through those grim years. “I think it’s important that everyone knows what our grandparents lived through because it marked them as a generation. They were incredibly strong.”

China's Xi holds talks with Egypt's Sisi
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
08:59:15 UTC
17:59:15 KST

Breadcrumb
China's Xi holds talks with Sisi in first Egypt visit in a decade
Egypt's President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi on Wednesday received his Chinese counterpart Xi Jinping on his first visit to Cairo in a decade, as Beijing seeks a greater foothold in the region against the backdrop of the US-Iran war.
The 21-gun salute at Cairo's Ittihadiya Palace marked the start of a day of talks expected to cover the Middle East war and its fallout, including on maritime trade security, as well as boosting Chinese investment in the Arab world's most populous country.
The two BRICS members are expected to sign a slate of economic agreements, including on artificial intelligence, transport and manufacturing.
Egypt currently estimates Chinese investments at around $10 billion. Beijing has key stakes in the Suez Canal Economic Zone, which are only expected to grow as the US-Iran war threatens global maritime trade.
Beijing has also played a key role in Sisi's megaprojects, the crowning jewel of which is the New Administrative Capital 50 kilometres (30 miles) east of Cairo, large swathes of which have been bankrolled by Chinese investment.
China is a major exporter to Egypt, with its trade surplus reaching $12 billion in the first seven months of 2026, according to Chinese customs data.
Across Cairo, a megalopolis home to over 26 million people, major streets have been lined with Chinese and Egyptian flags, as well as billboards showing Sisi and Xi.
Street signs boast of "generations of Egyptian-Chinese friendship flowing like the Nile River", while residents have been warned to plan for substantial traffic delays on their commutes.
Xi is expected to traverse the entire capital during his visit Wednesday, including a stop at the Grand Egyptian Museum overlooking the Giza Pyramids.
'Independent foreign policy'
According to analysts, Cairo will use the summit to underscore its strategic autonomy, showing it can leverage its close ties with both Washington and Beijing.
Sisi, in an op-ed published in Egyptian media on Tuesday, highlighted Cairo's "independent foreign policy", days after a branch of Egypt's second-largest bank was targeted by US sanctions.
He wrote that Egypt and China were partners in "strengthening the role of the global south" in an increasingly polarised world.
Washington vowed last month to isolate Iran economically, threatening expanded sanctions that could also hit Chinese banks, among others.
China, a major buyer of Iranian oil, has vowed to safeguard its interests.
In the lead-up to an expected meeting between Xi and US President Donald Trump this month, it has also sought to shore up ties with US-friendly regional nations.
Egypt is one of the largest recipients of US military aid, and historically a key Middle East mediator.
Last week, the US Treasury announced sanctions on the Emirati branch of Egypt's Banque Misr for alleged support to Iran.
Egypt—which under Sisi's administration became one of the world's top weapons buyers—hosted major joint air combat exercises with the Chinese military in August, featuring Beijing's powerful J-16 fighter jet.

Power grid near Cologne hit by suspected sabotage, German police say
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
08:58:37 UTC
17:58:37 KST

An electric substation near the German city of Cologne was the target of a sabotage attack, police said on Wednesday.
“Based on the current state of the investigation, we do not believe this was a technical malfunction, but rather a deliberate act — a criminal offense,” a police spokesperson for the western city of Essen told the German Press Agency.
The cause and circumstances of the incident in the Rhein-Erft district remain unclear. The investigation is in full swing.
According to the spokesperson, the police were called to the substation in the Rheidt district of Bergheim around 8 pm local time (1800 GMT) on Tuesday evening due to a technical malfunction.
A short circuit caused several power lines to fail. Based on current information, there was no outage of the general power supply.
Energy provider confirms incident
The facility belongs to the energy provider Amprion, which confirmed the incident.
“An incident occurred on Tuesday evening in the vicinity of Amprion’s Rommerskirchen substation in the Rhineland that affected the operation of power plant feeders,” the company stated early on Wednesday morning.
This reportedly led to equipment failures at RWE Power.
The Dortmund-based company added: “The general power supply was not affected at any time, and system stability was always ensured.”
Experts from Amprion are working with the relevant safety authorities to clarify the facts as quickly as possible and assess the impact.
Suspected sabotage at Brandenburg power plant
The incidents came after unidentified suspects carried out a sabotage attack on an electrical facility at a major power plant in the eastern state of Brandenburg on Tuesday, according to authorities.
Brandenburg Interior Minister Jan Redmann said the suspects used projectile devices to cause a short circuit in an extra-high-voltage line near the Jaenschwalde power plant.
“We cannot currently confirm that an explosive device detonated there or anything of that sort,” Redmann said.
Police earlier said devices apparently made from pyrotechnics had been found at an electrical substation, although reports differed over whether any of them exploded.
Daily Bild reported that police had confirmed an explosion and discovered several improvised incendiary and explosive devices, not all of which detonated.
Public broadcaster RBB, however, quoted police spokesperson Stefanie Pilz as saying that no explosion had occurred.
Grid operator 50Hertz said unknown perpetrators damaged several transmission lines, briefly interrupting operations. All lines were later restored, and the public electricity supply was unaffected.
The Jaenschwalde facility near the Polish border is one of Germany’s largest lignite-fired power stations.

Ryanair warns air fares in Europe will jump next year if oil price stays high
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
08:58:04 UTC
17:58:04 KST

Ryanair has warned that air fares in Europe will jump next year if the oil price remains high and that some airlines could go bust.
The Irish budget carrier has cut its passenger target for the year to 31 March, down from 216 million customers to 214 million, to help reduce its exposure to “unhedged winter oil” during the unprofitable off season, with jet fuel currently trading at $140 (£104) a barrel.
Ryanair expects passenger numbers between November and March to be broadly flat compared with the same period last year.
The company said: “If high oil prices continue through to summer 2027, Ryanair believes short-haul air fares in Europe will increase materially to reflect higher oil prices, as some less well-hedged competitors will struggle to maintain capacity or even survive this coming winter season.”
Brent crude, the global oil benchmark, touched $97.04 a barrel on Wednesday, the highest since late July, after renewed clashes between the US and Iran fuelled concerns over supply. It later eased back to just below $95.
Ryanair expects the cut to its winter schedule to reduce its winter losses by €70m (£60m) to €100m. But, because it has hedged 80% of its jet fuel at $67 a barrel, it expects to record another profitable year, albeit below last year’s record profit after tax.
The airline said it was on track to increase summer passenger numbers – between April and October – by more than 5% from 138 million to 145 million. Fares are drifting “modestly down” between August and September compared with last year, as flagged in July.
The rival budget airline Wizz Air reported on Wednesday that its passenger numbers had grown by 25.9% last month compared with a year earlier, driven by a jump in flight capacity.
Ryanair was forced to reassure travellers in July that its planes were safe after a passenger was saved from being sucked out of a window mid-flight. Ljubisa Karović was sucked out headfirst after an engine failure resulted in parts smashing an acrylic window during a flight from Thessaloniki in Greece to Memmingen near Munich in Germany.
His wife, Svetlana Grković, saved her 61-year-old husband by holding on to his legs and managed to pull him back in with the help of two other passengers.

Istanbul State Opera and Ballet to open new season on Sept 19
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
08:56:00 UTC
17:56:00 KST

The new season will feature the premieres of two operas, two ballet productions, two modern dance works and a children’s ballet.
Istanbul State Opera and Ballet (IDOB) will open its 2026-2027 artistic season on Sept. 19, featuring new opera, ballet and modern dance productions alongside a wide range of concerts at Istanbul’s Atatürk Cultural Center (AKM) and the Kadıköy Municipality Süreyya Opera House.
IDOB General Director and Artistic Director Caner Akgün told state-run Anadolu Agency that the season would open with Ludwig van Beethoven’s Symphony No. 9, featuring the IDOB orchestra and choir under the musical direction of İbrahim Yazıcı.
Akgün said the institution aims to highlight the healing power of art through its productions.
“We will stage Turgay Erdener’s ‘Afife,’ one of the most valuable ballet works in the history of the Republic. The IDOB ballet company is excited to bring this important work back to life under the conditions of AKM, with Beyhan Murphy’s concept. Our production of ‘Lucia di Lammermoor’ will also return,” he said.
Highlighting the importance of AKM for IDOB, Akgün said the institution had gained international recognition through the venue and its experienced artistic staff.
“IDOB has made a major impact not only in our country but also internationally, thanks to the influence of Atatürk Cultural Center and our strong and experienced team. We have created an environment where our international connections have grown and where we can convey our messages to the world from AKM. This is one of our greatest sources of pride,” he said.
William Shakespeare’s “Romeo and Juliet” ballet will also meet audiences in November.
Akgün said IDOB was focusing on Turkish values and supporting contemporary Turkish composers by staging both new works and pieces that had not been performed for many years.
“One of our most important works is Ahmet Adnan Saygun’s ‘Gilgamesh’ opera. We presented its world premiere for the first time in many years,” he said.
He added that “Edusa,” by Güldiyar Tanrıdağlı, the first female Turkish opera composer of the Republican era, would return to the stage. The work combines Tanrıdağlı’s music with a libretto by writer İskender Pala.
Akgün said IDOB was also creating opportunities for contemporary Turkish composers at the Süreyya Opera House and supporting new and experimental Turkish works.
The operas “Tehlikeli Oyun” and “Deli Dumrul,” which were staged last year, will return this season.
“We will stage the world premiere of Selman Ada’s ‘The Overcoat’ at the Süreyya Opera House this year. Selman Ada will also conduct the premiere of his work. It was inspired by Gogol’s ‘The Overcoat,’ and we are very excited about it,” Akgün said.
IDOB to perform in Italy
Gounod’s “Faust” will be staged in French in a contemporary ballet interpretation by the modern dance company, while Giuseppe Verdi’s “La Traviata” and “Falstaff” will continue to be performed.
The IDOB ballet company will also undertake an international project in December, performing “The Nutcracker” at Teatro Lirico di Cagliari, one of Europe’s leading opera houses.
The production will feature a reinterpretation by Turkish choreographer Mehmet Balkan.
Akgün described the project as a major source of pride and excitement for the company.
Akgün said IDOB had established protocols with the state opera and ballet companies of Sofia and Bucharest and was also collaborating with international artists at festivals.
The company’s classical ballet repertoire includes “Giselle,” which will return in February.
In March, IDOB will stage a neoclassical interpretation of a work by George Balanchine, founder of the New York City Ballet. The choreography, based on Pyotr Ilyich Tchaikovsky’s “Serenade,” will be accompanied by Philip Glass’ “Circle of Fifths.” Ulvi Cemal Erkin’s “Köçekçe” will also be incorporated into the program.
“We believe that, after detailed work with our principal choreographers and ballet company, we will present a very special evening,” Akgün said.
The season will close in May 2027 with Giacomo Puccini’s “Turandot.”
Italian director Roberto Catalano will stage the production, while Ayyub Guliyev, music director of the Azerbaijan State Theatre, will conduct the orchestra and serve as musical director.
Akgün said “Turandot” would have a special significance for the institution and remain an important part of its repertoire for many years.
IDOB will continue its projects for children and young audiences alongside its opera, ballet and modern dance productions. “Cinderella” and “The Little Prince” will remain in the repertoire, while auditions for the children’s choir will be held in October.
Fernando Melo’s “Wind Tree” will open the Istanbul Theatre Festival, organized by the Istanbul Foundation for Culture and Arts, on Oct. 24-25. The work will be added to IDOB’s repertoire from January.
The Modern Dance Company will continue its “Pinocchio” project, while “Delirium” and “Dance Adrenalin” will also remain in the program.
The new season will also feature Mozart’s “The Abduction from the Seraglio,” Wagner’s “The Flying Dutchman” and Britten’s “The Turn of the Screw.”
Akgün said producing works in different languages and styles helped raise the company’s artistic standards, adding that the depth and diversity of its repertoire were among the priorities of its artistic management.
IDOB aims to welcome around 200,000 spectators during the new season. Akgün noted that productions reaching occupancy rates of up to 90 percent demonstrated strong audience interest in high-quality performances.

Iran, US exchange new attacks: Who was hit in latest strikes?

Iran, US exchange new attacks: Who was hit in latest strikes?
Iran said the US bombed a wedding near the Strait of Hormuz, before Tehran launched missiles at Kuwait, Bahrain, Jordan, and Iraq.
The United States and Iran have exchanged a new round of attacks – the biggest in more than a month – raising fears of escalation into a wider regional war.
The US Central Command said it struck dozens of military targets along Iran’s southern coast.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4Top US lawmaker Mike Johnson says lying is part of some Iranians’ religion
- list 2 of 4US strikes on Iran kill child at wedding ceremony
- list 3 of 4Mark Ruffalo comments spark pushback against anti-Semitism ‘smear campaign’
- list 4 of 4‘We had an ordinary life’: Iran fisherwoman navigates uncertainty of war
US President Donald Trump on Tuesday said Iran will be “totally wiped out” if it retaliates against the US attacks. “If they do respond, they’ll be hit much harder,” he told Fox News in an interview.
Iran has responded by firing ballistic missiles towards Jordan, Bahrain, Kuwait and Iraq’s semi-autonomous Kurdish region. Tehran has accused the US of hitting a wedding party, killing at least four people.
Here is what’s happening in the US-Iran war.
Where did the US attacks hit?
Iran said that the US bombing of a house during a wedding celebration in the city of Kuhestak has killed at least four people. Esmaeil Baghaei, the spokesman for Iran’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs, called it a “brutal” attack, where more than 68 people, including women and children, were wounded.
Footage published by the Iranian Red Crescent Society showed a building with walls and windows blown out, and debris scattered on the ground.
The humanitarian group also published pictures of several children receiving treatment at a hospital in Sirik, which overlooks the Strait of Hormuz.
In addition to Kuhestak, the semi-official Tasnim news agency reported explosions in coastal cities including Konarak, Bandar Abbas, Jask, and Asaluyeh, as well as Qeshm Island.
The second consecutive night of US attacks comes as Washington is jostling to wrest control over the Strait of Hormuz, the global energy chokepoint, which remains under Iranian blockade and has become Tehran’s bargaining chip.
Two locations near the cities of Ahvaz and Aghajari in Iran’s southwestern Khuzestan province were hit in missile attacks, the province’s deputy governor for security affairs said, according to the state broadcaster IRIB.
Seven people were killed at three locations in the province, and eight others were injured in the attacks, the IRIB reported.
In total, at least 18 people have been killed across Iran.
Where did Iran hit back?
Iran’s military said it launched attacks on US bases and assets in Jordan, Bahrain, Kuwait, and Iraq’s Erbil.
Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said its forces carried out a combined missile and drone attack on US facilities in Erbil province in northern Iraq in retaliation for the US strike.
Iran claimed it hit the Sheikh Isa Airbase, which hosts US forces, in Bahrain. The IRGC said it launched a “heavy” ballistic missile attack on Prince Hassan airbase and a US Marine base in Jordan, and hit the headquarters and residence of the American commander of the Ali Al Salem airbase in Kuwait.
Tehran said its attack on Kuwait set fire to a drone hangar and a ramp through which UAVs participated in attacks on Iran, adding that several US drones were also destroyed, and claimed to have killed a number of US soldiers.
Kuwait reported intercepting drones and missiles but did not report any casualties. There was no immediate comment from Washington, either.
Jordanian armed forces said air defence systems intercepted and destroyed 10 of 13 Iranian ballistic missiles that entered the kingdom’s airspace earlier, with the remaining three falling in remote areas without causing casualties.
What are US, Iran saying?
Washington and Tehran have upped the ante in attacks and political rhetoric amid a diplomatic deadlock. Speaking at the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation Summit in Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said Tehran will reciprocate if the US returns to the terms of the June Memorandum of Understanding that halted the military hostilities. The two sides have failed to agree before the deal expired on August 17.
Iran’s Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei said his country “has unforgettable lessons for the American enemy”.
Baghaei, the Iranian spokesman, called for global action against the US strike on the wedding function.
“This cruelty cannot be separated from the chain of atrocities that preceded it,” he said, pointing to attacks on the city of Minab and Lamerd on the first day of the war.
In Minab, US forces struck an elementary school, killing more than 150 people, and in Lamerd, they hit a sport hall, killing at least 21 people.
“Iran will respond to these savage crimes with firmness,” Baghaei said. “Still, those governments and international institutions that remain silent in the face of such barbarism, or seek to justify such acts, must understand that their silence is not neutrality.”
In the US, Trump said he is not trying to force Iran back to the negotiating table, dismissing reports that Washington is seeking a new agreement with Tehran.
“I like our position now much better, with almost total control of the Hormuz Strait, and their economy totally collapsing,” Trump said in a post on Truth Social.
He added that Iran was “playing out the inevitable” and asked: “When are the Iranian people going to rise up and fight?”
Alexandru Hudisteanu, a maritime security expert, told Al Jazeera that the recent escalation in the US-Israel war on Iran is unlikely to be a one-off “because this war has not been settled in military terms and both sides have the impetus to go to war from time to time”.
It can become “a repeatable pattern” although the war is no longer “in an active phase”, he said.
He added, “there are still conditions that create these flare-ups, especially because the US is trying to show that Iran does not have monolithic control over the Strait of Hormuz and on who passes through the strait.”
The talks over the status of Hormuz have been deadlocked, with Washington demanding an end to the Iranian blockade without any conditions while Tehran wants the US to end its naval blockade on its ports.
The latest escalation comes a week after the US imposed a slew of economic sanctions to pressure Iran to come to the negotiating table. Tehran says the US economic pressure will fail.

17:53:19 KST

The weight-loss pill Wegovy is now available in German pharmacies. Its active ingredient semaglutide increases satiety and the adult dose costs 170 to 280 euros.
The Wegovy weight-loss pill from Danish manufacturer Novo Nordisk will be available in German pharmacies from 1 September. Following EU approval in July, Germany is the first country in which Wegovy is being sold. Novo Nordisk described the authorisation as a "milestone".
The prescription-only medicine is intended as an alternative to the weight-loss injection already on the market and works with the same active ingredient: semaglutide. It mimics a gut hormone that is responsible for the feeling of fullness.
The retail pharmacy price of the weight-loss pill is expected to be between 170 and 280 euros, a spokesperson for the manufacturer explained. While the injectable version of Wegovy has already been approved for children aged 12 and over, the tablet form is only approved for adults.
When taking semaglutide tablets, adults with overweight reduced their body weight by an average of around 13.6 percent, according to the OASIS-4 study, which essentially formed the basis for EU approval. It was carried out by an international team of researchers.
In the trial, 205 participants took the drug. A further 102 participants received a placebo. With the injection, the average weight loss was higher, at 19 percent. However, the treatment period in that study was 72 weeks, two months longer than for the tablet (64 weeks).
As with the injection, the oral version also comes with side effects: many patients who use the medicine experience gastrointestinal complaints, including nausea and diarrhoea. It can also lead to inflammation of the pancreas.
Compared with the injection, the tablet has to be taken every day. For the injection, administering it once a week is sufficient. For both products, however, what matters alongside regular use is diet and exercise, said Julia Szendrödi, president of the German Diabetes Association.
100 billion dollar market
"Whether injection or tablet: medicines against obesity are not miracle cures for optimising weight, but components of a therapy for a chronic disease," said Szendrödi.
The use of products such as Wegovy is always part of a broader treatment concept. These drugs do not replace prevention, Szendrödi added. There is a need for better nutrition labelling, quality standards for school meals and restrictions on advertising unhealthy foods to children.
Globally, the market for weight-loss medicines is fiercely contested. According to analysts, by 2030 it could be bringing in 100 billion dollars a year for pharmaceutical companies, business daily Handelsblatt reports. Various products are now available. In the United Kingdom, for instance, the pill "Foundayo" from US manufacturer Eli Lilly will be on sale from the end of August.
These weight-loss medicines are intended for people with obesity, with a body mass index (BMI) above 30. In cases of conditions such as type 2 diabetes or sleep apnoea that are linked to excess weight, they can also be used below a BMI of 30.

The French President and Dutch Premier will meet in Eindhoven to discuss how to strengthen ties, especially concerning the shared priority of bolstering European sovereignty.

The 11th-century Bayeux Tapestry, which famously depicts the conquest of England by William the Conqueror of Normandy, arrived in London in July for the sell-out exhibition, after leaving France for the first time in more than nine centuries.
Experts feared it could be damaged but the French culture ministry insisted it had arrived in good condition.
Macron is "very eager" to see the tapestry displayed "in optimal conditions" laid out flat at full length on a table, the French presidential official said.
On the diplomatic side, Britain's new Prime Minister will be looking for concrete outcomes from Macron, as he eyes closer post-Brexit cooperation with the European Union.
The British leader — who replaced predecessor Keir Starmer in July — has vowed to boost sluggish UK growth and keep pushing France for help stopping migrants crossing the Channel to Britain aboard small boats.
Burnham has largely focused on domestic policy since taking over, but has also appeared eager to project his standing on the international stage, in particular maintaining London's support for Ukraine following Russia's 2022 full-scale invasion.
Starmer had enjoyed some success in this area, working closely with Macron and winning admiration from allies. Macron built with Starmer the best relationship with any of the five UK premiers he has seen prior to Burnham, during his near decade in office.
The pair adopted lead roles in a so-called Coalition of the Willing of nations supporting Ukraine. The French leader has remained eager to press his vision of European sovereignty not dependent on the United States, where the United Kingdom is seen as having a crucial role to play even after Brexit.

Ukraine strikes Russian naval drone in Black Sea
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
08:50:43 UTC
17:50:43 KST

- Ukraine's Navy destroyed a Russian uncrewed surface vessel near Snake Island using a precision strike from a drone.
- The destroyed vessel was likely a Russian KAMA-class drone boat, first unveiled in June 2026 with a stated range of 700 kilometers.
Ukraine’s Navy said it destroyed a Russian uncrewed surface vessel near Snake Island in the Black Sea on Tuesday, according to Militarnyi.
Footage released alongside the announcement shows the drone boat being struck by a precision munition dropped from an unmanned aerial vehicle after being detected. The vessel caught fire and detonated following the strike. Based on the released footage, Ukraine appears to have used a Bayraktar TB2 drone, a Turkish-made system Ukraine has operated since before the full-scale invasion, to carry out the attack.
Ukraine’s Navy said the destroyed vessel was likely a KAMA-class uncrewed boat built by Russian drone maker ZALA, the same company behind the Lancet loitering munition widely used against Ukrainian forces and equipment.
ZALA first unveiled the KAMA publicly in June 2026 at the International Maritime Defense Show “FLOT-2026” in Kronstadt, near St. Petersburg. The company presented two versions of the platform, one with a waterjet propulsion system and one with an outboard motor, both intended for what ZALA described as civilian and dual-use missions, including hydrographic surveys, environmental monitoring, search-and-rescue operations, port and oil platform security, and cargo delivery to islands.
According to specifications ZALA released at the unveiling, the KAMA has a maximum range of 700 kilometers (435 miles) from shore and can carry a payload of up to 600 kilograms (1,323 pounds), allowing for a range of onboard equipment including electro-optical sensors and thermal imaging cameras. The jet-propelled version measures 6.5 meters (21 feet) long and weighs about 1,000 kilograms (2,205 pounds) with a fiberglass hull, while the outboard motor version is slightly larger at 7.9 meters (26 feet) and roughly 1,200 kilograms (2,646 pounds). Both versions reach a maximum speed of around 30 knots and can operate in sea states up to three, according to the manufacturer, navigating using satellite positioning, an inertial navigation system, and marine radar.
Defense analysts who examined the KAMA at its unveiling noted that despite ZALA’s framing of the platform around civilian applications, the design closely resembles other Russian uncrewed surface vessels already documented in offensive roles, including a camera-equipped variant used in a May 2026 attack on Odesa. No dedicated attack or “kamikaze” configuration of the KAMA had been publicly announced by ZALA prior to Tuesday’s strike, though analysts had previously said such an adaptation could not be ruled out given the platform’s modular payload capacity.
Snake Island, a small outpost in the northwestern Black Sea near the mouth of the Danube, has remained a recurring flashpoint throughout the war given its strategic position along shipping lanes used for Ukrainian grain exports. Ukrainian forces have conducted repeated strikes on Russian naval assets and reconnaissance platforms operating in the surrounding waters since retaking the island from Russian forces in 2022.

World leaders missing in action as UN warns of climate target breach
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
08:47:38 UTC
17:47:38 KST

1.5C global warming breach likely as Australia defends Pacific climate talks
In short:
The prime minister has hit back at criticism over the federal government's high-profile climate meeting for world leaders next month.
It comes as a UN report warns the world is unlikely to keep global warming below 1.8C.
What's next?
Pre-COP will be held in Fiji and Tuvalu in early October before COP31 gets underway in November.
The prime minister has defended the number of leaders attending a high-profile climate meeting in the Pacific Islands, as a United Nations report warns the world will breach the 1.5C global warming benchmark within the next five years.
The federal government had initially wanted world leaders to attend pre-COP next month, ahead of the main climate talks in Türkiye in November.
Fiji and Tuvalu are hosting the lead-up event as part of a compromise, after Australia's failed bid to host COP31, the world's largest annual climate summit.
Reports said Australia was struggling to convince leaders outside the Pacific to attend a special meeting in Tuvalu, before Fiji's foreign minister, Sakiasi Ditoka, gave the first public account of those going.
He said Antigua and Barbuda, Cabo Verde, Thailand, Maldives and Timor-Leste had so far agreed to send leaders to the event, and Germany, Mexico and South Korea will send ministers.
When questioned about attendance at the pre-COP while speaking to media at the Pacific Islands Forum in Palau, Anthony Albanese said the government had always anticipated that a pre-COP event would not attract the same level of patronage as COP itself.
"The fact that the pre-COP is being held in Fiji with a side trip to Tuvalu as well is something that is really welcomed because what it will do is provide a focus on what is happening in the Pacific.
"The entry fee for credibility at the Pacific Islands Forum and for bilateral engagement in the Pacific is taking climate change seriously."
The prime minister also voiced his displeasure with the line of questioning.
"You are being so disrespectful to the Pacific leaders who are here," he said.
"We need to actually have some respect for the process and respect for our Pacific leaders, and Australia has an absolute interest in engaging with the Pacific."
The government pitched pre-COP as an opportunity to show leaders the perils that climate change poses to low-lying island nations in the Pacific, and to drive greater global action on climate change.
However, the nations sending leaders are hardly major polluters, nor do they need reminding of the risks climate change poses to vulnerable countries.
Energy Minister Chris Bowen said pre-COP was a "key opportunity" for the Pacific.
"The Pacific said to us, 'We thought it would be good to invite some leaders.' We've done that," he said.
"There's a very small component in Tuvalu, which is a small country, with limited capacity to host people.
"But that will be important in terms of not only prime ministers, heads of multilateral development banks, cabinet ministers who often don't attend pre-COP either but are coming to this one."
'Every fraction of a degree counts'
The growing climate risks confronting Pacific nations have been underscored by a landmark UN report, which has warned the world will likely pass 1.5C global warming in 2030.
It found that a temperature rise peak of 1.8C above pre-industrial levels was now the best-case scenario and highlights what can be done to return to 1.5C after the overshoot.
Countries have been trying to keep global temperatures to well below 2C as part of the Paris Agreement, a legally binding international treaty on climate change.
That includes an agreement to "pursue efforts" to limit warming to 1.5C above pre-industrial times.
That target was chosen because the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) indicates that crossing that threshold risks unleashing far more severe climate change impacts.
Climate Change Authority chair Matt Kean said urgent climate action remained necessary, despite the likelihood that the 1.5C target would be exceeded.
"Every fraction of a degree that we can limit global warming will reduce the danger and reduce the cost," he said.
"There is a huge reason for Australia and indeed the rest of the world to limit global warming; the economic consequences will be dire if we don't, and the danger to lives and livelihoods will be severe if we don't.
"So the message is very clear: we need to speed up the pace at which we're reducing our emissions."
Malte Meinshausen, professor of Climate Science at the University of Melbourne, said the energy transition means some of the worst scenarios that were possible a few years ago are no longer likely.
But he added that failure to reduce global emissions quickly meant the ideal scenario of limiting warming to just above 1.5C was no longer available.
"Compared with our options five years ago, the new paths are more costly, come with more floods, fires and droughts and the need to draw, at some point, carbon emissions out of the atmosphere that we are currently emitting," Professor Meinshausen said.
"Acting now is still the cheaper option than not acting now, as we can still achieve 1.5C in the longer term."
Calls for Australia to do more
Speaking at the Pacific Islands Forum, Vanuatu's Climate Change Adaptation and Energy Minister, Ralph Regenvanu, said Australia was not doing enough to curb carbon emissions.
"Australia is a major producer of fossil fuels; we all know fossil fuels are the primary driver of the climate crisis,"
"The very least a country like Australia should be doing is stopping future expansion, and it's not doing that. You need to stop expansion, and you need to start transitioning away."
The comments come a day after Federal Resources Minister Madeleine King helped open a project that will feed gas fracked from the Beetaloo Basin into the Northern Territory's power grid.
Mr Albanese defended Australia's approach to the energy transition, saying the country was "highly regarded" on climate change.
"The Pacific leaders have respect for the position that we've taken, and they also understand […] because they're dealing with it as well, that the transition can't happen overnight.
"It requires strategies and policies to be put in place, and one of the things that renewables require is firming capacity, and gas has a role to play in firming capacity."

Spain sheds almost 163,000 jobs in August as unemployment climbs
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
08:44:26 UTC
17:44:26 KST

The Spanish economy lost 162,840 jobs last month with 44,419 registering as unemployed. The drop represents the smallest decrease in August since the Covid-19 pandemic.
August once again brought negative figures for employment in Spain.
Spain's Social Security system lost 162,840 contributors, while unemployment increased by 44,419 people, in a month traditionally marked by the end of the tourist season and a fall in hiring for sectors such as education.
Despite the drop, the loss of contributors is the smallest recorded in an August since the Covid-19 pandemic. On a year-on-year basis, the Spanish labour market has created around 680,000 jobs.
At the end of the second quarter of 2026, the unemployment rate in Spain fell to 9.87%, the lowest since the first quarter of 2008, compared to 10.83% in the previous period and forecasts of 10.7%.
In 2026, the figures are also influenced by the process of regularising foreign workers.
By the end of August, the Social Security system counted 337,917 contributors incorporated through this process, which has helped cushion the seasonal fall in those paying into the system.
In total, foreign workers already exceed 3.5 million contributors and represent 15.9% of the total labour force.
These figures have led Spain's Minister for Inclusion, Social Security and Migration, Elma Saiz, to describe the evolution of the labour market as "historic job growth".
Education accounts for the biggest job losses
Education is once again the sector hardest hit by the seasonal drop in registrations.
More than 78,000 teachers and other education professionals have ceased to be affiliated, coinciding with the holiday period and the interruption of numerous contracts during the summer.
The end of the peak tourist season has also contributed to the drop in registrations and the rise in unemployment.
"As it happens every summer, when the holidays end, unemployment rises because of seasonal work", explained Spain's Second Deputy Prime Minister and Labour Minister Yolanda Díaz.
The increase in unemployment is higher than that seen in recent years for this month.
The figures, however, are again partly shaped by the regularisation of foreign workers, as some of those benefiting from the process have registered as jobseekers.
The total number of unemployed people stands at 2,356,000 which is the lowest level recorded in an August since 2007.

BP shares fell as much as 9% following the announcement of his departure before recovering some of those losses.
Tyler joined BP’s board as a non-executive director in April 2025. He is a former chief executive of construction group Balfour Beatty and currently chairs building materials company Grafton Group.
BP said Tyler had worked alongside more than 15 chief executives during a non-executive career spanning listed and privately owned companies in the oil and gas, natural resources and engineering sectors.
“Ian brings significant experience providing challenge and support to executive teams, while maintaining strong governance and oversight on behalf of shareholders,” said Dame Amanda Blanc, BP’s senior independent director.
Tyler will lead the board as it oversees chief executive Meg O’Neill’s restructuring programme. Her priorities include simplifying BP’s portfolio, strengthening its balance sheet and imposing tighter investment discipline.
BP is seeking to reduce net debt to between $14 billion (€12bn) and $18 billion (€15.4bn) by the end of 2027. The company estimated in July that its net debt stood at between $22 billion and $23 billion at the end of June.
The debt target formed part of a strategic reset announced in February 2025, when BP shifted investment back towards oil and gas, reduced planned spending on low-carbon businesses and promised tighter capital allocation.
BP also announced that Blanc, who oversaw the searches that led to the appointments of both Manifold and Tyler, would not seek re-election at next year’s annual general meeting. She will leave the board once a successor has been appointed.

Signs before puberty could predict painful periods, study finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
08:40:46 UTC
17:40:46 KST

A new study has found that non-painful symptoms in young girls, such as fatigue and dizziness, could help predict who is at risk of painful periods later on.
Experiencing non-painful symptoms, such as fatigue and dizziness, before the first period might signal a higher risk of dysmenorrhoea — painful menstruation for the years to come, according to a new study published in The Lancet Child & Adolescent Health.
Many women struggle with period pain, which starts in adolescence and can affect their lives for years after. Researchers hope that addressing some of the symptoms before a person's first menstrual period could reduce the burden of dysmenorrhoea on young women.
“Identifying risk factors for dysmenorrhoea, especially severe dysmenorrhoea, has the potential to improve outcomes for female adolescents through early and more targeted treatment,” the authors wrote.
The researchers analysed data from over 2,000 adolescents and found that non-painful somatic symptoms – such as fatigue, dizziness, gastrointestinal problems, nightmares or sensory changes – and advanced pubertal development at ages nine to ten are strong indicators of future menstrual pain.
Dysmenorrhoea is common in adolescence and is often dismissed as inevitable or left untreated, the authors wrote. It can interfere with daily functioning and lead to other chronic pain conditions; however, little is known about its risk factors, and the lack of research before the first period is hindering efforts to identify those at risk.
Previous research has found that approximately 70% of female adolescents experience menstrual pain, and in 20% of cases it has a significant impact on their daily activities.
The study also found that sleep problems were strongly associated with a greater impact of pain on daily activities. Researchers say that addressing sleep disturbances before the first period could help to reduce the pain burden.
For example, cognitive behavioural therapy targeting this issue in adolescents with chronic pain shows promise for easing both the sleep problems and the resulting pain interference.
“These findings raise the possibility of identifying at-risk individuals before pain becomes a lifelong issue,” the authors wrote.

The current owner’s family bought it in the mid-1970s for 2,500 Belgian francs, equivalent to a good 60 euros. It is expected to fetch between 40,000 and 70,000 euros.
During the Zoute Grand Prix, the classic and luxury car event in Knokke-Heist, a very special car will be auctioned: the Cadillac Series 62 Convertible in which King Boudewijn was often driven in parades in the early 1950s. Value multiplied by 1,000
The current owner’s family bought the Cadillac from another collector in 1976. The original invoice, which is still with the car, shows a price of 2,500 Belgian francs. That is equivalent to just over 60 euros. Broad Arrow Auction House estimates that it will now fetch 1,000 times that amount, roughly speaking.
The auction will take place on Friday 9 October, but the car will be on display two days beforehand.

====================================================================================================

Sharp rise in utility bills pushes Russia's inflation further off target
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
08:34:54 UTC
17:34:54 KST

The October increase follows a January rise and is the first double tariff hike in four years. The central bank warned it would push annual inflation further above its 4% target in an economy already squeezed by the costs of its war, sanctions and a 21% key interest rate.
Russia is raising utility tariffs for the second time this year, with an average 15% increase taking effect on 1 October — a move the central bank says will push inflation further above its target in an economy already under severe pressure from war costs and sanctions.
The increase will range from 8% to 22% depending on the region. Residents of Stavropol Krai, Dagestan, and the Tambov and Tyumen regions face the steepest rises, while Moscow tariffs will go up 15% and St Petersburg 14.6%.
An earlier 1.7% increase took effect in January. Raising tariffs twice in a single calendar year is rare in Russia — the last time it happened was in 2022, the first year of Moscow's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
The Kremlin has justified the increases by citing ageing communal infrastructure and the need for modernisation.
Utility networks across much of the country date from the Soviet era and have received insufficient investment for decades. Repeated harsh winters and deferred maintenance have accelerated their deterioration.
Sanctions imposed because of Russia's war in Ukraine have restricted access to imported equipment needed for repairs, and the workforce available for infrastructure projects has shrunk as labour has been absorbed by military production and conscription.
The Bank of Russia said the October tariff rise would contribute noticeably to faster annual inflation. Its baseline forecast puts annual inflation in 2026 at 6-7% — well above its 4% target.
Measures affect the small and the poor
After the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, Russia faced a combination of external pressure and internal restructuring.
Western sanctions restricted access to financial markets, technology and equipment. Trade flows were rerouted. State spending rose sharply, concentrated on military procurement and related industries.
The economy avoided deep recession, but the adaptation came at a cost. Growth became increasingly dependent on state contracts and military production, while civilian industries faced labour shortages, expensive borrowing and limited access to technology.
The central bank raised its key interest rate to 21% in late 2024 in response to inflation, making credit extremely expensive for businesses and households. It has kept rates high since.
High borrowing costs have depressed private investment and squeezed smaller companies that cannot access state financing.
Utility bills are a fixed cost that households cannot cut. For lower-income families, a 15% rise in heating, water and electricity charges directly reduces money available for food, clothing and other spending, at a time when food prices have also risen sharply. For higher earners, the same percentage increase matters far less.
Businesses face parallel pressure. Factories, logistics companies, shops and offices all depend on utility services. When costs rise, operating margins shrink, and companies pass costs on to consumers, adding further to inflation.
The Russian economy has relied significantly on domestic demand to sustain growth since 2022.
A squeeze on household spending power from rising mandatory costs works against that dynamic, particularly in regions where wages have not kept pace with inflation and where military contract income is less prevalent than in major cities.

Twelve Israel Prison Service staff indicted over 2023 alleged assault, death of security prisoner
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
08:34:35 UTC
17:34:35 KST

The prosecution indicted 12 Israel Prison Service (IPS) personnel and former employees on Tuesday over the death of security prisoner Thaer Abu Asab and the alleged assault of eight other inmates at Ketziot Prison in November 2023.
The indictment, filed with the Beersheba District Court, charges all 12 with reckless homicide, aggravated serious bodily harm, and multiple counts of aggravated assault causing bodily harm.
The shift commander and shift sergeant are also charged with obstructing an investigation.
The filing moves a case that began with the questioning of 19 prison personnel nearly three years ago, in formal criminal proceedings.
According to the indictment, the shift commander had earlier shared with some of the defendants his distress over the deaths of Druze soldiers in battle. Later that afternoon, Abu Asab, who was being held with eight other security prisoners, asked the shift sergeant whether there was a hudna (“ceasefire”) in the war. The sergeant relayed the question to the commander.
Commander allegedly led group into cell, ordered attacks
Before the evening count, the commander allegedly told the personnel taking part that they would depart from the normal procedure and enter the cell to show the prisoners that there was no ceasefire.
The indictment alleges that the commander told the group he would take responsibility for whatever happened and said prison management was aware of what was taking place. He also allegedly warned female officers attending the briefing not to enter the cell so that they would not be hurt.
Shortly after 7 p.m., the commander led the group to the cell and began the count. Prosecutors allege that he then ordered the other defendants inside, where they jointly attacked Abu Asab and the eight other prisoners with punches and kicks. Some allegedly used batons.
The commander is accused of directing the assault from inside the cell and personally striking at least one prisoner. After several minutes, he ordered the group to stop, according to the indictment.
None of the defendants reported the alleged assault or recorded any unusual incident during the count, prosecutors said.
Abu Asab collapsed and lost consciousness shortly after the group left. Other prisoners called for help, and medical staff took him to the prison clinic. He had no pulse and did not appear to be breathing. He was resuscitated and transferred to Soroka Medical Center in Beersheba, where he was pronounced dead at 10:22 p.m.
Cardiac, respiratory injuries from beating deemed cause of death
Prosecutors attribute his death directly to the beating. The indictment says he suffered multiple broken ribs and tears in the walls of his heart, causing cardiac failure and bleeding around the organ. His broken ribs also damaged his respiratory system and prevented his lungs from expanding properly.
The combined cardiac and respiratory injuries ultimately caused his death, according to the prosecution. The other prisoners suffered bruising and injuries to their backs, arms, shoulders, and other parts of their bodies.
Early reports following Abu Asab’s death said an autopsy had found extensive signs of violence but had not conclusively established that he died from the blows. The indictment now presents a specific medical account connecting the alleged assault to his death.
The second charge concerns what prosecutors describe as attempts to interfere with the subsequent police investigation.
The shift sergeant allegedly instructed one of the defendants, before he was questioned, to tell investigators that no batons had been used.
The shift commander is accused of contacting another prison officer after his own questioning and asking him to relay instructions to female officers who had not yet been interviewed.
They were allegedly told to say that the defendants entered the cell only after the prisoners caused a disturbance and that any force used was part of a legitimate attempt to regain control.
One of the officers initially gave investigators a false account but later admitted that she had lied and provided her version of the incident, according to the indictment.
Abu Asab, 38, was a Fatah member from the Kalkilya area who had been imprisoned since 2005 following convictions for attempted murder and other security offenses.
The IPS said the incident occurred under the previous prison commissioner.
It added that the current commissioner had ended the service of some of those involved after taking office, saying the organization would not tolerate breaches of the law or its disciplinary rules.

Suspect in Jerusalem baby food contamination case named as Yan Shemla
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
08:34:31 UTC
17:34:31 KST

Yan Shemla was named on Wednesday as the suspect arrested in connection with the suspected deliberate contamination of baby fruit-puree jars with sedative drugs in Jerusalem.
The Jerusalem Magistrate’s Court extended his detention on Tuesday until September 6 after finding that the investigative material established a “significant” reasonable suspicion of his involvement.
Police suspect Shemla of deliberately inserting sedative substances into jars of Prinok fruit puree sold at two Zol Begadol supermarket branches on Jaffa Street.
The offenses under investigation include using poison in a manner that endangers life, theft, and negligent handling of medication.
Shemla, a resident of southern Israel, was arrested at his home on Monday after police reported a breakthrough in the investigation. Officers searched the property before taking him for questioning.
The Magistrate’s Court initially allowed his name to be published but temporarily delayed the decision at the request of his attorney, giving the defense time to consider an appeal. His identity was released on Wednesday morning.
Attorney Zecharia Shenkolevsky, who is representing Shemla through the Public Defender’s Office, said his client has a mental-health condition and is in a complex psychological state.
Several young children hospitalized in Hadassah Medical Center
“The investigation is in its early stages, and we expect it to be conducted while protecting his rights, certainly in light of his medical circumstances,” Shenkolevsky said. He added that Shemla was cooperating with investigators.
The case began in June after several young children were hospitalized at Hadassah-University Medical Center in Ein Kerem with drowsiness, weakness, and apathy after consuming Prinok fruit puree.
They were later discharged in stable condition.
Laboratory testing found clonazepam and lorazepam in five jars examined during the investigation. Both are prescription medications from the benzodiazepine family and can cause drowsiness, weakness, and confusion.
The Health Ministry said all five jars appeared to have been opened or tampered with before they were purchased.
Tests of products obtained from the importer found no contamination, and the ministry said it had found no indication of a manufacturing defect.
The findings shifted the investigation toward the possibility that the substances had been inserted after the jars left the importer. No general recall of Prinok products was issued.
Involved Zol Begadol branches close, then reopen with restrictions
The two Zol Begadol branches where the jars were sold were initially closed and later prohibited from selling food and cosmetic products until stricter quality-control measures were introduced.
Shemla’s detention is currently authorized only through September 6.
If police want to keep him in custody after that date, they will have to return to the Magistrate’s Court and explain what investigative work remains and why his release could endanger the public or interfere with the investigation.
The court could then extend his detention again, release him under restrictions, or order his unconditional release.

Canterbury Bulldogs coach Cameron Ciraldo wants the NRL to communicate rule changes for next season well in advance.

What's next?
Ciraldo's Bulldogs will wrap up their 2026 season with a clash against the Broncos on Thursday night at Stadium Australia.
Cameron Ciraldo wants rule changes for 2027 to be communicated to clubs well in advance of the season's start date as Canterbury prepares to become the latest crash-test dummies in trials for the NRL's kick-off experiment.
With the Bulldogs and Thursday's opponents Brisbane both out of finals contention, the NRL has again opted to stress-test changes to the kick-off rules, where teams conceding a try can opt to kick or receive from the restart.
The concept was widely panned by players in Melbourne's win over Brisbane, and Ciraldo claimed on Wednesday he only learned his team would be guinea pigs in their regular-season game via email.
Ciraldo would have a right to feel aggrieved by the NRL's constant tinkering, given his side were firmly entrenched in the top four last year.
The Dogs slipped back in the pack when the NRL changed the six-again threshold from the 40-metre line to the 20-metre mark weeks out from the season starting.
Canterbury has righted the ship since officials have eased off on calling six-agains.
And while Ciraldo won't solely attribute his club's early-season form slump to the changes, he would prefer clearer communication so clubs can plan their conditioning and roster management accordingly.
"If you look at our form at the start of the year you can blame that, but I think there's a lot of factors that went into our results at the start of the year," Ciraldo said.
"We'll look to address those over the next few weeks.
"As the rules came back to what they were last year, we sort of found our rhythm a little bit more, and were able to get back to our style of footy.
"I think it coincides with a number of other things as well.
"I think everyone would like to know what the rule changes are to start the pre-season and not find out about them during the trial period."
Ciraldo said Canterbury had little time to put the trialled kick-off interpretations into practice this week.
"I don't check my emails that often, so someone had to tell me," Ciraldo said.
Canterbury's clash with Brisbane will be the last for Bronson Xerri (Melbourne) and Josh Curran (Perth) before they move on to new clubs in 2027.
Ciraldo paid tribute to the pair for being key parts of the Dogs' revival, and confirmed Sean O'Sullivan had agreed to a contract at Belmore for 2027, despite interest from the Super League.

Sadiq Khan fined by fast-track court over untaxed car City Hall says is not his
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
08:30:27 UTC
17:30:27 KST

Sadiq Khan’s office has revealed he was the victim of a scam that led to him being fined for failing to tax a car that did not belong to him.
The London mayor was found guilty last month under a system of “conveyor-belt justice”, in which magistrates decide on hundreds of cases a day, sometimes spending less than a minute on each.
City Hall officials say the 24-year-old Nissan Micra did not belong to Khan or Transport for London.
The mayor has been the focus of protests by motorists angry at the expansion of the ultra-low emission zone in London. Some said they planned to register cars in Khan’s name to make him liable for the £12.50 daily charge.
The prosecution was undertaken by the Driver and Vehicle Licensing Agency, which accused Khan of being the keeper of the vehicle when it was spotted as being untaxed on 24 January. In a move that paves the way for the conviction to be erased after a court hearing on Thursday, the DVLA said on Wednesday evening that the case had been withdrawn after a review and it was investigating the circumstances.
“This is a scam, which is a crime,” said a spokesperson for Khan.
“It’s not the first time the mayor has been the victim of a scam involving people falsely stating that Sadiq is the owner of a vehicle. Such behaviour is illegal, and the DVLA are aware.”
A magistrate, sitting in a private hearing of the single justice procedure in Herefordshire, convicted Khan in his absence and ordered that he pay a £220 fine, £85 in costs and settle the £35.84 bill for unpaid tax on the Micra.
PA Media alerted the DVLA to the criminal conviction on Tuesday and its officials confirmed they were reviewing the case and investigating the circumstances of the prosecution.
Court documents show that DVLA letters addressed to the mayor about the unpaid tax bill were sent to a Gordon Ramsay restaurant in east London instead of the nearby TfL offices.
The mayor faces the possibility of having to appear in court to try to overturn the conviction.
The single justice procedure was introduced in 2015 as a cheaper method of dealing with low-level criminal cases, allowing magistrates to sit alone and in private.
The system, which is under government review, was criticised in 2024 when about 59,000 train-fare evasion convictions were overturned for being unlawful. It also emerged that children had been wrongly convicted in the secretive courts.
More scrutiny has come over repeated incidents of sick and incapacitated pensioners being convicted for not paying their household bills.
In Khan’s case, court records show he was prosecuted by the DVLA after the annual tax on the Micra, which was first registered in 2002, ran out last September.

How the SCO chips away at US power without an alliance system
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
08:30:06 UTC
17:30:06 KST

How the SCO chips away at US power without an alliance system
The SCO’s significance is practical: it gives those who do not want their future defined in Washington a forum to coordinate and hedge
The timing is important. Russia’s invasion of Ukraine remains unresolved, while the war between Iran and the US has turned the Persian Gulf into another theatre of strategic competition, with energy markets again exposed to disruption around the Strait of Hormuz. The SCO now brings together China, Russia, India, Iran, Pakistan, most of the Central Asian republics and Belarus, alongside partners including Turkey and multiple Gulf states.
Its 10 full members represent more than 3.4 billion people and roughly a quarter of global GDP. However, its growing importance is not simply a matter of size.
Calling the SCO an anti-American alliance is a mistake. Its members have different interests. India and China remain strategic competitors; India and Pakistan have long-standing tensions; and Central Asian governments want room to manoeuvre between Moscow, Beijing, Ankara, Brussels and Washington. Turkey remains a North Atlantic Treaty Organization (Nato) member while pursuing a larger Eurasian role.

'It’s not 19th century': Kerala CM Satheesan slams cleric over 'women should stay home' remark
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
08:30:05 UTC
17:30:05 KST

Satheesan’s remarks came amid mounting criticism of Aboobacker over his comments defending restrictions issued by the Kanthapuram faction of the Samastha Kerala Jamiyyathul Ulama on women’s participation in religious events.
NEW DELHI: Kerala chief minister VD Satheesan on Wednesday rejected Sunni cleric and Grand Mufti of India Kanthapuram AP Aboobacker Musliyar’s call for restrictions on women’s participation in public life. He said women must join the mainstream, asserting that such views have no place in a developing Kerala.Speaking to reporters, Satheesan said the state government did not agree with Aboobacker’s position that women should remain at home, adding that even Islam did not require women to be confined to domestic life.
"We don't agree with his statement that women should stay home. It's not a suitable stand in our developing Keralam. It's not the 19th century that one should make such statements. Even Islam doesn't say that. Women should not stay home, but join the mainstream. That is our stand," he said.Satheesan’s remarks came amid mounting criticism of Aboobacker over his comments defending restrictions issued by the Kanthapuram faction of the Samastha Kerala Jamiyyathul Ulama on women’s participation in religious events.Labour minister Bindu Krishna also criticised the cleric, saying such remarks undermined women’s constitutional rights and sought to push them "centuries back".
"Constitution of India assures equal rights to women and men, irrespective of sex. The people have the right to live a free and liberal life. And also, these types of statements push women centuries back. So, we can't accept such statements. Our women are free to move. They are best rulers. Our girls are always coming through this society, and we can't accept such statements," Krishna told ANI.The controversy followed remarks made by Aboobacker at the Hubbul Rasul Conference in Kochi, where he defended recent directives issued by the Kanthapuram faction of Samastha to local Mahalls on women’s participation in religious celebrations.A circular issued by the organisation directed Madrasas not to allow women to be present among unrelated men at religious events. It also advised against displaying young women on public stages and having them participate in road processions alongside unrelated men.
Defending the directives, Aboobacker said women should remain within the home and invoked the Quran to support his position."Women should remain confined within their homes. They should not enter the public sphere. The Holy Quran says so," Aboobacker said, while defending the purdah system as a practice intended to protect women’s dignity.He argued that allowing women into public spaces without restrictions could result in "great destruction", insisting that the measures were intended to honour and protect women rather than diminish them.Aboobacker also said Islam had granted women property and inheritance rights centuries ago to improve their status without requiring them to leave domestic life. He maintained that he was not concerned by opposition or political criticism and said no one could silence him or force him to change Islamic doctrines.
Vijaya Srivastava is a journalist and feature writer whose expertise lies in covering human-centred developments. Her stories explore how policy, technology, economic shifts and social change influence people's everyday lives. Her work also focuses on bringing depth, context and a human perspective to complex issues.
Her reports primarily cover society, healthcare, safety, public policy and emerging trends, alongside other political developments.

5,000 evacuated in Azerbaijan after arms depot blast
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
08:29:49 UTC
17:29:49 KST

Azerbaijani authorities evacuated 5,000 people after a fire triggered explosions at an ammunition depot overnight from Tuesday to Wednesday, officials said, adding that there were no casualties.
The blaze broke out at a depot near Nizami village in the western Goranboy district, the emergency situations, defence and interior ministries said in a joint statement.
Emergency and defence ministry personnel, working with police and local authorities, launched an operation and brought the situation under control, they added.
People living nearby were evacuated as a safety precaution, the statement added.
Residents of Nizami and the neighbouring village of Khoylu were moved to nearby areas, Goranboy deputy chief executive Seymur Nazarov told journalists.
"The total number of evacuees is 5,000," said Nazarov, who heads the district's emergency commission.
He said the fire was still burning and sporadic explosions could still be heard, but that efforts were under way to prevent the blaze from spreading and to extinguish it.
No homes had been damaged and no deaths, injuries or serious losses had been recorded, he added.
Security measures were in force at the entrances and exits of both villages, while evacuees were being accommodated in safe conditions, Nazarov said.
