German Navy tests Israeli LORA ballistic missile
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
07:52:55 UTC
16:52:55 KST

- Germany's Navy conducted a successful dual firing trial of IAI's Naval LORA ballistic missile under its OPEX testing program.
- Germany is reportedly moving forward with plans to procure the missile system, which has a range of more than 500 kilometers.
The German Navy successfully completed a dual firing trial of Israel Aerospace Industries’ Naval LORA ballistic missile, launching the weapon from an operational German vessel and hitting its target with precision in both test scenarios, IAI said.
The trial was conducted as part of the German Navy’s Operational Experimentation program, known as OPEX, a testing initiative the service launched to support its “Marine 2035 and Beyond” plan. IAI said the missile was launched from a configuration comprising a command trailer and a launcher aboard the German vessel, and that the weapon system met all the trial’s objectives in both scenarios.
Separately, Reuters reported that a German frigate tested the Lora system in the North Atlantic, between Ireland and Iceland, in a previously undisclosed operation. According to that report, Germany now plans to move forward with preparations to procure the missile, which has a range of more than 500 kilometers (311 miles).
LORA, short for Long Range Artillery, is a quasi-ballistic missile developed by IAI’s MLM Division that can be launched from land-based mobile launchers or naval vessels. The missile has a publicly listed operational range of 90 to 430 kilometers (56 to 267 miles) and uses a combination of GPS and inertial navigation for guidance, with a circular error probable of 10 meters (33 feet), according to IAI’s own published specifications. It is unclear whether the range Reuters cited reflects an upgraded or export-specific configuration.
The missile has seen combat use by Azerbaijan, which deployed the system during the 2020 Nagorno-Karabakh conflict against Armenia.
“This is an unprecedented achievement for IAI and the Israeli Ministry of Defense,” said Boaz Levy, IAI’s Chairman. “The successful trial of the LORA missile, launched from a naval vessel and striking its target with exceptional precision, took place overnight in Germany, the country where the world’s first ballistic missile was developed. This trial demonstrates Israel’s technological strength and the unique cooperation between Israel and Germany. It marks another significant achievement alongside the deployment of the Arrow 3 system on German soil, further strengthening Germany’s defense and deterrence capabilities and deepening the strategic partnership between our two countries.”
“Israel Aerospace Industries is proud to take part in strengthening the strategic cooperation between the State of Israel and the Government of Germany,” said Guy Bar Lev, IAI’s CEO. “This significant milestone is underscored by the operational live-fire exercise (OPEX) of the LORA system, one of the world’s most advanced and combat-proven ballistic missile systems.”
Germany separately fields IAI’s Arrow 3 missile defense system, which has been operational on German soil as part of the country’s broader air and missile defense buildup.

The collision occurred 18 nautical miles (33 kilometres) off the Silivri district on the western edge of Istanbul province, the governor's office said on X.
A Turkish cargo ship carrying 10 crew members sank on Wednesday after colliding with a tanker off the coast of Istanbul, with no immediate signs of survivors, Turkish authorities said.
A lifeboat and other debris from the Tugberk Imamoglu have been found, but there has been no sign of the crew, Turkey's General Directorate of Maritime Affairs said in a statement.
“There are 10 seafarers on board, including the captain,” Transport Minister Abdulkadir Uraloglu said. “They are all Turkish. We can say that the sinking occurred rapidly in 11 minutes. No one has been found alive.”
Two helicopters and 12 search and rescue vessels were searching the area.
The ship collided with the Turkish-flagged tanker Alsu in the Marmara Sea at around 3 am (2 am CEST), according to the General Directorate of Maritime Affairs. An emergency signal was received from the Tugberk Imamoglu, with the first rescue vessel reaching the area at around 4:10 am (3:10 am CEST).
“It is assessed that the Tugberk Imamoglu vessel sank, because it did not respond to any calls and the mobile phones of the personnel on board went unanswered,” the maritime directorate said.
The Alsu's captain had reported the collision as happening at 3:15 am, with 14 search and rescue vessels dispatched to the area backed by a helicopter, it said.
What do we know so far?
The directorate's head, Unal Baylan, said the ships had been communicating with each other by radio immediately prior to the collision indicating “that the two captains saw each other and were talking to each other to adjust their routes,” he told a news conference.
The owner of the Tugberk Imamoglu said the ship's captain had contacted the Alsu before the collision, warning that the tanker was entering the cargo vessel's shipping lane.
“Despite this, according to our initial findings, the collision occurred as a result of M/T Alsu’s navigational movements and our ship sank shortly afterward,” the statement from Imamoglu Denizcilik said.
Turkish news agency DHA reported that radio recordings showed the Tugberk Imamoglu's captain warning the Alsu to steer to port in an attempt to avoid the collision.
The Alsu's owners did not immediately respond to the claim.
The 90-metre cargo ship was travelling from the Mediterranean port of Iskenderun to Eregli on the Black Sea. The 91-metre Alsu, an oil or chemical tanker, was sailing from Kocaeli, east of Istanbul, to Aliaga on Turkey's Aegean coast, according to MarineTraffic.
The Silivri Public Prosecutor’s Office said it had launched an investigation into the sinking.

Fake 10 Downing Street listing on Booking.com highlights security failures
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
07:45:12 UTC
16:45:12 KST

Successive politicians have clawed their way past colleagues over the years to call the residence home. Yet in an offer that probably seemed too good to be true, the property site Booking.com has been accused of “systemic security failures” after it was able to set up and accept payment for a fake listing for 10 Downing Street.
A property listed as a “1 bedroom apartment in the heart of London” – with the exact address and a picture of the prime minister’s home – was listed on 18 June by researchers from the consumer watchdog Which?.
The listing, which promised a four-minute walk to the Houses of Parliament, was set up so that users had to request a stay and were unable to reserve and pay automatically.
The booking window opened briefly and closed so that a test could be carried out by a researcher from Which?. The consumer watchdog said a payment for a week-long stay had been processed by the digital travel site that enables users to book hotels and other accommodation as well as flights and car rentals.
The money had still not been refunded more than six weeks after it had been set up, according to Which?, which is associated with the Consumers Association charity.
A fake review was also uploaded to the site, describing the stay as “exceptional” and enjoying the experience of “hanging out with Larry the cat”, in a reference to Downing Street’s resident feline.
Despite Booking.com sending a message saying the review would be checked by a team of moderators, the consumer watchdog said it had been added almost immediately.
The team of researchers were also said to have used Booking.com’s mailing system to send an external URL asking the representative for credit card details to confirm the booking, Which? said.
The watchdog claimed the travel site had told them it had the ability to block URLs being sent through the messaging system if it suspected fraudulent activity, but it had not done so.
The listing was finally removed on 27 August, six weeks after it went live.
Rory Boland, the editor of Which? Travel, said: “If Booking.com’s so-called sophisticated AI systems can’t spot that 10 Downing Street is not a holiday rental, then it’s no wonder scammers can exploit the platform so easily.”
The watchdog said its investigation had “uncovered systemic security failures across the platform” and urged Ofcom, the UK’s communications regulator, to investigate.
A Booking.com spokesperson said: “This limited test is not a true reflection of the experience of millions of listings on our platform. The property added by Which? was not visible to customers or ‘live’ for the time period referenced.
“We use a range of checks, verification measures and artificial intelligence, which help us detect and remove the majority of fraudulent listings within 24 hours.”
It said that as the property was not open and bookable, some of its automatic fraud controls were not triggered to completely remove the fraud listing.
An Ofcom spokesperson said platforms have legal duties obliging them to take down illegal content generated by users once it is known. “Booking.com is not in scope of future rules that will apply to paid-for fraudulent advertising, and any change to that would be a matter for government,” they said.

New photo shows Wolf XM30 hidden under tarp
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
07:43:53 UTC
16:43:53 KST

- General Dynamics Land Systems released the first photo of its Wolf XM30 prototype, shown wrapped in a tarp during transport following its August 21 delivery to the U.S. Army.
- The vehicle's design remains concealed as it competes against American Rheinmetall's Lynx XM30, with the Army expected to select a winner in 2027.
General Dynamics Land Systems released the first publicly available photo of its Wolf XM30 prototype in transit this week, showing the vehicle wrapped entirely in a black tarp and strapped to a flatbed trailer.
The image follows the company’s confirmation that it delivered the prototype to the U.S. Army at Aberdeen Proving Ground, Maryland, on August 21, a delivery The Defence Blog previously reported based on a social media post from Geoffrey Norman, a retired Army brigadier general who now serves as director of strategy at General Dynamics Land Systems.
The tarp keeps the vehicle’s actual shape and design details concealed. General Dynamics has not released an uncovered photo of the Wolf XM30 or said when the vehicle’s full appearance will be shown publicly. The transport photo is the closest look the public has gotten so far at the physical hardware behind the program.
Norman, who spent 30 years in the Army as a tanker and cavalryman before joining General Dynamics two years ago, worked on the Next Generation Combat Vehicle Cross Functional Team at Detroit Arsenal before leaving the service. In his earlier post announcing the delivery, he said the Wolf uses what the company calls a Modular Open Systems Architecture, intended to let new software and hardware be added to the vehicle without a full redesign, a “born-digital” approach he said was built specifically for future upgrades.
Norman said the August 21 delivery is the first of several Wolf XM30 prototypes General Dynamics plans to complete and hand over to the Army. Additional vehicles are expected to go to Fort Hood, Texas, where the Army will run them through an evaluation process that could lead to a full-rate production decision. General Dynamics has credited teams across six sites, Sterling Heights, Lima, Scranton, Tallahassee, Grand Rapids and London, with building the vehicle.
The Wolf XM30 is one of two competing designs in the Army’s program to replace the M2 Bradley Infantry Fighting Vehicle, which has been in continuous service for more than 40 years. American Rheinmetall Vehicles is building the program’s other entrant, the Lynx XM30, and delivered the first of eight Lynx prototypes to the Army within days of General Dynamics’ Wolf delivery. That delivery put the Lynx into government-led developmental and performance testing under the program’s Phase 3/4 Engineering and Manufacturing Development contract, worth approximately $764 million. Rheinmetall has said it will deliver its remaining seven prototypes later this year for use in operational unit training, running in parallel with technical evaluation as part of the Army’s Transformation in Contact 2.0 initiative.
Both companies are developing and testing their prototypes in Michigan, drawing on the state’s concentration of Army ground-vehicle expertise centered on Detroit Arsenal, home to the Army’s Tank-automotive and Armaments Command and the Combat Capabilities Development Command Ground Vehicle Systems Center.
The Army is expected to select a winning XM30 design in 2027, with the design and prototype phase of the program alone valued at $1.6 billion.

Gaza's fishermen face shrinking fishing grounds and arrests
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
07:36:52 UTC
16:36:52 KST

Breadcrumb
Gaza's fishermen face shrinking fishing grounds and repeated arrests by Israel
For fishermen in the Gaza Strip, the sea has become increasingly difficult and dangerous to access, as Israeli naval forces continue to restrict their movement, open fire on fishing boats, and arrest fishermen, according to local fishermen's representatives.
On Tuesday, Israeli naval forces arrested 10 fishermen off the coast of al-Zawayda in central Gaza and Sheikh Ajlin, southwest of Gaza City, according to the Union of Fishermen's Committees.
In a press statement, the union said Israeli forces opened fire on the fishermen's boats before taking the detainees to the Israeli port of Ashdod.
Seven of the fishermen were later released, while three remained detained at an unknown location at the time of reporting, the union added.
"The arrest of these 10 fishermen adds to a series of daily violations, including killing, arrest, and the destruction of fishing boats and equipment, in addition to preventing fishermen from accessing the sea for more than three years," Zakaria Bakr, an official with the Fishermen's Committees, told The New Arab.
"The arrests were part of broader restrictions and violations affecting Gaza's fishing sector, including the destruction of boats and fishing equipment and restrictions on access to fishing areas," he said.
The number of Palestinian fishermen arrested by Israel since the Israeli genocidal war began on October 2023 had reached about 150, he explained.
Under constant fear
For fishermen who continue to venture into the sea, each trip has become a source of uncertainty.
"We go to sea not knowing if we will return," Salim Hamouda, a Gaza-based fisherman who has worked in the profession for years, told TNA.
Hamouda said the sea had previously provided his family with a stable source of income but had now become associated with fear and insecurity.
"We go out to sea not knowing what will happen to us. We might return with some fish, or we might lose our nets or boats, or we might be shot at or arrested. The sea has become a path to death for us, not a path to livelihood," he added.
Hamouda noted that the decline in fish stocks, rising fuel prices, and the high cost of fishing equipment had further undermined the profession.
Many fishermen and their families were now dependent on debt and humanitarian assistance, according to Hamouda.
"No one asks about us. Organisations talk about farmers, displaced people and workers, but fishermen have been forgotten," Hamouda lamented. "We have families and children who need food, medicine and education, and we have no other source of income."
Mohammed Saadallah, another fisherman from Gaza, said the fishing community had been living under a constant sense of fear and uncertainty, while many fishermen had lost their boats and nets during the war.
"We used to live off the sea, but today we cannot work," Saadallah told TNA, "A boat that used to support an entire family can be destroyed in minutes, while nets that we buy at great expense can be lost in an instant."
"We are not asking for the impossible. We simply want to work safely and return to our families. But even this right has been denied to us," he said.
Heavy losses
The restrictions have affected not only fishermen but also thousands of people who depend directly or indirectly on fishing for their livelihoods.
According to the Union of Fishermen's Committees, around 4,000 fishermen in Gaza work on more than 700 boats, while around 70,000 people rely on fishing and the sale of fish for income.
Bakr estimated that the fishing sector had suffered direct losses of about 120 million US dollars, with around 95 per cent of its infrastructure damaged or destroyed through bombardment, fires and the destruction of fishing equipment.
He estimated indirect losses at approximately 7 million dollars per month, as the fishing catch has fallen to about 2 per cent of its pre-war level.
Bakr described the restrictions and attacks on fishermen as violations of international humanitarian law and the Fourth Geneva Convention.
He also said the ceasefire had failed to provide meaningful protection for fishermen, as restrictions and attacks continued.
He called on the international community and relevant countries to pressure Israel to halt violations against fishermen, ensure safe access to fishing areas and support the rehabilitation of Gaza's fishing sector.

Belgians’ commute to work longer than an hour a day for the first time
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
07:35:56 UTC
16:35:56 KST

For the first time, we are spending more than an hour each day travelling to and from work. This emerged in an international study by HR services provider SD Worx, the findings of which appeared in Flemish daily Het Laatste Nieuws. The average Belgian worker’s commute takes 61 minutes a day, which is well above the European average of 48 minutes.
Belgians’ commute to work longer than an hour a day for the first time
With an average commute of 61 minutes a day, Belgians are Europe’s commuting champions. Sweden (57 minutes) and Ireland (56 minutes) complete the top three.
Part of the explanation lies with ‘long-distance commuters’, says SD Worx. More than one in eight Belgian workers (13 per cent) commute for two hours or more a day – the highest proportion of all the countries surveyed. This group often travels more than 120 kilometres a day. The international average is 8 per cent.
“Belgians live quite a long way from work, but traffic jams undoubtedly play a role too,” says Veerle Michiels, a mobility expert at SD Worx. The majority of Belgian commuters travel to work by (company) car.
The study reveals that public transport remains an area for concern: only 25 per cent of women and 28 per cent of men find public transport convenient, reliable and easily accessible. This is lower than the European average of 36 per cent across the countries surveyed.
A symbolic threshold crossed
“The one-hour mark is more than just a symbolic threshold,” emphasises Michiels. “It crosses the line that employees themselves still consider acceptable.”
Nevertheless, Belgians seem to have largely accepted long journey times as part of the job. One in three Belgian employees (34 per cent) say that their commute takes up a significant amount of their working time, which is barely above the average of 32 per cent across the countries surveyed.
Men’s commute longer, women prefer to work from home
The SD Worx study reveals clear differences between men and women. For instance, men spend longer travelling to work (65 minutes) than women (56 minutes). There are also twice as many men (23 per cent) as women (12 per cent) who commute more than 100 kilometres a day.
Women live closer to work, and they also have a lower threshold for acceptable commuting time (47 minutes) than men (67 minutes). They are also more likely to say they would prefer to work from home more often (35 per cent compared with 28 per cent of men).

Apple joins Google in renaming Lake Ontario 'Lake America'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
07:35:37 UTC
16:35:37 KST

Apple Maps now shows Lake Ontario as "Lake America" for US users, following Google's lead in complying with US President Donald Trump's order as trade talks with Canada sour.
Apple has become the latest company to adopt US President Donald Trump's new name for Lake Ontario — Lake America — on its Apple Maps platform.
The move came less than a week after Trump formally ordered the change in an executive order. Lake Ontario is one of North America's five Great Lakes, alongside Superior, Michigan, Huron and Erie.
The name change was driven largely by the collapse of trade talks between the US and Canada at the end of August, after the US imposed new 50% tariffs on around $20 billion (€17.3bn) worth of Canadian goods.
Apple Maps users based in the US will see the lake as Lake America, while those in Canada will still see the original Lake Ontario. According to US Interior Secretary Doug Burgum, Trump personally approached Apple and urged it to implement the change on its navigation platform.
Trump has since posted a number of AI-generated social media videos, including one showing him kicking over a Lake Ontario sign and replacing it with one reading "Welcome to Lake America".
At the lake itself, however, Canada has installed a new sign reading "Lake Ontario. Now and Always."
"Long before President Trump, this lake was called Lake Ontario. Long after President Trump is gone, it will still be called Lake Ontario," Ontario Premier Doug Ford said, according to the BBC.
Canada has also said it will implement "dollar-for-dollar" counter-tariffs in response to Trump's new levies.
Google under fire
Google made the same move over the weekend, drawing significant criticism on social media, with users accusing the tech giant of capitulating to the Trump administration.
This is despite the fact that while the US president can dictate how the federal government refers to geographic features, he has no authority to force private companies, foreign governments or even US states to do the same.
"The US Geographical Names Information System has formally changed the name for 'Lake Ontario' to 'Lake America' in the United States," Google said in a blog post.
"Since we update Google Maps to reflect name changes in official government sources, which is GNIS for the US, people using maps in the US will see 'Lake America', those in Canada will continue to see 'Lake Ontario', and those outside of the US and Canada will see both names."
However, other map services such as MapQuest have refused to change the lake's name. Last year, MapQuest also declined to rename the Gulf of Mexico as the Gulf of America.
The latest stand has driven MapQuest to the number one spot on the US Apple App Store's top charts, as of 1 September, ahead of even long-time favourite ChatGPT.

Why Greece is betting on Israel’s Achilles Shield
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
07:35:08 UTC
16:35:08 KST

Why Greece is betting on Israel’s Achilles Shield
The defence deal between the two countries fits into a larger shift in regional alliances amid the US-Israel war on Iran.
On Monday, Greece and Israel signed a $3.5bn defence deal to build an integrated, multilayered defence network to protect Greek territory dubbed the Achilles Shield. The package brings together the David’s Sling and Spyder interceptors, the Barak air and missile defence system and multimission radars, alongside a separate deal adding Drone Dome systems to protect strategic sites from UAVs.
It is the largest defence deal ever concluded between the two countries. It is also one of the most significant export agreements in Israel’s recent history.
What makes the agreement particularly striking is that it comes as Israel’s global standing is at one of its lowest points in decades. And Greece is no outlier, given that 65 percent of its citizens now view Israel unfavourably. Why, then, has Athens now chosen to openly deepen its ties with Israel in the most politically sensitive of areas: defence and military technology?
Firstly, the shadow of Israel’s conflict with Iran looms large. In early March, an Iranian drone struck Cyprus, Greece’s neighbour and close partner. This likely reinforced anxieties that were already visible in 2024. After Israel, with the help of the United States, downed approximately 300 Iranian drones and missiles, Greek Defence Minister Nikos Dendias called on Athens to develop its own antidrone “dome”.
The deal is therefore partly the product of pragmatic necessity as countries scramble for military solutions to growing drone threats. Saudi Arabia, Qatar and the United Arab Emirates, for example, are acquiring antidrone technology from Ukraine, another country able to market its products as battle-tested.
Despite its political disadvantage, Israel has a practical head start, given that it has long practised “arms diplomacy”, using its defence industry as a springboard to cultivate deeper bilateral ties with prospective buyers.
The second factor driving the Achilles Shield deal is another longstanding tenet of Israeli grand strategy: the “periphery doctrine”. This advocates that Israel develop ties with non-Arab states and peoples on the periphery of the Levant to counter the hostility between Israel and its immediate neighbours. It is a recognition that shared threats can produce strategic partnerships. And in the case of Israel and Greece, that shared threat is Turkiye.
The irony is that Turkiye – as a non-Arab state and the gateway between the Middle East and Europe – was Israel’s close partner in the early days of the periphery doctrine. In 1949, Turkiye was the first Muslim country to recognise Israel. In subsequent years, Ankara and Tel Aviv developed robust but clandestine security ties.
This worked as Israel intended in that it opened the door to increasingly public and broader bilateral relations, which continued even after the Islamist-oriented AK Party, or Justice and Development Party, came to power in Turkiye in 2002.
But both sides fell out in late 2008 after Israel launched an offensive on the Gaza Strip. Subsequent divergences over Israeli policies towards the occupied Palestinian territory have gradually unravelled their deep ties.
Bilateral trade has collapsed since Ankara imposed an embargo on Israel in 2024. There are no longer direct flights between the two countries. In June, US President Donald Trump claimed that US pressure stopped Turkiye from joining the war on Iran, on Tehran’s side. This may sound far-fetched, yet it illustrates how Israel and Turkiye not only disagree on many geopolitical issues, but increasingly see each other as rivals and even threats.
What is remarkable is how quickly Greece has filled the void. In previous years, Tel Aviv’s partnership with Ankara precluded closer ties with Athens. But no more: in late 2025, Israel, Cyprus and Greece signed a “Joint Action Plan” that mandates enhanced military cooperation.
Energy has reinforced this strategic convergence. The discovery of substantial gas reserves in the eastern Mediterranean encouraged Israel, Greece and Cyprus to cooperate on pipelines and maritime security.
And, as was the case with Turkiye, more extensive bilateral ties followed security cooperation: some 744,000 Israelis visited Greece in 2025, compared with the peak of 558,000 Israeli tourists who travelled to Turkiye in 2008.
The increasing regional division into competing blocs has also driven the burgeoning Israel-Greece relationship. In February, Israeli Prime Minister Netanyahu floated a “hexagon alliance” of Israel, Greece, Cyprus, India and unnamed Arab and African countries.
Six months later, Saudi Arabia, Turkiye and Pakistan signed the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement. This alliance broadly overlaps with what commentators earlier labelled the “Islamic coalition”.
This is an evolving dynamic and inter-bloc collaboration is as common as intra-bloc divergences. But it demonstrates that the crisis of confidence in the US as a security guarantor extends beyond the Gulf states and predates the recent war on Iran. It also portends headaches for Washington’s policymakers, given that these increasingly competing states are all US allies.
The Achilles Shield deal is therefore the new manifestation of an old Israeli strategy that has been accelerated by the US-Israel war on Iran. Public scepticism may complicate Greece-Israel relations, but Israeli-Turkish ties deepened for decades despite similarly unfavourable public attitudes.
In short, in the eastern Mediterranean and elsewhere, growing popular outrage at Israel’s policies will continue to coexist uneasily with deepening security cooperation at an elite level. The irony is that the same conflicts that have damaged Israel’s international standing have also increased the value of its military experience and defence technology.

- Work is being performed in Beavercreek, Ohio, under Air Force Research Laboratory management, with completion expected by February 2028.
The U.S. Air Force has added $11.2 million to a contract with BlueHalo LLC for a program called Aiman Improved Readiness, bringing the deal’s total value to $41.2 million, up from $30 million, according to a Department of War contract announcement.
The modification adds scope to a cost-plus-fixed-fee contract Air Force Research Laboratory originally awarded to BlueHalo. Work will be performed in Beavercreek, Ohio, near the lab’s headquarters at Wright-Patterson Air Force Base. The contract is expected to be completed by February 13, 2028.
Fiscal 2026 research, development, test and evaluation funds totaling $32,147 will be obligated at the time of this modification. Air Force Research Laboratory at Wright-Patterson Air Force Base, Ohio, is the contracting activity managing the award.
BlueHalo, based in Huntsville, Alabama, and Arlington, Virginia, is a defense technology company that works across space superiority, directed energy, counter-drone systems, autonomy, radio frequency and signals intelligence programs. The company has held multiple prior contracts tied to the Wright-Patterson research ecosystem.
In February 2026, the Department of War awarded BlueHalo a separate sole-source contract worth up to $19.95 million to develop AI-enabled frameworks for human biological modeling, work performed in nearby Dayton, Ohio, and managed through the same Wright-Patterson contracting activity. That program focuses on integrating large-scale biological data with artificial intelligence to support monitoring of warfighter health, performance and exposure risks, with work running through February 2029 and options extending to 2031.
BlueHalo has separately built up a portfolio of space technology work. In March 2025, the company said it successfully demonstrated a long-haul, two-terminal laser communication system designed to simulate conditions across low-Earth, medium-Earth and geosynchronous orbit, advancing the technology to Technology Readiness Level 6, a designation indicating the system has been proven in a relevant environment and is ready for accelerated development.
The Air Force has not disclosed the specific technical scope of the Aiman Improved Readiness program, what capability or system it supports, or how this funding increase changes the program’s objectives beyond the added dollar value.

Germany successfully tests Israeli ballistic missile, officials say
BERLIN, Sept 2 - Germany successfully tested an Israeli ballistic missile in the North Atlantic overnight, military officials said on Wednesday, as Western powers scramble to acquire long-range weapons to counter what they see as an increased threat from Russia.
The test of what officials said was a LORA missile built by Israel Aerospace Industries came hours after Berlin publicly blamed Russia for an attempted drone attack at Leipzig/Halle Airport last month and ordered measures in response.
Germany does not currently have ballistic missiles, which fly at much higher speeds than the cruise missiles in its arsenal. The Israeli-built system has a range of up to 500 km (310 miles), Germany's defence ministry said.

Navy chief Jan Christian Kaack said the test was a success.

Germany is also working on an upgraded version of its Taurus cruise missile, currently its only weapon with a range of several hundred kilometres, with production scheduled to start in 2029.
The upgraded Taurus NEO missile will feature an extended range, improved shielding against interference, and advancements in navigation and seeker head technology, according to a budget document.
German forces have about 600 Taurus missiles with an official range of more than 500 km (310 miles) in their inventories, that can be launched from fighter jets such as the Tornado, the F-15 or the F-18.

Pakistan’s Punjab allows ‘secret’ terrorism trials: Why it’s controversial
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
07:25:51 UTC
16:25:51 KST

Pakistan’s Punjab allows ‘secret’ terrorism trials: Why it’s controversial
A single unnamed official can order anonymous judges, prosecutors and witnesses in terrorism cases, with no time limit.
Islamabad, Pakistan — Politicians in Punjab, Pakistan’s most populous province, have passed a law allowing terrorism trials to be held in near-total secrecy, with the judge, prosecutor and witnesses permitted to remain anonymous.
Under the law, a person facing the country’s most serious criminal charge could be convicted without learning who heard the case against them, who prosecuted it or who testified.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4What are Pakistan’s controversial constitutional amendments about?
- list 2 of 4Pakistan passes amendment empowering parliament to pick top judge
- list 3 of 4How would Pakistan’s 27th Amendment reshape its military and courts?
- list 4 of 4Pakistan’s Punjab police kill 900 people in eight months: What’s going on?
The trial record can be sealed, and an appeal could be heard by judges never told who presided over the original trial.
The Anti-Terrorism (Punjab Amendment) Bill 2026 passed the Punjab Assembly on August 31, after opposition politicians staged a walkout in protest.
Four days earlier, the government had appeared to relent, agreeing to have the bill reviewed by the law department or a parliamentary committee.
When it returned to the floor, it was unchanged and passed without amendment on Monday.
The law has drawn criticism from opposition politicians, lawyers, rights groups and analysts, who say it concentrates enormous power in a single, unnamed official and could be used against government critics.
What does the new law do?
The law lets the government appoint a senior bureaucrat as a “designated authority” tasked with deciding what cases are to be heard under the special provisions earmarked in the legislation.
The official’s identity is kept confidential, known only to the chief justice of the Lahore High Court.
The official can declare any terrorism case, or even a whole category of them, a “special security case” if they conclude that the people involved need special “protection”.
The law does not clearly define the parameters that need to be met, and the accused cannot contest being placed under this category. Once the official requests it, the chief justice assigns the case to a sitting anti-terrorism court judge. A panel of five public prosecutors is drawn up, and the official picks one.
From there, the identities of the judge, prosecutor, police officers, witnesses and defence lawyers cannot be disclosed under any circumstances. Official titles are used instead of names, and court orders are signed without revealing who signed them.
Witnesses are identified only by codes. Hearings can be held over videolink, including from inside a prison, with voice-altering technology used to disguise participants.
The case file is sealed and held jointly by the chief justice and the official.
The law includes no expiry date, and a final clause allows the government to adopt “such other measures as it may deem appropriate”, leaving room to add further powers without further legislation.
Why is the government doing this, and why now?
The government’s official justification, laid out in the bill itself, points to increased cases of attacks by armed groups, and rising threats faced by judges, prosecutors, investigators and witnesses. It argues that the existing law does not adequately protect them.
Speaker Malik Muhammad Ahmad Khan, on the floor of the assembly, invoked Pakistan’s toll from terrorism over the past two decades to argue that the assembly was the right forum to strengthen prosecutions.
Khalid Mahmood Ranjha, the legislator who tabled the bill, told Al Jazeera that the chief justice, not the designated authority, nominates the trial judge.
“There is no interference of the executive,” he said.
He dismissed fears that the law could be used against political opponents.
“It is just an apprehension,” the politician said, calling the criticism “propaganda to politicise and make the law controversial”.
“This law [is] only for hardened terrorists.”
But no single attack or case has been publicly named as the trigger.
Punjab also records only a small share of Pakistan’s terrorism-related deaths each year.
The vast majority occur in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and Balochistan, which together account for more than 90 percent of the country’s terrorism deaths.
Al Jazeera contacted Azma Bokhari, Punjab’s provincial minister for information, Marriyum Aurangzeb, senior minister in the Punjab government, and Rana Muhammad Iqbal, Punjab’s law minister, but did not receive a response.
What are critics saying?
Rida Hosain, a Lahore-based constitutional lawyer, said the threats facing judges, prosecutors and witnesses in Pakistan are real.
“There is no denying that Pakistan’s people and land have paid a devastating price for terrorism,” she told Al Jazeera. But she said no one who has actually read the amendment “can reasonably claim that it is consistent with due process”.
Opposition politicians argued the law violates the constitutional right to a fair trial and hands judicial-style powers to an unelected official with no oversight.
Ahmer Rasheed Bhatti, the independent legislator affiliated with jailed opposition leader Imran Khan’s Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaaf (PTI) party, led objections on the floor.
“It creates a parallel procedure in which the executive, not the court, decides what a fair trial will look like,” he told Al Jazeera.
The designated authority must consult the chief justice, he said, but does not need their agreement.
Hosain said the secrecy itself removes a basic safeguard.
“By introducing faceless courts, an accused is deprived of the ability to challenge judicial bias and safeguard judicial impartiality,” she told Al Jazeera. “While this law remains in force, the right to a fair trial and due process is effectively suspended in Punjab.”
The Human Rights Commission of Pakistan (HRCP) also raised the alarm.
“The bill does not adequately define the circumstances in which these extraordinary powers may be invoked,” the commission’s spokesperson told Al Jazeera.
That, HRCP said, creates scope for abuse against ordinary citizens, political opponents or protesters in the name of security.
Mian Dawood, a Lahore-based constitutional lawyer, said existing law already lets courts protect witnesses and hold closed hearings under a judge’s control.
The new law, he said, moves that control to the executive rather than filling a gap. He said someone wrongly caught up in the system would have little recourse. Remedies such as a malicious-prosecution claim exist on paper but are “impracticable” in Pakistan’s courts, he said.
“A citizen has to suffer the misuse of powers by the state authorities,” the constitutional expert said.
Majid Nizami, a Lahore-based analyst, told Al Jazeera that Punjab province’s original antiterrorism law — enacted in 1997 and now amended with the controversial new provisions — was also misused.
“It looked very good on paper too,” Nizami said. “But what happened, eventually, was that it was used for political point-scoring and political manoeuvring.”
He said the law has, since 1997, been applied against nearly every major political party in Pakistan.
Nizami said he could not identify a Punjab case in the past decade where witness intimidation had derailed a prosecution — the ostensible justification for shielding the privacy of prosecutors and judges under the new amendments.
But there are older precedents. One case that stands out involved rebel commander Malik Ishaq. Ishaq co-founded Lashkar-e-Jhangvi, a sectarian group blamed for killing hundreds of people, most of them Shia Muslims.
Named in more than 200 criminal cases, he repeatedly walked free after witnesses and even judges grew too frightened to move against him, until he was killed in a 2015 shootout after armed men freed him from police custody.
Has Pakistan tried this before?
Punjab itself passed a law last year giving authorities the power to detain terrorism suspects for up to three months without charge, part of a wider wave in which Balochistan and the federal government passed near-identical detention powers in 2025.
Balochistan passed a similar law in September 2025, letting a senior official anonymously flag cases for the same kind of concealed proceedings. It has been in force for about a year, without any publicly known case of its use.
Ranjha told Al Jazeera that Balochistan and Sindh had “already passed this law,” and that Punjab needed to follow.
While Sindh has amended its own antiterrorism law, it is only to let the provincial government resize or abolish antiterrorism courts based on caseload. It introduces no comparable anonymity or secrecy provisions. Khyber Pakhtunkhwa has not amended its law along either track.
Salman Ghani, a political analyst, said Punjab’s situation differs from Balochistan’s for a simpler reason. “Punjab is still governable, and we don’t see terrorism incidents here every other day,” he told Al Jazeera.
Bhatti argued that gap was telling.
Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, which, alongside Balochistan, faces the overwhelming majority of the country’s terrorism violence, has not adopted secret trials; Punjab, which faces almost none of it, has.
“The federal government looks instrumental,” Bhatti told Al Jazeera. “Provinces appear to have been asked to enact similar amendments.”
He does not believe Punjab’s government developed that appetite on its own. “You are not looking at a local caseload,” he said. “You are looking at a request.”
What happens next?
A legal challenge looks likely.
Opposition politicians have argued that the law conflicts with the constitution’s fair-trial guarantees and oversteps what a provincial assembly can legislate, since antiterrorism law falls under federal jurisdiction.
With no sunset clause built in, the law does not expire on its own; whether it survives will most likely be decided in court rather than by the assembly that passed it.
Bhatti drew a comparison with the last time Pakistan departed this far from ordinary courts: military trials for civilians, introduced only through a constitutional amendment after the 2014 Peshawar Army Public School massacre, and built with a two-year limit unless parliament renewed it.
“You do not need a faceless provincial trial in the safer province,” he told Al Jazeera, “Unless the facelessness is the point.”

U.S. Army awards AV $464.8 million laser weapon deal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
07:31:46 UTC
16:31:46 KST

- The US Army awarded AV a $464.8 million contract for 26 LOCUST X3 laser weapons under its first formal directed energy program of record.
- The Other Transaction Agreement runs five years and follows a June demonstration where Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth watched the system shoot down drones.
The US Army has awarded defense contractor AV a $464.8 million contract to produce high-energy laser weapons under the Enduring High Energy Laser (E-HEL) program, the Army’s first formal directed energy program of record, according to Laser Wars.
Under the Other Transaction Agreement, AV will deliver 26 of its 30 kilowatt LOCUST X3 laser weapons to the Army over the next five years. The systems are meant to counter low-cost weaponized drones.
The X3 was formally unveiled in March and built specifically for the E-HEL program. It is the latest version of AV’s LOCUST Laser Weapon System, which American troops have already used for counter-drone missions from the Middle East to the US-Mexico border.
The Army’s fiscal year 2027 budget request called for the procurement of two E-HEL systems at $17.4 million apiece, with plans to field up to 24 additional units over the following five and a half years, according to a draft request for proposals from the service’s Portfolio Acquisition Executive for Fires published in January.
“This award marks a defining moment not only for AV, but for the future of modern defense,” said AV Chairman and CEO Wahid Nawabi.
“The transition of directed energy from experimentation to an enduring, fielded capability reflects years of collaboration, innovation, and operational success alongside the US Army. We are proud to deliver these production systems and support the Army’s mission with scalable, modular, and cost-effective defense solutions.”
The Army first announced E-HEL in a July 2024 special notice, describing it as a modular system built on lessons from two earlier LOCUST-based programs. One is the 20 kilowatt Palletized-High Energy Laser, which conducted live-fire testing from the flight deck of the aircraft carrier USS George H.W. Bush (CVN 77) in October 2025. The other is the Army Multi-Purpose High Energy Laser, a vehicle-mounted system tested over the past year from the back of the service’s Infantry Squad Vehicle and Joint Light Tactical Vehicle.
The Department of War has gradually expanded its use of laser weapons overseas to protect troops from drones. The Army sent several Palletized-High Energy Laser systems to an undisclosed location, likely within the US Central Command area of operations, starting in 2022. Four Stryker-mounted, 50 kilowatt Directed Energy Maneuver-Short Range Air Defense systems followed in 2024 for in-theater testing before that program was later canceled. In July, the US Air Force disclosed it had deployed several Boeing Compact Laser Weapon System units across Europe as part of a layered air defense network.
The Army’s requirements for E-HEL call for three distinct engagement profiles: 30 one-second shots per minute against high-density target sets, six nine-second shots per minute against low-density sets, and three 17-second shots per minute against hardened targets. The system must also sustain full power for a full minute, with a recharge cycle capped at four minutes.
The draft RFP also required that an E-HEL system arrive with production capacity already in place. AV said it met that requirement with a $30 million manufacturing expansion in New Mexico announced in March.
The contract follows a June demonstration at White Sands Missile Range in New Mexico, where Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth personally observed AV’s LOCUST shoot down drones, according to Laser Wars, which first reported the event. That demonstration also featured nLight’s “P5 version” of the DE M-SHORAD system and Lockheed Martin’s 300 kilowatt Indirect Fire Protection Capability-High Energy Laser prototype, known as Valkyrie. Weeks later, the Pentagon awarded nLight and Lockheed Martin contracts for the 300-500 kilowatt Joint Laser Weapons System, part of the “Golden Dome for America” missile defense effort.
Earlier Army laser efforts struggled to reach production. The Mobile Test Unit, the first vehicle-mounted laser weapon, was judged “neither scalable nor robust enough for Army standards,” while the Government Accountability Office found the DE M-SHORAD system “not mature enough” for full production.
Separately, the US Air Force’s Recovery of Airbase Denied by Ordnance system, a 3 kilowatt Zeus III laser mounted on a Cougar 4×4 MRAP vehicle, is already in sustained production, with contractor Parsons under contract for 29 units.

Vietnam court sentences 11 to death in major drug trafficking case
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
07:32:51 UTC
16:32:51 KST

Sarah binti Haironnine
03 September 2026•Update: 03 September 2026
A Vietnamese court in Ho Chi Minh City sentenced 11 people to death on Thursday for drug trafficking in a major case involving 227 defendants, local media reported.
The Ho Chi Minh City People’s Court handed down the sentences after a two-week trial in the case known as VN10, according to the VnExpress media outlet.
The court identified Ha Danh Nam, 52, as a key figure in the drug trafficking network, saying he was involved in several branches of the operation.
Two other defendants, Hoang Sy Thang and Bui Van Anh, were sentenced to life imprisonment for illegally transporting drugs.
The case came to light in March 2023 when customs officers at Tan Son Nhat International Airport in Ho Chi Minh City detected drugs in luggage carried by four flight attendants arriving from France.
Authorities found more than 8 kilograms (18 pounds) of ecstasy and more than 3 kilograms (7 pounds) of ketamine and cocaine in the luggage.
The four flight attendants were initially detained but were later not prosecuted after investigators found insufficient grounds to establish their involvement in the trafficking.
The investigation expanded to more than 2,700 suspects in 477 cases, while transactions linked to the network totaled nearly 29 trillion Vietnamese dong ($1.1 billion).
The court is continuing to announce sentences for the remaining defendants.
The VN10 case involves charges including drug trafficking, illegal transportation of drugs, drug possession and organizing illegal drug use.

Danish intelligence says Russia preparing sabotage attacks against defense industry
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
07:25:22 UTC
16:25:22 KST

Seyma Erkul Dayanc
03 September 2026•Update: 03 September 2026
Russian intelligence services are actively preparing sabotage operations against companies in Denmark's defense industry, public broadcaster DR reported Wednesday, citing the Danish intelligence service.
"We see that Danish companies are also targets for concrete Russian sabotage planning, and that Russian intelligence services are actively preparing sabotage operations aimed at the defense industry in Denmark," said Emil Graesholm, head of counterintelligence at the Danish Security and Intelligence Service (PET).
Graesholm also told Danish newspaper Berlingske that authorities had uncovered specific Russian plans for sabotage operations against companies in Denmark.
"Therefore, this is not just a warning that it might come to Denmark one day. We are already seeing the planning now. Very concretely," he said.
The companies that could be targeted include firms in the defense industry linked to military aid to Ukraine, according to PET.
The intelligence service said it has identified "concrete examples" of Russia attempting to recruit ordinary Danes through social media and other online platforms.
Such individuals could be asked to perform tasks including photographing companies or installations for use in planning sabotage operations, PET said.
"It is extremely serious if ordinary Danes help Russian intelligence services – either intentionally or unknowingly," Graesholm said.
PET said it works closely with Denmark's Defense Intelligence Service and the Danish Agency for Social Security and Preparedness, and regularly updates police districts on the threat assessment.
"We have continuously briefed selected companies and industry organizations on the threat picture, and together with other authorities we have advised on specific security measures," Graesholm said.
He added that the defense industry broadly needed to take the “necessary security measures" to protect itself.
Graesholm said PET considered the threat sufficiently concrete to publicly warn about it.
"It is such a concrete identification and preparation that we find it necessary to go out with the message that it is a threat that must be taken seriously," he said.
The Confederation of Danish Industry said it was taking PET's assessment seriously and was in close contact with relevant authorities.
"The changed threat picture calls for increased attention from companies, but also for calm and proportionality," said Rasmus Anderskouv, head of security and preparedness at the organization.
Anderskouv said companies should assess their specific exposure and ensure their security and emergency preparedness measures were functioning properly.
Flemming Splidsboel, a senior researcher at the Danish Institute for International Studies, described PET's announcement as serious and said the threat was "new," "concrete" and "advanced."
Former Defense Intelligence Service chief analyst Jakob Kaarsbo said PET's decision to speak publicly could be intended to signal to Russia that Danish authorities were aware of its activities.
